product_reviews: ['    **INTRODUCTION.**Jimmy Tock was born on a night when strange things happened.JImmy s father Rudy spent his time running between the ICU where his father was dying following a stroke, and the expectant fathers lounge which he shared with a very strange clown-Konrad Beezo.The enraged Beezo tells Rudy all about the circus he works in and how his wife will give birth to the most wonderful clown the world has ever seen.  Driven out of the fathers lounge by the very angry ranting clown, Rudy arrives in ICU to see his father sitting up and talking.His joy is short lived however when his father begins to make dire predictions for his unborn son s future.Rudy and his wife are not even sure their child is a son, but his fathers determination to warn them of the evil that is to come convinces Rudy to write the information down.He foresees five days in the boy s life where pain and death will seek him out, days of great terror and torment.Rudy faithfully records his fathers warnings on the back of a circus flyer.After his message is imparted, Rudy s father abruptly dies leaving both him and the medical staff stunned.Overwhelmed by grief, Rudy returns to the fathers lounge to see Beezo and the delivery doctor in the middle of a formidable argument.Beezo s wife, an aerialist from a famous circus family has died in childbirth.Beezo believes the doctor has assisted in her death at the instruction of her father, patrician Virgilio Vivacemente.Beezo shoots the doctor and points the gun at Rudy, however he decides to let him live as he has not taken part in the  plot  to deny him the fame of his son.Rudy, a lowly pastry chef has only one concern, and that is to protect his wife- Maddy and their child.Finding Maddy unconsious with her nurse and their baby gone, Rudy has no choice but to go back into the hospital to find his child and protect him from the insane clown.Beezo is set to escape with his son after shooting his wife s nurse.As soon as Rudy catches sight of Maddy s nurse hiding with their child, he is happy to let him go to save further bloodshed.==================================================I have given you quite a long intoduction to the story to demonstrate how  much detail is put into the book itself.My condensed version of events does not convey the feeling of the story or explain details anyway near as well as the book. You will have to read it yourself for that.*I will only give you a brief taster of the rest of the story as i do not wish to ruin it for future readers.*==================================================**MAIN STORY.**Jimmy has a healthy happy life with two loving parents and his Grandma Rowena.The Tock family lead a simple life, they take joy from each other, the community they live in and from food.Jimmy is following in his fathers footsteps to become a master baker, and dinner at the Tock home is all about enjoying each others company and celebrating the wonders of pastry.As the first day of his grandfathers predictions daws near, Jimmy and his family try to prepair themselves for an unknown threat.Jimmy is taken hostage at the library with Lorrie Lynn Hicks, by a good looking fellow with an axe to grind against the town.Lorrie is a sassy, life loving, beautiful woman and Jimmy is instantly attracted to her despite their desperate situation.While trying to figure out a way to escape, Jimmy discovers that thier captor is non other than Konrad Beezo s son- Punchinello.Unfortunatly he is as psychotic as his father and has been bred on hatred and told a very doctored version of events that occured on the night of his birth.Jimmy and Lorrie have to improvise and think on thier feet to escape. The second of Jimmy s dark days occurs after the birth of his first child.In comparison to the day the child was born, and all the other horrible days, this one is a walk in the park, but the message that is given will scare the family for years.The third of the five days will have repercussions for the family that could never be forseen.Attacked in his own home and having to fight for the lives of his wife and children, Jimmy has to confront Beezo the insane clown.The fourth of Jimmy s five days is family related.His eldest child is ill and he has to invite evil into his life to ensure her survival.In this part of the story you can read what every parent knows.There is nothing you would not do, or say to save your child.Last but by no means least.The finale brings a new twist and a new tradgedy to the Tock family.It proves that you have to confront the past to be able to embrace the future.It makes everything clear, and even if the truth is disturbing, it has to be faced.============================================I hope i have given you sufficient information without ruining the book.I have been deliberatly vague when describing the main story, as to tell you any more would make it worthless when reading.==================================================*CONCLUSION / INFORMATION.*I come from a family of readers and my Dad picked this up for me, so am unaware of how much it cost.The whole family have read Koontz but i have emerged as the biggest fan as the rest prefer sci-fi (yawn).I have read many of his books and have never been disappointed,  likewise with Life Expectancy.The Tock family are so genuine in thier love of life and thier belief that they will get through anything life throws at them, including loony clowns.You cannot help but care about thier characters and find yourself rooting for them the whole way through.This is not to say that thier characters are vapid and they rely on divine grace to get them through.Each situation brings out personal strengths they never knew they had.The humor they display in even the toughest situations makes you wonder if you would react the same if you were faced with adversity such as they are.**As is evident, i enjoyed this book immensly and would highly recommend this to anyone.**My hardback copy was published by Harper Collins and has 401 un-putdownable pages. Thanks Sue.     ', '    We all know that clowns are evil.  Almost as evil, in fact, as sheep.  But throughout the history of horror movies and from Stephen King s IT to the clown that resides under your five year old s bed, we ve all learned that clowns are not the funny, face-painted entertainers we re lead to believe, but cruel, ruthless killers of satanic birth.But as Dean Koontz weaves the story of Jimmy Tock, he intricately includes a clown like you ve never seen one before - without make up, without funny nose or sinister smile, without self-imploding car, but just as murderous as the next slightly insane clown.On the night of his birth, Jimmy Tock s grandfather makes ten frighteningly accurate predictions, then he died the very moment little Jimmy s mother gave birth.  The older Tock predicted that the baby would be twenty inches in length, would weight eight pounds ten ounces, would be born at ten-forty-six pm, would suffer from syndactyly; he predicted everybody would call him Jimmy despite his birth name being James and he predicted five terrible days that the little Tock would suffer during his life: September 15th 1994; January 19th 1998; December 23rd 2002; November 26th 2003; April 16th 2005.  And then he died.At the same time, Jimmy Tock (nobody ever called him James, even people he d only just met) was born.  But while Rudy Tock, son of Josef Tock and father to Jimmy, was both grieving for his dead father and elated at the arrival of his son, in the maternity suite next to the Tock s a far greater drama was playing out.Natalie Vivacemente Beezo, wife of arguably the world s greatest clown - Konrad Beezo - and daughter to the greatest aerialist that ever did live - Virgilio Vivacemente - was struggling with a traumatic childbirth, one that ultimately killed her.Konrad, unable to contain his grief, blamed the doctors for her death, saying they were agents for the evil Virgilio who hated the fact his daughter, a beautiful aerialist, had married a clown   He grabbed the newborn baby from a nurse and shot her and the doctor delivering the news of his wife s death, before going on the run.Jimmy Tock grew up with the loving guidance of his parents, Maddy and Rudy, and became a master baker.  But as September 15th 1994, the family came together, apprehensive of what that day might bring... To tell you what happened on those days would be to spoil the story line.  The scene is set and if you re a fan of thrilling fiction or Dean Koontz, then this novel is one I can highly recommend.  The narrative is written as if the story teller, Jimmy Tock, is uncomfortable with telling stories yet Koontz weaves his magic with the prose and the story flows quickly and entertainingly.  The chapters are short but fulfilling and the page-turning effect of Koontz s latest story had me through 400-page hardback in just a handful of nights.As the Tock s life becomes inextricably entwined with the history of the circus, as the might of the clowns and the aerialists comes to bare on Jimmy and his beautiful wife, they are forced to make life changing decisions in order to keep their loving family together.  Koontz writes the story so well that you find yourself willing the Tocks to succeed, not to fall foul of the traps the Beezos and the Vivacementes may be setting for them in the future.By chapter 63 your heart is in your mouth as you try to understand just what has happened to the hero of the story; to find out, you have to keep turning the pages.To a pedant like me, the only negatives in this novel were a couple of inadvertent uses of poetic license.  In 1994, Lorrie Lyn Hicks makes a reference to e-mail as if everybody is using it, yet in  94 e-mail was still in its infancy and was the realm of academics, scientists and the rich, who could afford the gargantuan fees to connect to their 9.6kb Internet providers.Likewise, in 1998, friends and neighbours bring the Tocks piles of DVDs to watch to see them through a period in their life, yet in  98 DVD players and discs were as rare as e-mail was in  94 and the cost of players, not to mention the films themselves, were still extraordinarily high, yet Koontz writes as if the Tocks have a player in every room. The notion was as absurd as houses having more than one TV in the nineteen fifties.Neither of these inadvertent uses of technology detracts from the story, however, and it is incredibly well written, incredibly enthralling and, above all, it contains a level of light-hearted humour that is often missing from dark tales; this humour makes you love the brilliantly woven characters more.Whatever your usual genre of choice, Life Expectancy has enough of a level of romance, comedy, excitement and terror to suit all tastes and it s a highly recommended read.If you re looking for any clues as to  quot;who dunnit quot;, the only thing I shall say is: syndactyly.       ', '    *~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~* LIFE EXPECTANCY BY DEAN KOONTZ*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~* quot;When the hand of fate reaches out to touch an ordinary man..... quot; quot;The Master of our Darkest Dreams quot; THE TIMES*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~* THE PLOT *~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~* Life Expectancy  is a tale told from the point of view of Jimmy Tock, whose life we pick up at the time of his birth where his anxious father, Rudy is separating his time between his labour-pained wife, Maddy and his father, Josef Tock, who is in the same hospital on his deathbed. As a frantic Rudy rushes between his loved ones, he encounters a strange and embittered man in the waiting rooms, a man whom Rudy finds highly disturbing - however, he is distracted from this as his father suddenly sits bolt upright in his hospital bed to inform Rudy that not only is he about to die, but he also has information in the form of dates concerning Rudy s impending son.He predicts the child will be  Jimmy  never be James and the intensity of his demands that Rudy write down five dates to beware frightens Rudy and he hurriedly complies. The dates the dying man gives are the following: SEPT 15TH 1994; JAN 19 1998; DEC23RD 2002; NOV 26TH 2003   APRIL 15TH 2005, on these dates, Jimmy will be great danger and must beware. As Josef demands his son write down the last date, he promptly dies but in his raving he had also warned Rudy to beware of the clown - who is the disturbing man in the fathers-to-be waiting room.As Rudy hurries back to his wife he finds a doctor shot dead and a nurse lies stricken in the corridor - the clown, Konrad Beezo cradles a child under his arm and in gun in the other - he claims the hospital staff have killed his wife due to the demands of his over-zealous and evil father-in-law, Virgilio Vivacemente, with this he makes his escape and we pick up Jimmy s story once more where he is an adult, happy with his kooky family but with the first of the  danger dates  looming the next day.....We then follow Jimmy through his life as he meets each danger date and the impact it has on his life and that of his wife Lorrie and eventually, their three children, Annie, Lucy and Andy. As they face each new danger with courage and near fatalities, the Tocks come to realise how the clown Konrad Beezo is enmeshed in their lives and struggle to extract themselves from each new danger only to know they face another....*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~* MY THOUGHTS *~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*It was an enjoyable plot and but I found it to be lacking something that Dean Koontz usually finds - the story was entertaining enough and was a real page-tuner with each, short, chapter linking well into the next - I found I didn t really need to concentrate very hard and that I read it very quickly - well, in one day, even though it is quite a big book. The twists in the tale at the end of the book probably saved it from getting a bad review from me as I really wasn t expecting them. I didn t find the book to be in Dean s (I m sure he will forgive me the familiarity, I do own most of his books )  usual style, though a few of his  Christopher Snow  series had a similar tone to them that I also found over-easy to read. Usually, I find his prose to be descriptive and at times quite searching in his quest to embroil tension by building conspiracy into the plot - not the case with this book - I would describe it as fast-paced but lacking tension until the end of the story. This book did have a fair interjection of humour which helped to keep the reading light with the banter between Jimmy and Lorrie entertaining if a little tiresome occasionally.The characters were also quite lightweight - I liked the main characters, but found them lacking in substance and wondered if that is why Dean injects so much of the  humorous banter , even Jimmy sometimes came across as quite childlike - though the feeling behind the family unit is well constructed and quite nice.Overall, if you are not looking for heavyweight literary prose, then the book is enjoyable and fast-paced. Although Dean is considered to be an author in the Horror genre, I would describe this book as more of a thriller - this is a perfect book for the beach to while the day away in the hot sun on fine, sugary sand... (god I need a holiday ) *~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~* OTHER STUFF *~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*Publisher: Harper Collins2005 ~ www.harpercollins.co.ukISBN: 0 00 719695PAPERBACK lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; MORE BY DEAN KOONTZ  lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; lt; gt; ODD THOMAS  lt; gt; THE TAKING  lt; gt; THE FACE  lt; gt; FALSE MEMORY  lt; gt; lt; gt; MR MURDER  lt; gt; LIGHTENING  lt; gt; ICEBOUND  lt; gt; THE VISION  lt; gt; lt; gt; THE EYES OF DARKNESS  lt; gt; SHATTERED  lt; gt; INTENSITY  lt; gt; STRANGERS  lt; gt; lt; gt; STRANGE HIGHWAYS  lt; gt; WATCHERS  lt; gt; THE BAD PLACE  lt; gt; TICKTOCK  lt; gt;AND MUCH, MUCH MORE ........ ;)Hope this is helpful, thanks for reading  Kes :)     ', '    The only thing worse than a bad book, I feel, is a book which should have been so much better. For all the distaste a real stinker of a story can cause, it s quickly forgotten, whereas the remnants of the nearly-novel seem to linger for some time, an unsatisfying aftertaste of something that appeared so appealing. And that s enough of that tenuous analogy. Dean Koontz s Life Expectancy suffered from exactly such a problem, for me. The premise is a fantastic, tantalising one; setting out with the end of one life and the start of another in quick succession. The dying man, one Josef Tock, awakes from the grip death was increasingly applying to him, and makes a series of prophesies concerning his soon-to-be-born Grandson, whom he is destined to miss by minutes. The first set of his ten predictions concern his birth; he precisely the child s size, weight and time of entry to the world. However, it is the second five which are to be of most consequence. Five dates he names, each signifying a terrible day in the life of young Jimmy Tock. Having made his prophecy, he dies, and the child is born, instantly fulfilling the first five predictions, giving his parents cause to believe the likely accuracy of the second set. Thus Jimmy s life begins, and must continue, taking in all five days. What lies beyond, and of what nature is the evil that stalks him? For me, this is a gripping, teasing premise; one can t help but read on, if only to reach each of the five days. Sadly, however, it was gradually downhill from here. Although I ve heard of Koontz, I d never previously read any of his work. Doubtless others would better be able to fill me in, but I was under the impression that he was a horror/thriller writer, and had certain expectations of his style. Of course, it would not necessarily be a negative to find contrary to what I expected, but the author s writing nonetheless confused me somewhat. The humour that characterises the opening part of the book, before the first day, works well; it brings life to the Tock family unit which is so important to the story, and adds an element of depth to the characters as you see them bounce off each other. However, when this tone continues into the first of the terrible days, things work less effectively. Throughout the book, Koontz litters the narrative with dry asides to the reader and little quips that sit rather uncomfortably alongside what are meant to be dates of  quot;terror and violence, malice and perversion quot;. Add into that the at times far-fetched actions of the hand of evil, and this, just occasionally, reads like a bad Dan Brown satire. As I say, this is a great shame. Alongside the excellent set-up, there are many good things about the story itself. The main characters, at least in the Tock family, are exceptionally well defined, and Koontz does a fantastic job of quickly filling out his protaganists, really giving us a sense of what s going on in their minds. The little interchanges between family members are always fairly amusing, and Jimmy and his wife play off each other especially well, even if it s a fraction unclear what exactly she sees in him. The villains of the piece are slightly less developed, which can be a pity, particularly in the case of the  quot;big quot; baddie, who only makes a fleeting appearance at the end. Aside from these minor grievances with tone, the plot is the biggest problem with Life Expectancy. Maybe it was just over-expectation on my part, but when the blurb spoke of  quot;an Evil so pervasive quot;, I couldn t help but conjure up some pretty grand images. Sadly, none of these are even nearly realised; the terrible days featured here involve some very run-of-the-mill stuff, with a very unremarkable twist thrown in towards the end - one which isn t so much predictable as simply unnoteworthy. I can t say as I remember even raising an eyebrow; it just doesn t really affect the book in any meaningful way. Frustratingly, the only really decent perpetrator of evil is only given a cameo role, in and out too late to impact upon events too consequentially. I m probably making the book sound a lot worse than it actually is, to be honest. It is an entertaining read for the most part, and it kept me going enough for me to whip through it fairly greedily, even if much of this was driven more by a hope something rather more epic would ocur than anything else. The exhanges between the characters are well written, and the story is well narrated by the central protaganist, and despite its shortcomings, this wouldn t put me off reading Koontz again. Indeed, I d like to see if the style he exhibits here is characteristic of him as a writer, or merely a bad choice of tone in this one effort. Yet, as I mentioned in my first paragraph, the disappointment I felt having finished the book was made all the greater by the hopes it generated with its own opening. All in all, it s far from a bad read, but it simply could have been so much more.     ', '    This book has a great storeyline ( I do not know where this guy comes up with all the ideas.)The book tells the story of a man, who on his deathbed leaves a prediction for his grandson, Jimmy Tock  who is born at the same time as his grandfather dies. It follows the life of Jimmy and how these predictions came true throughout his life and how these predictions affect his family and friends and some not so friendly people who keep crossing paths with Jimmy.This book will keep you on the edge of your seat and keep you turning the pages.Mr Koontz keeps the suspense throughout the book and make you live the whole storey, right to the last page the twists and turns continue. I think that this book is one of his best recent books and reminds me of the old Dean Koontz, if you have read some of his early work then you will love this one.Life Expectancy uses clever words that are easy to understand and the pages flow, each more gripping than the last, you share the charactors ups and downs as they progress through life, and makes you wonder what will happen next, i wanted to read the last page quite early on ( This is always a good sign of a good book for me, but i did resist and it was well worth it)I reccommend this book to any one, as its not too frightening but does hold the suspense throughout.it will be in my top 5 of Dean Koontz books      ', '    I am a big Dean Koontz fan and have read most of his books with great enjoyment. Lifw Expectancy was all I expected it to be.The book begins with the death of Josef Tock who makes a series of predictions about his grandson who is yet to be born including details of his birth weight, height and so on. Shortly after his death, Jimmy Tock is born and sure enough the predicted weight etc was spot on.But now comes the rub, the grandfather also predicted that on five specific dates, Jimmy Tock would experience terrible things. And with the accuracy of the first predictions, what else could Jimmy s parents do but believe them?At the same time, another baby was being born, the child of  the world s greatest clown, Konrad Beezo  This time the birth did not go well - the mother dies  Unable to contain his grief, the clown blames the doctors for her death. And the story beginsKoonzt tells the story with all the  magic  we could expect. The story flows quickly with chapters are short and enthralling. Koonzt s main ability is to carry you onwards through the book. Life Expectancy is a page-turner without a doubt. I read it just a few days.       ', '    I was given this novel as an unexpected gift and having never read Dean Koontz novels before I was a little dubious as to whether or not I would enjoy it. Like most people I have that touch of coulrophobia which made me apprehensive about whether it would just spook me too much to read about a family of evil clowns.  The Times  recommendation  quot;The master of our darkest dreams quot; on the back of my copy also added to this image of forthcoming nightmares; but proved to be quite an exaggeration, as I didn t find it scary at all.At first I was intrigued by the premise of the novel, Rudy Tock moves between being witness to his own father s death and his wife s labour with their first child in a bleak and sinister feeling hospital. Ten predictions are made by Rudy s father, Josef, about the son that is about to be brought into the world. This is not a pleasant introduction to the world, for Jimmy. Five terrible days lie in his future and the fates have a very clever and disturbing life ahead of him.Sadly I found the writing style a bit clunky and disappointing given the expectations I had of Dean Koontz as an author. Later it occurred to me that this style, which lacked much character development and a real feel for the locations and motivations in many parts, was due to the story s autobiographical protagonists telling it, rather than Koontz as a writer. Perhaps it wasn t representational of Koontz usual style, but it made it harder to have faith in the books momentum and to be sufficiently absorbed in this fictional world in order to really feel for the characters.As the story progressed I found this inexperienced writing style less cumbersome, but still found it a bit forced in places. Twice the storytelling protagonist(s) try to trick the reader and this I found a little patronising, and led to a removal from the fictional world s momentum. Although the first person narrative allowed the reader to get a grasp of how he felt about family and therefore demonstrated that this was the strongest motivation, it didn t allow for an omnipotent perspective to show other character s motivations and therefore many of them lacked substance.As for the plot, I found that in places it dragged; and while some days which were not prophesied to be terrible turned out pretty awful, therefore bucking the trend, it also had terrible days that weren t given enough inner motivation to be really terrifying. It did however keep me turning the pages and having enough connection to the characters to want them to make it through. There were two rather dark descriptions of events in the story which touch upon dark themes and horror, but by and large this seemed a very comfortable read.Lorrie lacked soul for me and I couldn t understand why she was so drawn to Jimmy for most of the story, she should have been more than banter and quips, plus Jimmy s somewhat over flattering view of her. She fed a lot of the plot and she and the other generations of the Tock family lacked depth.Despite my initial misgivings about clowns, I found them to be less the stereotypical evil and more understandable or, in a way personable, than some of the other characters. I was quite disappointed in the end that we didn t get more description into Punchinello s motives and thinking; as he seemed to be, for me, the one charismatic character in the whole thing. It didn t make me fear clowns as much as it made me want to avoid the circus altogether and hospitals for that matter.There were two significant twists in this story which I won t go into too much detail about. While both surprised me, neither was as shocking or horrifying as I had been expecting for a  horror writer s  novel. The first seemed to come out of nowhere, given all the padding there was for a few earlier  days  in the story. It also lacked adequate description of personal reactions from all the characters involved, which I would have loved to have known more about.The second twist drew a mixed reaction from me. It seemed blunt and underdeveloped, but also encouraged a few deeper thoughts into the earlier parts of the novel which had seemingly been brushed over. Here I felt Koontz s writing shone above that of the first person chronological narrative. A few suggestions in the mind came out at this truth telling near the end and you had to change your opinions of a few characters. Unfortunately it was all a little too late to really score points with me.I liked the optimism and humour in the book, as it was quite surprising to see this given the story s dark premise. Although I guess if the Tock family hadn t have had an optimistic view of their chances of coping with these awful days ahead, Jimmy would have topped himself long before they came along. I liked the family atmosphere of many parts of the novel but felt disappointed that we only had Jimmy s explanations of their thoughts and deeds, rather than the characters speaking for themselves or being spoken for by a third person narrator. I know that some very good tales have been told in the first person, but given that  fate  is probably the most prominent figure in the tale, perhaps this one would have been better told by someone removed from events. Though this would no doubt make for a very different story altogether.I m very glad that this was a quick read, I think that I put on three pounds while reading this for the last fortnight, thanks to all the mentions of cake and pastry, by it s master baker narrator. ', '    This is the first Dean Koontz Book i have read and i read it in 3 days whilst sunbathing in Egypt.The book is about a pastry chef s son named Jimmy Tock and in the moments before he is born, Jimmy has a strange destiny thrust upon him,  Jimmy s grandfather, who was in a stroke induced coma, suddenly awoke and predicted, among other things, five  quot;terrible days quot; for his grandson, between his twentieth and thirtieth birthdays and then dies as Jimmy is born. ', '    What can I say, it has suspense, it has killer clowns....On a serious note, I got this book from a friend of mine who worked next door to me...I never heard of Dean Koontz until I read this book, it was an action packed suspense thriller, that had me biting my nails the whole story through. You won t be dissapointed I assure you all of it        ']

s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
Dean Koontz’s *Life Expectancy* offers a compelling blend of suspense and emotional warmth that aligns well with a reader who values both thrilling narratives and rich character dynamics. Told through the eyes of Jimmy Tock, the story gains a personal and intimate tone, allowing readers to deeply connect with his journey as he faces five ominous days foretold since birth. This narrative choice enhances the emotional resonance, making the suspense not just external but intimately felt.

What stands out is Koontz’s skillful balance of dark themes with light-hearted, comedic elements. This approach makes the story’s heavier moments more approachable without undermining their significance, a nuance that adds depth to the reading experience. The portrayal of a close-knit, loving family further enriches the narrative, providing a heartfelt backdrop that explores human connections and the complexities of relationships—elements that invite reflection on love and loyalty amid chaos.

The pacing is brisk and engaging, with twists and suspense that maintain momentum throughout, satisfying readers who appreciate a well-structured thriller. However, while the fast pace keeps the story entertaining, some readers might find that the emphasis on plot-driven suspense occasionally overshadows deeper thematic exploration or historical context, which could have added further layers to the narrative.

In summary, *Life Expectancy* is a gripping, emotionally textured thriller that combines humor, family bonds, and suspense in a way that is both entertaining and thought-provoking. For readers who enjoy character-driven stories with a personal voice and a mix of light and dark tones, this book offers a rewarding experience—though those seeking profound thematic depth or historical richness might find it somewhat lighter in those areas.

product_reviews: ['    I eagerly waited for this book to come out and when it did I wasn t disappointed. The book is very long but for someone who can t get enough of the story, it s perfect The story begins with Harry angry that none of his fellow wizards are contacting him often enough after all he has been through in his previous year at Hogwarts, seeing a death and his arch enemy return to power. I don t think the films capture the excitement and suspense created in the books. I don t know how they are going to make a film out of this one but the film might be a long one- we should be so lucky, it is more likely they will cut out endless amounts of information that doesn t seem to be important but will prove to be in a future book The characters are extremely well defined in this book and you find yourself hating a certain woman in this book and wanting nasty things to happen to her- you ll undersatnd if you read it  What worried me in the book was Dumbledore s distance from Harry throughout the book but it is all explained at the end.The ending is the most exciting portion of this book and doesn t disappoint. It s worth it and you will find youreself not wanting it to end. I unfortunately read it in under a week but I can still read it again and again       ', '    Harry Potter the boy wizard is attending his 5th year at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.Haunted still by his evil nemesis Lord Voldemort and some wierd dreams. He has to depend upon the unlikeliest of people to help get him through the year, Neville Longbottom and Severus Snape, to name just two.There is a struggle of power within the walls of of Hogwarts mainly between the regular staff and the pupils and a new member of staff who is rather obviouly a spy planted by the Ministry of magic to control the goings on at the school - she also wants to torture Harry a lot more than is healthy for 1 person.it is more adult than the last 4 in the series and they all seem to be getting darker.Dumbledore is still barmy, Sirius is still gorgeous but moodier, Snape is still evil, vinictive and greasy and hates Harry just as much if not more, Harry is huffier - must be all those hormones , and Ron and Hermione are still giving me the impression of a couple in love.Voldemort is indeed back and wanting to get to power and of course do away with Harry. Harry, this time however, is given an additional foe to battle in his spare time - while he isn t getting into trouble, breaking school rules, snogging girls and plotting against the evil Lord Voldemort.This book is an excellently clever mixture of hilarity, hormonal mood swings, evil plots and vengeful notions.It was highly enjoyable and very hard to put down, and even harder to have to stop and explain what i was laughing at to every one in the room.The thing is everyone wants to know the story as you re reading it, so you end up spending more time reading extracts to your friends rather than actually reading the book itself.a little long-winded in parts with some un-necessary bits to add extra length.     ', '    I thought I was going to burst with anticipation waiting for this book to come out   Yes, I was one of those sad people who had read almost the entire book within a day of its release.  Was it worth the wait?  Without a shadow of doubt, yes J K Rowling does not disappoint with this 5th instalment of Harry Potter s battle against He Who Shall Not Be Named.  Her writing and story telling style remains clear and entertaining although at times it felt a little slow paced (although maybe that was because I was far too keen to find out which character died...)The book is undoubtedly long at something over 700 pages and as I have said the pace can feel a little slow but this does not detract from the undoubted quality of what is, without question an amazingly good read from a truly talented story teller.I think that it might be difficult to pick this book up and read it without having read the previoius 4 books first, but then they too are great reads so why not treat yourself to all 5?On the whole, I felt that the storyline was pretty strong throughout - my only criticism would be that the ending was a little weaker than Goblet of Fire and there seem to be less unanswered questions at the end of this book than there were at the end of Goblet of Fire.  But having said all of this, I am certain that book 6 will be totally worth the wait The character development was, as ever excellent and believable.  Harry in particular has grown older, wiser and seems very angry - unsurprising given what he has gone through - and J K Rowling puts this across well.All in all, definitely worth the wait, definitely gets 5 stars and comes highly recommended.  If you haven t read this book yet go and buy it now   Roll on book 6      ', '    I started reading the new Harry Potter book whilst on a number fifty-two bus, but I didn t unwrap it from it s crinkly little plastic bag and just throw myself in. I kept it in the bag, hidden from the world, for a few minutes, and then read a chapter. Then I put it back. And let the first chapter swill around, savouring the flavour that a fever of anticipation had caused. I m not one to bath in fever pitch anticipation but even I had to admit:  quot;the wait was sort of worth it quot;.I d like to warn all non-reviewers that the way I m advocating is not the way to read this book. While I didn t go down the Guardian route of reading it and reviewing it in an hour after it s release, I did blast through it as soon as I got home. Reading it in a day may seem slightly less restrictive, but at 766 pages Rowling s fifth tome is well, rather tome-like to be frank.So the big question (other than  quot;who dies? quot;) is - is it any good? Well, a few of you are probably screaming out for the news on what happens at the end but I m afraid that if you ve taken the time out to buy the book, it s your responsibility to read it and find out yourselves  And it s not Ron.The book is split in to thirty eight chapters, and at the start it rolls on in a slightly predictable manner, but it s not like we weren t expecting it. Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia are not only  quot;horrid quot;, but probably the best parody of 4x4 driving yuppies you can find in print this side of Private Eye. They are absolutely fantastic, if they have lost their charm a little. Rowling, in this instance, extends this further by making the Dursleys the winner of fabricated prize of the Best Kept Suburban Lawn award. Sprinkler-me-do After that the plot rumbles along quite merrily, if a little slowly for my liking. We do see a rather fantastically described courtroom passage in the early stages of the book that almost makes you believe that the ghosts of Rumpole and Kavanagh are going to pop out and get involved in some madcap legal antics. But, um, no. Instead we see the introduction of the ever lovable Dumbledore (with his rather excellent hat), and have a little rumour impregnated in to our heads that certain people aren t trusting him as much as he d like. This trial links in with what I believe to be one of the main emerging theme in the book - the idea of injustice. Building on the previous books, the Ministry of Magic are involved heavily. In the forerunners to this part of the series, justice prevailed - protagonist beat antagonist (Harry beats Voldemort, or equivalent) and manages to spit in the face of his critics (lovable baddie Draco) - and all live happily ever after. But book three introduces Sirius Black, and the inevitable question of his miscarriage of justice. While the first two lay down the ideas that if you commit an evil, someone will punish you, the third demonstrates the moral message that if you don t commit an evil, there is always some idle busybody who ll find a reason you did it, And they won t let silly things like innocence get in the way of it.In book 5 meanwhile, the actions of Harry almost happen out of necessity. Hence the old adage of 2+2 being 5 comes in when he gets punished for what is, inherently, a good thing. They describe him as getting off on  quot;a technicality quot;, but the technicality happens to be the overriding point - mens rea and all. The old phrase  quot;get the specifics sorted and the rest will sort itself out quot; seems appropriate. As I recently wrote on a message board, I am almost tempted to sit down and pray every night and thank the Great Geezer Upstairs that while he has inflicted a lot of bad on us - war, concentration camps, the Bush administration, Victoria Beckham, television etc. that he has not once given us a justice system as corrupt as the one in Order of the Phoenix. Hmm... I am almost tempted to find a bat and wallop the Cornelius Fudge round the head with it and beat the concepts of judicial independence, separation of powers and  quot;innocent until proven guilty quot; in to them by whatever means necessary. Now if only David Blunkett could read this book and understand it as a piece of social commentary. I wonder, is the Harry Potter world governed by the European Convention on Human Rights? I do wonder indeed...**Now... Tom... calm... deep... breaths... soothing... blue ocean...**Okay, we can proceed now that I ve got my temper under control.Just briefly back to those political/legal issues - while some people may be amazed that they came up, it s not like we didn t expect them: I mean with the current context  n  all.On the way to the school itself, the merry crew meet a new character, one of many, the rather curious Luna Lovegood who then reveals that her father is editor of a wizarding magazine, The Quibbler, a kind of Daily Sport with magic spells in (and with the omission of women with inconspicuous chest-mounted plastic appendages), which seems, at first glance, just like a fill-in character. Which in fact she is. Later on though, she comes in to her own and fills a void that some of the other characters have left. One criticism that could be levelled at Number Five is the number of characters that get introduced, many of them just become names. While fantasy fiction aficionados will have no problem with this amount of characters (I mean, they have to put up with titles like  quot;Betrayal of the Duke: The Fall of Krag aroth-Asgard quot; so what s a few extraneous characters at the end of the day?). Tonks is okay, and could be developed. The other members of the Old Brigade are back in force (Moody, Lupin etc.) and it s umm, okay.What else has changed? Harry has morphed from being a saint - he could almost have applied to join a Buddhist monastery with his self-denial and lack of egotistical ramblings. Ron has come in to his self and become more than just a sidekick. Hermione has taken her fanatical house-elves lark to an almost feminist-level of nonsense. And at the risk of becoming a slash-reading fanboy, I d like to say that Malfoy does absolutely nothing in this book. While he served as the figure of evil, this has been replaced. There is no discernible evil, just stupidity.That s where the latest addition to Rowling s lineup, Professor Umbridge comes in. Her detention scenes with Harry are some of the most gut-wrenching bits of torture I ve read recently. Cliche maybe, but Room 101 seems like it s entered popular culture - she is what you d find inside. But, as with all this post-modernism, instead of being the sadistic boot-wearing figure of evil that we ve come to expect from the realms of totalitarianism (almost a cliche in itself), she has gone for the modern figure of evil - the kind cardigan-wearing pseudo-academic who  quot;knows best quot; but has  quot;her ways quot; of making you agree. It s as if Adolf Hitler and Bridget Jones had kids - she d take the drive and determination of the father but reject all his posturing, saluting and uniform wearing and come up with a feminine version far more vicious than the SS shining bright lights in your eyes. Umbridge is that daughter - a kind of fluffy evil (but malicious not sarcastic, although she probably has the latter up her cardie sleeves somewhere). Reason Online described her as  quot;banal evil quot;. And I think that s rather a good description. And she s coming to a secondary school near you Rowling s only downfalling with this latest book is the length is partly responsible for the  quot;overdescriptiveness quot;. While I m not one who dislikes extraneous descriptions, at times this book can be silly. At times it adds atmosphere, and you can almost feel the textures and picture the places (and allows you to argue more readily with the  quot;movie quot; version of the books).There is a strong theme throughout this book of necessity. The courtroom scene focuses on a reasonable necessity of protection and all through out the book there continues this thread that Harry must do what he is doing. It did have the most disappointing ending of all of the books, literally because it just stops. I d like to explain, but for fear of ruining it for you all, I will just leave it at that. This book begins, as ever, with Harry staying in Primrose Drive, under the  care  of his Dahlishly grotesque Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia.  He is feeling very frustrated, because he has not heard from any of his friends.  He is also worried that disaster will strike after the return of Lord Voldemort, which he witnessed at the end of book 4.  In addition, he is having to deal with his horrible cousin Dudley, who is now a gang-leader in the neighbourhood and a worse bully than ever.  One evening, while on his way home from a walk, keeping a little distance behind Dudley, Harry is suddenly aware that they under magical attack  Being Harry, he manages to save his cousin as well as himself - although as usual he is blamed for the attack rather than thanked for rescuing Dudley   Unfortunately, having now used magic in the muggle world, Harry is summoned to appear before the Wizengamot, the court of wizards, and threatened with expulsion from Hogwarts.From that point, things do take a slight turn for the better.  Harry is taken to London, where he is reunited with his friends Ron and Hermione, the rest of Ron s family, his godfather Sirius, and some characters from previous books - including the werewolf Lupin, who was a teacher in book 3.  Still Harry is not told much about what is going on.  Although happy to be with his friends, he feels more and more frustrated at being treated like a child, when he is now 15, and has taken part in more battles than most wizards far older than he is.  When the date of the trial comes up, Harry is taken to the Ministry of Magic by Ron s father, and we discover that wizard beaurocracy is every bit as bad as that in the muggle world   Naturally Harry is not convicted and sent to Azkhaban (or the book would have had no more content ) - he is acquitted, since underage magic is permitted in case of life or death.  Nevertheless, many of the Wizengamot do not believe that he was actually attacked, and it becomes clear that the wizarding world is split between those who believe that Lord Voldemort has indeed returned, and those who think that Harry likes being the centre of attention, and has been telling a great many lies.And so to Hogwarts for a new term, albeit with Harry anxious, irritable and frustrated at all that has been going on, combined with general teenage angst.  When he discovers that Hagrid is not around, he becomes more worried still.  When he realises just how much work and pressure there will be, as his year is working towards the OWL exams at the end of the year (the wizard equivalent of GCSEs) he is horrified.  When he meets the new Defence against the Dark Arts teacher, Professor Umbrage, he begins to feel that he might almost have been better off if he had not returned to school at all.  Professor Umbrage not only  dumbs down  the entire curriculum, insisting on rote learning of facts rather than any practical application:  she also turns out to be cruel and vindictive.  As the year progresses, life at Hogwarts becomes more and more difficult, as Professor Umbridge is appointed to be the school inspector, and proceeds to create more and more new rules which restrict students in increased ways.  This, no doubt, is a way of making fun of the current UK government s increased restrictions in the state schools, and caricaturing the dreaded OFSTED inspections.  (I expect this book is a great hit with teachers )  Inevitably Harry gets into trouble more than anyone, mostly undeserved, but as he continues to be bad-tempered and does not always guard his tongue, it s perhaps not surprising.  There are some humorous moments,  many of them provided by Ron s incorrigible elder twin brothers, and their friend Lee Jordan.  One of my favourite moments occurred after Harry did an interview for a newspaper, giving the full truth, in detail, of what happened at the end of book 4.  Because so many people refused to believe that Voldemort was back, the magazine is immediately banned in the school.  Harry is upset by this, but Hermione is delighted:  she points out that banning something is the surest way to ensure that EVERYBODY will read it, one way or another.  I can only assume that this is a gentle dig at the many readers in the USA and elsewhere who tried to ban the Harry Potter books - only to see them turn into the world s fastest-selling phenomenon Towards the end there is the usual exciting climactic battle of good vs evil, this time taking place in the Ministry of Magic which we were introduced to earlier in the book.  The book ends with Dumbledore looking over his half-moon glasses and giving the explanation which all the pre-release book reviews said he would give - although in fact we don t learn much more than we knew or could have guessed already.   And so the way is open for the last two books, where we are promised further surprises and an increase in the  dark  aspects.Conclusions:I think this is probably my favourite of all the Harry Potter books so far.  I wasn t so keen on book 4, but found this one a lot more interesting.  It s an excellent book to read aloud:  each chapter is well-written and has plenty to enjoy, so there s no sense of a long and boring start.  I read two or three chapters per day for about ten days - then nearly wore my voice out completely by reading about ten chapters on the last day, since we all wanted to know how it would end   It was very satisfying to have such a long book, so that it was not finished in a single day.  Reading aloud made it take longer still.  I felt quite sorry for the people who queued for hours, bought the book the minute it was released.. and then read it straight through immediately.  All that hype... for what? I know people have criticised the emergence of a new, angry Harry - but to me this did not seem unbelievable at all, given his age and the circumstances surrounding the book.  It also fit well with his mostly compliant personality, having repressed so much anger over the years in order to stay out of trouble - as far as possible - with his muggle relatives.  Sooner or later anger must be expressed, and it s finally happened to Harry.   He handles it well, for the most part, although he does make some silly mistakes.   Nevertheless I think this makes the book less suitable for younger children, and more appropriate for teenagers.  I was a little disappointed at the increase in bad language.  Nothing too major, but quite a few minor and unecessary words were used.  Perhaps this reflects teenage culture to some degree - but since Harry and his friends are not exactly typical teenagers, it hardly seemed necessary.   My only other disappointment was in what seemed like a plot flaw:  Harry is given, early in the book, a mirror which will enable him to communicate with Sirius if ever he has need.  During the book there are some occasions when Harry desperately needs to communicate with Sirius, and each time chooses a  dangerous method - apparently forgetting completely about the mirror.  This seems so unlikely as to be slightly ludicrous, and we wondered why the mirror was brought into the story at all.Still, those are only minor whinges.  On the whole, I highly recommend this book - although I would suggest reading all the others beforehand, or much of it won t make sense. ', '    The postman rattled my letter-box impatiently on the morning of the twenty first.  When I finally opened the door, in my jammies, wiping sleep from my eyes, he was busily writing out a card saying how sorry he was to miss me.  He looked up, recoiled somewhat from my 6.30am face, then recovered bravely.   quot;There s your Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix. quot;  He announced and thrust the Amazon package into my hands.  I can only imagine the number of times he got to say that, throughout that day.The Harry Potter books have been rather popular in our house since the first of the series was published in 1997.  My eldest was ten at the time and took to the world of JK immediately.  Since, I have read every new adventure after she s devoured it and two years ago started reading them to my younger daughter.  None of us is wildly keen on the films, preferring our imaginary visions of Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.When I was a child, I was hooked to the Chalet School series of books.  The Harry Potter books remind me strongly of these.  The action takes place in a boarding school in each.  An adventure will begin, necessitating the bending or breaking of rules, and our protagonists risk punishment.  There are school houses to root for, sports to follow and school bullies to watch out for.  The children we sympathise with are at the mercy of teachers who dislike them, or can gain sympathy from those who understand them better.  Of course, it is a long time since I read the Chalet School series, but I don t recall the girls forming a coven at any point.  The introduction of magic is what gives Harry Potter that little bit more excitement and mystery, in a child s eyes. quot;The Order of the Phoenix quot; is the size of a small house.  I implored Jill not to say anything, or even show any expression on her face, as she read.  Like the rest of us, I knew that a regular character would be killed off in this book.  I wanted to discover who it would be, by myself.  Some two days later, she passed it over, looking smug.  I ordered her to clean her room and started reading.The structure of the book is as before, following the school term, with the bulk of the story taking place at Hogwarts.  Harry has spent the summer holiday at his hateful relatives, the Dursley s, home and is not being treated any more kindly than usual.  Immediately, we can tell that both Harry and cousin Dudley are beginning to grow up.  Unfortunately, Dudley had taken to hanging around with a group of thugs, enjoying such past-times as vandalising property and bullying children younger than himself.Harry is huffy and angry, because he has had no real word from his friends, Hermione and Ron.  His attempts to follow the news are thwarted and he has difficulty in keeping tabs on whether Voldemort has made a move on his plans to overthrow the wizard world.Following an attack by the dreaded Dementors on Harry and his cousin one night, Harry is brought to the headquarters of The Order of the Phoenix, for safety.  This turns out to be the family house of his godfather, the handsome Sirius Black.  He is put out to find that Ron and Hermione have been ensconced there for much of the holiday and is angry with them for keeping information from him, although this was on the orders of Dumbledore, the Headmaster of Hogwarts.  Because he has used magic out of school, to save himself and his cousin, he must attend a hearing to decide whether he will be expelled from school.  Of course, Harry makes it back to Hogwarts for his fifth year, when he must sit his dreaded OWL exams.I like Harry in this book.  He has definitely become a teenage boy.  His moods swing erratically and he is often dealing with anger and frustration.  Much of the story deals with Harry s quest to find out exactly what s going on in the fight against Voldemort and he rails against the decision of the adults to keep information from him.  He wants to be respected, as the young man who has already defeated the Dark Lord more than once, and included in their plans.Harry is disappointed to find that he has not been made a prefect, although Ron and Hermione have been awarded the position.  Much of his frustration is vented on his closest friends, who cope admirably, but are obviously tiring of his moods.  All of the fifth year pupils are under tremendous exam pressure, and homework takes up much of their time, energy and emotional well being.  As a reader, I found myself berating Harry, who on many occasions doesn t follow the advice given to him by people who obviously do know the full situation and have a plan formed with which to handle it.As many of us do at this time of our lives, Harry has to reassess his view of his parents, particularly his father, who does not appear to be the saintly figure Harry has previously supposed.  He has his first kiss, too, along with his first botched relationship.The school in this book has changed from the welcoming haven Harry has always found it, to a place of punishment and imprisonment.  He has to accept a lifelong ban on Quidditch, an enormous blow for sports fans.  At one point, Harry would even prefer to be in Privet Drive, rather than Hogwarts.Hagrid is missing for the start of term, off on his own adventure, and a new teacher, Dolores Umbridge, has appeared to take up the jinxed Professor in Defence of the Dark Arts post.  Dolores dresses in pink fluffy cardigans and has pictures of gambolling kittens on her office walls.  Don t let this fool you, she has a toad like quality and has been sent there by the Ministry of Magic, to keep an eye on Dumbledore and bring some discipline to the school.McGonagall is her supportive self, Snape is greasy and treats Harry with disdain as usual, and Draco Malfoy and his gang are again present to threaten Harry and his friends.Despite the warnings from the Sorting Hat that the school must stick together because they are in a time of great danger, the children cannot help but split into factions.  Some believe the warnings about Voldemort that Harry and Dumbledore have been giving during the previous year, while the majority have a view, actively encouraged by the establishment and the Daily Prophet, that they are both either slightly mad or plain attention seeking.The story fairly gallops along, while the protagonists try to find ways of fighting the establishment.  They must spread the truth of Voldemort s return whilst trying to ensure that they have covered all of the work required for their OWL s, not an easy task when practical exercises are banned from the Defence of the Dark Arts class.  Harry Potter s dreams become more and more disturbing, as it seems a link has been forged between himself and the Dark Lord.  Harry has to deal with his increasingly bad temper alone, and is frustrated and hurt that Dumbledore has kept aloof from him throughout the year.  The activities of The Order of the Phoenix, designed to thwart Voldemort s efforts, do not appear to be particularly successful to Harry and he feels forced to take action in order to save the day, again.  As Hermione says,  quot;Are you sure you don t have a  quot;Saving People thing quot;? quot;  Ah, of course he has, and it is his fatal flaw.Yes, one of the regular characters is killed off.  I have to say that JK does a good job in throwing in a few false leads along the way.All in all, I enjoyed Harry s latest outing and appreciated the evolution of the younger characters.  I hope that his next will show how his experience with the  quot;Order of the Phoenix quot; has matured him.  I d like to see him trust someone else s judgement, for a change.     ', '    Harry   s back, and don   t we all know it  Three years of eager anticipation on the part of children and adults alike finally culminated in the release of the fifth book of the seven-book series in the third week of June. Rowling has recaptured the ability that the other Potter books have to keep one turning page after page, late into the night. Throughout nearly 800 pages, there isn   t one opportunity for the reader to get bored, even in the early stages when the plot seems to sag under the weight of all the information thrown at the reader.It   s difficult to define what makes the Potter series so immensely readable, and so hugely popular. Have you heard much about him lately? Have you read the odd opinion about him? I thought so. The release of the fifth instalment of J. K. Rowling   s immensely successful Harry Potter series brought new levels of hype to our already hype-ridden world. Usually I can   t see what all the fuss is about, but this time, having read the previous Harry Potter tales, I joined in with the excitement. So much so in fact that I bought my copy of    Harry Potter and the Order Of The Phoenix    within hours of it being available to pre-order from Amazon (www.amazon.co.uk). At 50  off the RRP (i.e.    8.49 not    16.99) I was extremely pleased with myself. Sadly, however, I had to wait some six months or so before the postman finally delivered it to my door on the fine, sunny morning of Saturday 21st June. Even more sadly I was booked in for a double shift at work that day. Never mind... So, as the first tentative opinions on the book began to appear on ciao, I was still eagerly reading the first few pages. A month later and I   ve read the whole book not once, not twice, but thrice  (No, I didn   t spend quite the entire month reading it, I did manage to do a few other things as well). It is, fortunately, as entertaining as I hoped and expected, and its 760 odd pages make sure that the entertainment lasts as long as possible, and we   re able to immerse ourselves deeper in the wonderful world of magic than ever before.   Saying it was    as entertaining as I hoped    is quite a complement considering the huge level of my expectations. It   s over two years since I first read the first four Harry Potter books (in the space of a few weeks) and the waiting has been at times almost excruciating, especially given the amount of hype that this latest release has received. Secrecy was (fortunately) well maintained prior to the release date, and I   ll certainly try not to spoil anything for future readers and hence  won   t be giving a blow-by-blow analysis of the plot. However I will try and elaborate slightly on the clues that J.K. Rowling gave away, namely about the death of an important character, the characters growing up into adolescence and the    relationship of sorts    that Rowling revealed Harry would have. I will also analyse other key issues in the book, such as authority, injustice, narrow-mindedness, careerism, responsibility, guilt and culpability. For any of you who aren   t yet aware, Harry Potter is a young wizard who attends Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, where he learns all sorts of magical disciplines under the watchful eye of Albus Dumbledore, the headmaster. With his friends Ron and Hermione he enjoys various adventures, often involving his arch-enemy Draco Malfoy. His parents were killed by a powerful evil wizard Lord Voldemort, but his    killing curse    bounced of the infant Harry and reduced Voldemort to a shadow of his former self. Returning to power many years later, he attempts to gain revenge against the now teenage Harry, as part of a  wider battle between good and evil wizards. The magical world is superbly created in the first four books, and this continues in book five, as we learn ever more about the people, creatures, customs and institutions of this wizarding wonderland. The ups and downs of Harry   s discovery of this world (he didn   t know he was a wizard until his eleventh birthday) provide the backdrop to the wider plot of the struggle between good and evil. In this respect book five differs little from the previous stories. Good still battles evil and Harry, although na   ve at times, is a typical hero. He excels at nearly everything and is a very powerful wizard (magic seems to be more about natural brilliance than about effort and learning, although the latter are important too). In his first four years at Hogwarts he has defied Voldemort three times, won innumerable quidditch matches (the wizard sport) and assisted his school house to victory in the house championship every year. So, in the fifth book too he defies Voldemort, wins at quidditch, remains a hero among his peers  and performs well in most wizarding pursuits. Those with no experience of Harry Potter may wonder how on Earth this can span over seven hundred pages and be interesting. In fact I   ve wondered that on many occasions too. The way Rowling creates a fantasy world, in-depth and in some respects realistic, yet free from everyday pressures and worries, is masterful. Reading Harry Potter is an escape from a real world, yet at the same time it is exciting, tense and even upsetting (note the death of an important character). We feel emotions even more than ever, but at a different level to the everyday matters that bother us. This is primarily because Harry is such a good hero; although not perfect, shallow or boring, we know that he will acquit himself well in his wizarding world, leaving us free of concerns about how we will acquit ourselves in the real world. The books are an inspiration: empowering yet relaxing; exciting yet peaceful; tense yet free of worry. It would be wrong however to characterise this plot as a clone of the previous plots. In keeping with the development throughout the series, it is in many ways more complex than before, with important themes being developed and a greater blurring of the boundary between good and evil, right and wrong. Indeed the main plot (i.e. the battle between good and evil) is less pronounced than ever before. Rowling appears to building slowly for a grand showdown between Voldemort and his opponents in the final instalments, since his involvement in book five is infrequent and simple. The main plot is therefore weak in comparison with the previous books and builds very slowly. Partly this is because it is not so self-contained as before, and hence merely increases expectations for the climax to come. However I do feel that more could have been made of the goings-on of the Order of the Phoenix, and J.K. Rowling could have allowed for Harry to find out more about this mysterious organisation. Moreover there are various sub-plots that, although interesting, do seem to be space-fillers to some extent. In attempting to give value for money for punters by producing almost quarter of a million words, I feel that Rowling has sacrificed some of the    tightness    of the earlier novels. By this I mean that, like book four, there are points in book five where the pace slows down and there is slightly less of a compulsion to turn the next page. In some ways this is good though, as the book ebbs and flows between points of greater and marginally lesser interest, thus providing fairly exciting climaxes and also allowing for points where you can put the book down temporarily and grab a bite to eat or a few hours sleep    The much hyped death of an important character was pretty predictable; I was virtually certain who it was before I   d even begun reading the book. There were a couple of points however when Rowling made  me think that I might be wrong, and these    red herrings    provide added entertainment as well as being essential to other aspects of the plot. The death allows Rowling to consider aspects of guilt and culpability. Harry feels guilty about the death of the character, and believes that he is responsible for it, which are emotions often felt by the bereaved. There are several    if only       moments where we realise that the character might not have died if someone had done this or that or t   other. There is an important message here about not    crying over spilt milk   , i.e. we can   t change what is done. In respect to culpability, Dumbledore attempts to claim responsibility for the death of the character (in an attempt to ease Harry   s mind) but it is clear to the reader that the death, like all things, is caused a huge number of unique circumstances, actions and people. Nobody rational would believe the crackpot stories of  Potty wee Potter  The Biggest Book Yet ==================At a whopping 766 pages, the fifth installment of the Harry Potter series resembles a large brick. I found it very surreal, almost as if Harry was still dreaming, and of course very very disturbing and sad.The Missing Link:==============This is a huge book, and despite the lengthy story line I ve given, I feel that there is so much in the book that I ve given only a fraction away. That much was obvious when he interviewed JK Rowling for BBC 2 recently. Did he read the books as research for the interview? Unlikely. Then why does such an eminent TV journalist read a series of books conceived, first and foremost, for children? The answer is, of course, that he cannot afford not to. His job requires him to be up with the latest literature, and the Harry Potter series most certainly falls into that category.The key to the success of Harry Potter is that the age of the audience range from 5 to 105. Almost everybody has read at least one book in the series and many more have read them all, myself included. Am I ashamed to admit this? Perhaps a little. Reports that JK had writers block and was unable to finish the series, or that she was too caught up in married life to write, have proved to be unfounded, since the fifth book is not only here, but it is several thousand words longer than the New Testament. Religious groups who previously called for the books to be banned will doubtless use this as evidence of malicious intent, claiming that they show too much evil.The book was released at one minute past midnight, which reeks of some king of marketing ploy. The books themselves are the size of house bricks, but as the saying goes, you can  8217;t judge a book by its cover.The Order of the Phoenix sees Harry living back with his Uncle Vernon, Aunt Petunia and their son Dudley. Nobody objects to a bit of descriptive filler in the right places, but this is the wrong kind of story for that sort of thing.But credit where credit  8217;s due, the story kicks off properly soon enough in the style that readers are used to. All the characters are up to their usual magical, mischievous, muggle-bashing ways. The kids will be pleased. And what about the more mature reader? Well  8230;The problem I have with JK Rowling  8217;s books is that they are simply unrealistic. But before you all screw up your face and sneer at my stupidity, I understand the irony of such a statement. The Lord of the Rings is the classic fantasy novel. Unrealistic certainly, but not in it  8217;s own terms. I am certain that half of the problems in the Order of the Phoenix could have been avoided with a bit of common sense.At one point early on in the book, Harry has to stand before a jury on trial. Not because I am in any way special, but because the whole situation was ludicrous.The problem is that the Order of the Phoenix is a children  8217;s book, and makes no secret of that fact. It is understandable that more mature readers will pick holes in the writing; perhaps unavoidable.All excuses aside though, there are some things about which I feel I must object.JK Rowling has stressed in interviews that Harry will suffer from hormones just like any teenage boy, and that we will see evidence of this in later books. And, sure enough, the Order of the Phoenix contains adolescent rumblings aplenty from the young Harry, who has, it seems, finally entered puberty in earnest. Aged fifteen. Am I the only one who finds this odd? But still, better late than never.And since late starters are not uncommon, we  8217;ll let that one pass. But there  8217;s something else. Aged fifteen, Harry has his first kiss. It is the first sexual contact with a member of the opposite sex he has ever had; and he is fifteen years of age. Whatever the case, he needs to make up for lost time.It  8217;s very easy to criticise the Order of the Phoenix. There are countless pages of very little action, the book does little to progress the plot on a grander scale and so on and so on. But when all  8217;s said and done, this is a book that entertains the reader. And if you want more than entertainment from Harry Potter, you  8217;ve completely missed the point. Though Im back, Hollz x     ', '    Harry Potter is, as surely everybody now knows, a young wizard who attends Hogwarts School for witches and Wizards. He is, however, not just any young wizard teen. He is the only person to have survived a direct attack from the most feared wizard of his age, Lord Voldemort; he is the boy who lived. First killing his parents, Voldemort turned his wand on Harry, only to feel his spell backfire and destroy his own body. Harry was left with a scar on his forehead, and grew up with his human (muggle) relatives, only to discover that he was a wizard at age eleven and that he has gained entry to Hogwarts.J.K.Rowling  8217;s series has come a long way since the first book six years ago. Harry Potter has become the children  8217;s fiction phenomenon of the last decade, prompting comparisons with C.S.Lewis and even Tolken. Rowling has created a surprisingly engrossing fantasy universe that revolves around the guarantee that pretty much everyone who reads her books wishes they could go to Hogwart  8217;s School for Young Wizards. This, the fifth instalment of the series, has been delayed for over a year, giving Rowling time, now that the pressure is on to finish the series in style, to prepare the storylines for this novel, and the final two in the series that will follow.The last couple of novels begun to set the scene for a story of some grandeur, filled with many characters across several generations (primarily Harry and his school friends, and those remaining from Harry  8217;s father  8217;s friends from his time at Hogwarts). Whilst reading the previous book, it occurred to me that perhaps the story should be picking up somewhat in pace, as the target audience grow up (Rowling often said that each book shows a year at Hogwarts, and that her audience would grow old with the characters) and as the audience in general (the books remain massively popular with readers of all ages) become more involved with the characters and overall mythology. Whilst I enjoyed   8216;The Goblet of Fire  8217;, I found it lacking in pace. It ends with Harry  8217;s blood being used in order to resurrect Lord Voldemort, who calls his followers to him, presumably preparing a second coming.It falls to this book, therefore, to begin this war, and whilst it fails in some ways it is imbibed with an intensity throughout that the previous book was lacking. Before its release we were told that it would contain a death of a major character, and a great revelation from Dumbledore (the headmaster of Hogwarts, and the only wizard who Voldemort fears). The death, I thought, was not entirely necessary (although perhaps I will be proven wrong as the series continues). The revelation is quite shocking, and promises to move the series forward and towards its conclusion.The new year at Hogwarts may prove to be Harry  8217;s toughest yet. His claims that he saw Voldemort reborn are believed by very few of his classmates, most of whom consider him a liar.  This image is cultivated by the wizarding newspaper, The Daily Prophet, who, under careful control from The Ministry of Magic (who adamantly deny Voldemorts return), take every opportunity to bad mouth Harry. Dumbledore is ignoring him for reasons Harry cannot fathom, and those who are involved in the secret fight against Voldemort are unwilling to keep him updated. This, coupled with recurring dreams and frequent eruptions of pain from his scar, and the fact that Harry is now a fully-fledged teenager, raging hormones and all, all add up to Harry  8217;s trickiest year yet. He is angry at everything, having frequent arguments with his friends, and getting himself into more trouble with his potions teacher, Snape, and even picking a fight with his cousin, Dudley. What this novel shows us first and foremost is that Harry has quite a temper on him. He rages against everything, and is constantly at odds with the world around him.To see Rowling develop Harry in such a realistic way is quite satisfying. Harry is growing up, as are his friends. Ron and Hermione continue to impress. Ron begins to break away from Harry  8217;s shadow, a place he has always been a little unhappy. Hermione continues to prove her worth, although Harry ignores the majority of her advise. Other characters, such as Ginny Weasley and Neville Longbottom are given more of the limelight. Neville, in particular, always shown as the class clumsy kid, begins to come into his own, developing into a characters whose future I look forward to see develop.From previous books, Lupine and Mad eye Moody make a welcome return, as does Siruis, Harry  8217;s godfather. We visit a few new places, perhaps most notably The Ministry of Magic, where much of the action unfolds. Everything we expect from a Harry Potter novel is present; a foray into the forbidden forest, a few new creatures are revealed, Harry discovers a few more things about his past and his parents, and we are left, mouths watering for more.It is hard to describe the most satisfying parts of this new story without giving things away. Suffice to say that this year at Hogwart  8217;s is undoubtedly the hardest for all the pupils, least not Harry himself. I often thought that one of Rowling  8217;s greatest challenges would be to develop this huge story about an event that will shake the whole wizard community to its very core, whilst keeping the main characters in school, largely away from the action. In this she proves her skill as a writer. The effects outside events have on life at the school are given priority for the majority of the novel. The characters are given valid reasons to leave the confines of the school on several occasions, breaking the book up well, and keeping us in contact with the turmoil of the wizarding community. The overall story is such a compelling one, that I often wished I were simply following the story of the adult wizards. But it isn  8217;t their story, it is Harry  8217;s, and when he comes into his own and takes action like a true hero, he is undoubtedly the star. In Order of the Phoenix, Rowling picks up the pace and leaves us wondering what jaw-dropping events she has for the final two instalments in the series.
