', '    For many years I ve been hearing a lot of talk about some gun-totin  gangsta going by the name of Harry Potter. Well actually I m told he s more into toting his magic wand, but I m guessing the less I know about his sordid private life the better. Well anyway, turns out that this pimp daddy is some kind of children s book phenomenon about a teenage wizard who goes out and saves the world every year at his high school, fighting against one full-on cunning, badass wizard going by the name of Lord Voldemort. Now being a crime-fighting, soldier of fortune DJ superstar as I am, I can kinda relate to this, although I would admit that my arch-nemesis, Roger Foxby, is neither cunning or particularly badass, but he sure gives it his best shot So I jumped in the Danger Mobile last Tuesday (Having extracted Ern, who d been cruising in it again) and put the pedal to the metal all the way to popular bookstore Waterstones to score a copy of Harry s latest adventure Harry Potter And The Order Of The Phoenix. Once out of the bookstore I began to notice that virtually every other person I saw was also carrying a copy of this not inconsiderable tome: it s about the size of a small brick. There really is no underestimating this phenomenon. I d read the other books in the series once when I d been locked in the dungeons of a Gay German neo-Nazi called Heidrich Meershwanschenwurst (Now there s a story...), but having travelled 500 ks across Europe tied to a mini-scooter being chased by six demented members of an avant-techno  quot;collective quot; intent on whipping my buttocks raw, the whole hype thing was lost on me. I figured I d enjoy this one better seeing as I wasn t handcuffed to a seven foot bass player called Gunther (The only English phrase he knew was,  quot;Could you pass the twiglets quot;), I didn t have to use my teeth to turn the pages and I didn t have a German guy wearing a gimp mask dancing in front of me and intermittently licking a picture of The Queen Mother. But I determined there and then that, firstly, I d read the next in Harry s adventures and, more importantly, that would be the last time I ordered Weisswurst after midday (They do warn you...).Well I got home and paused only to go to the toilet, before settling down in my favourite chair and reading the whole thing cover to cover. At first I was quite confused by the fact that Hermione was now known as  quot;Big Mandy quot; and Harry went around servicing women of a certain age, but then it dawned on me that Ern had swapped the dust covers with one of his... specialist... novels. Being a full-on extra-terrestrial, he d read it by the time I realised my mistake (He s a bit like Short Circuit. Who remembers that movie?), and after threatening to take him back to the secure compound I d broken him out of in the first place, he returned the book to me. With an evil grin on his face he told me he knew who died, but I d already worked out who was for the chop in Goblet Of Fire. And if you didn t see that one coming you should feel ashamed of yourselves - I d cottoned on to who it was and I was cuffed to a guy who kept engaging in lewd acts with stuffed toys as we fled through France...I can safely tell you that Harry gets into more scrapes, the books have continued their development of the characters and it deals with more mature subjects. This time Harry returns to Hogwarts High safe in the knowledge that wizard bad-ass Lord Voldemort is back and kicking ass, despite the fact that the wizarding press and the Ministry of Magic are denying Harry s story (A bit like our world in reverse then). To make matters worse everyone, including head honcho wizard Dumbledore, seems to be ignoring Harry right up until the point that events conspire and he ends up at the headquarters of The Order Of The Phoenix and slowly things start to be revealed. But in the meantime he has to get through a year of school with his famed scar hurting every minute and the ministry having sent a sadistically evil teacher called Professor Umbridge to spy on the school. Cue Quidditch, tight spots and bitch fightin  with the Slytherins as normal.First up I should tell you that Harry gets p*ssed in this book, and that s strictly in the good old US of A sense (Although pupils at Hogwarts are able to go down to the local pub to get butterbeered-up). Being as he is fifteen in this one, he s sure to get hormonal rushes, and things can t be easy seeing as he now feels it when Lord Voldemort is happy or angry, so he spends the entire book screaming at various friends and members of the Hogwarts staff that he hates them. When he s not screaming at people he s in a sulk and when he s not doing that he s having visions of the mysterious Department of Mysteries through the eyes of Voldemort. That s a lot to cope with when you ve got important exams round the corner and it s no surprise he s as angry as Heidrich was when he realised that, not only had Gunther and I escaped and handcuffed him to his dancing gimp, but that we d also managed to wrest the Jade Statue of Les Dennis from his grasp.To be fair Harry s not always angry - he even gets romantic with the object of his affection, Cho Chang - this isn t a straight-forward teen romance though - you see Cho was going out with Cedric Diggory who bought it in the previous book, which is quite an interesting situation to introduce children to as it poses all manner of moral questions which are pretty complex for what is basically a kids book. Harry Potter presents a lot of complicated situations and ideas to the kids - The Philosopher s Stone had Voldemort getting all Nietzsche on Harry s ass. Chamber Of Secrets... that s all a bit of a blur to tell the truth - I made the mistake of giving Gunther some twiglets while reading it and... well... the pages were pretty unreadable after that (Although Gunther was pretty complicated - turned out he used to be a she. That posed me a few of my own romantic moral dilemmas...). Prisoner Of Azkaban was just clever as it had you suspecting Sirius Black throughout but then turned the tables at the end when it turned out the rat was evil all along. And Goblet Of Fire featured the whole start of that twisted love affair and also the concept that a creature born into servitude - the House Elves - might not actually want to be set free, and might actually enjoy their lot. This hit home to me particularly as I watched the Dancing Gimp and his gyrating hips - he seemed to be quite enjoying himself. But I didn t stop to ask after I bludgeoned him over the head with the complete works of J. K. Rowling and made a run for it still tied to the scooter... Another great touch is that we see hot-head Harry take the law in his own hands and actually get out one of the old unforgivable curses and use it on someone - could it be possible that Harry is actually totally evil? He does have a bit of Lord Voldemort inside him (I very nearly had a bit of Heidrich inside me, but it was in the cause of escape, and I do still have the scar...).Things take more of a scary turn in this one with some rather disturbing scenes - Umbridge s detention with the pen that writes in the writers blood and scratches out the words in the back of their hand, the graphic attack in Harry s dream when he s the snake, the sinister archway with the tattered, wafting curtains in the Department of Mysteries. Rowling seems to have gone out of her way to make things darker, scarier and a lot edgier in this one as we head towards the inevitable showdown between Harry and Voldemort in the final book. Her writing style s the same as ever - it s not poetry but you can t stop reading the darned things, and the world of Potter grows ever more complex and lovingly described, with more magic and monsters cropping up in this one. My personal favourite is the Thestral - a big leathery eerie horse thing that you can only see if you ve seen death. Kind of reminds me of Heidrich s lair - all those leather sofas, leather chairs, leather rugs. Amazing how slippery leather rugs are, especially when you re grappling a megalomaniac with a seven foot German cuffed to your other arm trying to get hold of more buffet snacks. Good thing Heidrich had been indulging in some bizarre auto-erotic S M ritual which had involved him tying himself to a Highland Cow, otherwise we d have had nothing to pin him to the floor with. He said it d make him  quot;Ein Gross Herren, quot; or something.Good to see some new characters appearing at Hogwarts - there s a couple of new Aurors (Dark wizard hunters) who re both on Dumbledore s side, but they don t get up to much. The best addition to the cast is the diabolical Professor Umbridge, who tortures and brutalises the students inflicting a particularly evil reign of terror on the school to try and oust Dumbledore and discredit Harry, including her sadistic detention and her delight in starving Harry of all happiness. It s the fact that Rowling can come up with unforgettable characters like this that make the Potter books all the more worth reading - you pick your favourite and root for them. My personal hero, and I share this with my good friend The Divine Cheese, is Professor Snape the potions master. This guy is great - an anti-hero, he hates Harry and uses every opportunity to get at him and yet he s still on the side of good, although he trips the light fantastic on the dark side. And best of all we get an insight into him as we find out how come he can spy on Voldemort without the bad-ass gettin  mediaeval on him and why he hates Harry so much. In fact we discover that Harry s Dad was once a bit of an a-hole, and I really felt sorry for Snape, more sorry even than when I discovered that the reason that Heidrich wanted a genocide on all countries beginning with the letter D was because he d been turned down by record companies in Denmark, Dominican Republic and Djibouti.Lastly, I m given to understand there s a couple of movies based on the first two novels, and they ve scored big hits in the theater. Well I don t know too much about the movies - I hadn t even heard of this Harry Potter guy when the first one came out and the second one was in the theater when Gunther and I were hiding out in a remote Dutch farm from the Techo Ninja Hitmen who d been sent by Heidrich to kill us and get back the Les Dennis statue. Anyway, reading Phoenix, you can tell that she s got the movies in the back of her mind - favourite characters make a return such as Gilderoy Lockheart (I hear Ken Branagh was the highlight of Chamber Of Secrets) and there s some fairly beefcake action scenes towards the end as Dumbledore takes on Lord Voldemort in a majorly flash-bang rumble. I d love to see someone make a movie of that, although my desperate last stand after the ninjas got Gunther and I was airlifted to safety by Ern in the Danger-Copter having only been armed with a packet of twiglets would also make a great movie.So whether you re a convert to the cause or you ve never had the slightest inclination to read Potter, Phoenix is another great yarn which answers a whole bunch of questions from the last books and poses another bunch more - is Neville actually the greatest wizard in the universe? What s through that sinister archway in the Department of Mysteries? Are Harry and Hermione finally going to get it on? Is Draco Malfoy going to confess his true feelings of undying love to Harry? And which character is obviously going to get nixed in the next book? I hope y all be finding that out sometime soon. I ve got to run now seeing as those Ninjas just caught up with me again, but Ern is supercharging the Danger-Mobile and I ve been practising my unforgivable curses, so I ll be speaking to you again soon I m sure. Bring it on  cause this one s for you Gunther.Thanks for your time, I m Dick Dangerous.Dedicated to the memory of Gunther. Man, he felt like a woman... s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix continues J.K. Rowling’s masterful blend of fantasy and character-driven storytelling, appealing to both younger readers and adults alike. The book’s richly crafted world expands intriguingly with new magical creatures, spells, and hidden secrets, which will certainly satisfy a curious mind eager for imaginative world-building. The narrative’s ability to weave fresh mysteries and leave some questions unanswered cleverly sets the stage for future installments, inviting thoughtful speculation about the wizarding world’s deeper complexities.

However, from a character development standpoint, some new additions feel underdeveloped and somewhat peripheral, which may frustrate readers who value fully realized personalities and meaningful growth. This lack of depth in certain characters slightly weakens the otherwise cohesive plot, which occasionally meanders amid the sprawling storylines. While the book’s length and complexity offer a rich experience, the unresolved plot threads might feel less satisfying to those who prefer tighter narrative closure.

The story’s thematic layers—touching on authority, resistance, and the nuances of power—offer fertile ground for reflection, aligning well with readers who appreciate philosophical undertones beneath the fantasy veneer. Rowling’s occasional wit and humor continue to enliven the narrative, providing welcome levity amid darker developments.

Overall, Order of the Phoenix is a compelling installment that balances imaginative expansion with thoughtful themes, though it stumbles slightly in character focus and plot cohesion. For readers invested in the series and those who enjoy exploring layered fantasy worlds with a mix of mystery and social commentary, this book offers substantial value and plenty to ponder. Just be prepared for some narrative threads to remain tantalizingly open-ended.

product_reviews: ['    To continue on the theme of John Grisham books comes the next one I found on my shelf as I work through all the old Books I  8217;ve read. In fact looking at my bookcase there are more books by him in there than any other author, which I suppose really shows the kind of effect The Brethren had on my reading habits. The Testament is another of my favourite books by Grisham. As far as I  8217;m aware before we go any further, this is one of the few yet to be turned into a film.As a former Lawyer Grisham bases most of his books on this field and although at first this probably doesn  8217;t sound appealing he somehow manages to bring it to live and turn it into a gripping read. He pulls on his own knowledge of law and criminal proceedings in such a way that it makes it interesting to read and simple to understand. And although the majority of his characters are lawyers or legal students this shouldn  8217;t put you off.When the 10th Richest man in America, Troy Phelan decides at 80 years old that rather than continue suffering he needs to end his life. He gets out of his wheel chair and throws himself off the balcony from the 14th storey of his company Head quarters. Leaving behind a number of possible heirs to his fortune, who are all rather happy their father is dead and they can get their hands on the cash.With his 6 kids desperate to get their hands on the money that they  8217;re father had assigned to them in his will all gather to find out that after the psychiatrists had found him of sound mind to sign his will, he almost immediately ripped it up with his lawyer still there and hand signed a hand written revocation of the original will and left everything to his illegitimate daughter Rachel Lane, just moments before he plummeted to his death.It  8217;s then down to his lawyer Josh Stafford to find out who this Rachel Lane is and inform her of her fathers death and what he wishes to do with his vast fortune. The only clue to where she may be was a note saying she was in Brazil working for a small tribe as their village doctor as part of her missionary work. So Josh dispatches Nate O  8217;Riley to Brazil to try and find her, but Nate has his own problems, as he is currently in a drying out clinic trying to beat his drinking problem.Of course his kids really aren  8217;t happy about this and despite a clause saying he will pay off all their debts, which there are a lot of, if they don  8217;t contest the will they decide to push ahead anyway. So having forfeited their right to any money, will they be successful in contesting the will? Can Nate find Rachel in amongst the Brazilian rainforest? Well I wont be telling you why not read it and it  8217;ll all fall into place.Like all of his early books this one had me hooked from the first word. I read almost 200 pages of this on an afternoon, when I was actually suppose to be going out I got that much into it. As I  8217;ve mentioned on previous ops the basics of Law I was taught at College bored me but the way Grisham writes makes it simple for everyone using Key phrases and sayings but in ways that are very simple to follow. This helps to make the book a much easier read.Now the majority of the book focuses on Nate and his struggle against booze whilst he tries to find Rachel. He seems a very odd character but his plight into the forest really grips you from the start. Before the book really gets going you get a lot of background and general information on Nate, which makes you feel a little for him at times. Like with Darby in The Pelican Brief, Grisham builds up his characters well. The original, multi-millionaire character Troy Phelan makes you feel sorry for him even after his death and this is all down to the way Grisham writes. The further into the book, the worse Troy  8217;s family gets and you can almost understand by the end why he rewrote his will and left them all out of it. Again this is all down to Grisham  8217;s writing skills and his ability to bring characters to life. To be honest the book is almost flawless with little to bring it down at all. Although the length of time it takes to find Rachel may be too long for some I found it to be just about right. The usual addictiveness of a Grisham Novel is there as I mentioned and once you read that closing paragraph you feel content that your desire for a good story has been fulfilled.If you fancy buying this then it  8217;s available from all your high street bookshops for    6.99 or from Amazon for    5.59.     ', '    Eighty-year-old Troy Phelan jumps out of his wheelchair, practically runs across the room out onto the terrace and dives from the top floor of his 14 storey building to his death. The sick, sad, lonely self made multi billionaire knew that he wanted to die, knew that his family wouldn t mourn him much and wanted to cause them as much grief as he could by setting the scene for the last act of his life.A short time before his death Troy who was one of the richest men in the USA was examined by 3 notable psychiatrists and pronounced sound in mind. Then he signed a 90 page professionally prepared will sharing his billions out equally amongst his 6 children from 3 broken marriages. All of who were in the room with their individual lawyers at the time of the examination and signing. His families, their lawyers and the psychiatrists then left the room totally satisfied with the filmed proceedings.Camera still running, and with just 3 others remaining (Josh Stafford, a partner in the law firm and Troy  8217;s gofer Snead) Troy shredded that will and produced and signed an handwritten 1 page will revoking all others and leaving his billions to illegitimate daughter Rachael Lane.  Only Troy knew of her existence and nobody including him had more than a vague idea where she was. In a letter to Josh he ordered the contents of the will not to be disclosed until January 9th, one month after his death. In that final testament all he left his 6 legitimate heirs was payment of any debts incurred before the reading and that would be only on condition that none of them contested the will. Immediately after signing the will he jumped to his death leaving behind a great deal of controversy and uncertainty.His slick lawyer Josh Stafford was faced with the problem of finding Rachel Lane. All he had to go on was that she was a trained doctor and a World Tribes missionary in Brazil working for a religious outfit who had been sworn to secrecy about her. As far as his 6 children were concerned they were his heirs and had no idea that the final will had cut them out. Their problem was in getting enough credit to buy the expensive things that they desired and would be able to afford once they inherited the money.At this stage I pondered on the fairness of a man that can play games with his children and detest them so much that he can disregard the security of their futures yet leave a massive fortune to a daughter that he had only met once and 20 years earlier. We learn that he had little interest in them as children and that each had received a trust fund of  5,000,000 on reaching 21, excepting for his weird 14 year old son Ramble whose money was waiting in trust for him. The 5 who had received their trust funds had gone through most or all of the money and some were in debt. Troy had worked hard for his money and was certain that his incompetent children and their partners would fritter the fortune away. I can understand that point of view but heck what  8217;s the point of having money if you live austerely as Troy did and don  8217;t enjoy it.Josh decides rather strangely to send 48 year old food litigation lawyer Nate O  8217;Riley to Brazil to look for Rachael. At the time of Troy  8217;s death alcoholic Nate is drying out in a rehab centre for the umpteenth time and hardly the most suitable choice for the task and the temptations on the way. With 2 failed marriages and children that don  8217;t like him, Nate  8217;s excess baggage includes self-pity and to a certain extent the self-delusion of an alcoholic who has often stumbled at the hurdles of reform.Nate travels to the Brazilian jungle while the Phelan heirs and their many legal advisors wrangle greedily over the inheritance. The book swings back and forth between both aspects of the story but my favourite parts were the descriptions of Nate sailing down an alligator infested river in a storm and the settlement of hostile semi-naked Ipica Indians and their surroundings.I won  8217;t say any more about the plot except that the will was read 2 weeks instead of a month after Troy  8217;s death as he specified. I found that rather odd and there was no real reason given for not carrying out Troy  8217;s last wishes, certainly not enough to affect the plot.I haven  8217;t read anything by John Grisham before and only picked this book in the library because of reading enthusiastic opinions about some of his other books. I wasn  8217;t disappointed in my choice and found the storyline interesting enough to want to read to the end and find out what happens although it didn  8217;t totally absorb me to a point where I couldn  8217;t put the book down. I found some of the plot implausible but it seemed to strengthen rather than weaken this piece of fiction.The main character Nate was well described and it was quite easy to build up empathy with him, but in parts I wanted to give him a big nudge with an extreme part of my anatomy. Part of the implausibility of the book was the speed in which Nate managed to travel to a remote part of Brazil called the Panatel, have some adventures and find Rachel with little information to go on.When Rachel finally comes into the story I found it hard to find any empathy with her. She  8217;s a good woman, dedicates her life to her religion and caring for natives in a remote part of the world with little access to what we call civilisation. Suffers unimaginable hardships every day stoically. A tough lady yet disappointingly little of her personality is exposed.My favourite character was Jevy, Nate  8217;s guide and translator in Brazil. Jevy had lived in the USA for a while and one day wanted to go back there. He came across as a caring, loyal, humorous and intuitive young man and was used in the story to keep Nate  8217;s feet on the ground. I would liked to have seen the character expanded upon and explored more.The Testament drew to a satisfying conclusion, leaving me with lots of things to think about. We all have to die sometime but wouldn  8217;t it be awful dying knowing that the uncaring vultures waiting to pounce on what we leave behind are our children and the ones that we would most want to mourn us. It made me think about the lives of children with rich parents who spend time making more money instead of loving, raising, guiding and enjoying their children. I learned something about the perils of the jungle and the way primitive tribes still live even now. I thought about the value of missionaries who apart from bible bashing offer invaluable medical care and knowledge making a not always welcome good and real difference to the existence of people from remote areas.Greed was the motivation of many of the characters in the book, including some of the lawyers. You learn that those who uphold the law are not always honest when millions are at stake and hope that the storyline isn  8217;t too true to life. Once the scenes with the lawyers came in I expected to find the book boring. I didn  8217;t, I found myself curious to know how the Phelan heirs would react and just how low they and their lawyers would stoop. The switches to the jungle adventure were perfectly timed to stop me from ever feeling bored.Although classed as a thriller it wasn  8217;t thrilling, just a well told story with adventure, a hint of romance, a delve into the lives of spoilt filthy rich, an insight into the mind of a reforming alcoholic and the amount of money that lawyers can make out of other peoples deaths. Not the best book that I  8217;ve ever read but still eminently readable and recommended for long winter evenings curled up in front of the fire. I shall certainly read more of John Grishams work in the future.Paperback copies are available at Amazon for    5.59. Talking books are also available and cost    11.70 for Audio Cassette,    14.99 for Audio CD     ', '    I love reading. I used to absolutely loathe it, but now (faced with huge volumes of modern poetry (what?) and inexplicable olde English) the novel has become a huge relief to a tired english student.John Grisham is a writer with what is known as  real talent .  The Testament  certainly puts this to use and it is very successful in using a unique plot-line and bringing it to life for the reader. It follows the story of a dying multi-millionaire, his shocking last will, an undetectable heir to his fortune, and the search to find her. I think that this novel is so successful because of its enchanting descriptions of Southern America. It is almost travel writing - the details are so exact that it seems that you, too, are travelling in a river boat in search of a lost tribe. Grisham perfectly captures the atmosphere in his narrative and the reader is lost in a plot of suspense, danger but also light humour. It is impossible to put this down once you have started reading.     ', '    The Testament, another hefty best-seller from John Grisham. Just how well does it stack up against his other novels?The Plot~~~~~~~~Ageing billionaire businessman Troy Phelan, tiring of life, draws up a new will before committing suicide. The hopes of his six children and three ex-wives are confounded by the surprise naming of a previously unsuspected illegitimate daughter as the major beneficiary. The bequest is complicated by the fact that no one knows the whereabouts of the daughter who is thought to be serving as a missionary somewhere in Brazil.The story develops on two strands; the legal challenges of the children and the quest for the missing daughter. The defence of the will is led by the late Troy Phelan   s lawyer, Josh Stafford. The quest for the daughter, Rachel Lane, is undertaken by Nate O   Riley, a partner in Stafford   s law firm. O   Riley is newly discharged from rehab for his drug and alcohol addictions.This novel has far less of the legal technicalities than other works by this author. The emphasis is far more on the second strand, the search for Rachel Lane, than on the legal battle. I do have one point that I just can t figure out, see the footnote if you have read the book and tell me if you understand.The Characters~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Frankly it is difficult to describe many of the performers in this story as characters. We really learn little about any of the characters other than O   Riley. The characterisation overall is so shallow as to hardly merit the description two-dimensional. Not a stereotype is left unturned; the putative heirs are uniformly drawn as irredeemably greedy and stupid, the lawyers are unscrupulous and manipulative, the police uninterested, the judge ambitious and publicity seeking. Nate O   Riley, the only character to have any depth, is himself little more than a quick sketch     ambitious and brilliant trial lawyer, burnt out by 40, dependent on drugs and drink between periods of rehab. The effects of the search for Rachel Lane on O   Riley are the sole area of character development in the whole novel.The Background~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~The search for Rachel Lane takes place in an area of Brazil called the Pantanal. This is a vast area of rivers, tributaries and swampland that is home to a number of surviving indigenous peoples. Ten years ago the research apparently carried out by Grisham would have looked impressive. Today it took about thirty minutes to extract from the internet all the geographical information that Grisham so liberally scatters in his narrative. At times the text smacks more of a travelogue than the gripping thiller presumably intended.My Critique~~~~~~~~~~~The story relies on a very broad suspension of disbelief. The initial premise is just incredible (and I use the term in its proper sense of unbelievable) that a man would be so petty and spiteful as to snub his family in such a convoluted way. The story then progresses through improbable (would you really choose someone coming out of rehab to travel into the untamed wilderness looking for the heiress to an  11 billion fortune) and back to incredible. The coincidences that are required to carry the story forward to its conclusion beggar belief. And yet    Having said all this, the story does rattle along at a tremendous pace. Regardless of its deficiencies it is, to use a clich   , a real page-turner. I bought this book passing through an airport and read it at a single sitting. I later reread it so that I could make a proper assessment of it here. Even on a second reading it remained enjoyable, although less so when the element of surprise was removed. I would heartily recommend this as a relaxing holiday read. Unlike some other Grisham works, the storyline is uncomplicated and the focus is on the fast moving action rather than complex legal argument.Footnote~~~~~~~~The one legal point that I don t follow is this; the instruction of the late Troy Phelan to his lawyer, Stafford, is to delay disclosure of the contents of the will for one month after his death. Why, therefore, is Stafford so happy to have the will read on 27 December, two weeks before the date Phelan instructed. I have reread this a number of times and it doesn t seem as if he makes any opposition to this move. Indeed he appears to welcome the opportunity. This seems at odds with his otherwise dogged determination that Phelan s wishes be carried out. Are we supposed to think that he feels sorry for the supposed heirs? Any suggestions gratefully received.     ', '    The Testament is another of John Grishams later novels and shows a change of direction. The story surrounds the search for a missionary in Brazil who has inherited a multi-billion dollar media company. She is tracked by a washed up alcaholic lawyer who is a member of the firm dealing with the estate. The journey to the Brazilian tribal jungle is a test for the lawyer whose addictions are tested to the limit.  The ability for Grisham to dream up diverse storylines and characters is part of his enduring culture. This is a must for Grisham fans     ', '    I don t get much chance to read novels nowadays, but I read some of Grisham s earlier books some years ago, so I picked up The Testament in Heathrow s bookshop before a long haul flight and I am very glad I did.  A curious but un-putdownable mixture of Grisham s grasp of legal procedural (which as an ex-lawyer he brings to every book), old-fashioned but enjoyable adventure in foreign parts and un unexpected dose of spiritual mystery reminiscent of Graham Greene.The central character is very fallible and very believable, and as almost the whole book except the gripping opening chapter is seen through his eyes, perhaps it doesn t matter that most of the other characters are ciphers.The only real failing is that the ending is rather quick and a bit of a disappointment - it reads as if Grisham was half way through an epic work, noticed the page count, dashed off an ending in 20 pages and mailed it to his publisher.Don t let this put you off, though.  The rest of the book is both gripping and thought-provoking.     ', '    Grisham added to his legal thriller oeuvre with this at times subdued, at times fantastical novel, which always assures that you will not rest until you have reached its satisfying climax. The book opens from the first person perspective of Mr. Troy Phelan, self-made tycoon and octogenarian, worth approximately  11.5 billion. Troy is a very unhappy, bitter old man, with several ex-wives and six wastrels as his legitimate children. He has made the decision that he would prefer not to remain on earth, and has resolved to end it by leaping from the top of his Virginia business tower, 100 floors to his death.Troy has one last, twisted trick up his sleeve: in a bizarre ritual, he first makes a will with his solicitor, leaving all his wealth to his ex-wives and children. Following a psychological examination that concludes that he is sound in mind, he signs the will with the words   8220;Mickey Mouse  8221;, produces another, handwritten will, signs it, then leaps from his wheelchair, runs across the board room and hurdles the protective barrier, plummeting to the pavement below to the amazement of his lawyers and butler.The handwritten will leaves virtually none of Troy  8217;s fortune to his ex-wives and children: almost his entire estate is bequeathed to one Rachel Lane, a missionary in the wilderness of Brazil, and an illegitimate daughter of Phelan  8217;s. So begins Grisham  8217;s most sensitive novel to date, which goes on to explore the contrasting characters of the members of a family with far too much money for their own good, and a woman on the edge of civilisation with no interest in money. The bulk of the novel centres on the character of Nate O  8217;Riley, a Washington lawyer who specialises in suing doctors, drinking and drugs. Coming out of his fourth stay in rehab, Nate is commissioned to find the sole benefactor of the world  8217;s largest inheritance, at all costs. Thus begins a journey to the deepest depths of the Brazilian rainforest that will fundamentally change Nate  8217;s perspective on life forever.During the trip, questions of addiction, self-worth and religious belief are considered without a didactic tone, and Grisham illustrates the remarkable recovery of a lost soul with a great deal of sensitivity and subtlety, and very little sentimentality. The book ultimately demonstrates mankind  8217;s need for religion, without persuading the reader that he or she should necessarily become religious themselves. Yes, the religious characters in the story are presented as happier than their clearly miserable and unlovable opposites; but there is no pressure on the reader from Grisham.I can do no more than strongly recommend this cleverly written, yet fairly straightforward novel, which I believe rivals The Firm as Grisham  8217;s best.     ', '    Ever picked up a book, and not been able to put i down?  Here is one of those - an ideal last minute Christmas present, perfect Birthday present for almost anyone.  Whatever the excuse for buying a book, make sure you buy this one.Its a book which covers more of human nature and life in general than it would first appear to.  The plot at first glance is a super one, with a multi billionaire passing away, leaving his fortune to a missionary locked away in a jungle.  Whilst she is being found, the money grabbing relatives try and get their share.Not only does it follow this general plot, but opens up thoughts of the whole meaning of life.  It explores the real importance of money in the greater scheme.  It puts  quot;success quot; in its place - after all, what is success?A great read, which really makes you think - more than just your average book.  Highly recomended.     ', '    I believe this is one of John Grisham s most recent books. I have only read a couple of John Grisham books, but this is definitely the best yet.The StoryThis book is about a billionaire called Troy Phelan. He is old, has acquired a fortune of  11 billion, and has a large, alienated family. He is a bit of a womaniser, and this is reflected in the number of ex-wives. He is bitter and depressed and believes the money is the root of all his problems. He also despises his children and ex-wives. All of them are total losers, and have wasted the  5 million he gave them on their 21st birthdays (except the youngest who isn t 21 yet). And they all expect a massive sum to be left to them in their will.Troy has had a massive will prepared by his trusty lawyer Josh Stafford, and to satisfy his family, has a thorough videotaped psychiatric examination to ascertain his state of mind. He passes with flying colours. Then he produces a self-written will, and jumps out the window.But what does the will say? I suppose I can tell you, its right at the start. He leaves his kids nothing, except he will pay off their debts - but if they contest the will they get nothing. he leaves everything to an illegitimate daughter who is a missionary in Brazil. Heavy stuff.After that, the story is about finding this missionary, the case the kids launch against the will, and thast all i m going to say.Actually, the story about the missionary is a bit predictable when you think about it, but it is still great reading. Its less up-and-coming-wall-street-WASP than most Grisham books, which is refreshing, and the story isn t so long for it to get boring. Its fun reading about the waster kids, and the story of Nate O Riley when he goes off to Brazil to find her. OK, thats all I m saying.Its a very good book, an easy read and very interesting and original. I recommend it.     ', '    A dramatic suicide starts this novel, and I expected great things after the opening chapter. Unfortunately, this book fails to deliver, as Grisham s characters are less interesting and well-developed than usual. The plot is reasonable but somehow Grisham fails to execute what could have been another great story. It misses the certain mystery ingredient common to his other books, and while still being a good read, doesn t live up to the master writer of legal fiction s high standards. It is also overly long, yet the ending appears suddenly, which is unusual since Gisham nearly always takes time to carefully structure a good ending. Disappointing.     ', '    This book is another legal blockbuster from John Grisham.  It is a story that mixes legal suspense with a remarkable adventure that will alter the characters lives forever.It centres around the search for the beneficiary for a billionaire   s will, the self same billionaire who has left his fortune to an unknown heir, alienating his family and friends in the process.The hero is a rather pathetic individual who is trying to resolve his personal problems (drinking, womanising, etc), whilst being a last ditch shot at keeping his job.The plot is complicated, but enjoyable.  All in all, a thoroughly enjoyable typical Grisham novel.     ']
filtered_hist_vote_written: ['    Are You Being Served seemed dated when it first appeared on the small screen.  Mr. Grace with his doddery gait and his broken voice creacking and crackling with age was most amusing as he whispered  quot;You re al doing very well. quot;It was the sort of programme which had stereotypes by the dozen.   Mrs. Slocombe with his pink hair, Mr. Humphrey s - Gay as the proverbial Lark and Mr. Lucas the caddish youngster after the ladies. All this was part of the charm of the piece however and it worked really well.Feew comedies can take the double entendre to the extent that it was employed in this one.  Somehow it all gelled.     ', '    Why do people always feel that difficult issues should be kept from the younger generations. Junk is a very interesting and enlightening book. It deals well with drug addiction and gives an honest and accurate discription of the affects of it. Its obvioulsy quite controversial which I think is a very good aspect of literature now days. The storie follows a young girl who runs away from home and slowly turns to drug addiction. This storie is true and follows characters that Melvin Burgess knew. ', '    If you ve read the mallorean and belgariad then you will be dissappointed by this latest adventure from david and leigh.The characters reach nowhere near the level of silk, garion and c nedra to name a few. ', '    The Testament is another of John Grishams later novels and shows a change of direction. This is a must for Grisham fans     ', '    i have many books by Leslea Newman so when this one came out i went out to buy it straight away  The jacket was bright and eye-catching          (designed by Newman s lover, Yohah Ralph) and the blurb on the back cover promised an exciting read  The book was extremely funny and tongue in cheek and proved to be a exciting read. It makes a fresh change from a typical romance in that it concentrates on Bridget herslef and shows her whiny side.  Her weight, smoking, and 1471 obsession is highly entertaining as are her rowdy feminist bunch of loyal friends.This book is very loosely based upon Pride and Prejudice and is a must for everyone   Although some of her mishaps seem almost impossible, this woman seems to attract all disasters her way and realistic or not, Helen Fielding keeps you engrossed in her book Her ditziness is loveable and you end up feeling sorry for this poor woman as well as laughing out loud at her crazy fate  Follow this book with the movie and then with the second book - Edge of Reasoning. ', '    When Salinger wrote this, his most famous book, I doubt most seriously that he could have comprehended the lasting impression that it would have on the lives of so many people world wide.I first read about the exploits of Holden when only 15 years old and was hooked on the style and content of the book immediately. ', '    Bumps, by Zoe Barnes. Well, as the name and cover of the books suggests this book sees the main character, Taz Norton, through the rocky road of her life at work as she finds out she is pregnant.First  mishap  (or is it) - Taz gets dumped, her boyfriend leaving her for her flatmate second, Taz finds out she is pregnant just as she is asked to handle this huge important task at work. third bump, well that s as the book puts it  quot;the one in front of her quot;.Basically, once you start reading this funny book it is not possible to put it down.Although the main character is Taz, and the book centres on her, there are many other fab characters to meet along the way, from the granny/grandad to be, friends, work collegues, the boss, friends made at pre-natal etc etc.One of the best other characters is a young girl called Mandy who Taz becomes good friends with. ', '    Before University I completed an HNC in Business Information Systems, although there was no specific text recommended for the course I decided to buy a text book called Business Information Systems published by the Financial Times. This text is absolutely essential if you are studying HNC/HND/Degree in Information Systems, Information Technology or even as a general book for Business students.The text covers in detail the elements of how information is distributed in the business environment. The current edition was published in 1999 with 640 pages, so it is fairly up to date, but the business practices remain the same. Essential stuff.     ', '    I think Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire is the best of the four Harry Potter books so far. It is the biggest of the books, and it has over 600 pages. (My review tells most of the storyline.)In the book, Harry is chosen mysteriously as a champion to the Triwizard Tournament. The Triwizard Tournament was established 700 years ago. John Grisham’s *The Testament* offers a story that, while not his most thrilling, unfolds with a measured blend of adventure and subtle romance. The narrative centers on a complex legal and spiritual journey, highlighting mankind’s intrinsic need for religion without veering into preachiness—a nuance that adds thoughtful depth to the plot. The conclusion, in particular, stands out as both satisfying and thought-provoking, leaving readers with meaningful reflections beyond the courtroom drama.

However, from a critical standpoint, the book leans heavily on improbable coincidences that challenge the story’s plausibility. The initial premise involving Troy Phelan’s actions strikes as somewhat petty and unbelievable, which may detract from the overall cohesion for readers who prize originality and logical plot development. This reliance on contrivances somewhat undermines the narrative’s potential impact.

Character development is a mixed bag here. Nate’s guide in Brazil, Jevy, brings a caring and humorous presence, yet his character feels underdeveloped, missing opportunities for richer complexity. Similarly, Rachel Lane, portrayed as a dedicated missionary, lacks deeper exploration of her personality, which could have added emotional weight and nuance to the story. For readers who prioritize layered, fully realized characters, these shortcomings might be disappointing.

In sum, *The Testament* is a well-told story that balances legal intrigue with spiritual themes, suitable for those open to a reflective rather than a high-octane thriller. While it may not satisfy readers seeking tightly woven plots or deeply intricate characters, it offers a thoughtful narrative with moments of warmth and insight—making it a worthwhile, if imperfect, addition to Grisham’s oeuvre.

product_reviews: ['    I read this novel as part of a module for my degree and thoroughly enjoyed it.  The module was called  Fallen Women of the 19th Century  but the story of Tess is about so much more than that.  It combines childhood innocence and girlish naivete with the real world of cruelty and down right bad luck.  Tess s story is one of betrayal and heartbreak, it is tragic and yet, despite the negative events in the novel, like Steinbeck s works, Hardy keeps the reader enthralled throughout without feeling miserable.  Although written a long time ago, the novel addresses issues that are still important today and instills real empathy in the reader on behalf of Tess.  An excellent read whether it be for study or for pleasure.     ', '    When Tess of the d   Urbervilles was first published 1891, it caused a great stir. This story was one of the first to include a great variety of topics such as murder, rape and violence. Written by Thomas Hardy, it is a rather depressing novel that follows the life of Tess Durbeyfield who seems to have continuous theme of bad luck throughout her life. The novel begins with John Durbeyfield begin informed by a Parson that he and his family belong to a long line of rich ancestors, the d   Urberville family. With this in mind, he sends Tess out to go and claim kinship. This is when she meets Alec d   Urberville, a person we will get to know very well. What we find out after Tess has left though is the fact that Alec only bought the name d   Urberville to replace their actual name the Stokes. Alec obviously takes a liking to Tess, but Tess is a little wary and shy and soon leaves.A few days later Tess gets invited to go and work for the d   Urbervilles. When she arrives to work, she instantly becomes Alec   s favourite maiden and because of this, not so popular between the rest of the maidens. After a night out, Tess becomes on the receiving end of one of her colleagues comments, which soon turn quite. Luckily for Tess though Alec comes to her rescue and takes her away. But has this placed Tess in more danger? Alec says he is in love with Tess but we get the feeling that is only in the sexual way. He doesn   t actually care for he, so with Alec purposely riding in the wrong direction, he takes advantage of a vulnerable Tess. While she is asleep, he seduces her. This is a major part in the novel and is very significant for the rest of it. Throughout Tess    life she has a series of miss-timings and this could be seen as the starter of them all. There is a huge consequence to this moment. After Tess leaves a month later, she gives birth to baby Sorrow out of wedlock. But unfortunately it dies and Tess has to perform an emergency baptism. With all this tragedy already struck upon Tess, she decides to leave and get more work. Tess eventually finds work on a farm in Marlott. Here she immediately falls in love with the farm boy, Angel Clare. Angel appeared earlier in the novel at a dance. But unfortunately he didn   t choose to dance with Tess, and chose someone else. This backs up the idea of miss-timings. Soon Tess and Angel get married but then yet more tragedy strikes on her wedding night when she decides to inform Angel about her past life with Alec.That is where I will leave it about the novel to avoid spoiling it for you. I will say this though     Fate has yet more tricks in store for Tess and it the novel doesn   t have a happy ending. Tess of the d   Urbervilles is a very depressing novel. Bad luck continues to strike upon Tess. As the novel progresses, more and more tragical elements are visible. For instance the rape scene, Alec takes advantage of a vulnerable Tess and that event leads to Tess having a baby out of wedlock. Once again this is tragical for Tess as this was not really her fault. There is no resolution for Tess    problem. Even as early on as some of the first chapters, there is miss-timings and bad luck for Tess. When Angel turns up at the dance, he just picks the first girl he sees to dance with, and unfortunately that isn   t Tess. If their paths had crossed there and then, then Tess would not have had a line of bad luck in the future. Even when they met later on you could say they were fated to have bad luck. Just after they had wed the cock crowed. This is an omen of bad luck and tells us something bad is going to happen. It heightens our thoughts of Tess    bad luck and it shows us Tess cannot escape tragedy and bad luck. This is the way Hardy demonstrates these. Just when we think Tess might have some happiness, he brings on more bad luck. He also teases us and leads us to guess what is going to happen for a while. He drops little hints for us to pick up on such as the superstitions. He tells us something bad is going to happen here. Hardy demonstrates tragical elements by hinting at events. For example just after Tess and Angel   s wedding, Hardy puts in the crowing of a cock in the afternoon. This is a bad omen and tells us something bad is going to happen. It heightens our thoughts and this event is tragically because just as we thought Tess might find some happiness at last, we have a bad omen and the idea that yet more bad luck is coming Tess    way. Hardy displays the novel as Tess is part of a game with bad luck and fate. She cannot win this game and cannot escape it. Bad luck will continue to haunt her and she is fated to have a tragical ending. It is like an uncompromising hand that is continually dealing out disappointments and bad luck to Tess. Tess is hopelessly resigned to doom. Hardy is really to blame for Tess    tragic life. He doesn   t make it easy for her at all. Almost every chance that Tess decides to take and every coincidence she encounters, it brings her sorrow and bad luck in the long run. For example she took a chance to tell Angel about her life with Alec but that backfired on her and she ended up without him. Hardy believes a woman is helpless in the hands of fate and Tess is trapped in the web of fate. Hardy carries out fate   s work for them.Overall, from what I   ve read, the novel does appear to be tragical. It would be hard to say it isn   t tragical. After all Tess has had so much fate and bad luck that her life has to be tragic. Hardy displays the novels in patterns and never makes it easy, even right up to the very end. A definition of tragedy for this novel in relation to Tess would be a series of tragical events in Tess Durbeyfields life that have been fated onto her. She cannot escape them and everything she tries to do to avoid them just leads to another disaster for her. Tess could never escape the bad luck in her life. Tess of the d   Urbervilles is a great read but does drag on a little and can become a little depressing. Although it is thought provoking and Hardy uses his techniques well. He makes us feel pathos for Tess a lot and wonder how so much bad luck can be portrayed onto just one character. The story is set in seven phases and at the end of each phase something tragical takes place for Tess. Hardy displays many patterns and very efficiently. If you haven   t already read it, I would advice that you should.Thanks for reading. Rob :)     ', '    Tess of the D   Urbervilles Plot:    Tess of the D   Urbervilles    is a classic Victorian tragedy about the life of an impoverished and virtuous Wessex country girl who becomes a victim of her society and the forces of fate. Her destiny will be both in the hands of the changeable morality of her fellow humans and the consistent forces of nature. When the rural peasant John Durbeyfield is given delusions of grandeur by a well-meaning amateur genealogist a series of events are set in motion that will spell disaster for John   s eldest Daughter. Through a misplaced a sense of guilt Tess seeks kinship with a noble family who use the D   Urberville name. They are, in fact, no relation and a member of their family bought the name. One family member, Alec, takes a fancy to Tess and will spell her downfall in many ways. Meanwhile another man, Angel Clare, seems to be her salvation. In a world where self righteousness and hypocrisy co-exist as almost the same entity, Tess will soon have to decide whether she should reveal her unfortunate past with Alec or remain silent.  Review: I am surprised how few people draw parallels between Thomas Hardy   s penultimate tragic novel and the Marquis de Sade   s    Justine   . Both novels focus on the plight of a completely virtuous female protagonist who is a victim of both the conventions and hypocrisies of their times as well as cruel coincidences. The major difference between them, of course, is in their execution. Despite being considered a controversial novel at the time of its release, Hardy   s novel does not use regular overt pornography nor does promote the nihilistic atheist philosophy that Sade uses throughout his works. However, there is a lot to suggest that Hardy   s book is more pagan than Christian in its view of the world and by that token more than a little critical of the theistic conventions for the time. From the May dance at the beginning to the Stonehenge venue at the end, Tess is a pawn of the    President of the Immortals    used to pay for the sins of her noble ancestors and a victim that will receive no comfort from institution of the Church. Unlike    Justine    there is nothing you could describe as horrific in the text. However, the great horror writer Stephen King has cited Hardy as one of his favourite classic writers. His reasons for discussing Hardy when he is being interviewed about horror are interesting. King says that when you start a Hardy novel you just know everything is going to go horribly wrong. It is this pessimistic presence that comes in the form of providence in    The Mayor of Casterbridge    and fate in    Tess    that arguably makes his works possibly even darker than Sade and the Gothic novels that became popular in the 19th century. Hardy doesn   t need the overt or even implied presence of the supernatural to encourage his reader   s mind to explore uncomfortable places and ask difficult questions. Unlike the Gothic novel there are no brooding castles or manor houses and, if anything, Hardy is known for his beautiful descriptions of his beloved Wessex. This certainly comes out in    Tess    and is used to contrast the legacy of the industrial revolution, as the impoverished peasants    miserable working days are described with Hardy   s vivid descriptions of the farmhouse machinery. This machinery is one of the novel   s most memorable pieces of symbolic imagery. Such backdrops and themes, however, are nothing compared to the amount of investment Hardy puts into the story   s heroine. Tess Durbeyfield is not the one dimensional figure of virtue that Sade presented for his brutal philosophising. She is na   ve, dutiful and loving, but she is not a weak victim. Tess endures tremendous hardship, faces her hypocrites and does eventually fight back. She is not merely a victim of her own naivety, but of both the unfair manmade systems of her time and the forces of fate. When she confronts the men in her life she speaks with the words of the sympathetic reader and we experience with her a sense of learning as she ultimately faces her tragic destiny. I would recommend    Tess of the D   Urbervilles    to any reader who is looking for something that on a superficial level will offer insights into the plight of the impoverished countryside residents and women in general of the 19th century and on a deeper level will ask some very human questions about morality.       ', '    Tess of the D Urbervilles is a novel that frequently comes up an A level reading lists. It s a well known Hardy novel (helped by the Roman Polanski film of the book)  and a particularly depressing one at that.I m going to do a plot spoiler, so If you don t want to know what happens, don t read the next paragraph.A chance remark by the local vicar causes Tess s father to realise that his family is descended from nobility. When a freak accident leaves the family on the brink of poverty, tess is sent to relaations at Transome. It turns out that the family living in the ancestral home have merely bought the title, but are happy to offer Tess work. The young man of the house, Alec, seduces Tess. She leaves, and later gives birth to a child, who dies not long after. Tess then goes to work on a dairy farm where she meets Angel Claire, a vicar s son. They fall in love. Tess writes a confession of her past and posts in under Angel s door, and under his carpet so he never finds it. She repeats her confession on her wedding night, he is unable to accept her past and abandones her. Tess then works in some very unpleasant plaes, and ends up having to support her family after her father dies. Alec offers to pay for her family in exchange for her, and she agrees, becoming his mistress. Angel Claire returns, having forgive Tess. She murders Alec and follows after him. The police find her at Stonehenge and she is hung for her crime a while later.Hardy subtitled this novel  quot;A Pure woman quot; which at the time caused total outrage. Tess is, by Victorian standards, a fallen woman and Hardy  sympathetic treatment of her did not sit well with many of his readers.Hardy in this novel looks back at the rual past and suggests the ways in which it is already being erroded by machinery. There are new and alarming machines present in the fields, and all is clearly not well. Hardy mourns for the loss of a culture and an era.There is a great deal of sexuality in this book - Tess and her relationship with Alec, Angel having had a lover before Tess, but being too much of a hypocrite to accept her past - hardy explores the double standards applied to the genders in his time, and the cruelty with which women are punished for their mistakes. Virginity and chastity are rpized in women, experience is expected in men, and fallen women are an inevitable consequence of this. Fate. You can watch the threads of fate controlling Tess from the moment the book opens through to the very last page. Coincidence drives her life in unlikely and fatal dirrections. I noticed studying this book that at key moments, when fate s hand moves most surely over tess, there is invariable an image of red and white - a red ribbon against a white dress or the like - these often come up and are well worth watching for. Red tends to symbolise passion in most systems, white is associated with purity and so the combination seems especially apt for Tess.Tess as a character. I found Tess a difficult heroine to get along with and not an easy individual to understand. At times she is amazingly headstrong, resourceful and self willed, at others she lapses into a terrible apathy and lets anything at all happen to her - as far as I can make out, there s not much logic to this. At the beginning of the book we see her as innocent, pretty, well meaning and willing to work. She is largely formed thereafter by the events in ehr life, becoming what the situation demands. She is proud enough to not take advantage of those who could have helped her, too honest to do the sensible thing and not tell Angel about her past. It is commented in the book that she isn t much like a village girl, and perhaps it is the nobility in her blood that leads her into such difficulties - in the Victorian era, the idea that blood would show was prevelant - cases like Oliver Twist for example. One can be born noble (Or so they thought.)I would recomend watching the Roman Polanski film if you read the book - it does follow the plot fairly well and it s nicely done. Obviously, it s a simplifiaction, but it gets the main points across.     ', '    The most under-appreciated aspect of Hardy is how he delves fearlessly into tackling issues which were, at the time, taboo and even still have a certain stigma attached to them. In Tess, a young girl is taken advantage of by her employer and raped; the plot also deals with an alcoholic father, pregnancy out of wedlock and even murder. This could easily be the tagline for a contemporary novel, but contemporary authors have a distinct advantage over Hardy: they can write about these issues explicitly without criticism. Hardy could not. People tend to lose sight of this nowadays, viewing Hardy as a talented but unadventurous author; they forget that in the nineteenth century, it was considered obscene to write about some of the things Hardy did and to have it all happen in a rural setting was especially maverick in a world where all English literature revolved around London and country-folk were ignored. Hardy therefore had little choice but to be subtle while describing such issues (or risk not being published at all), so his temerity is often over-looked by twenty-first century readers and some may find it difficult to understand what is happening - several members of my English Literature A Level class were oblivious to the fact that Tess had been raped and were surprised to read that she had a baby A major criticism of Hardy s works, including Tess, is that he tends to rely too much on coincidence and his plots are very fatalistic and therefore unrealistic. While I understand this viewpoint, I love the plot with its tragic turns of events and coincidences and would argue that sometimes life is stranger than fiction, so Hardy s fatalism has a place in literature. The plot is varied and does get a little dull in places, although my English Lit class all loved and hated different sections so there s probably something for everybody. There are some sickly-sweet places where Hardy seems to get carried away a little (the utopia of Talbothays, for example), but I think these are balanced out by the harshness of other sections of the plot.Tess herself is a very likeable tragic heroine whose major flaw is her naivety and sense of responsibility. I think that Hardy does desperately want her to be happy, but knows that that could never happen due to the turn of events (I don t want to give the plot away ). Yes, there are times when you want to slap her for not being a little wiser and more independent, but these flaws are due to Tess being such a product of her upbringing (look at her parents: a drunk with too much ambition because his ancestors were knights and a mother who looks in a fortune-telling book to make decisions). This is an unusually sympathetic portrayal of a woman who has fallen victim to fate and circumstance and even committed crimes herself along the way - unusual for both a Victorian novel and a male author, another under-appreciated aspect of Hardy s work.Angel Clare was the subject of a heated debate in my Lit class: most of the girls hated him and my teacher loved him. I m sitting on the fence here and saying that he is a balanced character who offers a stark contrast to the repulsive Alec D Urberville, likeable enough but he betrays Tess too much. I think Angel acts as the Victorian conscience: deeply religious and  good , he has a sickening holier-than-thou attitude and makes Tess feel guilty about her  crime . This is the hardest bit to digest, but it s vitally important to understand: rape was viewed as adultery in Victorian society, so Tess s rape is basically her own fault according to that attitude. Hardy obviously disagrees with this view and is critical of Angel Clare for not being more supportive (a view which I concur with) and while he portrays Alec as the villain of the story, Angel never quite fits the role of hero.I could write all day and all night about the characters, plot and issues, trying to persuade you to read this novel, but it is too easy to ignore the most obvious and best part of this novel: your personal emotional response. I m not ashamed to say that although I have read this novel several times over 7+ years, it still has the ability to make me feel sad, angry, happy, frustrated...It can also make me bawl like a baby  Technically, Tess is a good novel with all the details you could wish for (even the minutae of a  red  motif, recurring references to graveyard trees, etc.), but emotionally, it is a masterpiece.     ', '    Tess of the d UrbervillesA brilliant book written in the first person, by Thomas Hardy. He acts like a  god like narrator  controlling his main charchters Tess s fate. However, this novel has many hidden messages, the love for the natural countryside, the hatred towards the upper classes, the despair for the dying social classes, and the rejection of religion, which he believed to be man made. The story itself is brilliant, we follow the plight of a peasant class, and the problems that face, but her beauty and naivety get her both in trouble and make her fall in love. Troubled by her pass, she his dumped by lover on her wedding night. This is a book which must be read, although it is very descriptive it is non the less excellent.     ', '     Tess of the D Urbervilles , one of Hardy s eleven novels, is considered as one of his better works throughout his career as a novelist.  The book was first published in 1891 under the name  A Pure Woman  and received a mixed reception.  The book is currently in my English  A  Level syllabus and with good reason too.  From it we can appreciate how important effective characterisation is and obviously we can see how Hardy s views on such topics as fate are communicated through his books.  The story is set in the bleak and forbidding Dorset landscape (South West England), referred to as  Wessex  (this was actually the name used for the Ancient Anglo Saxon kingdom of King Alfred) in the novel. Almost all of Hardy s fiction is set here.  As critical readers will notice, each different place in the story is associated with different experiences of Tess.  As you probably noticed, the plot is about the story of Tess.  Early on in the novel Tess Durbeyfield finds out that she is a descendent of the nobel D Urbervilles.  After the death of the family s horse,  Prince , Tess is made to visit Alec D Urberville who lives in a neighbouring village to ask for financial assistance.  Little does she know that she is employed not because Alec actually needs her but because he fancies her.  This leads to several encounters between them where Alec tries to approach Tess in a more than friendly manner, if you know what I mean.  However, Tess being so young and innocent does not know what to do and rejects him.  However an important event happens during her time with Alec, that is, she is raped by the latter.  This makes her leave Alec only to find out she is pregnant.Anyway some time later, the baby dies and Tess is off to new pastures to find work.  She goes to Talbothays where she meets Angel Clare and falls in love with him.  These turn out to be the happiest days of her life, however after they get married, Angel gets to know the truth of Tess s history and things get complicated for Tess from then on.  Obviously I m not going to tell you how the novel ends just that it is rather surprising.The characters in the novel are very well developed, especcially that of Tess, Alec and Angel Clare.  They are all very beleivable and give us an insight on the country people, their way of life and their beleifs.  In fact this was one of the reasons why Hardy actually started writing novels.  He wanted to preserve the country people s way of life in a time where industrialisation was on the increase. Tess of the D Urbervilles  is divided into seven phases and each phase is broken down into several chapters.  The chapters are not too long and I found that this helped me since some parts of the novel can be quite boring.  Most chapters start with descriptions of the setting and here is where Hardy really excels at what he does.  If my memory serves me correctly, in one chapter he described the setting so detailedly that it took about 5 to 6 pages.  In my opinion, the descriptions are very important as they add a lot of symbolism to the novel.As I said above, we can clearly see Hardy s views on fate and how he beleived that our lives are planned out the day we are born (if not before ).  In fact, the theme of the book can be described as follows: quot;The struggle of man against the indifferent force that rules the world and inflicts upon him a great deal of suffering quot;All in all, the tragedy that is  Tess of the D Urberville  was quite an enjoyable read, even though everything about the plot is depressing.  However it gives an idea of how things were durng the Victorian era and Hardy s description of setting are a must for any budding writers such as myself.  Price :    4.49 from play.com incl. p pPublisher : Penguin Books Ltd (UK)ISBN : 0141439599Format : Paperback - 592pgs     ', '    I ll warn you before I start - this review gives away the ending.I had to read this as preparation for my A Level English course, and it completely put a downer on my summer holiday, which was, in hindsight, not the best situation in which to read a book this depressing.  Since this was a  quot;classic novel quot;, I was already expecting not to enjoy it, and I was proved right.  For this is a novel which gives the reader absolutely no pleasure at all in reading; just 450 pages of endless depression, angst and misery.  It tells the painful story of Tess Durbeyfield, who struggles to overcome the problems of ignorance and poverty, and gets herself into all manner of heartbreaking situations.  She is raped, contemplates suicide several times, and the book finishes with her capture and execution for murdering her attacker.  However, don t be fooled, none of this is as exciting as it sounds.Some of the other unimportant issues contemplated by Hardy are the way in which traditional agricultural life is being destroyed by machinery; how unforgiving religion can be, and the rigid class system of Victorian Britain.  Some of these could still be relevant today, but it is definitely a novel which is incredibly dated, written as it was in 1891.I would not have so much dislike for this book if it was at least well written, or even interesting.  I understand it was published in the 19th century, so the language was always going to be old-fashioned, but Hardy s style is so detailed in its descriptions and elaborate in its style that it is often difficult to read.  He spends a whole chapter describing Tess milking a cow on a dairy farm.  Sentences such as  quot;One may, indeed, admit the possibility of a retribution lurking in the present catastrophe quot;, appear on every page, as if just to emphasise that Thomas Hardy knows lots of long words and is not afraid to use them.  Sometimes simpler is better.  The scene in which Tess is raped is written in such flowery language that I didn t even realise anything had happened until she had had the baby.The structure of the book is fairly unusual, since it is separated into 7 distinct parts, or  quot;phases quot;, with chapters within these.  These phases split the tale into manageable chunks, with different storylines and background characters in each one.  These help to show different periods in her life, and I do think that this worked quite well.While I m on the positive points, I ll admit that Tess herself is a very empathetic character, and you can feel for her all the way.  But the two main male characters, her attacker Alec d Urberville and her lover Angel Clare, seemed to me to be very irrational, and their changes in character were too simple and unrealistic.  One minute d Urberville is an evil man, then he suddenly becomes a religious preacher, then he changes right back again.  At the end of the day, a good book needs a good story, and this one just isn t.  It gets extremely repetitive, since it is basically the same problem and the same emotions over and over again.  You could easily sum up the sixth phase of the book, in which she is pestered by d Urberville, in about a chapter.  I found Tess  constant moaning very annoying, as was the endless  quot;he will never love me, oh how my heart breaks quot; kind of self-pitying.I can understand why people will say that this is a moving novel and one which grips the imagination; and it was probably really shocking and brutal for its time.  But for today s audience it will seem really quite tame, and its language would put most modern readers off from the very first chapter.  Read it if you really want to, but just don t expect any ray of light at the end of this extremely long, slow and tedious tunnel.________________________________________________If for some reason you did want to put yourself through reading this, you can buy it for    3.37 plus    1 postage from www.thebookplace.co.ukHope that helps      ', '    Tess of the d Uerberville is in my opinion one of Thomas Hardy s best book. It s about a tragic heroin, who s life is  blighted  like the stars. Her social class, society, her fate all  doom  her. When she reluctantly goes to  claim kin  she meets trouble. Alec Durberfield, who embodies money, the higher social class, who sues his superiority against her, exploiting her, and eventually raping away.Whether she was raped or not, it doesn t really matter, her innocence is taken away, and leads to her downfall. Her baby dies, and rumours in the village spread. Again, she sets on a journey, this time to a natural environment, a dairy, where she finds happiness, and agrees to marry Angel Clare, but her conscience plays on her mind, and on her wedding night she tells Angel Clare about her past.He comes from a strict family, a religious family, and cannot forgive her, forcing Tess to go back home. Her drunken father dies, and she is forced to go back to Alec for the sake of her family, but when she realises that Angel wants her back, she kills Alec.But the reader get a sense that justice is done, when Tess and Angel are re-united at the end, and Tess is hanged. The story-line is very good, but what is more pleasing abut this novel is that you get a a lot of Hardy s own views. He doesn t like society looking down on people. He dislikes strict morality, and he emphasises the importance of money, as it is money which Tess goes to claim, and he emphasises the dying breed of the peasant class. There is some brilliant imagery, when Tess is at the natural environment, she finds happiness, the season is summer, and their is plenty of  milk, in contrast to the end when she leaves the milk is  running out  Read the book a couple of times, and you will understand it more. Tess is a victim, but of what?      ', '    I read Tess of the D Urbervilles for English in my final year of high school. It was the second Hardy novel I d read and wasn t a novel that I enjoyed particularly.I find Hardy and Dickens quite similar, but I personally find Dickens to be a wittier writer with more of a knack for characterisation than Hardy. With Hardy, it is sometimes hard to connect with his characters, and this was certainly true in  quot;Tess quot;.For a start, the events in the book can seem almost archaic to a modern reader and extrememly hard to relate to. Secondly, Tess seems to meet disaster after disaster and after a while you start to believe she is beyond unlucky. Worst of all, Hardy can be overly descriptive. I felt that he often spent more time illustrating the beauty of the fields than elaborating on his storyline or characterisation. quot;Tess quot; is a fairly well-known novel, and is certainly worth reading once or twice, although I don t personally find it is a book that I d want to return to again and again.     ', '    Do not read Tess if you are in one of those grumpy moods and need cheering up. It is horridly bleak. Hardy explores all the avenues of chance and fate and comes up with a devastatingly heart wrenching outcome. I won t tell you what it is but just be prepared for it all. Symbolism, imagery and the link between one motiff and another is well done giving the chapters a sense of continuity. Every character s actions are intricately linked to another s and this explores the idea of accountability and how each person s course of action decides the path of another person s actions. It is important to note that Hardy was greatly influenced by the Theory of Evolution of Darwin and thus there are certain comparisons of the different classes of not only society, but religion. Look out also for the influence of John Stuart Mill in this novel. Hardy also examines the relationships between Man and nature, the environment, the rural countryside and the more urban areas, along with some gender issues. the book on the whole is a good read and leaves you quite in awe of Hardy s powers of description. Excellent man      ']
