s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
Thomas Hardy’s *Tess of the D’Urbervilles* is a deeply moving exploration of a young woman caught in the unforgiving grip of Victorian social norms and fate. Tess’s journey is tragic yet thought-provoking, as Hardy masterfully portrays her as a victim of rigid class structures, harsh morality, and the double standards that condemn her for circumstances largely beyond her control. The novel’s emotional core lies in Tess’s innocence lost through Alec’s exploitation—a pivotal moment that triggers her social ostracism and personal downfall. This exploitation is not just a personal tragedy but a sharp critique of the era’s gender dynamics and social injustice.

Hardy’s use of vivid imagery and symbolism, especially the recurring motifs of red and white, enriches the narrative by contrasting passion and purity, underscoring Tess’s complex inner world. His narrative style, emphasizing fate and coincidence, reinforces the sense that Tess’s misfortunes are not merely personal failings but the cruel workings of an indifferent universe. This fatalistic tone invites readers to reflect on the broader societal forces at play, including Hardy’s clear disdain for the upper classes and strict religious morality that compound Tess’s suffering.

Angel Clare’s inability to forgive Tess’s past, shaped by his strict upbringing, adds another layer of emotional complexity and highlights the destructive power of rigid moral judgment. Yet, amidst the bleakness, Tess finds fleeting solace in nature, moments that contrast sharply with the oppressive social environments she endures.

For readers who appreciate rich character development and social critique, this novel offers a compelling, if heart-wrenching, study of human vulnerability and societal cruelty. While Tess’s story is steeped in tragedy, Hardy’s nuanced portrayal ensures it remains a powerful, empathetic reflection on fate, injustice, and resilience.

The only hitch is the use of a Ford Focus which I guess some people will be put off by, and opt for BSM with their smaller Corsa   s.Scruff9/10/01     ', '    This review is going to be updated regularly as i embark upon the journey of learning to drive woo Choosing between driving schools and organising lessons...Ok so i never got lessons when i was 17 which is what most of my friends seemed to do. Due to studying for A levels and having no money what so ever it was never really an option, and plus, its not like i really needed a car. The bus and train was good enough However i am now 21, just finished my second year of uni and really need to start driving. I want the independance and will need it for work and such. So i got my provisional and set out to find what driving school shoud i opt for. This was between the AA and the BSM. I have ruled out using a local driving school because i will be moving back and forth from uni and home and wanted a school which could give me lessons anywhere. To be honest there isnt much difference between BSM and The AA. The cost is similar, ie expensive. BSM offer    2 off each lesson if you are a student. AA offer    2 off each lesson if you book 12 in one payment.In the end i went with AA because my sister had used them. They also had a policy of not picking extra pupils up during your lesson, i feel this is good becaue who wants other people in the car when your trying to learn?  So i went on the AA site and theres a form in which you obtain a quote based on how many lessons you wish and where you live by clicking on your postcode. 12 lessons in june 2006 cost me    264, this includes the    2 discount on each lesson. Yes its alot of money  Once i paid using a debit card online i was given a pupil identity code which you can use a reference when dealing with the AA. The page then stated that someone from the AA would ring me up shortly to arrange a lesson with a local instructor. I booked on 29 June. They took my money from the bank on the 3rd  July. By the 14th of july i still hadnt had a phone call. Obviously this was disappointing. So i rang them up myself and spoke to a member of staff who apologised and then arranged my first lesson. My local instructor is called Fred and i have arranged a lesson in a weeks time. The lesson is 2 hours long. AA recommends this be 2 hours but its up to you if you prefer a one hour lesson. I have been told that after my first lesson all my dealings will be direct with the instructor. You can cancel lessons but must do this within 2 days. The car i will be driving in is a new ford focus. These are replaced every 6 months. Im pretty nervous about the whole thing, will my instructor be ok, will i be able to get into driving without crashing and stalling? All will be revealed over the next few months So far, the staff seem pleasant, but disappointed with the no call back as promisedUpdate 18th July 2006 So my lesson with Fred is supposed to be for tommorrow morning at 10. The AA just rang this afternoon and a pleasant phone operator informed me that Fred is unavailable for the lesson, wasnt told why. Instead we have arrange my lesson for thursday morning. My new instructor for the area is called Mitch Ray. Classic names. Good that they ring you and you arent left waiting. However as a pupil you have to give two days notice if you cancel, whereas they can just cancel whenever. Update July 20th 2006  - FIRST LESSONFirst lesson was excellent  My instructor rang the doorbell to collect me and i was sooo nervous. Showed him my provisional license and was visibly shaking from nerves haha  Anyway he was really good at putting me at my ease. He asked about what experiene i had, which was none  And that wasnt a problem. He drove me to a quiet industrial estate and we spent the first hour or so talking through what everything in the car did, how to adjust my seat, mirrors, steering wheel and all that. Was a little boring but still was essential info for my. Then the next hour i basically drove about  Got up to 20mph, and changed into 2nd gear, go me  haha. He explained what everything did in an easy to understand way and was really really patient. The AA have a syllabus booklet in which all the information and tasks to master are written on a chart. the instructor can then mark down and date what has been learnt so you can chart your progress. At the end of my two hours he drove me back to my house and we arranged the next lesson which we wrote down in the AA booklet i had so easy to remember. The car itself, a ford focus was pretty easy to control, nice and clean. Dont be put off by its bigger size, once your in the car its fine. The car gets replaces every 6 months as well. My instructor is a qualified one, and not passing on the job which is what other schools use for instructors. He also told me he used to be a driving examiner  So things bode well for me All in all it was really exciting and fun. And believe me, i was a nervous wreck to begin with, so dont worry if you are anxious. Obviously it depends on what sort of instructor you get, but AA do have a code of conduct for thier instructors which should ensure high quality teaching. SECOND LESSON   My instructor was late today, but he rang me 15 minutes before my lesson was due to start and told me he would possibly be 15 minutes late. So at least i knew what was happening. Incidently, he was late because the AA main offices had given him a pupil who was a far way out of the main area which he teaches. I think the AA offices need to realise how far apart some places are Anyways, as usual i was picked up from my house. He drove me out to the quiet industrial estate where i had my first lesson. I had forgotten a bit of the basics but it wasnt a problem and we went through it again. Started the car up and drove round a while changing gear up to 2nd and so on. Then we went through the theory and basic rules of mirror signal, manouvere and how to do junctions. He drew out diagrams on some paper and we talked it all through. Then i had a go a doing left junctions, obviously forgetting the most simple things like looking in my mirrors because i was still trying to sort out what my feet were doing Then we did right junctions and they are hard  You have to turn the wheel so much to negotiate the turnings and what not, as well as the traffic. This week there seemed to be more traffic and a few people walking about. My instructor had to break for my on his dual controls to stop me nearly crashing woops. Oh yes and i stalled a few times. But i wasnt made to feel stupid or bad at driving and so all was good. My instructor has the patience of a saint  Also, other drivers were very considerate when i was trying to turn and stuff like thatSo excellent lesson, again i would recommend the full two hours because by the time youve gone through theory and what you are going to do that lesson you need lots of time to practise over and over. Its still fun though My instructor told me about another AA driver who would take his pupils to macondalds during the lesson so he could eat. I couldnt believe my ears  Very unproffessional, luckily for my, my driver wouldnt do this.      ', '    BACKGROUND BUMPH I put off learning to drive for as long as I could manage because of nightmare experiences as a youngster. I crashed a quad bike injuring myself, and the course tyre wall and was banned and put on the   8220;Worse Driver Ever  8221; list at a local go-kart track.However I reached the point where I was desperate for independence and thought been free to go wherever I wanted whenever I wanted was the key.  I dragged out the Yellow Pages and searched through the driving schools in my area.  A few of my friends had been with independent schools and had more than a few horror stories to tell about their experience and none of them had passed first time  8230;so I decided to give one the national driving schools a try.THE AA AS AN ORGANISATION...The main reason I chose the AA over BSM was the price.  At full price both schools charge    18 in my area, but if you book a slot of 12 lessons with the AA, then the price is cut to    16 a lesson.  If you  8217;re a student BSM offer a discount making each lesson    16.40.The AA telephone operators were both polite and reasonably helpful.  However, there were a few items that let their service down.  Some people prefer and feel more comfortable been taught by a female instructor whilst others prefer a male one.  The AA does not offer you a choice of instructor gender and the instructor you get will depend on your postcode.  There was also some slight pressure put on me to take my lessons on a Saturday, which is impossible for me due to work commitments.  I had to be firm and insistent that Friday was the only day suitable for myself.The AA sends a starter pack to all their customers, which consists of information about the AA, a year  8217;s free membership to their breakdown service and a    100 holiday voucher.  I received the pack within the promised 28 days and was particularly pleased with the holiday voucher and am using it off next years trip to Grand Canaria.  However I feel my years free AA membership has been pointless and wasted.  Like most learner drivers I do not yet own my own car and will not until I pass my test.  The free year starts from the day they send it out.  Personally I think a voucher that you send back when ready to claim your free years AA membership would be a much better idea and would ensure that everybody can make full use of the   8220;generous  8221; offer.THE INSTRUCTOR AND THE LESSONS (PLUS MORE ABOUT THE AA)...My actual instructor is female and I have to say that so far I cannot say a bad word about her.  She is patient, explains things well, does not get angry at my mistakes and gives me lots of positive encouragement.  As a result I feel relaxed and confident when driving, exactly how it should be.The AA asks what driving experience you  8217;ve had and how confident you feel.  As I was a complete novice my instructor started right at the begining and for the first few lessons I only drove on quiet country roads where other traffic was minimal.  I did not progress onto busier roads until my instructor felt I was ready.  This was good because it allowed my confidence to build up and meant I felt in control of and familiar with the cars controls before the daunting task of dealing with other vehicles.The AA  8217;s policy is to provide its pupils with a syllabus that starts with the basics, such as setting off and stopping, and gradually progress to more advance techniques such as town driving and reversing.  At the end of each lesson my instructor talks thru where I am on the syllabus and what we  8217;ll be doing in the next lesson.  This is very beneficial because it means as a learner you are kept up-to-date with your progress and can judge how well you are doing.  My instructor also often uses the DSA Driving Manual to explain certain things, for example clutch control.  This made certain things more clear although sometimes I felt it wasted valuable driving time.Another good thing about the AA and other larger driving schools is that they can afford to renew their cars every few month, meaning you never a drive an unreliable old   8220;rust bucket  8221;.  I have had two cars since starting to drive, and the only thing that was different about them was the colour.  The make, model and engine size are always kept the same but because the pedal sensitivity in every car varies you have to get re-used to the clutch and brake.I wasn  8217;t pressured, although my instructor did suggest I buy the AA Theory Handbook.  I paid half the normal price for the previous years, which is practically the same as the current one, and found it very useful when revising for my theory.  However most theory books are similar and answer the same purpose. I have now been driving for 5 month and am due to take my test in a few weeks.  The AA don  8217;t seem to rush putting their pupils in for their test, preferring instead to ensure they are ready and likely to pass first time.  My instructor has not encouraged me to take more lessons than I need to and now I am ready for my test has reduced my lesson from two hours a week to two hours every two week.AND FINALLY...All in all I have been reasonably pleased with the quality of service I have received from the AA.  I have enjoyed learning to drive and look forward to my lessons, however this is more to do with my actual instructor than the AA themselves.  This suggests that providing you are happy and comfortable with your instructor the company you choose, national or independent, is a minor detail.~~~~~~UPDATE~~~~~~The AA have switched from using a 1.2 Ford Fiesta Ghia, to using a 1.6 Ford Focus.  These are large, powerful cars and manouvering them is a nightmare.  I found it difficult despite been at test standard, therefore unless your a fan of bigger cars I would no longer recommend the AA, at least until they change to a car more suited to learners.     ', '    Well, I ve had five lessons with the AA Driving School now, so I guess I m just about qualified to write an opinion on them.The salespeople on the phones were very quick to promise lots, and deliver nothing. I have yet to receive my  welcome pack  which I was promised. I don t seem to be making much progress, and my instructor seems to be very quick to anger which causes me to lose confidence. I was provided with a syllabus, but the instructor has made no attempt to follow this. I m putting this down to my bad driving for now. The instructors also seem very  keen  for one to buy the AA Theory Test book.One bonus to the AA Driving School is that its fairly cheap for a national driving school - my lessons were    16/each if I paid in advance for twelve (which I regret now).     ', '    When I decided it was time to learn how to drive, I chose the AA because I had a voucher for a free lesson and I thought they were a reputable company, but little did I know what I had let myself in for. My instuctor nearly always turned up late and wasted my time.  He was very impatient and did my confidence no good.  AA s strategy is to make you take as many lessons as possible so they can leach you dry of money before your test.  Another annoying thing is that they change your car every few months so you have to get used to a new clutch, and this adds yet more lessons to your bill.  I found it to be a very impersonal service and as a result I failed my test with them.  Thinking that it was just my bad driving to blame, I left the AA Driving  school  and started lessons with an independent instructor.  He told me my driving was fine and after a few lessons I easily passed my test.I don t know if this was just a one off, but my advice to any learner drivers is to boycott large, money making driving schools such as the AA and BSM and learn with independent driving schools who are far more successful.     ', '    It was 3 months after my 17th birthday when my Dad decided he d had enough of driving me to and fro and would like to be the one who can drink at the pub and be driven home. That decision made, we needed to choose a driving school. I left that bit to him and he booked up some lessons with the AA.The thing I like about having lessons with the AA is you know that they are a reputable company. They aren t suddenly going to run off with your money and they aren t going to give you a death-trap to drive. In fact they change the cars relatively frequently, I ve driven two in 6 months. They change them to exactly the same model and it took me one lesson to get to grips with the slightly different sensitivities of the pedals but otherwise it was fine. The lessons cost about    17 each but there was a discount for bulk buying. They also gave me a holiday voucher (not sure that I ll use it but it was kind all the same). They also gave me 1 years free AA Membership. Hoorah Hooray  Except that I won t be doing any driving in my own car at the earliest 6 months into that membership. Never mind, at least I get their lovely magazine.So, the lessons. My first lesson I was really nervous, as you might imagine. I m a very little person (5ft small and not massively built with it) so I was worried that the Ford Focus the AA use would be totally uncontrollable for a midget like me. However, no booster seat for me as it was surprisingly easy to see over the steering wheel and reach the pedals. I find the car really easy to use and extremely comfortable, which always helps. The skills and techniques are gradually built up so you don t really notice. I was surprised how quickly I was on the major roads and turning right a traffic lights and roundabouts.Obviously the AA Driving School as a whole can t be judged on individual instructors but I d like to praise mine for being really patient and friendly. It s nice to know that if I make a mistake he ll explain it and not make me feel like a total idiot. But like I say, it s a very personal thing whether or not you like your instructor or even if you get a nice/competent one.What else is there to tell you, well I can t really say whether they/I are successful as my test is in 2 weeks but, as long as the manouevres are OK I think it will be OK.I think the best advert for the AA is that I have always looked forward to my driving lessons, and I m not a person that looks forwards to much.UPDATEWell I passed my test for the first time of asking on Monday 1st July, so that must say something about how well they teach  Actually I m a bit sad cos I won t have any more lessons now      ']

', '    I have previously had driving lessons with a private company - Grimsby Intensive Driving School, and now learn with the AA. product_reviews: ['    For my 400th review, I would just like to write a review on the new car that I have just recently bought - that being, the wonderful Citroen Saxo 1.1. It is a second hand car, and it is a T reg and so therefore it is about 12 or 13 years old. I bought it from a local secndhand car garage, and they sold it to me for    750 with a full 12 month MOT and service and a three month warranty on the major parts should anything go wrong. My only gripe is that there is no tax on it, but as the guy came down by nearly    100 in the price I shall let him off  For a car this age, it doesn t have a CD player - there is a tape player and a radio, but I know a man who can get me a CD player quite cheaply  It has got a sunroof, and it is only a three door car but I can cope with that. It s not fun trying to get in to the back seats without two further rear doors though... In terms of road handling, what with it being a small car it is extremely light and easy to run. There is no power steering on it, but I really don t see the need for it on a car this size. And due to its small engine size, it is also quite cheap to run in terms of petrol usage - I have to drive 20 miles each way to work every day at the moment, and    25 worth of petrol lasts me for three complete 40 mile round trips and most of the way there again (so about 130 miles in all on country roads). I have also driven it at high speeds (but keeping within the national speed limit for motorway driving of course ), and the road handling is just as good. It is also an extremely comfortable car to drive in, and although it is quite small and near to the ground you wouldn t really notice the bumps on the road too much. It must be my natural good driving  Many people get this type of car mixed up with a Peugeot 106, and I can see why as from sideways on they do look very similar. This is I guess because they are French made (no real significance I suppose ), but according to the man who sold it to me the engines are pretty much identical and so therefore parts are quite easy to come by. All in all, I was very happy with my purchase and should you ever find yourself in need of a small car then this is one that you should at least think about. And if you get a good deal just like I did on actually buying it, then you will be laughing all the way home  Many thanks for reading my review, and I hope that it has been of some help to you       ', '    The Citroen Saxo 1.1 First is a vast improvment in the old entry model Ax and is a suprisingly nice drive.The 1.1i engine has enough power to weave in and out of city traffic and keep up with the fast moving traffic on main town roads but feels stressed on motorways as it only has a 1100cc 4 cylinder 60bhp engine which accelerates suprisingly quick.The French made Saxo has decent bulid quality and looks a solid car.If its looks you will definetly not be bringing this car home.The saxo looks a little dated alongside rivals which is why it is not so popular on UK roads.Peformace                   *** 3 star 3/5The Saxo pleasingly arrives at 60mph from a standstill in 12.8 seconds which is around the same as the Peugeot 306 HDI lx  Which has 90hp.The Saxo goes on to a lessimpressive top speed of 100mph which is enough for motorway journeys but feels underpowered and lacks overtaking power at high speeds.                      **** 4 star 4/5Running costsThe Saxo is cheap and cheerful to run.  A maximum service cost will only set you back around    705.The Saxo 1.1 First is only group 2 insurance so expect a typical quote of around    290.Economy             **** 4 star 4/5         The Saxo 1.1 First has a official combined mpg figure of 46.5 mpg.In Extra Urban surroundings expect around around 56.5 mpg.Equiptment      * 1 star 1/5The Saxo has a very low standard equipment level as you would expect for it to be a entry model and have a price tag of    5,995.The following equipment is as followed.  .Immobilizer                STANDARD  .RDS radio cassette     Optional  .No extras avalible in the First modelOn the roadOn the road the Saxo is at acceptable level.Steering can become heavy when arking in tight gaps where theres lots of manovereing to be done.The handling on the Saxo could vastly be improved,For starters add power steering .The Saxo does not feel sluggish around town and theres a bit of power around town when you need it.The Saxo is a quiet car to drive and windnoise is low but occurs at high speeds (60mph+).ReliabilityThe Ax was a reliable run around so i would imagine this would be the smae.The small engine is simple to ork on and cheap to maintain at A1 standardsRecommendationsI would not reccommend this car to anyone i would recommend the Seicento S which includes Power steering and has optional Metallic paint ad manula or electric sunroof.     ', '    I don t know too much about cars so it will probably come to no surprise to those is similar positions to me that I took my husband along with me so i didn t get ripped off After many searches and looking at many varieties of small car I chose a Saxo East Coast,1.1i 3 dr.The first thing to say about my nippy little car is that I love it. I chose a special edition, which really only meant I had a CD player rather than cassette radio, sporty seats with lovely upholstery and a different coloured seat belt on each seat, yellow gear knob, metallic paint and blue colour on the speed dial etc. Basically the differences were visual rather than any thing different to the mechanics of the car. ', '    Probably my biggest motoring mistake to date.......Don t get me wrong, the Saxo is a great little car. ', '     AAAhhh, it s a little Citroen Saxo. Yes, for about a year now I have been driving around in my little Saxo, and I now feel qualified to tell you something about it. This review, I m afraid, comes four years too late, as the Saxo went out of production in the year 2000. It has since been replaced by a more 21st century, bubble-like car, the C3. There no question that the C3 is the nicer of the two, with its chic French curves, however at    9.000 it s not to everyone s liking. And so we come to the humble Saxo. Weighing in at 805kg the Saxo is very small, so obviously would not be suitable for big families, or indeed for people with big legs which invariably get crushed if they sit in the back seats. An avid Saxo-spotter, I have found they come in a spectrum of colours, the most offensive and most striking being bright yellow. It is not what I d call a  pretty  car, in fact it is near identical to the Peugeout 106, but having said this it has lines in the right places, and almost looks sporty. Unfortunately looks are deceptive, and the Saxo is about as sporty as Lisa Riley. I have a 1.1l engine, which can manage 0-60 in 12.4 seconds, and has a top speed of 102mph, a fact that will raise a gasp from some readers. Admittedly a sloth could probably accelerate quicker, but driving the Citroen Saxo is not about speed. Nor, in fact, is it about driving in comfort and luxury: The seats are perfectly comfy, but the interior seems to be made exclusively of black plastic. My car, the Saxo LX does not have air con, it does not have a sun roof, it does not have central locking, nor does it have electric windows, heck, it does not even have a CD player. But, it does have one redeeming feature- character.Far from being resentful towards Citroen for the small imperfections the Saxo boasts, I am quite grateful for them. This is because they all contribute to its character; for example when I turn up the bass on the radio, the windows rattle in their frames, and then the whole plasticky door starts to rattle. It is little things like this which save the driving experience from becoming monotonous. Or maybe I m being slightly harsh on the Saxo, as even without the quirks I think driving it would remain fun. Before this car I drove a Corsa, which was reliable and solid, but it became rather tedious to drive. The Saxo has not yet had the same effect on me. This is probably because it always poses challenges when you to drive it- I get a certain thrill from trying to reach the same speed as other cars whilst driving up a slip road, however much the Saxo might want to continue at its own leisurely pace. Parking is of course a doddle, with the power steering and because the car itself is so minute. I do, however have one concern about driving the Saxo. I am over 6ft, and I have size 12 feet. Irrelevant? Not when driving this car. The reason is because the foot well is incredibly cramped: to change gear I have to push down the clutch with my toe for it to touch the floor. I also have issues with the accelerator, as it is not wide-feet friendly, meaning that when I accelerate I often inadvertantly end up nudging the break with the same foot. This can make a more exciting driving experience, though as you can imagine, not a very pleasant one Before I bought the Saxo, I became an obsessive, hunting down articles and photos on my future car. It was somewhat disconcerting, therefore to find after typing  citroen saxo  into the google image searcher, hundreds of photos of crushed Saxos. This leads me on of course to the safety. As you may have guessed, this is not the Saxo s strong point. Upon impact the airbag, which you would assume is comforting to have,  bottoms out  meaning that the drivers head can come into contact with the steering wheel. There is also no structure in place to lessen side impact, so if you get hit, the Saxo is likely to crumple like a tissue. Obviously this is not a laughing matter, and can be a cause of serious concern. In a crash test the Saxo gained an overall score of 38 . Not very impressive, I m sure you will agree. In 2000, the last year of production, Citroen introduced many safety measures for the Saxo to help combat these concerns, and passenger and side airbags became optional extras. I suppose a similar issue is that of car security; my Saxo has a factory fitted immobiliser which will hopefully keep greedy fingers at bay. Unsurprisingly for such a small car there is no alarm, or any fancy security equipment, I get the impression that once again, Citroen have adopted the  no frills  approach. Moving away from the rather grim prospect of crashing, and the dark world of car crime and it is possible to become more upbeat. It would be downright wrong to write a review on the Saxo without mentioning the accessories or modifications you can have. One man allegedly spent    30,000 on modifying his Saxo to be the emitome of  boy racer . Admittedly I do not fit this stereotype, far from it, however you can help to notice the multitude of Saxo s with vast ineffective spoilers and exhaust pipes as big as dustbins. So, if you are that way inclined, there are many mock-chrome accessories and many body kits on sale, costing about    300 to make your car look truly,  bling ?Probably the main selling point of the Saxo is its money-saving ways. According to the manual, a 1.1l Saxo will squeeze in 46miles/ gallon, which is very economical. Thus far it has also been money-saving in the respect that I have not had to fork out a fortune on repairs or services. So it would seem that the Citroen Saxo is not always small and fun, but also reliable. With respect to Citroen themselves, I have been very impressed. Their customer service is superb, especially considering that I did not buy the car new, and that it is now four years old. For example, my car was missing the user manual, so as a long shot I emailed Citroen about it. Naturally it was no fault of theirs that I had lost it, but about two weeks later a brand new manual fell from my letter box. This reassured me that Citroen are a solid company, after all it s the little things that count Although you can not now buy a new Saxo, if you are desparate to get one, there are plenty of 2nd hand cars for sale. Of course I can not give you a fixed price, because you have to consider milage and age, but I can say that my car, now four years old, with a low milage of about 25,000, cost me    2,200. If you are buying a used car you can celebrate in the depreciation- a new Saxo used to cost about    7,000  Of course this also means insurance premiums that are not too scary. Because of this the Saxo is an ideal car for new drivers. A trip to Ebay.co.uk is always worth it if you are searching for a Saxo, as it should give you an idea of how much you should pay. I should end by saying that the Saxo sold remarkably well during the four years it was in production, because of its universal appeal. Like Harry Potter, this car can be enjoyed by both the old and the young. Primarily it is a small and cheap car, and I hate to use the expression, but  it gets you from A to B . That is, as long as you do not crash having departed from A, as then your motor will be going nowhere but the scrap yard. Although peppered with imperfections, the Saxo remains a fun car, bursting with charm- one my favourite things to have crossed the Channel. Although being nine years old and bought second hand from a private trader, it has been very reliable for me and i haven t had to fork out a penny on it (other than petrol), i had looked at several different makes and types of car on autotrader, ebay, and other internet websites, but this was the first car i went to look at and it appealed to me very much, i bought it straight away, it was very easy and comfortable to drive.  Other benefits for the citroen saxo 1.1 includes low maintenance, easy and cheap to run, small but spacious inside, and excellent value for money for this good looking car   The citroen saxo 1.1 comes very highly recommended in my opinion, especially to first time car buyer s.       ', '    This is a great little car which I highly recommend.  Yes, it s got a few faults (which car hasn t) but so far it s given me 2 years of pretty much trouble free motoring.It s nice looking (MUST have foglights or it looks incomplete ), stereo is adequate, has central locking, sunroof, keypad immobiliser, economical (450 miles of town driving on a tank), electric windows.Mine has been nicknamed Saxo-van due to its great carrying capacity.  The back seats are quick and easy to fold down, and we managed to get a large sideboard in it (with the boot closed too ) which wouldn t fit in a new golf It s very nippy, and smooth and quiet to drive.  Even when travelling at 70 - 80 mph it s still got some oomph Two little niggles:-1) the pedals are too close together - takes a while to stop hitting the accelerator when you want the brake 2) my front windows rattle when down My only other gripe has not been the fault of the car but of the main dealer - avoid them like the plague.     50 to replace a bolt in the sunroof ( ) and    120 for a service   And there customer service is poor too.  I have since found a small citroen-approved garage which is great and very cheap.  My 27,000 mile service only cost    40.Overall, a great car      ', '    The Citroen Saxo has got to be one of the most affordable and reliable small cars around. It is very popular among students who are attracted to the wide range of colours, good promotional prices and its good street cred.The size of the Saxo works to its advantage, it is easy to manoeuvre and park and now comes with power steering as well. The different models are designed to suit a range of needs from the ultra sporty to the very basics.I have been driving my second-hand Saxo for over a year now and have experienced no problems whatsoever. It continues to sail through its services and M.O.T   s without much bother and its fuel consumption is low.  I would definitely recommend this car.     ', '    The Citroen Saxo was first brought out in 1996, and to its credit it was better than the old AX. The model however was still old and not particularly well built. The mk II (W reg Onwards) however is a vastly improved machine with much better looks and an engine which is the same but still manages to pull better. The colour coding of the interior is also fantastically sporty, red seatbelts and dials.The cars 60bhp engine is well enough for anything, and the drive is fantastic (I knew a guy who had a BMW Z3 and a saxo, and came to work every day in the saxo simply because it was a better drive). The only problem here being that the pedals are too close together making it difficult for drivers with big feet, I m a size 9 however and never had a problem here.I read a review on here that slated the saxo s handling, which I can only say is brilliant, because I used to throw it round corners and it never once grumbled. I m convinced it has claws to hold it on the road. The guy paid over 9,300 for his saxo and sold it 4 months later for 4k something. Which makes him a slight idiot for accepting that price. Ours is a 2 year old model (Y reg) bought for    6500, has been crashed,and is still worth over    3000, so to accept a    5000 loss on any car after only 4 months seems crazy to say the least.Another brilliant advantage to the saxo especially for younger newer drivers is their tendancy to throw things away, like they will pay your vat or something like that, or free insurance for over 21 s making it a brilliant buy at a very cheap price.The main thing that bought the car for me was the extras, rear headrests that up until recently only the corsa offered on all standard models as well. A CD player which to get on a corsa you need to buy an SXi model, and which even on the new model of fiesta is still not fitted as standard (shows how shockingly bad ford are at being slightly generous) My friend has a V reg fiesta with alloys front fog lights power steering and NO CD PLAYER      I don t care about alloys I can t see them when I m driving, power steering is pointless on such a light car, and front fog lights get used in conditions which it s plainly stupid to go driving in anyway. The saxo also has a rather generous boot for its size and it s interior is well laid out. Worth noting at this point that the saxo and the 106 are exactly the same car, just look at them and it s obvious. The only difference is the badge as a status symbol and seeing as citroen are not as fashionable (Although getting better) the price is much lower for much more.The service we recieve from the citroen garage is second to none. for example I got in the saxo one day and tripped a switch which disabled all my instrument panels somehow, bit of a pain in the backside, so I rushed upto the garage before it closed (It was about 4:30) and the mechanics had all gone home. My parents were on holiday and I had no way of proving who I was, but the showroom manager came out wearing his suit and got absolutely filthy looking around my car and eventually fixed it for me too. I felt really guilty about his previously brown now black patched suit, but he still told me to come back later on before 6:30, when he went home if it did it again and he would have a better look at it for me, what a guy   Another comment generally made which I disagree with is the fuel consumption. At 80 the saxo was doing nearly 4500 revs and at 80 my 306 does only just over 3500 revs making my bigger engine much more economical. I found it quite uneconomical, it cost me over    20 to get to stoke and back, whereas in my 306 I got to Birmingham and back for the same money. Plus my 306 has done about 100,000 more miles than the saxo. My final complaint is that there are no deadlocks on the car so smash in the window pull up the lock and you are in, making it not very safe at all. Just don t leave your mobile inside.In all an excellent little car, which it was indeed a pleasure to drive, cheap to insure and which was extremely fast indeed. I now drive a 1.4 75bhp 306 which is not as fast as the old saxo. A good car, well worth considering or investing in. Hopefully the problems will have been resolved on the C2 set to replace the Saxo in 2004.     ', '    Fiery?  No.  Understated but cool? No.  Adjectives that I would normally like to have associated with items that I may purchase are definitely not affiliated with the Citroen Saxo 1.1 East Coast.With only a 1.1; it lacks the power and aggression of its VTR counterpart.  And with a multicoloured interior (e.g. each different seatbelt is a different colour; yellow gearknob) it s not exactly the cool image that one may be looking for.  However, despite the lack of these vital elements, it is a fun car.  In fact, it is as a result of an absence of these characteristics, that makes it a fun car.Let s return to the beginning.  Why buy a car when it s rather lacking in some of one s idealistic qualities?  Well, coming with a free 2 year full insurance (no age limit); it is a rather attractive purchase at about 7000 pounds new.  For the newly qualified driver, insurance is a huge problem, often being over 1000 pounds in the first year.  Though it is an expensive first car, with either a healthy bank balance or generous parents, it is a sensible buy.Now let s return to the car itself.  As said, it s not exactly a tiger and it certainly doesn t purrr but with half a tank of petrol (a full tank is too much and slows the car down) and only yourself in the car, you can still leave some poor souls behind at the traffic light.  Being small, it is excellent for getting into those tight spaces in the city which larger cars (and some women drivers?) have trouble getting into.  In addition to this, it is very economical, petrol-wise; and furthermore,  with the impending road tax according to engine size, it is bound to save the owner a couple of bob.But still, a multicoloured interior   , I hear you moan.  That is true, it does take a little getting used to, and you may have to live through jokes such as  your car looks like its from playschool , but for the wackier people and those with a sense of humour, it can be rather nice.How does it drive?  Well, it is quite nippy and so great for the city though I frequently drive it on the M1 where it is a little underpowered.  Furthermore, though there is no power-steering, steering is suprisingly light anyway and gear change is supprisingly smoove compared to the like of VW Golf .  The pedals are rather small and the size of the car itself is not suited to those of considerable length.  However, space in the back is adequate and boot space is great.  And with them combined when the seats are let down, one can fit long objects such as snowboards in the back which is quite handy.All in all, if you can t be bothered to read this whole comment, just read this last bit.  It s quite nippy so good for city used and will not burn a huge hole in your finances.  However, it s not for the boring due to its crazy interiors nor for people with long legs.     ', '    Myself and my son recently visited our local Citroen dealer because we organised a test drive on a 1.1i Saxo First. This was because my son is currently looking for a new car to replace his very reliable but ageing current motor, a Citroen AX.The Saxo has always attracted my son with its good looks and decent performance, but interestingly enough he was interested in the smallest engine option of the First. There are several reasons for this, all unbelievably and unusually sensible coming form my son   Firstly the 1124cc engine keeps insurance costs down and also it is very light on the drink when it comes to the petrol pump. Despite this you musn t get me wrong because it is certainly no slouch, the lightweight of the body ensures that. It can accelerate very nippy around town and from traffic lights, a suprise for such a small engine. In fact it accelerates form 0-60 in a suprisingly fast time of 12.4 seconds and boasts a solid 60 bhp.An interesting point for me was to see how the gearbox fared on this car. It s predecessor the AX, was reknowned for having a clunky gearbox and in fact my son s own AX was the same. However I am very happy to report that the Saxo Firsts  box is a very sweet and smooth changing 5 speed manual box.Load space is very deceptive in this car. It doesn t look like it has a bulky boot but it is deceptively large inside. It will hold a good amount in standard position but when the back seats are down it is like a small van inside. I would estimate that the Saxo s loadspace has the edge over other cars in the supermini category like the Fiesta and the Corsa.The other features that come as standard with the Saxo First 1.1i are as follows: heated rear window, rear wash/wipe, tinted glass, digital clock, rev counter, drivers air bag, anti-roll bars, immobiliser, radio stereo/cassette with 4 speakers and a whole lot more.It s remarkable that you can get all of this for an impressive    5940 brand new, with a number of special offers on top of this on offer from Citroen at the moment. In the end however my son didn t make the purchase as it was slightly out of his price range but he is on the look out for a Saxo First a year or 2 old so that it fits into his price range.     ', '    I seem to be one of the lucky few with this stunning looking car, with its colour coded bumbers and side strips    It is packet full of features  Power steering, electric front windows, CD Player, sunroof, very comfortable interior  The list goes on  I am 6ft tall with size 12 feet  At first i found this car hard to drive because of its small foot well but i got used to it  I find it not too small and not too big, it fits me and 4 of my 6ft or so friends in quite comfotably without loosing any of that nippyness it has. The boot is very big and I really enjoy the drive. I drive a fair distance on the motorways and find i m always in the fast lane keeping up and even overtaking the BMW s without pushing the car to its limits. I love my Saxo and i ve only seen a few of the Desires about but anyone with one is very lucky and anyone with the chance to buy one is even luckier           ']

product_reviews: ['    Introduction~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~~ ~ Through my contacts in the motor trade here in Dublin I got a sneak preview of the all-new Mini from BMW that is due to hit the car showrooms both here in Ireland and in the UK most likely some time next month. (July, 2001)The car I got a peep at is the Mini Cooper version, and is tagged to enter the Irish market at around the    15,500 (Irish Punts) mark.What it will retail at in the UK is anyone  8217;s guess, but it will unquestionably be less expensive than here in Ireland.There is even talk of the entry level version being priced at less than the    10,000 mark (Sterling) ~ ~ The car it is replacing, the much loved old Mini, was (some would say still is) a British icon, ever since it was first produced way back in 1959, the brainchild of the great Sir Alec Issigonis. At the time, it set entirely new standards in car design, and lasted literally unchanged for generations in its original form.Two years later, in 1961, the race car expert John Cooper assisted in the building of the very first Mini Cooper, and the name Cooper has had a close association with performance Minis ever since.~ ~ The new Mini is the work of a guy called Frank Stephenson, an American working for BMW in Germany.In the BMW advertising, Mr. Stephenson says,   The Mini Cooper is not a retro design car, but an evolution of the original. It has the genes and many of the characteristics of its predecessor, but is larger, more powerful, more muscular and more exciting than the old Mini.  8221;~ ~ Straight away, let me say that I don  8217;t entirely agree with Frank Stephenson  8217;s assessment.The new Mini bears little or no resemblance to the earlier product, despite BMW  8217;s insistence to the contrary.About the only thing it has in common with the old Mini is the fact that it will still be built in the UK, at Oxford, but it is thoroughly German in every way and a BMW through and through.Interior~ ~ ~ ~ The new Mini Cooper is surprisingly roomy in the rear, and there is room enough for three grown adults, (at a push) even if there isn  8217;t exactly a lot of space to cross your legs. Inside it has been deliberately designed to remind you of the old Mini, and still has the characteristic central (and very large) speedometer.The switches, buttons, dials, and levers all have the same look and feel as the old car, but the very wide-opening doors, adjustable driver  8217;s seat and steering column, and the remote central locking are all latest technology, and ensure that it is extremely practical and adaptable for both driver and passengers.You can open the boot remotely from inside the car, and while it is still very small with not too much luggage capacity, the 50/50 split-folding rear seats increase luggage space dramatically when required.A panoramic sunroof can be fitted as an optional extra, which gives the car an even airier and larger feel.Exterior~ ~ ~ ~ ~~ ~ Perhaps predictably, the new Mini is both longer and wider than its predecessor, although it has to be said that it is still very much a compact car, the overall length  being only 11ft. 10in.Looking at the car from the front, the bonnet, lights and grille give it a cosy and friendly look, while at the rear, the wide and steeply raked body and flared wheel arches give it the compact,   8220;stick-to-the-road  8221; look that we have come to expect from a Mini.All the side pillars are tucked away behind the glass, making it look like it has a continuous window extending all the way round the car. Engine, Performance, and Roadholding~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~ ~~ ~ The car I viewed had a Brazilian-made 1.6 litre, 16-valve engine capable of developing some 115bhp.The entry level car of the Cooper range will have a slightly less powerful 90bhp version of the same engine, but I am told that BMW plan a Cooper   8220;S  8221; version for release in 2002, which they promise will have a 163bhp supercharged engine. ~ ~ The 1.6 litre is quick enough, with a 0 to 60mph time of only 9.0 seconds, a quoted top speed of 124mph, and with a return of 42.2mpg in fuel economy.The less powerful entry-level version has a 0 to 60mph time of 10.8 seconds, a top speed of 115mph, and fuel consumption of 43.5mpg.No figures have yet been released for the Cooper  8221;S  8221; version. ~ ~ A fault that has been levelled at this car is its lack of low-speed torque, and I would agree with this criticism, as it could definitely do with a bit more pulling power at low speeds. Forget the Honda Civic Typer R or the Seta Leon cupra this is the only small car .     ', '    Ever wanted to know how famous people feel? Buy the new BMW Mini Cooper. Its drop dead gorgeous looks turn heads wherever you go. I picked mine up last week and nothing prepared me for the attention I would receive. Its a Chilli Red Cooper with white roof (a tradional Cooper colour). Wherever I drive people stop and stare. Wherever I park, I return to an audience, my girlfriend is gettin jealous.So what about the car. Well for a start its not mini in dimensions. Park it next to a classic Mini and you will be shocked at how big it is. Its in a similar class to a Fiesta. As I mentioned its looks are nothing short of stunning. Clever design has created a look thats is unmistakenly Mini yet almost futuristic. With the exception of the Audi TT, thaere is nothing on the road to rival it.The interior is equally retro-modern. The large central speedo of the Mini is there but in a very modern form. The cabin design is very well laid out with easy to read dials and a rev counter placed behind the steering wheel. A couple of critisms of the interior are the lack of storage space, no glove compartment and limited door storage and the plastick feel of the indicator and wiper stalks. These are more than compensated for by the comfortable sporty seats and the infinately adjustable driving position.The performance in mid range hot hatch, 0-60 in 9 seconds and limited to 125mph. Its a little wheezy in low revs but hit the sweet spot at 35000-4500rpm and the Mini is just delightful. The gearbox is possibly the slickest and smoothest I have ever encountered, the brakes are superb, the 60-0 time similar to a Ferrari or Porche. ABS is standard but fortunately I have not had to test the abilty of this. What sets the Mini Cooper apart is its handling. Its is simply superb. The ride is like that of a car 3 times the price, cornering go-kart like,with it wheels at the corners design mirroring the old Cooper.One other critism apart from the interior space is the size of the boot, you could get about one medium suitcase in it.For    12000 you get a car that turns heads, handles like a ferrari and is more fun that you would ever imagine was possible in a car. You get BMW back up and opting for the TLC package gives you all major services and oil changes for 5 years for an incredible    100 all inclusive     ', '    Mini CooperBackground of the Mini.The original Mini was designed by one man, his name was Sir Alec Issigonis, as was primarily released in the United Kingdom on 27th of August 1959. In its first 40 years of production, there was almost 5,300,000 Mini   s made, many cars have tried to replace the Mini, such as the    9X   , however none have succeeded.After the Queen was sighted in a Mini in the early 1960s the cars popularity rocketed, with other famous stars such as The Beatles, Steve McQueen and Clint Eastwood all owning the British icon.The original Mini   s made by were just over 10 feet long and however with released such as the saloon and the van the Mini has become a versatile car, catering for many drivers.  The original Morris Mini-Minor had an 848cc engine, and was produced by the British Motor Company, [BMC]. In 1964 sportier upgrades of the successful Mini were introduced, theses were the Cooper with a 998cc engine, the Cooper S with 1275cc Engine. The Mini is known for its superb handling, and this is an important factor that led the sports edition of the car was such a successful racing car, with the three time Monte Carlo winners, being the most famous.After the formation of Austin Rover in 1981 Mini   s in all its variations continued to be manufactured, however it wasn   t until Bayerische Motoren Werke AG, or BMW as most commonly known took over the Rover company, selling Land Rover to the Ford Motor Company and keeping the rights to the Mini.The BMW Mini one and Cooper went on sale in the UK on the 7th of June 2001, and across Europe in September 2001, with a vast array of extras, to personalise each car; the Cooper s was later released in May 2002.The Mini continued as released until early 2007 when the Mini MK2 was released in the UK. Sticking with the 1.6 litre engine that is across the board for the New BMW Mini, with both interior and exterior modifications, changing the look of the Mini again, as it become a modern depiction of and motor vehicle.Prices.The Mini One, starting price is    11,595The Mini Cooper, starting price is    12,995The Mini Cooper s, starting price is    15,995Overall view of the Mini CooperThis review will be related to a late 2005 Mini Cooper.I ve driven a 3-door petrol Mini Cooper since I passed my test a little over 2 years ago, so I cannot compare it too any other car apart from the car I learnt in; a  Peugeot 307 diesel , however at the age of 20 I could never imagine driving anything but a Mini. The car was bought brand new in 2005 for slightly over    15,000 and was worth very penny, there has not been any major problems with the car, except when there was a problem with the steering column, but did not make any difference to driving, just made a squeaking noise when the car was in motion.Exterior.The Mini   s exterior is reminiscent of the classic Mini but in many ways is very different. With visual and performance upgrades available from the dealership, such as colored wing-mirrors, aerodynamic body kits, spoilers, tinted windows and most famously a trait of the Mini, go fast stripes and roof decals. The addition of aerodynamic kits and spoilers will not only improve they sportier aesthetic of the Mini but it will improve the handling of that Mini, with the aerodynamics being improved by the body kits and spoiler, making the car stick closer to the road.The exterior of the Mini is a British icon and the new Mini has reinvented this iconic symbol globally.Exterior Rating - ****Interior.The interior of the new Mini is based on the classic Mini Cooper S, the rally edition Mini had bucket seats and a central column that housed the controls for the car and the speedometer. The speedometer was in the centre to both the driver and the navigator could see the speed that the car was traveling.The central column in the new Mini houses the controls for the electric windows, air conditioning, radiator system, fog lights, and stereo-system, along with the speedometer.The standard Mini seats are sports bucket seats, with upgrades available, including the John Cooper Works Sports Seats, and new Park Lane seats. The back seats are of similar design and look great and are fairly comfortable. The ceiling in the Mini comes as grey as standard, however the consumer may choose a black ceiling upgrade. I think this upgrade is worth having because with the tints it makes the car look much more private. The boot space is average, on a par with the Citroen C2 and despite it seeming small is deceptively big, the seats also fold down for extra storage space.Interior Rating - *****Engine and Driving.I m pretty sure that the car in more capable than doing 124-mph, and is quick off the mark and for a 1.6 petrol engine has such power when it accelerates, I have driven other Mini s, such as a Mini one and despite the same engine size, the tweaks under the bonnet make so much difference to the drive that the car offers.With the 5speed gearbox and the low biting clutch, changing gears and acceleration is such a dream while driving. Unlike many other cars, the Mini was an acceleration pedal that comes from the floor, meaning the driver must push down on the pedal, rather than pushing forward on the pedal like many other cars. The Mini is known for its handling and the Mini Cooper does not let you down in that respect, with the Mini   s ability to hold close on corners and move on straights to take full advantage of the acceleration.Engine and Driving Rating - ****Overall Review of the Mini Cooper.I love the feel of the car, aesthetically both the exterior and interior of the car is great, the rounded smooth body can be enhanced by bigger and bulkier aerodynamic kits [or body kits].The interior of the car is both modern and easy to navigate, with a large speedometer in the centre of the dashboard with the stereo and all the switches, for air con, windows, fog lights etc all in the central column, making it easy both the driver and the passengers to operate the extras within the car. The Mini has quirky parts that drivers are attracted to such as the central column, that set it apart from conventional cars. I could not imagine driving any other cars and I   ve used the Mini website to create my dream Mini for future reference, with their growing popularity throughout the world Mini is forever improving. I would recommend this car to everyone, with concepts for saloons, vans and pickups, the BMW Mini is slowly becoming available for drivers from all walks off like.Over all Rating - ****If there is anything I have left out, just give leave a comment and I   ll be sure to improve it as soon as I get the chance. Thank you.     ', '    My mini cooper     do I love it or hate it?  I have had the little beauty now since the second week in January (so around 2 months as it is now mid March when I am writing this).Mostly I love it, what I hate about it at the moment is the cracked mirror, scuffed wheel arches and scraped door handle that I now have on the drivers side thanks to meeting a white van on a narrow bridge    (although estimates are around    180 all up to fix it)She is gorgeous     chilli red with a white roof and large, deep eyes     a drivers seat that you can position how you want to     hunched forwards or way back, up to the roof or down through the floor, upright or laid back, well supported or slouching.  This is a car to get in and loose yourself for at least 20 minutes at a time (fortunately my commute is around 25 to 30 mins)I am not going to give you stats on the car     after all if that is what you want you can go to the mini web site (www.mini.co.uk     what a surprise ) and they have them all there     including the new mini cooper S due out in July (don   t forget to wipe the drool off the keyboard).  What I am going to give you is emotion     Pure and from the heart.I used to drive a Honda CR-V so I know what it feels like to drive a car with space inside.  In the Honda you had to stretch or lean if you wanted to keep your hand on the knee of the person in the passenger seat (Only ever did that with my wife though) in the Mini you don   t it is a comfortable distance.  OK so we have established that it is smaller     not a great surprise     but after being in such a large car does the Mini feel cramped?  NO   Absolutely not, in fact the    cabin    space for the driver actually feels larger to me     probably something to do with the fact that there is no metal in the top of the doors, just the glass and that the windscreen is at a steep angle so appears to be giving you a wide view of the world.The only thing I really miss is the height so you can see the scenery, but to be honest you need to keep your thoughts on the drive or the spirit of the Mini will run away with you     and find the nearest metaphoric small bridge and a white van.The Cooper (and even the standard Mini) has put exhilaration back into driving and put fun into a commute I dreaded.  Just in case you had not picked up the vibe yet     I love the car and would not hesitate to buy another one.So the emotional side of things gets big thumbs up from me, but what about the practicality of it?As I said     I used to drive a Honda CR-V (another car I highly rate) and I have 2 children     boys aged 3 and 5 so practicality has to be a consideration.They can both get in the back in reasonable comfort with my partner and me in the front.  The best arrangement though is the 3 year old behind me with my partner next to him and the 5 year old in the front with the seat forward to make ample legroom in the back for her.  This car does have plenty of seating space for a family of 4     trust me I live it.What about luggage space though? The boot is not massive     certainly not compared to the vault of the CR-V     but it is easily big enough to get the weeks grocery into.  It is also big enough to get two cabin baggage roll on cases into (My sons have one each which their take to their grandmothers with them) and still leave some room for coats and wellies.Also in the boot there is a cigarette lighter hole (or 12v power take off if you prefer)     why?  So you can keep your mini fridge in there and look cool? It is probably something to do with the fact that I can not find a spare wheel.No one at the dealership mentioned it.  I guess the manual might, but I have not got through it yet.  If you look in the boot where you would expect to find a spare wheel     it is missing.  What is there is a jack, some interesting tools for undoing valves, a can of some sort of sealant and a tyre pump that powers from a 12v socket.  I really do hope that I do not get a puncture until after I have read the manual on how this is all supposed to work OK so working forwards from there     the rear seats do split fold, and they do fold down without lifting up the rear bench so if there are only two of you I am pretty sure you could get a weeks luggage in the back to go to the airport.The rear seats are a type of bucket seat, so the rear passengers do get a bit of extra legroom from that and also have plenty of headroom     there are only 2 seat belts though so do not try to get 3 in There are 2 nice size speakers in the rear panelling and some very handy sized moulded plastic pockets at the side that will hold a beaker or can.  In the back of the front seats you will also find a couple of nets, so there is plenty of storage space for things there.Moving into the front     as I said the seats have an incredible amount of adjustability.  I challenge anyone to not be able to find a comfortable sitting position.  Be upright, prim and proper, or sink to the floor and get sporty it is your choice.In the front you have your controls too     a fiddly bit here is the mirror adjustment lever under the end of the hand brake, but it works OK.  The gear knob is wonderful     it is so big and round and your hand can just sit on it as if it were an extension of your arm.In front of that are two cup holders (or one and the ashtray) and the lighter socket.Travelling upwards you come to the central console.  Window controls on both sides, fog lights (if you chose them) and a door locking switch     handy for the lady on a dark night stopping at traffic lights in a dodgy part of town.  Also you have your ASC+T on/off switch.  This is basically to turn your traction and skid control on and off depending how racy you are feeling.Next the environmental controls     level of heat, fan speed, rear de-mister, air recycling and if you choose it air conditioner     choose it, even in England we need it.  It really does make a massive difference to the speed in which you can demist all your windows if you can turn on air-con. Above that you have your radio     your choice, tape (with or without auto-changer), CD or minidisk. These pieces all fit in together wonderfully and look fantastic.Above that you come to the mark of the mini     the BIG (and I do mean BIG) central speedo     modernised with a digital read out of mileage and trip counter (with a count down to your next service each time you turn the engine on) and dials for Petrol and Water Temperature.Over to the passenger   s side there is no glove box, just a shelf (underneath the passenger air bag) and a big door pocket for your map.Moving back to the driver   s side you have your adjustable height steering wheel and a big rev counter (came with my chilli pack)The lights and wipers are easy to operate and you have a couple of little push buttons on the steering wheel for the horn (which is a nice little tootle).Finally something on the fuel economy - it sips.  It uses more if you have the air-con on, but generally you can get around 300 miles out of around 40 litres of petrol.The other thing at the moments is that you can get a TLC package - but a mini and take this out at the same time and for    100 you have covered all the standard servicing costs for the first 5 years or 60,000 miles.If you have gotten this far     congratulations.  I hope it has given you some excitement     the car certainly does it for me and I would recommend it to most people unless you really would prefer to be in a Yugo (I have had one of those too, but not by personal choice ). If that were the case though you would probably not be reading this in the first place.Go get it     you won   t regret it, as long as you remember not to get too carried away.     ']

', '    The Vespa ET2 and ET4 are the most popular scooters on London s streets, and have been for a couple of years now. It s a position they well deserve.I ve been riding the four-stroke, 125cc ET4 since 1999 and have felt no desire to change. When I first saw the smooth curves and sleek metal skin I knew I wanted this machine. It was an incredibly original look, evoking models from the scootering heyday of the 1960s yet not out of place in the 21st century. A timeless design.Less striking but no less important, the performance lives up to the appearance. Incredibly reliable, as you would expect from Vespa, cheap to run and a smooth ride. Claimed top speed is 65mph, but I have touched 70. The ET4 is capable of handling motorways and long-distance trips, but it s on city streets that it really shines. It sticks to the road, steers beautifully and is incredibly manoeuvrable, nipping through gaps that a bigger bike can t manage. Features like the handbag hook, underseat storage space and digital dashboard clock make life easier for the commuter.The price of a new machine has dropped, making the ET4 one of the best bargains in its class. Look out for two limited edition colour schemes this year, too.My only complaint is that the ballooning sides make it uncomfortable for a pillion passenger. But that s his problem, not mine.Every manufacturer now has its  retro  beast. But Vespa were the first and their scooter still looks cooler, cleaner than the rest.     ']

s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
If you’re drawn to compact cars that blend spirited driving with iconic style, the MINI Cooper remains a compelling choice—though it’s evolved quite a bit from the classic Mini many of us nostalgically remember. Thanks to BMW’s engineering, reliability has improved significantly, with fewer maintenance headaches than older Minis, which is a big plus if you value peace of mind alongside fun.

Performance-wise, the MINI Cooper delivers a lively, engaging drive. The manual gearbox is notably smooth and slick, and the brakes inspire confidence—perfect for those twisty back roads or city streets. Handling is where this car truly shines, with go-kart-like cornering and a low center of gravity that make every journey feel thrilling yet composed. That said, the engine can feel a bit light on low-speed torque, so don’t expect muscle car grunt, but the responsive throttle keeps things exciting.

Design-wise, MINI nails the retro-modern vibe inside and out. The large central speedometer and sporty, comfortable seats create a cockpit that’s both charming and driver-focused. Outside, the MINI Cooper’s head-turning looks still command attention, though it’s lost some of the cult mystique of the original. Still, it’s undeniably a cool and cheeky presence on the road.

On the practical side, the MINI tlc servicing package offers excellent value, covering five years at a reasonable price—something to consider given the car’s premium positioning. Optional packages like Pepper and Chili add worthwhile features, but be prepared: the base model feels a bit barebones, and extras can quickly push the price up, making it an expensive small car, albeit good value within the BMW family.

Finally, if personalization is your thing, MINI’s aftermarket scene is rich and varied, letting you truly make the car your own. Overall, the MINI Cooper balances nostalgic charm, sharp handling, and modern reliability—just be mindful of the cost if you start ticking all the option boxes.

product_reviews: ['    I have been the proud owner of a Sapphire blue Peugeot 206 1.4 GLX for 2 years - and i m still in love   This makes it the most successful relationship i ve ever had Not only does this car look good, i look good in it   It s easy to handle and quite quick which makes me appear to have as good a driving ability as Michael Schumaccer - which obviously i do not have   (there is a small dent on the back which can vouch for this ).After a few years of managing with a Ford (Fix Or Repair Daily )Fiesta, i ve never looked back.  I do alot of motorway driving which this car loves, gone are the days of vibrating steering wheels and so much noise you have to turn the stereo up full blast to drown it out. ', '    After many happy years with the Renault Megane coupe (see previous op ) it was time to trade in and get something a bit newer.After looking at many, many cars, we finally chose the Peugeot 206 1.4 LX (although Ciao call it a 1.3?) okay, it s a 1360cc engined car.
