Plenty of leg-room and a comfortable seat   Being a fairly small car, passengers in the back don t perhaps get quite as much leg room as they d get in a larger car, however it is certainly not cramped even with adults as back seat passengers.PRICES***************It s very hard to comment on prices as these can be affected by dealer s offers, your choice of options / colour, and a multitude of other factors, however as a rough guide the total on the road price of my car was    11,295 (including registration / tax etc).  When buying a new car there are always plenty of different financing options available and it wouldn t really be suitable for me to list those that were available to me here as no doubt they have changed in the couple of months since I ordered my car.TO CONCLUDE***************I m sure that you can probably tell that I m extremely happy with my car and would certainly recommend it to any potential new car buyer.  There s bound to be some features I haven t mentioned within this review, however I have tried to include as many of the features that I think make this car better than others I have driven.  If you want more technical details about the vehicle they can be easily found on Peugeot s website or from a dealer.  Thanks for reading, and I hope I didn t do too bad a job of my first car review Angeelu :o)     ', '    Only a month ago did I purchase my Peugeot 206, and having driven a Fiat Seicento beforehand, how could it disappoint me? The answer is... It hasn t  It s an absolute pleasure compared to the loud rumbling annoyance that was the fiat. The Fever is the latest special edition and comes with a cd player with 6 speakers, metallic paint, electric windows, and front and rear fog lights. The disadvantage to the Fever is that it only comes in 3 colours: moonstone, aluminium and black. But that s pretty much it. I opted for a black 3 door hatchback with a 1.4l engine. The engine is efficient and quiet, and has quite a lot of poke for a small engine. The cabin is quiet, the cd player is good, and the ride is quite smooth. I have found the handling good and responsive and better than most of the cars I ve driven. Visability within the car is good.The look of the car is classically cute and the styling is unrivalled although the onyx black version gets dirty at the drop of a hat. The interior is interesting, as on the black model you get a black and orange fabric interior. It sounds horrible, but its a relief when you find out that its burnt orange, and looks really cool. If I had to pick any holes in this car, I would criticise the lack of fabric and paint choices, but then again, when the price for the base model 1.1 fever is only    7995, you cant really complain.The dealership that I purchased my car through were very helpful, and with my finance package, RAC cover was included. I would recommend the 206 and peugeot to anyone.     ', '    Don t expect technical stuff in this opinion.  But, I have had my Peugeot 1.4 LX 206 for just over a year and consider its about time I gave an honest appraisal of the car.THE STARTI decided to change my car (Fiesta) for a newer model.  So off I went to visit Ford, Vauxhall and Peugeot garages.  After not a lot of consideration (I was put off by the first two sales people) I ended up at Peugoet.  I spied this red car on the forecourt, and fell in love with it   Fab shape, great colour, interior was brill.  Okay, I m only 5ft, could I see all around?  The salesperson (good move , it was a woman), came out and showed me all the essentials.  The driving seat is adjustable up, down and back, the steering column is adjustable, excellent all round vision through the tinted windows, easy gear change, electric windows and wing mirrors, air conditioning AND a CD player with surround sound.  Could I test drive.  YES -take it out -unaccompanied.  I loved it   Great handling, smooth ride. Want it - got it THE MIDDLE BITIt cost me nearly    9k for this 10 month old used car.  Peugoet Finance -did a deal with them, hung out for what I wanted to pay per month   Mileage was low, just over 9500 on the electronic clock.  Anyway, I reckon I got a bargain.  I love driving this car.  Its easy, the gear change is smooth, it accelerates in all the gears and it looks good.I like the way the driving seat can be raised and lowered to suit whoever is doing the driving.  This was a major selling point, along with the adjustable steering column.  It has power steering, making the actual driving a dream, it responds instantly.  Fingertip control of the usual lights, indicators wipers AND you can set the headlights to four different positions.  Electronic counters, so no chance of turning the clock back, good displays including a rev counter.  Nice interior design, and comfortable seats. It will stop on a sixpence, thats the ABS for you - Peugeot have an excellent braking system.  It has air bags, central locking and seats 5 people effortlessly.  Fine.  Can it move - yes, it is fast and nippy.  Ideal for town or motorway driving and I do a lot of both.  Fuel economy is excellent, although the air conditioning does run off the fuel, it doesn t use that much. Under the bonnet - found the oil stick thing (if I can anyone can ), water bottle for the wipers and the other essentials.  Nearly everything else has a protective cover, the battery etc, which I think is a really good idea.  Starts first time, every time, no knocking, shuddering or anything like that.  Has excellent suspension. Security, well it has central locking, remote locking, immobiliser fitted as standard and the keys are chipped - so, unless you have my keys, you can t start it Can it pull fully loaded.  Let me tell you, I ran my son, (he s 21 and nearly 6ft) and three of his friends (one of whom is really a big guy) to play football.  Down the motorway, no problem, flew at its usual speed, up a rather horrible hill to get to the field - no problem.  I changed from 5th to 4th and that was it  I was impressed Did I mention it has a CD Player/Radio with surround sound?  Amazing sounds and it has a little stick on the wheel, so you can change tracks/radio stations/volume without taking hands off the wheel.It also has the wheel sizes and tyre pressures on the uright sill of the drivers door -neat or what Boot wise, not bad, but who needs a massive boot?  I can get all the shopping in the boot and it doesn t fly around everywhere.  Back seats all fold down, there s a compartment under the passenger seat for storing those valuables away and my insurance is cheap (Churchill - the one with the nodding dog)NEARLY FINISHEDAll in all I am really impressed with this car.  Here is a the best recomendation - I DIDN T take my hubby with me when I went looking for a car.  He thought I d made a HUGE mistake.  Guess who loves driving my car - his only complaint is that its not got enough height.  SO what did he do -three weeks ago he went and bought a Peugeot 1.4 LX 307   thats how impressed he was with the make.  The parts are really inexpensive, although if you loose a wheel trim it does cost to buy just one - around    10 -    12. I will be shopping around when it is due for its first full service.  Would I have another Peugot - Yes.  DO I think the 206 is ideal for me -YES.  Do I let my son drive it -NO (aren t I mean, he drives the 307, finds it more comfortable).   Not bad for someone who isn t all that car mad   Thanks for reading.     ', '    I have the current advantage in my job that I require hire cars on a number of occasions, typically I get the standard Vauxhall Astra which is boring the first time you sit in it and goes steadily downhill from there   Well, last week I accepted delivery of a Peugeot 206 in metallic Sapphire Blue.  I jumped into the car with a chorus of  where s your hairdryer?  and  I ll have a trim  ringing in my ears leaving me with some prior mis-conceptions about the general use of the 206.  The engine size was 1.4 and boy did it move, pulling away from the office I noticed that the car was extremely responsive and quick off the blocks.  The car moved very easily through the gears and took the corners extremely well.  Generally driving around town the car was in a class of its own, fast away from the lights and nippy through the traffic it is small but doesn t drive like your typical small car.  A Fiesta this ain t  This car handles very well on the motorway also, none of the typical shuddering and juddering at higher speeds that you usually experience with a car of this size.  I was also surprised at the inside layout of the car, very clean and concise with a lack of the over-engineered look that is so often seen in cars these days.  The trim was well placed and matched the bodywork well - I am unsure what options are available with this model but would be interested to know what could be added.All in all a very nice car that I wouldn t mind owning myself, maybe put some alloys on and a CD changer in the boot, a darker colour but hey, beggars can t be choosers       ', '    Hi ihave owned my peugoet 206 now for a few months and have found it an amazing car. I have a 3 door version which not only looks sporty, but is also big enough inside for all of my mates to fit in.It is a great car for everyone, sporty enough for young, and big enough for the family, an all round great car.This car boast group 4 insurance so cheap for most to insure but not slugish with its 1.4 engine. I drive mine everyday for a few miles at a time and it doesnt seem to use up any petrol at all.I am looking forward now to doing mine up which will make it an eye catcher and hopefully the idol car of the town.Specification of my 2061.4 engine (petrol)ABSPower SteeringRemote Central LockingAir Conditioning****** NOT THE SUNROOF MODEL*****Metallic Platinum SilverRoof SpoilerGTI Fuel CapCD PlayerAdditional  FeaturesThese cars are great for the young drivers around not only are they cheap to run but parts are widely available and easy to find. There are many peugeot garages around so i am sure you can find the items you require.The car looks smooth and stylish with only a few additional extras such as -  alloys, gti fuel cap and lexus lights which wont set u back too much.I decided against the sunroof model as they look abit weird and with AC although it uses up a little bit of petrol the overall look of the car is great increased.***** If you are looking to buy have a look at the 1.6 engine range as it is abit quicker - similar fuel consumption and only 1 insurance group higher.*****I am only 20 and Fully Comp for me on a 1.6 was only 750 compared to 700 for the 1.4 engine.This is an ideal first (for young drivers) or second family car witha roomy boot and all the things you need for a pleasant journey.According to a few websites the average miles for a Y reg pug 206 are between 30-40,000 miles and you are looking at round about    3000 for poor condition up to    5000 for excellent condition.Who the car is for  -  - The youngster - cheap, economic, ideal to modify and a great car to learn to drive in. - The family - smooth driver, ABS, good security, very spacious, fits the family and the shopping - The Business Man - Stylish, good looking, big enough inside for the 4 other business men in a stylish 5 door.     ', '    I wanted this car soooooo badly that after much persuasion my boss got me one as a company car   I was in heaven.I have never had a new car before and this was my dream.However,  I thought it would be a bit like my old 205 - nippy, reliable.  Unfortunately not so.I dread overtaking as there is just no power at all - in fact I call it  The Slug  - it takes an age to get going.The back door hinges went rusty after about a year - admittedly I don t open the back doors very often but Rust on a nearly new car      The brakes have squeaked since I have had the car   I have just got it back after the brakes not working properly   the handbrake not working (which a friend of mine has just experienced on hers too).The company are paying all repair bills as it s a company car   it s a good job too -    475 for the last service/MOT.It s such a shame as I am getting a convertiable next and would have liked the Peugeot 206 CC but will be going for an MG instead as this car, although lovely to look at, has put me off Peugeots for good.     ', '    This has to be one of the best looking cars on the road. There s an unsightly air vent on the bonnet but no car s perfect. Looks count for little when you re actually driving though and the 206 doesn t disappoints here either. I m not sure of the current price difference between this and the LX but when you can get them in the same engines why bother with the lower spec? The 1.4 engine is a little underpowered and, although it s fairly quiet, it does allow you to realise how much road noise there is (not much but it s there). The 1.6 is better and doesn t drink much more petrol. The dashboard is well laid out, reasonably well made but far, far to bulbous. A car this size should really have a dash not much above half the size of this car. Having said that, and the fact you can t seen ANY of the bonnet from any driving position, this is still probably the best supermini around - at least until the new Fiesta is launched, given Fords current form.     ', '    My 206 really is quite simply the best car i ve ever had, in metalic paint it looks absolutly fantastic  the steering is really light million times lighter than on my old clio  This makes gettin into tight spaces that bit easier.It is also extremely economical, you can fill up the tank and it lasts about 300 miles which is really good compared to my old clio.Whats great about the 206 1.4 LX is that it comes with a cd player as standard so you can really get the tunes going.It also comes with electric windows and electric door mirrors which i wouldnt be without now, it just makes driving that bit more comfortable.One bad thing about the 1.4 is the 0-60, it hasnt quite got that little bit of kick that you need when you need to overtake that car in front.     ']
filtered_hist_vote_written: ['    Normally I view cars as four wheels and engine to get me from place to place but that view has changed since I got the Jazz.  It is great little workhorse and very economical to run.On country roads I can get 50+ mpg and even driven hard on the motorways it is still very frugal on fuel.  The thing I love most about it (and the feature which made me buy it) is the flexibility of the storage.  Quite apart from the standard split rear seat etc it has this amazing feature which allows you to fold up the rear seat and create storage in the seat well for large packages, plants etc.  I expect my car to take on a lot of varied roles and the Jazz is just great at doing that.I find the roadholding excellent, it is nippy in traffic and a dream to park.  Visibility is good all round and I like the styling.  I am not surprised that it gets great reviews everywhere and scores high on customer satisfaction.Thank you Honda for a lovely little car that is fun to drive.  The only downside from my point of view is the fact that the  range  is only about 300 - 325 miles.  Personally I would have preferred 450+ but to be honest that is the only thing I can fault it on and all it means is on long journeys I just need to be aware and fill up.     ', '    I have had this scooter for about 4 months now. 1 previous owner, 3 years old, and not a fault with it yet. I have found this personally to be a very reliable 50cc, PERFECT for getting from A to B. Although like everything it will need the occassional servicing but I ve found once repaired, the parts will last a long time.As well as being a GREAT commuter, it s the type of veichle you don t feel ashamed riding. It looks stylish and slick, and whilst it is still only a 50cc  hairdryer , I have tended to find that the exhaust sound is a lot more bearable than most scooters.You should be able to pick up one of these baby s for as little as 500 pounds, and insurance for me is just 200 ish for the year (first time driver). tax is jack all. About 15 quid for the year. Also, if it is fairly new it is worth buying as it won t need its MOT for the first 3 years of its life.Uncle Harris Recommends.     ', '    Wow just to start off with, what a great little car   I bought this car second hand off my sister so, i soupose that i got a good deal with it just being a few years old and a good spec car. my version is a 1.4 SE trim. The SE trim adds, aloy wheels automatic headlamps and rain sensitive wipers (which are useful)the standard spec of this car is, alloywheelsrain sensitive wipers auto headlights remote central locking drivers and passengers airbagsABSAlarmclimate contraolair conditioning electric and heated mirrorsthe car is excellant for new or learner drivers as it is really easy to drive and with a turning circle of just above 9.8 meters its easy for parking in those tight car parks too, this car is also quite economical as i am currently getting an average of  40 mpg which is excellant considering its engine size being larger than the common 1.2 versions in other cars such as  the vauxhall corsa. im really happy with this car and im sure that it wont fail to impress you either, my advice to  you is, go book the test drive now and see for yourself However i have suffered from some minor electrical problems with this car and the garage informed me that this is quite common ??? but these were inexpensive to reapair apart form that its a cool car.The electrical faults were in the brake lighting. the brake lights were staying on even when the brake pedal was not depressed and even whilst acceleration i do soupose that this could be potentially dangerous but aparently there have been a couple of similar cases with problem s with indicators etc and this was due to fault electrical wiring. i hope this helps further      ', '    When I was younger I use to have more money to spend to buy a car, it was a good period enjoying life and having fun.The Swedish Saab 9000 for me was like a status symbol, almost a dream...and after some years saving money I could buy it.It was 1987, and I bought  a Saab 9000i 16v color silver grey, 140 HP, it costs me about 20.000     ( it was in Italian Lire).It s a powerful car,looks very good with a good acceleration and handling, but really reliable when you have to stop, and the fuel consumption was not so bad compared to others two liters.The seats are very comfortable,heated, with electric regulation.The chassis derives from the Fiat Croma, but very improved especially in aerodynamics( you know that Saab produce also component for airplanes and truck)The dashboard is complete it s seem like to drive an aeroplane.The automatic air conditioner is silent and efficent.Also people oversize (like me) can seat easily and comfortably.There were also some defect: it doesn t have a good value like used car,in few years you lose almost all the commercial value.The customer service was quite reliable, but the cost of the spare parts was really, really expensive.      ', '    I have been driving this car over a year and will really recommend you this car.First of all it is a low range car.It runs on unleaded petrol and is a tall body car.The air conditioner is amazing and cools my car within 90 seconds flat.The other reason why I chose this car is its heater,Its one of the best heaters available in cars.There are additional features steering lock and also a good storage space.Even if you store your stephanie still you have place to keep 3 huge bags.Safety wise it has seat belts for every person that would sit in a car.The power steering eases the drive.The wheels being small the car does not stick to the road and swings a bit after you reach speeds of 120 kilometres per hour.Also there are no safety bags available.There is little leg space for the back seat.Its a bit cramped.The looks are a bit tacky as it looks like a box.     ', '           What is the first thing you look for in a vehicle you are considering buying? The Rover 418 has some but not all of these features. If you’re considering the Peugeot 206 1.4, here’s a balanced take based on detailed user insights that should resonate with your practical and detail-oriented approach. 

Starting with the positives, the 206 impresses with its thoughtful features and solid build quality typical of European cars—no rattles or interior wear reported, which speaks well for its durability. The driving experience is comfortable and engaging: the ride is soft yet corners confidently, with light steering and smooth gear changes. The driver’s seat and steering wheel offer multiple adjustments, ensuring good support and comfort, especially for longer drives. Fuel economy is another strong point, with averages around 40-50 mpg depending on driving style, and a tank that can last over 1,000 miles in mixed conditions—great for keeping running costs low. Safety-wise, it includes both driver and passenger airbags, with the passenger airbag easily deactivated, which adds flexibility. The boot space is generous and practical, featuring flexible rear seat folding and a clever secret compartment under the front passenger seat, ideal for everyday errands or weekend trips.

On the flip side, the 1.4 engine can feel underpowered on steep hills or narrow lanes, requiring frequent gear changes—something to keep in mind if you often drive in hilly areas. Some minor annoyances include heated wing mirrors that aren’t electrically adjustable and a lack of an internal door lock button, which might affect convenience. Also, some boot fittings are flimsy, and there have been reports of rear window misalignment causing dampness inside, so a thorough pre-purchase inspection is advisable. The GLX trim offers nice extras like digital climate control and a 6-CD changer, but it lacks modern audio features like shuffle or random play, which might feel dated.

Overall, the Peugeot 206 1.4 is a stylish, reliable, and economical choice if you prioritize comfort, practicality, and low running costs, but be prepared for modest engine performance and a few small quirks. It holds its value well, making it a sensible buy for those who appreciate a well-rounded, no-nonsense hatchback.

', '       PETROL SOON TO COST AS MUCH AS YOUR PINT     read an alarmist tabloid headline of a couple of decades or so ago. Well, if you could find me a garage dispensing a gallon of fuel for the price of a beer these days, I   d shower you with all my worldly goods and offer to have your babies, or at least start a few off, leaving a false name and address as I get    me kecks    back on (men need not apply for this position).I don   t want to get embroiled into the    UK motorists pay the highest price for petrol under Labour    debate, for the simple reason that high fuel tax is here to stay, neither major party has done anything to reduce it, and unless you are fully acquainted with the entire tax regime, of, say France, then comparing a litre    here    for a litre    over there    is irrelevant.Besides which, petrol is a finite resource, its use pollutes the atmosphere and is a health risk, particularly in the field of respiration. You could argue that it SHOULD cost a lot under these circumstances, since we are, in effect paying a licence to use a    poison   .Whatever you think of the Chancellor, it therefore makes extreme good sense, both economic and environmental, to use as little petrol as possible. There are of course several ways in which this could be achieved. Below are a few of my suggestions.THOSE PESKY SHORT JOURNEYSBear in mind that it is the short journeys with relatively cold engines that cause a disproportionate percentage of local pollution. I   ve heard it said that the    school run    accounts for 10  of traffic-generated pollution. Another little publicised fact is that the air quality inside a car in a traffic jam is worse than that outside, so if you thought you were doing your children   s health a favour by running them down the road to school, think again. I realise that in the case of schools with a wide or rural catchment area, then to do otherwise wouldn   t be practical, but those of us who live in towns, with the school half a mile away, could start to address this. After all, as the Countryside Campaigners are quick to point out, we outnumber them. It therefore follows that we can have the greatest effect on the environment, for good OR bad.A cold engine will be running on choke, or its equivalent, which is, in itself inefficient, as extra    neat    petrol is added to the normal mixture of fuel and air, called the fuel/air ratio. This even happens in hot weather, as long as the engine has not been used for a long time. Diesel users have no need to be smug here, as anyone who has seen a cold diesel started will attest. Well, that   s just the point - you CAN   T see a cold diesel being started sometimes, thanks to the smokescreen being emitted from the back  Before the Citroen BX Tdi Owner   s Club lynches me, I would point out that not all diesels are like this, but they do add their own unique form of pollution to the air in the form of    particulates        I think they mean soot Anyway, all cars will go through some sort of inefficient start-up process, every time they are used from cold. In the case of a longer journey, this is a necessary evil, which gets better after five or ten minutes, but as the government-sponsored TV commercials exhort us, walking or cycling to the corner shop to buy a Sunday paper would be so much more healthy all round AND money saving.    Couch potatoes    could even decide not to bother at all     well done guys, Britain is proud of its slobs, and needs more like you  Another approach would be to combine this short trip with a longer one, stopping off to buy the paper whilst off on that other weekend religious experience, out-of-town shopping  However, out-of-town shopping brings its own pollution problems, but killing two birds with one stone would be a start.PLAN AHEADMy current part-time work with schools in a neighbouring borough leads me to plot a new road route nearly every week. Unfortunately, to get to the Richmond area from the Hounslow area has one limiting factor called The Thames, limiting my fording of it to either of Kew or Richmond Bridges. The fact that they want me to start at 9.15 am doesn   t help either, as the    mini rush hour    created by the school run is only then subsiding.My own car has a fuel computer, which can be reset before every journey to allow for the fuel consumption, and average speed to be calculated. What is most surprising, even in the most dense stop-start conditions, is that I can even achieve more than 30 m.p.g. at all, let alone exceed it by 5-10 m.p.g. However, what is most interesting is that the route which FEELS the most inefficient by being longer, is in fact more fuel efficient, to such an extent, that not only is the m.p.g. reading higher, but when you come to calculate how much actual fuel has been used, it really is less. For example, route    a    which is 5.4 miles, gives me 32 m.p.g., whilst route    b    which is 6 miles gives me close on 40 m.p.g. Therefore, despite the disparity in route length,    b    costs me 0.15 gallons compared to    a   s    0.17. Ok, so the saving is 2  of a gallon, but multiply that by 2 for the return journey, and by the number of times I make that journey, and it starts to add up to some real savings.On a larger scale, for instance, my recent trek to the Scottish borders, getting up early enough to leave home in West London and be through the Birmingham area before 8 a.m. helps to conserve fuel, since a car sitting in a jam at the confluence of the M   s 5 and 6 is achieving Zero m.p.g., and polluting the good people of Birmingham   s air for no reason. I have only ever achieved a smooth transit through this area by employing this tactic     at all other times, IT WILL be congested. I have ceased to use the various road check services, since on any long journey, you can guarantee that at least one scheduled and probably one un-scheduled delay will occur. If you pay heed to Delete or information telephone numbers, you   d never go out  Too much information can get very depressing.A SLIPPERY CAR FIT FOR PURPOSEAssuming that a large part of your journey will involve passing through still air quickly (we hope ), it make sense to check that your car is offering as little resistance to being moved as possible. Correct tyre pressures relative to the load carried are vital, both to fuel economy, general wear and tear, and safety. I wonder just how many people give their tyres anything other than a cursory    nope, they   re all still up    glance. Carry as much luggage as possible inside the vehicle     a roof rack carries its own fuel economy premium just by being there. Loaded badly, it   s even worse, and if you find yourself putting the rack on, just to squeeze that bit extra on board, maybe a rethink is needed. Does Junior REALLY have to take his ghetto blaster and X-Box with him? If on a touring holiday, the rack will no doubt stay there once you   ve unloaded the car, costing you dearly over a two-week period of motoring in the Dordogne. Likewise, carrying bikes is problematical. On the roof, they are exposed to the wind, but at least they are end on, whereas carried across the back of the car, they are out of the main blast, but sideways to what air does flow over the tailgate. I   ve got a folding bike in the boot, so I   m not really qualified to comment on which is best. At least if you   re carrying bikes, then by implication, you won   t be burning petrol all the time once at your destination  When choosing new tyres, try to get those that claim to be eco-friendly, with ensuing fuel savings. Tyres that improves m.p.g.? Yes, even though radial-ply tyres, now almost universal, are more compliant and flexible than the older stiffer cross-plies, there is still some room for improvement. Some brands of tyre now claim to decrease the car   s resistant to being propelled, with ensuing fuel savings of around 6 . This may be done by improving sidewall flexibility, or by using different rubber compositions. Do check that any different rubber compound doesn   t carry a reduced grip penalty, or at least be forewarned. The payback on such a saving will be quite long, but if you are changing your tyres anyway, why not give it a try?As for the fuel penalty imposed by running air conditioning, as you speed down to Nice, you may like to bear this in mind. According to my fuel computer, using a/c at 60 M.P.H. costs me 10  more fuel, compared to a car with its windows closed, without the a/c running. However, who would drive with the windows closed in these hot conditions? Therefore the penalty is not so great whilst cruising at speed, because a car with no a/c and its windows open is not as aerodynamic, and the comparative loss from using a/c is more like 5 . You also benefit from a more hushed    office    which may lead to your driving less frenetically.Of course, at low speeds, a/c really does start to cost you, and I try to use good old fashioned outside air until I   m getting uncomfortable. Since the system stays cold for a minute or so, why not switch it off a couple of miles from journey   s endBUT I THOUGHT TECHNOLOGY WAS GOING TO BE THE ANSWER TO EVERYTHINGYes, so did I. According to    Tomorrow   s World   , we   d all have chimneybreast sized slim-line TV screens now costing    125. Well, they got the size bit right, but stick a couple of noughts on the price.It has to be said that technology has created a lot of potential for fuel efficiency, but in the US case, this saving has been squandered on the purchase of ever more powerful cars, the    recreational vehicle    being a case in point. We in Europe have no need to be smug either. In the 70   s, when a Ford Cortina had a 1600 c.c. engine pushing out 70-odd brake horse power, fuel consumption would have been around 35 m.p.g. Now what do we have? 2-litre Mondeos, pushing out well over 100 b.h.p., and still capable of similar consumption. All very impressive, but in the meantime, Mother Nature is still coughing her lungs out.To be fair, technology has advanced over the years I   ve owned cars. Many of the retro-fit devices from the 70   s, are now de-rigueur. An example is the engine-cooling fan. 30 years ago, cars had cooling fans driven directly off the fan belt. Yes, that   s why it was called that. This shouldn t come as too much of a shock as all these reviews seemed to have been written by rich, right wing Republican voters.  I would hope that few on this side of the Atlantic would harbour similar hopes of a flat rate of income tax.  But just to be sure, I feel the need to spell out why flat taxes are a very bad thing.The main reason for this is that any form of flat tax is regressive.  When a rich man buys petrol or a pack of cigarettes, he is technically paying more in real terms than a man or woman on a lesser income.  This does not sound particularly fair to me.Obviously VAT is important revenue for the government.  But its importance comes down to politics more than to finance.  There are plenty of progressive taxation plans that could bring in revenue to the treasury.  What the Tories call  Stealth Taxes  are an essential tool in staying in government for any political party.  Few take notice of these taxes and so governments can get away with introducing them without losing voters.On the other hand, a government who raises income tax by any significant amount will find themselves liable to be out of office very soon.  But this is a massive shame as a rise in income tax and a reduction in things like fuel duties would do the poverty gap no end of good.  If income tax was raised for the richest and slightly lowered for the poorest, maybe a Prime Minister could justly declare that we are all middle class.The rich would be up in arms at such a tax hike, but their decrease in income would only be for so long.  Increased wealth amongst the masses, or more precisely, increased disposable income would inevitably lead to an increase in spending in goods and services.  These are the very goods and services that the richest in the land control.  This in turn would increase revenue from the richest band of taxation and the circle of wealth would rotate again.What this would do for inflation might not be particularly good, but responsible measures by the Bank of England should curb trouble.  This is a simple plan written in simple form, but I believe it could be effective.  Whether you agree or not, I hope you have enjoyed reading it. The savings for the environment are immeasurable and beyond financial considerations. > - > - > - > - > > - > - > - > - > - > REDUCING FUEL CONSUMPTION. *************************Ever since a price was first placed on fuel, products have been introduced to the market claiming improved fuel consumption, some of which have undoubtedly enjoyed a degree of success. Owners of vehicles can maximize economy by simple maintenance, servicing and driving style. But of course in the real world mechanical parts and tyres do wear, driving conditions change and our driving style is not always as economical as it could be. Vehicles are not always serviced, as often as they should, and once they are serviced carbon deposits will immediately start to build up resulting in a reduction of efficiency. What will be the benefit of fitting an EcoFlow MAGNET to YOUR car fuel line? Improved combustion will provide greater power. This power can be used to go further (fuel economy) or to go quicker (better performance). The engine will run cleaner allowing parts such as catalytic converters which can be very expensive to replace, to last longer. As well as saving money on fuel and parts, fitting a magnet will help the environment by minimising exhaust pollution. Benefits will NOT be immediately apparent, as there is a need for a   8217;saturation  8217; period. 1,000 miles (1600 km.) should be allowed for a petrol engine and 3,000 miles (4,800 km.) for a diesel engine. Fitting a magnet will not allow the use of unleaded fuel as a replacement for leaded fuel unless mechanical modifications are also made. > - > - > - > - > > - > - > - > - > - > HOW DOES IT WORK? *****************The powerfull magnets ionise the fuel by directing a specific and powerful static magnetic field right into the fuel supply line. Through a process known as magnetohydrodynamics the fuels ability to combine with oxygen improves and greater energy is released from the fuel. > - > - > - > - > > - > - > - > - > - > AT WHAT PRICE? **************Our dependence on oil and gas to fuel our transport, heating and industry continues to grow, providing ever-increasing revenue and power to the companies that provide the fuel. A catalytic converter produces more carbon dioxide, the gas that is responsible for the greenhouse effect and the one that governments continually promise to reduce. This is due to a variety of reasons, one of which is the mighty power that the US public in general wield which we are lacking in this country. If we go back to the 1970 s and the two famous Oil Price Shocks in which the prices of oil were hiked up by the major oil producers in the Middle East, we can gauge what happened in our country and Europe in general compared to the USA.We had to increase petrol prices by a massive amount to compensate for the extreme hike in price of crude oil from which our petroleum is obtained. This was no-one s fault but the oil sheiks who realized that oil was going to run out at some point in the near future and therefore wanted to guarantee and increase their massive fortunes. Of course the natural progression was to pass the increase on to the consumer as simple economic theory dictates, and this is in fact what happened throughout Europe.So, what if we compare this situation to the US? Well, the people simply refused to pay this higher price for their petrol, and eventually the government had to climb down and subsidise the price in order to keep consumers happy. This can partially be explained by the massive size of the US - it is not uncommon for people to drive interstate, or across 2 or 3 states which are all the size of England or larger in a couple of days, and also they see the freedom of their cars as part of th good old American Way.Therefore, comparisons with the United States are irrelevant and futile. This subsidy of petrol despite hundreds and even thousands of percent increases in production was what sent their budget into a spiralling downturn leading to their national debt accelerating into the trillions. Is this the kind of problem people want to put the UK in?Now I would like to address the common misconception that people are paying over the odds for petrol. It is without a doubt very true that the government enforces a huge levy on fuel, but this is not to say that this in unfair. Cars are extremely harmful to the environment, and anyone who remarks that road tax is there to pay for the upkeep of roads is clearly extremely misinformed about exactly how much it costs to build and maintain only one mile of motorway. The basic stem of the problem is that people see it as their private right to own a car and drive it wherever they want to, without giving any considerations to social welfare.It is not commonly known that the social cost, i.e. the total burden imposed on society, of an individual travelling from A to B is very often far greater than the cost the individual incurs in road tax, petrol, insurance and depreciation. People give little consideration to the problems of pollution, and by this I mean noise pollution and emission of noxious gases, and just how much it costs society to reduce these important problems.It is often said that a price cannot be put on pollution, but from an economic sense this is not necessarily the case. If it costs the government x million a year to subsidise a firm in order that they use more environmentally-friendly production methods, and this reduces their output of pollution by amount y, then we can indeed come up with a theoretical price. Why should the government subsidise such schemes, you ask? Well, why should people be allowed to drive as much as they like with only petrol prices to put them off?In conclusion, it should be remembered that travelling privately and owning your own vehicles are great priveleges that are conferred upon us as a result of us having an industrialized economy. This car was also four years old and had already 100,000 km on the clock  Inside the instruments are basic but effective. Seating support was excellent although my friends thought rear legroom was a little restrictive for a grown adult. The boot was more then adequate for four peoples weekend luggage. Having driven a good number of more expensive family saloons, both petrol and diesel, i feel entitled to offer my opinion on this car and can only say if you are in the market for a diesel family saloon and you don t test drive this one the last laugh will definatley be on you.     ', '    When you think of Toyota, you think of a trampy Toyota Corolla. Well not this car, the soft top is beautiful, the interior impressive and the drive a thrill. I have owned a Toyota Celica for 8 years and I imported it from America I thought it was so beautiful, in fact the police pull me over so many times, just to have a look at it. They give lame excuses that  your licence plate is illegal  then I put them straight that I ve been through court and proved thats it legal so they p1ss off. The car has a lot of room in the front and an amazingly large boot, but the back seats aren t exactly big, and terrible for all you randy people out there, unless you like it squashed. Now after 8 years, it is still going strong and we have passed every MOT without any modification except a seatbelt that had been caught in the door. Overall a great car, with great endurance, the speed is improving with good acceleration. The look is very impressive and eye catching. It makes showing off so much easier. The new version do have a car alarm too, which is lacked in mine.     ', '    I owned a L reg 1994 corsa 1500 diesel which I bought four years ago for    4000.I sold the five door hatchback in October 2000 for    1850.When I bought the car it had 55000 miles on the clock and when I sold it I had done nearly 30000 miles in it and it only let me down twice (both times the same fault on the alternator burning out).    The car was slow upto 30MPH, but was lively after that upto about 80MPH.The greatest thing about the car is the fuel economy, it return 55 mpg plus all the time.Servicing was a pain, every 4500 miles you need to change both oil and filter.I would recommend you to pay the extra for PAS, as the steering is very heavy without.Three door cars in dull non metallic colours do not sell very well, but make an excellant cheap car.    Space inside is fine, even for me and Im over 6 foot 2 tall.The interior of the car has a well build feel, but its nothing to get excited about.The stereo even on the basic merit model was a quality sound from the four speaker set up.The car doesnot come with any electric toys , but window operation is light and it has mirrors with can be adjusted inside the car.Make sure if you buy one the engine is not smokey and if your not sure about the timing belt condition get it changed.It should only cost    100 pounds at the most.....its a lot cheaper than a new engine.     ', '    To call What Car? a magazine seems a little unfair - it is in fact a giant tome of motoring statistics published monthly.As a car buyers guide it has reasonable coverage fo the months new entrants to the UK car market, and three or four road tests or group tests along with a couple of features on safety or car security etc.The strenght of this magazine is its impressivly in depth and well laid out facts and figures listing.Every new car is listed detailing price, equipment, performance and economy. The databse of information is vast and accurate.However much of the detail is unchanged month to month so the regular purchase seems expensive at over    3 a copy. This magazine serves as a good reference for someone looking to purchase a new car who wants background before vising the showrooms or as a bi-annual purchase for the car buff,     ', '    Now that the Formula One season is in full swing, I have noticed the sells of Autosport has increased at my local newsagents, but what is this magazine about? Autosport is a weekly journal that covers most aspects of motor racing; from Formula One to Club Level and Rally racing. Vintage racing and Tin Tops are not forgotten either, making Autosport one of the most comprehensive magazines for the motor sport enthusiast to read in the UK today.Within its many pages there are interviews with the drivers, teams and even commentators within the sport. Autosport cost only    2.30 weekly. There are special editions produced, which cover the magazine  8217;s Birthday, New Season  8217;s Guides, for example.Auto Sport has its own website. This provides more in-depth information about auto motor sport. The journal as well as the website provide feature and reports, plus club news information. The magazine  8217;s articles tend to range from single paragraph articles up to approximately two pages long on average stories, with a wide selection of high quality photographs. It is written in a manner that is easy to understand. If technical language is used then an explanation is given.There are also competitions to enter and the public is encouraged to contribute in the form of a Letters Page. As with all glossy magazines there are the ubiquitous adverts, but how this magazine differs, is that anyone can place an advert in the classified section. There is a market place for selling racing cars as well as an Appointments page towards the end of the periodical.Autosport is well worth a look if you are into motor racing, but do not expect to find go-carting or hot-rods in this book, as you will need to purchase another publication.Web site address: www.autosport.com     ', '    The new drink driving ads have appeared on our TV screens.Our favourite christmas songs serve as the soundtrack to these extremely hard hitting visuals of road traffic accidents. Some still photography and some video clips run for approx one minute to show the devastating effects of drink driving.You see cars so badly torn apart that it is likely no-one would have been rescued alive, and the horrified expressions on the emergency service members faces sum up the total devastation of the whole situation. You see people covered in blood, trapped in wreckage so twisted and crushed that you can hardly imagine it ever to have been a car.The slogan to this years campaign...This is one christmas tradition we could do without.The only problem with this campaign, as with most drink drive ads, is that with the content being so graphic the ads tend only to be shown in the later part of the evening and unfortunately the majority of people who drink drive will either be down the pub or so drunk already that they wont get the message.I understand that we do not want our children unnecesarily exposed to and upset by these horrific sights but i really feel the ads need to be screened before the drink drivers hit the road.     ', '    Ive been member of the TSB motoring club now for 5 years, and this was the first time I had to use them on Saturday.Normally I have a car which I well service myself up to a high standard.If I breakdown I can normally get myself going again.  But on Saturday some little toerag decided to pinch my sporty looking 1600 Fiesta.After the police where informed a think the driver panicked when he saw a police car and decided to drive of across a field, but because of metal barriers the car didnot want to go, so it fell to bits in a bad way.  The police where going to arrange recovery but warned me if I didnot claim on my insurance they would charge me for picking up the vehicle.I rang Green flag and they asked the right details about what had happened.I think because they asked was the vehicle free wheeling.They sent the right kind of truck that could move it easily.This was arranged free of charge.   I found the telephone to be answered very quickly and both the operator and wagon driver very very helpful.The wagon arrived after only 35 minutes,which I thought was excellant.    Im glad I had the cover which cost about    12.00 per month which I can pay by direct debit on two cars and covers me for even home breakdowns.They give me a good 50 percent discount on the second car.   As I said its the first time Ive ever had the need to call them, but was pleased about the completely hassle free collection.       ', '    We bought our Honda Civic 1.5i VTEC-E in 1997 when it was 7 months old, but just had delivery mileage. Our local Perth dealer (Weir Honda) were offering what was a nearly new car with around    1500 off the new price.  We knew from looking at comparative prices that this was a good deal and managed to get mudflaps and carpet mats fitted as well.Broadly the experience has been very good - the dealer has been helpful in sorting out several minor problems. These were rattle in top end of the engine (a minor adjustment), a missing jacking point on the rear nearside, a silencer which gave out after 2 years  use, squeaky ventilation fan and a stuck sunroof (x2).  None of these prevented the car from running and all were fixed free of charge.  In the case of the silncer they really did not have to do this but decided to offer a replacement ex-gratia.In terms of running it offers excellent fuel economy at an average 40-42mpg, with the engine tuned for this. But it also offers a reasonable amount of performanc from the VTEC engine when overtaking power is needed.  Interior space and boot space are good and almost equivalent to the Accord.  Open road handling is sharp and it is well-behaved in town, with good weighting on the power steering and a slick gear change. Brakes are good - not too sharp on application bit they do anchor well.  A downside is the build quality as regards rattles and squeaks from the boot area and windscreen respectively. However we like the car so just ignore these minus points.      ', '    20 years ago I passed my bike test and have ridden alot of bikes in the past. However I have had a family and steered away from them until recently.Wanting to get back into bikes but not over powering myself I opted for a T reg Kawasaki GPZ500s. It was cheap enough to buy considering a lot of other makes and models of a similar size and age were more expensive.Then I found out why.The 17  wheel does absolutley nothing for handling. It was not the kind of bike to drop to the knees on an open bend, it was the type of bike to slide where it wanted to.She started first time though I did find the starter switch slightly sticky,perhaps a common fault with Kawasaki. Fuel consumption I found to be no more than an average car. I felt I had to put in as much petrol as I did if I used my car to travel to and from work.Her one advantage was comfort. I could of ridden it all day. The seat was well shaped and I found my botty fitted snuggly. The handle bars were not too far apart which I have found with other models.With this in mind my relationship with this model was short.The style was good, looked a sporty kind of bike but lacked acceleration, constant speed and  general oomph. To top it all the piant work was to say the least tacky.For getting back into bikes or if you are just starting out consider something else, A Bandit, or CBR600 gives you the balance and the street cred. Admittedly these are slightly more expensive but you do as they say get what you pay for     ', '    A new revolutionary method of paying for your car insurance may well be available to European motorists by 2001.  Pay-As-You-Drive , where drivers pay rates varying between 0.9 and 5 pence a mile instead of an annual premium, is already available to U.S. motorists. Using new G.P.S.(Global Positioning Satellite) technology to track vehicles, the insurance is then charged out by the mile or by the minute. The rates charged would vary depending on the age and experience of the driver, and higher rates would be charged for city and night driving, when most accidents take place. By contrast, motorists driving on mainly rural roads and during daylight hours, would pay much-reduced rates. This system has many attractions for the  low mileage  motorist, who covers less than say 5,000 miles per year. Several major insurers are considering piloting this scheme next year, and it is envisaged many motorists will save up to 25 per cent on their annual premium. But some safety experts have cast doubts on the scheme. They fear that the  by-the-minute  fees will encourage speeding, with many drivers trying to save money by making their journeys faster.      ', '     When s the next bus?    Ooooh, maybe Thursday. Okay, I exaggerate slightly. But only slightly. Because the car versus public transport element of the petrol price debate is a complete red herring. In geographical terms, the substantially greater part of the UK simply doesn t have a public transport option.I could walk five and a half miles to the nearest public transport route, to catch one of the three busses a day. Of course I could. Would you?I could maybe hitch the forty two miles to my nearest railway station. Would you? Would John Prescott or Gordon Brown?And then I hear the arguement, But you chose to live in a rural area, you could move to a town or city. But this is where my work is, and anyway, I would actually prefer not to contribute to the decline of rural Britain.I know of one community (and there are many more) on the shores of Loch Hourn in the West of Scotland, which is fifty six miles from the nearest bus route. They also have among the highest petrol prices in Britain.The fuel price question is about much more than how far our personal pound goes. It s about whether our rural communities live or die.And I appreciate that, if you live in the city, this may seem like a whinge. But if our rural communities continue to be strangled, you re going to have to settle for eating French beef, imported vegetables, and holidaying in ghost towns.     ']

s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
The ongoing petrol versus diesel debate reveals some frustrating contradictions, especially when you dig beneath the surface of government policies and market realities. Despite diesel cars generally being more fuel-efficient and producing lower emissions than petrol counterparts, drivers who opt for these greener diesels often face heavier taxation—both through company car tax rules and increased diesel fuel levies. It’s a classic case of policy lagging behind technology, where governments seem more focused on revenue generation than genuinely promoting environmental progress.

What really stands out is how green taxes are frequently used as a cash cow rather than a tool to improve public transport infrastructure. This is particularly ironic given that many people rely on cars out of necessity, not choice—poor public transport options and safety concerns leave them little alternative. So, while diesel vehicles offer better mileage and lower emissions, the government’s approach penalizes these choices, pushing some drivers back toward petrol or even less efficient options.

Adding to the complexity, both governments and manufacturers appear to stall the adoption of advanced green technologies, likely to protect existing revenue streams and profits. This delay undermines the potential for cleaner, safer, and more efficient vehicles to reach the market sooner. It’s a frustrating dynamic for anyone who values performance and environmental responsibility but also wants fair treatment and sensible policies.

In sum, while diesel cars currently offer a compelling balance of efficiency and lower emissions, the heavier taxation and policy inconsistencies create a confusing landscape for consumers. For those of us who care about safety, value, and environmental impact, it’s clear that the debate isn’t just about fuel types—it’s about aligning incentives, improving public transport, and pushing innovation rather than protecting outdated revenue models. Until then, choosing the “best” fuel option remains a nuanced decision, shaped as much by politics as by engineering.

product_reviews: ['    The HP 364 ink cartridges are of great quality and I was very impressed with their performance all round. They are currently selling at Amazon for around    5.50 each or    20 for a set of four, which sounds quite expensive, but is much cheaper than the cartridges we have had to buy for previous printers we have had.The HP Photosmart Printer C309g uses five cartridges at a time     one each of cyan, magenta and yellow plus two black cartridges. (One of the black cartridges is for photos, the other for general use.) The cartridges are colour-coordinated and have a little image of a different shape on each one too, so you can easily see which cartridge is which colour. They are small and compact rectangular cartridges, which come with a plastic clip you have to break off to expose the ink. You lift up the main body of the printer, then the cartridge unit comes out from behind its protective cover. At this point, you can place each cartridge into its designated slot, until all five are positioned correctly. You can tell they are accurately positioned as there is an audible click when they are inserted properly. They are then ready to use and the cartridge unit will return to its original position out of sight.The packaging on the cartridges suggests they have enough ink in them to print between 250 and 300 pages of text or 20 photos. It didn   t smudge afterwards either nor did the print rub off onto anything else. We scanned documents and again these were lovely and clear without any problems. On these, the ink did not absorb properly and parts of it rubbed off onto our fingers afterwards. So our lesson was learnt     only use HP photo paper with HP ink cartridges and an HP Photosmart printer After using the ink cartridges for three weeks, I did not notice a discernible difference between the quality of the items I printed at the start and those towards the end of the period. ', '    I can still recall my first ever printer; a unsightly bulky machine with equally unappealing ink cartridges. This was, for me, not too much of a problem to begin with. Well to answer my own question, I should have cared for the welfare of my poor family who had to tackle replacing fiddly ink cartridges with a lack of good instructions. Anxiety stricken, they d strap on the goggles and protective gloves, ready to tackle yet another annoying ink cartridge, prodding and poking in the hope that it would just  fall  into place...Okay, so perhaps I am blowing things out of proportion a tad. I ve always had printers only needed just one or two ink cartridges. Why? Well I guess I always just presumed that if the printer needed more than this, it would become far too expensive and not at all worth the money. I can now hold my hand up though and say that having tried and tested a group of ink cartridges which work as one, I could not have been more wrong. I hang my head in shame at my naivety.I had always heard words of positivity buzzing around the  HP  brand. Most people I know would recommend them in a flash. Unfortunately I had never had the chance to try out their ink, until more recently, and this occasion was to change my opinion forever. The particular ink in question is the 364 option, which is compatible with a variety of HP Photosmart printers (B8550,C53244,C5380,C63244,C6380, and D5460). I note that it is not listed on the side of the packaging, however they work with my printer model, which is C309g. In the complete          Pictures of HP Photosmart 364 Ink Cartridges     ', '    It was my good fortune recently to be asked to test Original HP Photosmart 364 Ink Cartridges.  I have previously experienced HP Ink Cartridges in a work environment and I was aware of their reputation regarding quality and longevity but had been using cheaper cartridges recently at home (as finances sadly dictate)     would the superior HP quality be evident when I tested them?The cartridges themselves are pretty dinky     the colour cartridges are only the size of a chunky credit card.  They are also clean and virtually idiot-proof to install     even for a post-natal, hormonal, sleep-deprived tester such as myself.  Just pull the tag to remove the cover, snap the orange plastic tab and slot to place.  I   m just about the clumsiest person I know and even I managed to fit the cartridges without dirtying my hands.So I   ve fitted my new ink cartridges     now to print   Luckily, I   ve just had a new baby and there are lots of printing opportunities so off we go   .PhotographsAnyone who has visited my homepage recently will have seen the images of our gorgeous new son and I wasted no time in printing off a variety of photographs of both him and his big sisters for the doting grandparents, aunts, uncles and great Grandma. No waiting for them to dry either, they are instantly safe to handle.  To my mind, the quality of the prints is superior that of the prints that my husband obtained recently from our local supermarket photoshop.Colour PrintingI also printed a number of photographs on ordinary printer paper as a small collage incorporated within personalised stationery for writing Thank You letters.  Although you do lose some of the sharpness of the images due to the more porous nature of the paper, the colour was still very true to the original photographs.  As we have been inundated with gifts for our new arrival, I produced a substantial stock of this stationery and there was no discernable difference in quality between copy number one and copy number thirty.Black and White Documents I used the ink to print off a number of pages with predominantly black text     spreadsheets of financial information. I found that the printing was still very clear and precise, and again, there was no smudging or    bleeding    of the print. My two five year old independent quality control inspectors declared them to be    Excellent      A ringing endorsement indeed, from two very fussy wee girls.Longevity I have taken full advantage of the cartridges provided to me for testing and I have printed a LOT. (I will update my review if, and eventually when, I am required to replace my cartridges)Overall  Obviously the overall quality of the printing achieved is dependent on printer and paper quality as well as the ink used, but I am very impressed with the HP Photosmart 364 ink cartridges.  No, they are not the cheapest ink cartridges but they are high quality and long lasting     this is one instance where you definitely get what you pay for.Technical Bits   BobsHP Ink Cartridge     Photosmart 364For HP Photosmart B8550, C5324, C5380, C6324, C6380, D5460, HP Photosmart Plus, HP Photosmart PremiumBlack     from    6.31Photo Black     from    5.21Magenta     from    5.37Yellow     from    5.24Cyan     from    5.37All prices include VAT but exclude P P charges and are taken from https://h30042.www3.hp.com/SureSupply/CountrySelection.do 1Photosmart Ink Cartridges also available in XL version which yield over twice as many pages/photos     ', '           Introduction Some time ago whilst reading a number of product reviews on this site, unusually for me, a banner headline caught my attention which was requesting HP product testers.  All you had to do was fill in a few simple details about yourself, provide details of your current printer and that was it.  In all honesty I didn   t expect to hear anything further regarding the test, so imagine my surprise when out of the blue on the afternoon of 1st July I received a telephone call advising that I had been specially selected to form part of the testing team. So what is the catch The only catch, if you can call it that, is that I have to use the HP 364 ink cartridges and then write a review of the actual cartridges.  The plus point is that I get to use a brand new photosmart printer for doing so, so I knew it was the perfect opportunity to print out all those photos which I had been waiting to take to the local developers because my current printer was not suitable for the task in hand.  I initially was under the impression that I would be loaned the printer for the duration of the test, but I was advised that it would be mine to keep after the review had finished. As I had thus only experienced both the joys (and frustrations) of an  quot;All-in-One quot; colour cartridge          Pictures of HP Photosmart 364 Ink Cartridges     ', '          Ink, yawn Ink is not very exciting. Ink manufacturers and dealers of the world may pronounce a jihad on me for pointing it out but most people will probably agree that it   s not easy to get excited by ink. It   s something I spend no more than a few minutes a year thinking about but as a result of taking part in a Ciao    product test    on HP printer cartridges, I   m now using at least the next 20 years worth of    ink-think    time to tell you about the HP 364 range of cartridges.The idea of writing about ink filled me with the desire to file my credit card bills or start work on my tax return     two things I put off as long as I possibly can. I checked Ciao to see if I could glean any tips on how to write about printer cartridges and I discovered that hardly anybody writes about such things. Lots of cartridges are listed but few are reviewed. Why? I go back to my opening statement,    Ink is not very exciting   . Printers are fun, the stuff they print may be of great interest, and major importance but ink itself has the same role in the finished printed item that diesel does in a trip to the seaside     it   s an enabler, something than makes the final outcome of a glossy picture or a Cornetto on the beach possible, but in each case, something that we tend to take for granted until it goes wrong.Me and InkIt   s been said that computer printer ink is more expensive gram for gram than gold, heroin, saffron and every other bench-mark of expensiveness. I don   t know if it   s true and I don   t actually care but I   m very mean about buying ink.  I have a cheap Dell printer that takes a single multi-colour cartridge. I   ve had it for two and a half years and I   m on my third cartridge so I   m not what you could call a    heavy user   . I buy cartridges as rarely as I can get away with, eking out every last drop until I   m printing in a strange shade of light mauve. If my printer can leave any kind of mark on the page, then that   s good enough for me. When that fails, I   ll google for cheap knock-offs and comparison shop like a demon to get the best deal, buy three or four new cartridges and then I   ll forget about ink completely until the next time     a long while later     when I can no longer read my documents at all. At work I have the privilege of unfettered access to multiple laser printers. So if I need to do some more serious printing I   ll do it at work. At home I very rarely print anything that needs to be of high quality. I do the occasional boarding pass when I   ve forgotten to do it at work, print maps, occasionally fire off a few pages from the          Pictures of HP Photosmart 364 Ink Cartridges     ', '          IntroductionAs a user of HP inks for 20 years since the days of the Deskjet 500, I have always been impressed with the excellent quality of the output.  When I took delivery of my new Photosmart printer, it gave me the chance to test out HP   s newest ink brand, simply known as the 364 ink.  My previous printer, the Photosmart 3210 ran on the HP Vivera 363 ink which gave me excellent results.InstallationThere are five different colours of the 364 ink, namely Photo Black, Magenta, Cyan, Yellow and Black.  The beauty of having different cartridges for each colour means that when you run out of a colour, you only need to replace that one as opposed to replacing the entire colour cartridge as you would need to with certain other types of ink.Installing the cartridges is a quick and easy job.  Once you have taken one out of its packaging and snapped it away from its protective plastic base you just push it into the correct bay in the print tray until it clicks into place.  That   s all there is to it, once you have done this for all the cartridges you need to replace, you are ready to print.Photo PrintingPhoto printing has come a long way in the past five years or so.  When printing photos with earlier inks it was obvious which was the original and which was the copy as printer inks were not far enough advanced to produce the true colours that a professionally developed photograph would give.  Slowly, ink manufacturers have got their act in order and are now producing almost identical photographs to the original.  The HP 364 ink is a frontrunner in this area as photographs printed onto  dedicated HP premium photo paper, when placed side by site with the original look identical.  In some cases, the only way to tell them apart is to look on the back of the photo for any HP logo or any other distinctive feature, the quality is really that good.A problem with inkjet ink is that it has always taken a while to dry, meaning that if you pick up your printout too soon, you leave a nice fingermark or smudge on your photograph which means you either have to live with the consequences or print out another copy, using up extra ink which is not going to prove popular.  The HP 364 ink appears to be very fast drying.  If you attempt to pick up your newly printed photograph within 10-15 seconds of it dropping into the tray, you will find that it is completely dry and ready to show off to friends and family.Document PrintingThe standard black printer cartridge is very impressive.  As someone who produces lots of professional looking documents, I took the liberty of comparing the output from my HP 364 ink with that from an original HP toner in the HP Laserjet M2727 printer.  In the past, the quality of output from laser printers has been significantly better than the output from inkjet inks.  With the 364 ink, this is no longer the case.  Characters are perfectly formed on the page and the document still looks extremely professional.  Add colour images and texts to the document and the combination of inks works really well with no bleeding or unintentional mixing of colours.Printing on different quality paperAs with any ink, the key to producing high quality documents usually comes down to the type of paper you print on.  The same is true of the HP 364 inks although, even on standard quality paper, the output is still excellent.  As a test, I printed out the same photograph four times on standard paper and then four times on photo paper to see if the ink quality degraded between each print and also to compare the outputs on the different types of media.  The results from this test were impressive.  Firstly, there was no degradation between the first and the last printouts and although, the printouts on premium HP Photopaper looked amazing, the ones printed on standard paper were still exceptional, in fact they were the highest quality photographs I   ve seen on standard paper in terms of being similar to the original for colour strength.The same test was conducted with a 15 page report.  This time HP Premium A4 paper was used along with standard supermarket A4 paper.  The quality of output on standard A4 paper was considerably better than any previous output I have seen from an inkjet printer, that was until I saw the output on HP Premium paper.  On this type of paper, the output from the ink in simply outstanding and could easily be used for producing high powered documents.  The character definitions are perfect, even scrutinising them at close range will not find any blemishes. The standard A4 output results are also excellent, considering the difference in quality of paper, the ink really does respond magnificently to lower quality paper meaning that you aren   t going to have to break the bank each time you need to print out an assignment or an internal report.In order to test the flexibility of the HP 364 ink, as one final test, I reprinted the initial four photographs on HP Premium photo paper to test the quality after the ink had gone through some serious tests.  I wanted to see if any more bleeding or decolourisation had taken place since printing different types of documents on different types of stationery.  The results I got from this test were not unexpected, I have to say.  The quality of the new set of photographs was identical to the very first set we had produced.  This result gave me confidence that the HP 364 ink would cope with any type of document that could be thrown at it, safe in the knowledge that the first page would be of equal quality to the last page.The life of the inkPrinter consumables can, over the lifetime of a printer, cost more to replace than the initial outlay for the printer.  As a user, you want peace of mind that you will not be changing your cartridges every other week.   HP boast that their original cartridges will give you up to 34  more pages than compatible inks which is quite a difference. As a guide, the photo black cartridge will give you 130 photos, the colour cartridges will produce 300 pages and the black cartridge will give you 250 pages. XL cartridges are available in each colour which offers you a considerable saving in price per millilitre if you are someone who gets through ink quickly.
