The plot is simple; Hannibal takes over from where Silence Of The Lambs left off.  The infamous Lector is now 10 years older and has secured a position in a library in Florence.  The heroine Clarrice, played by an actress, whose name is about as memorable as her accent in the film, is approached by one of Lectors victims with fresh evidence about his whereabouts.  Wait for it, Clarrice is given the task of, yep you guessed it, tracking him down again.  This film really did have the makings of a good sequel.  Times have moved on, special effects have no doubt improved, but there was no real evidence of this in the film.  I  8217;m not going to spoil the film, but it has more twists than a   8220;B  8221; road in the middle of Wales, and more cat and mouse than Tom and Jerry could ever muster up.But having said that, if the better half is giving you grief and you need a bit of   8220;Silence  8221; then take a look for your self, but you may be better off decorating the bathroom rather than wasting your time and money on this flop.     ', '    As the sequel to the infamous Silence of the Lambs, this long awaited film, Hannibal has had many doubters from the time the filming was announsed. Anyone whos read the  book will surely understand, I read it eagerly when it came out and was baffled at how anyone, even the legendary Ridley Scott would come up with a viable way to show some of the most gorey scenes imaginable.Those of you who are expecting a second silence of the lambs will be dissapointed, this film is very different altogether. Not so much the tense thriller as an almost arty direction involving some fantastic and romantic scenery combined with the most grotesque of images. I neednt explain that it is not for the faint hearted. My partner at the cinema left complaining of a very queasy feeling in his stomach. (which may have been down to the popcorn and hotdog of course )Hannibal  is a good film, but I did find it a little slow, and as already expressed by the media, anyone who has read the book will see a very different ending. I wont detail either here, in case someone hasnt read or seen either yet  There a characters in the book not shown in the film who I believe help with character developement and understanding, eg Mason Vergers sister is not in the film but was a viable character in the book.Go see the film if you have a strong stomach just for the sheer experience as any one who saw Silence of the Lambs will surely be curious as to what Hannibal Lecter is up to now a days, and how easy it would be for him to involve himself in your life.     ', '    Ever seen anything more uncomfortable than someone unwittingly eating their own brain?  You have? Oh yes; the  Tweenies  have been known to induce that sort of reaction in people...Given the success of  Silence of the Lambs ,  Hannibal  has got to be a let-down. And it is. The chances were slim that Ridely  Gladiator  Scott (bloody good director that he is) could ever produce a sequel that matched the first in terms of intrigue and pure class. The film has good areas - good actors, good directing, decent enough screenplay, etc - butstill just doesn t seem to slot together right. There s enough gory horror to keep you tense, but the story line just isn t as deep or involving as the first film. Perhaps because we ve seen it all before in  the Lambs  or maybe because now Claris Starling is a changed woman (literally)- no,it s not that. Julianne Moore gave a very good performance as Claris, the  I m-an-even-tougher-bitch-now  FBI special agent, even if the ten years seemed to have treated her just a bit too kindly to be believable. She s back on the case of the elusive Dr. Hannibal Lecter and basically tracks him from Europe to the States, becoming more deeply involved as Hannibal s obsession with her becomes creepier and more disturbing. (No wonder really that Foster turned the part down - probably got a tip off that the plot was a bit pap).  You just can t recreate a classic such as The Lambs by simply re-hashing the elements of the first film, but to a lesser degree. A sequel novel - fair enough, I can see the market for that. But to spin off a milder, meeker, Marlboro Lights version of the first film and expect it to draw the audiences the first did - now that s just lack of imagination. The only reason this film will do as well as it will ( albeit not  Gladiator well) is that people will watch it based on the success of The Silence of the Lambs (as I did) and will be really rather dissapointed (as I was).  And on a side note - it s not as gory as some people have made out. NOT that I like to see gallons of ketchup all over film sets, but there wasn t even that  shock-factor  to keep me interested. But don t take your Granny, just in case.      ', '    Two words that really make this film Anthony Hopkins. ', '    Being the third film in the dr lector trilogy (the first being the excellent manhunter), you could be forgiven for expecting more. Hannibal seems to try and take the trilogy into a new direction involving the deep rooted respect and possible love for starling rather than the sheer fear factor the hopkins produced in silence. if silence hadnt existed, this would be a pretty good film.  As it is Ridley Scott has done an amicable job, with a script which seems to have been more than deliberately toned down, possibly more to lure hopkins back in to the role, than to satisfy silence fans. I wanted it to be more, I waited for it for ages, and i cant help but think that, unfortunately, there s something missing. On its plus side, There are loads of special features included on a two disc set, but at the end of the day, the movie is average, and the special features dont even begin to make up for it. ', '    Hannibal Lector has been the feature of three films, though I did not know this until recently, when I was told that the first one, called  quot;manhunt quot; (or something to that effect) was screened on television the other day. ', '    Having seen the prequel and being a graet fan of it, I was looking forward to the release of Hannibal, the sequel, with great interest. s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
If you’re diving into *Hannibal* on DVD, be prepared for a film that walks a fine line between chilling psychological thriller and unsettling gore fest. Unlike *The Silence of the Lambs*, where the victims evoke sympathy and the tension is razor-sharp, *Hannibal* flips the script by painting its victims as morally repugnant—almost as vile as Lecter himself. This clever twist complicates your emotional compass, making it harder to root for anyone, which might frustrate viewers craving clear-cut heroes or victims.

Narratively, *Hannibal* stands well enough on its own, offering a rich, character-driven story that delves deeper into Lecter’s twisted psyche. However, it inevitably pales in comparison to its predecessor’s tight storytelling and emotional resonance. If you’re a fan of psychological complexity and moral ambiguity, you’ll appreciate the film’s attempt to explore these darker shades, even if it doesn’t quite reach the same heights.

Now, a fair warning: the ending is gruesome to a fault, arguably crossing into unnecessary territory. It’s a visceral finale that might feel more like shock value than a meaningful conclusion, which could leave you questioning the narrative choices rather than reflecting on the characters’ arcs.

In sum, *Hannibal* offers a provocative, if imperfect, experience—one that challenges your sympathies and tests your tolerance for graphic content. It’s a solid pick if you enjoy dissecting morally complex characters and don’t mind a bit of gruesome spectacle, but don’t expect the same emotional depth or narrative cohesion that made *Silence of the Lambs* a classic. Think of it as a darker, messier sibling: intriguing, but not quite as polished or satisfying.

product_reviews: ['    ~ ~ Now I know that Steven Spielberg has made many fine movies, and that which one is the best of the bunch is a very personal choice, but in the opinion of this   8220;mad cabbie  8221;, this offering, Saving Private Ryan, (1998) comes close to being his very finest.~ ~ This is a movie about World War Two.In the opening scene we see an old man searching a virtual forest of white crosses in a military graveyard, until he finally finds the particular one he is looking for, and falls to his knees.In the next instant we are transported through time to D-Day in 1944, and more specifically to the killing ground of Omaha Beach in Normandy, France, where the American forces made their landing.We are taken inside the landing craft, to where the mostly very young and inexperienced soldiers are sitting crouched, literally waiting for absolute hell to break loose all around them.Men are shaking and throwing up with fear, and praying for their lives.A young soldier clutches his silver crucifix close, and constantly chants a   8220;Hail Mary  8221;.Then the doors fly open, and they are on the wet sand, where they are met by an avalanche of bullets and steel from the well-prepared and dug-in German defenders.~ ~ The screen then explodes into a turmoil of action, with shells exploding everywhere, and soldiers dying horrifically.We see the young man with the crucifix, now clutched to his stomach as he tries in vain to stop his intestines spilling out onto the ground.Soldiers are flung into the air by exploding shells and grenades, incinerated by fire, and mutilated beyond all recognition.We see a young man praising his luck when a bullet ricochets from his steel helmet, only to be killed outright by a bullet in the forehead from the very next shot, which tears his brain out the back of his skull.Another is wandering about aimlessly, clutching his severed arm.Men are decapitated, losing limbs, seeing their friends die before their horrified eyes.There is nowhere to go, nowhere to hide, nowhere to run to, to escape this vision of hell.The soldiers hug the ground that is heaving all around them, and pray for survival.Whether they live or die is a matter of pure luck. Here in this nightmare, no amount of training or experience is of any use whatsoever.~ ~ Are you beginning to get the picture?There are no Rambos or heroic SAS men here.These guys are just ordinary men, terrified out of their wits and minds, and doing their level best to somehow survive.Some of the scenes you will witness in the first 30 minutes of this film will be indelibly imprinted into your brain forever.This has to be simply the best action sequence ever shot in a war film, and I challenge you to be unmoved by the graphic camera work and by the total sense of the futility of war that it portrays.~ ~ I actually cried while watching this beach scene.I remember as a young boy pestering the life out of my father, who was one of the first British troops to land on those very same Normandy beaches. I was looking for tales of glory and heroism, and was disappointed when he went very quiet and wouldn  8217;t tell me anything.He actually won medals for his part in the action, and when I used to ask him, as young boys do,    8220;What did you get this one for Dad?  8221;, he would always come out with the same answer.   8220;For being stupid, son.  8221;It was only in later life that he tried to explain to me that war wasn  8217;t the way it was depicted on the TV and cinema in all those famous John Wayne films, but that it was sheer, unmitigated hell, but I never truly understood what he meant until I witnessed the scenes in this movie.Then it suddenly became very clear to me just what he had been talking about.That  8217;s why I cried. ~ ~ Anyway, enough nostalgia.After this frenetic first half hour, Saving Private Ryan slowly begins to reveal some sort of a plot.The film stars Tom Hanks as Captain John Miller.The men under his command are an understanding and battle hardened sergeant (Tom Sizemore), an army medic (Giovanni Ribski), a translator with no battle experience(Jeremy Davis) , a Jewish soldier (Adam Goldberg) who takes the war against Fascism very seriously indeed and very personally, a   8220;good old boy  8221; from the deep South (Barry Pepper) who is the team  8217;s sniper and who prays incessantly to God for guidance, a loud-mouth from the Brooklyn area of New York (Edward Burns), and an Italian-American. (Van Diesel) ~ ~ After somehow managing to come through the carnage of D-Day unscathed, they are now ordered by the top brass to undertake a new mission.They are to go behind enemy lines and find a soldier called Private James Ryan (Matt Damon), who the authorities have discovered is the only surviving son from a family of four brothers, all the others having been killed in action.Private Ryan is a paratrooper, and the army brass want him found and returned alive to his widowed mother. The only problem is that his unit has been dropped somewhere deep in German held territory, and no one knows exactly where.Again Spielberg portrays the madness of war, as Captain Miller  8217;s men openly question the decision that they should risk their own lives in order to save the life of one man that they neither know nor care anything about.~ ~ But the mission is undertaken, and as the squad move deeper and deeper behind enemy lines, the film again shows the sheer horror of war, as the hand-held cameras follow the carnage of the ensuing battle scenes, including some very realistic street to street fighting in the French towns they pass through.Difficult decisions have to be made. Should they rescue a little French girl whose house and life has been destroyed at the expense of not completing their mission?Should they summarily execute a captured German soldier who has just shot and killed one of their companions, or let him go and take the risk of him rejoining the fighting and doing the same again?Spielberg intersperses these moral dilemmas right throughout the movie.Along the way there is another very poignant scene, where Hanks tells   8220;Ryan  8221; (who turns out to be the WRONG soldier) that his three brothers have been killed in action.Even when the right Private Ryan is eventually located, their problems don  8217;t stop. Far from wanting to go home to his mother, the bold paratrooper actually wants to stay with his unit and continue fighting  ~ ~ For me, this ranks as the best war film I have ever seen.Director Spielberg succeeds in taking us right into the confused hearts and minds of the soldiers involved, and so you really feel the pain when you see them dying for what you believe to be nothing and for no reason.The real strength of this film is not just in its spectacular battle scenes and special effects, (although they ARE brilliant) but also in its deep and highly emotional plot, that has the viewer practically praying that all will turn out well in the end.This movie is a living testament to the courage and fortitude (as well as the stupidity) of the ordinary soldiers who are the   8220;cannon fodder  8221; in any war, and to the memory of those who fought, and lived, and died in those dark days, so that our democracy could survive.~ ~ And the relevance of that opening scene where we see the old man falling to his knees at the graveyard?Well now, you can probably guess, but if not, do yourself a big favour and rent or buy this film.And for the full effect watch it on a wide-screen TV, with stereo sound.      ', '    Aggressive and artful photography lends this moving film a bleached, washed out hue, giving it a strong, nightmarish quality. Visually, the story is presented as reportage, which sits a little uneasily with the developing plot.  But the success of the film is in its simple storyline and in the realism of its presentation of the experience of war. The camera work, art and sound direction draw  you right into the experience, so much so that your own reaction to the events on screen seems somehow to implicate you in the unfolding drama. It s an intimate, terrifying vision. Bullets fly by and lives are wasted in an instant. Given the scale of the overall production, and what must have been happening on set, the achievement of the actors is remarkable. Fear seems to stalk them. It s a theme that Tom Hanks  portrayal of the central character examines in a precise and concentrated way. And Spielberg s direction is aggressive. His choices are unpredictable and give the film a lot of edge. As a viewer, you are relentlessly returned to the personal experience of the characters involved. They seem dazed, blasted. The value of their lives seem transparent against the background of events. The visual imagery and tonality are strong, coherent, mesmerising. The whole piece is just stunning. ', '    Dare I swim against the torrential tide of accolades heaped by masses of film critics   many of whom I thought were more discerning   upon Steven Spielberg   s    Saving Private Ryan   (1998)? I might be swept away and dashed against the rocks in the process, but I won   t go under without at least attempting to confront that tsunami of uncritical praise that greeted the film. Thanks to Jill Murphy   s wicked influence, I finally gave in and rented    the greatest war film of this generation.    Or so I was told.By now everyone must know the plotline. Captain John Miller (Tom Hanks) leads a motley group of weary soldiers who survive the bloody D-Day landing on Omaha Beach on an unusual mission, that of tracing the whereabouts in German-occupied France of a certain paratrooper named Private James Ryan, and bringing him home. The US military has just learned that all of Ryan   s three brothers have been killed in action within a short period of time, in different theatres of war. Recalling the words of Abraham Lincoln to a mother who lost five sons during the Civil War, General George C. Marshall (Harve Presnell) is adamant that Pvt. Ryan be returned to his soon-to-be-grieving mother before any more harm befalls her last living son. It   s a public relations move thought up by the military top brass, nevermind its patent lack of logic and practicality.The persistent trouble I have with Spielberg is his wont to stack the deck in his favor by choosing oh-such-worthy causes to make into movies. So I feel like an evil and blasphemous Grinch for not locking step with the rest of Them in worshipping at the Spielberg altar and pronouncing SPR    a masterpiece      because Spielberg made the film as a personal tribute to the D-Day veterans. I understand that we do owe a great debt to these everyday men who did their level best in carrying out their duty through the fear, with sometimes heroic action in some impossibly hellish circumstances of horror and death. There   s no arguing with that at all. But honoring heroes by simply throwing up Big Symbols of Heroism and Patriotism onto the screen does not make for great cinema. Not in my book, anyway. Ultimately, SPR is a good film at best. What deep respect and gratitude I felt for the veterans    efforts were eclipsed by Spielberg   s fairly clunky attempts to make his Great Masterpiece about war.I have to divorce Spielberg   s filmmaking from his subject matter, because he insists on melding the two into one, forcing me to feel a certain way about something by virtue of the innate and unquestioned goodness of his cause. He wrests from me the freedom to glean for myself what the onscreen events might impart to the viewer. Spielberg seems not to fully trust his audience. He fears I may not    get    his points, whatever those may be (often rather simplistic ideas about the world), so he must lead me by the hand as he would a little child and show me exactly what to feel and think, and when. Well, I find no joy or pleasure in the experience of being condescended to like that.Some vital technical elements served only to distance me from the film. Like    Schindler   s List,    there   s a clinical sterility to the film   s look   its colors and milieu, its composition, its use of light and shadow   that calls attention to itself and trumps the painstakingly re-created realism of the grime and sweat of the soldiers and the disorganized rubble of half-leveled towns. Spielberg isn   t one for originality and imagination. His films are well-stocked with cinematic clich   s. Note the Norman Rockwellian sweeping Midwest farms where the Ryan brothers    mother lives, the sharp contrast shot of almost black against light of Captain Miller   s group during a solemn moment, and that uneasy lull with Edith Piaf playing on the gramophone as the guys chat amid the rubble about things that guys do. Spielberg wants so badly to make his picture look    artistic    and does so with such self-consciousness   did you notice that dizzyingly    realistic    camera shake a la    NYPD Blue   ? the blood-spattered lens in the landing at Omaha Beach? the oversaturated colors and image flicker that look like they   d been through the Adobe Photoshop mill?Not having lived under a rock for the past few years (well, not technically, anyway), I haven   t escaped the gallons of ink spilled and the gigabytes consumed on impassioned claims of how those first thirty minutes are    the most realistic depiction of war ever    and all that. Coming to this film with that expectation just dulled the experience for me. I was ready for a horrifically graphic bloodbath, and I got it   literally, up to those crimson waters crashing onto the shore at the end of the half-hour of carnage   just in case you still missed the point that the landing of the Allied forces on D-Day was an insanely chaotic mess of seasick, terrified young soldiers being cut down in an unending hail of bullets and mortar fire coming from the German bunkers above. Pretty neat special FX there, with those yellow streaks and zip-zip sounds for the bullets. The horrors of war made more realistic through LucasFilm computer enhancement.  But this is realer than real, folks  Despite his supposed insistence on authenticity, Spielberg isn   t genuinely interested in realistic depictions. Once more this film showcases his intemperance, his penchant for overdoing everything and belaboring the obvious to ensure his point comes through   and is hammered home into your thick skull. Instead of drawing me deeper into the movie, Spielberg only succeeds in alienating me further. Well, then, on to the good parts. The fine cast deserve kudos for their strong ensemble work. Those pre-shoot days of actual boot camp did help to turn the actors into convincing grunts. I fell totally for the wonderful Edward Burns as Brooklynite Pvt. Reiben, and even the normally pallid Tom Hanks as Capt. Miller would grow on me by the film   s conclusion. I also learned to like Barry Pepper as the sniper, Pvt Jackson, who gives some nuance to his cross-kissing, Bible-quoting character. His clean and brisk hand signals fell in with his assumed skill with the riflescope. It also helped that, for a moment or two, I thought I was seeing Johnny Depp playing Jackson  (Why was he absent from the film, anyway?) The terrified paralysis of the young and inexperienced translator, Corporal Upham (Jeremy Davies), is heartfelt and painful, although his Big Grown-up Moment felt a bit forced (and what was the point of that scene? Killing a man makes you a man?).On the other hand, there   s the insufferable Matt Damon, whose reason for his continuing current popularity escapes me. He smacked so much of the late 90s and annoyed me no end with that self-satisfied look and big white teeth of his. He was the falsest note in this otherwise interestingly discordant group of soldiers. (And no, ex-Bennifer Affleck won   t do in the role, either.)I can pick out some well-done scenes that made me forget about Spielberg   s ubiquitous shadow, and a few that went even further and moved me to tears. There   s the early, almost throwaway chatter among the men whom Capt. Miller chooses for the mission, and I rather enjoyed the lively and surprising repartee as they march through the French countryside. Edward Burns    Pvt. Reiben first grabs my attention in this sequence. Here   s a guy who dares to question the orders from above, and I wanted to hear more from him. His character rang true for me through most of the film. An unexpectedly moving bit comes when the gravely wounded medic, Pvt. Wade (Giovanni Ribisi) stoically and vainly tries to save himself while the others remain helpless in their clumsy, desperate efforts following a brief but costly raid on a small group of Germans. Near the end, witnessing the scene of Pvt. Reiben coming to the aid of his badly injured captain touched me deeply, too. This might be the first of Spielberg   s works to offer a glimmer of redemptive hope for the reigning Naked Emperor of Emotional Manipulation. He and Robert Rodat (the writer) actually allowed some grayness and a faint hint of cynicism to seep into the tale. Doubts arise among some of Capt. Miller   s crew about the wisdom of their mission, one of whom (Pvt. Reiben) asks why Ryan gets to go home to his mother when all of them have mothers waiting back home, too. Midway through Spielberg presents our exhausted captain with another dilemma directly pitting one soldier   s duty against another   s. The resulting turn in the story would be a bit of a letdown, but at the same time felt true to the American spirit of making the best of what could be mildly called a crazy situation. However, Spielberg keeps shooting himself in the foot, or in the toe, at least. That well-directed, suspenseful, surprise encounter between the erstwhile hidden German soldiers and Miller   s troops in the French town was somewhat spoiled by the Spielbergian contrivance in its introduction and resolution, but it was still early in the film for me to get too upset. There   s a real tension generated when Pvt. Reiben makes an attempt at insubordination, but the explosive situation is defused with a mixture of plausibility and improbable melodrama   very tricky but not totally fatal here. Spielberg ruins some other strong parts by, for instance, having Miller   s men constantly repeat the newly minted platitude about    earning the right to go home   .SPR has a few interesting scenes of the funny-puzzling kind. The dead serious look on the faces of those military officers meeting with General Marshall about the mission almost had me bursting out with laughter at the funereal earnestness of everyone. And when that Panzer tank suddenly looms large behind the two GIs in that foxhole near the bridge, can you say that this wasn   t just another bit of tongue-in-cheek humor on Spielberg   s part? These were jarring and disorienting moments amid all that gravity   I couldn   t suppress a chuckle on recalling a similar move to the Panzer   s by that animatronic Great White, when it emerges with a startling suddenness from the calm waters behind the oblivious Roy Scheider in    Jaws   . Are these examples of effective storytelling? Or perhaps the black humor was intentional? Heck, not a bad idea, really.Manipulative and banal would describe some other bits. Never one for subtlety, Spielberg fails to disappoint yet again in some places. I felt annoyed at the exchange of warm and fuzzy stories in the dark church, especially those related by Miller and the medic, Wade. Not to mention the embarrassingly unamusing incident told by Pvt. Ryan to Capt. Miller. (Or was that the point   that even the most trite things become significant in such circumstances? Should I give Spielberg the benefit of the doubt? I think not.) What about those opening and closing sequences featuring the US flag waving majestically against the sun (was that a halo I spotted there, embracing the flag?). He continues to employ glib symbols, such as that involuntary tremor plaguing Capt. Miller, and Pvt. Mellish   s (Adam Goldberg) taunting of German POWs with his star of David. And what is one supposed to make of those inane questions in the Hallmark   Kodak moment in the finale, questions asked pleadingly by the elderly character of his wife who doesn   t seem to understand:    Have I led a good life? Tell me I   m a good man     The unbearably saccharine   almost farcical   scene just blew to bits the emotional build-up created up to this point. It ain   t Spielberg   s fault    it must be in his DNA because the man just can   t help it when it comes to dreaming up such onscreen scenes of counterfeit emotion and passing them off as the real thing.Once more Spielberg enlists the aid of composer John Williams. Williams holds nothing back, drowning the viewer in sonic rivers of sentimental schlock. I searched in vain for a button to cut off that maddening, wall-to-wall music that played without pause in between sections of deafening sounds of explosions, whizzing bullets and rumbling tanks. This nonstop musical wallpaper would swell at the approach of nearly every Big Moment, effectively depriving said Big Moments of their potential punch and rendering them as anticlimactic events left to unfold for completeness    sake. I   m not so sure that Spielberg even has an anti-war message in SPR. ', '    FILM REVIEW ONLY - NO DVD INFOI have resisted the temptation to read any other views or opinions about this film before putting pen to paper (or, more accurately, fingers to keyboard) as I want to make sure I give my own untainted opinion.  There will be no spoilers.~~~~~~The Plot~~~~~~The picture is set in 1944 and begins with the historic D-Day Landings in France moving beyond the beaches as a squad of men embark on a special mission to locate and bring back home a single soldier (Private Ryan) who is somewhere behind enemy lines in occupied France.  I will say no more.  This is a film with its own story to tell.~~~~~~~~The Actors~~~~~~~~The man leading the mission to find Private Ryan is Captain John Miller ably played by Tom Hanks.  Whilst Hanks is undoubtedly a fine actor there was something a little too gentle about him.  This may have been a conscious effort to show how war cuts no class, no status and takes no prisoners; men being pulled from all walks of life to fight the battle for freedom.  Hanks managed to portray the complex personality that was Captain Miller very well.  We saw the vulnerability, the fear, the unashamed following of orders and occasionally the strength.As a result of resisting the temptation to read any reviews of the film I cannot state who the other actors were.  However, all were equally skilled, if not more so than Hanks at portraying their characters.  We saw the fear associated with war, the questioning of actions, the struggle for survival and above all the courage of these men that fought for our freedom.  All were represented, all were well portrayed.~~~~~~~~The Music~~~~~~~~The music was suitable, nothing more, nothing less.  If it had not been there the film would have lacked nothing.  This is a film you will watch for the content not the cinematic experience.The sound effects were amazing - again, nothing that overpowered the message that was being given, but complementing it the whole way.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~The Cinematography~~~~~~~~~~~~~~The camera work was outstanding.  The film is no colourful Hollywood extravaganza.  It is khaki.  With the exception of a few moments the film is monotone, not through the use of black and white film, but through the determined nature of Spielberg to make this as real an experience as possible.  There are no glory shots, no idolising or glorification - this is real, grey, khaki, dull real.The special effects team put together a very convincing war   perhaps too convincing.  The first class combination made it very hard to remember that this is fiction and not the real thing.~~~~~~~~~~~The Psychology~~~~~~~~~~~Please bear with me on this rather unusual sub-heading.  This paragraph is intended, in part, to explain my title.Spielberg is undoubtedly a master of the cinema, able to portray anything from the fantastic to the realistic.  This film is no exception.  It does not glorify war, neither does it patronise.  Through the media of the story line, the acting and the direction we see a scene that appears as real to the viewer as a documentary of the actual thing.  I am of the generation that has never known war (at least not such that it has tainted these shores) but this film felt real.Spielberg, through his dialogue, lets us into the minds of the men fighting the battle.  Men question their orders and yet follow.  The Leaders of the squads listen to the questions yet expect discipline and obedience borne out of a desire to survive.  What surprised me most was the way in which such discipline was achieved - not through shouting orders and threatening non-compliance but through listening and respect for the fellow soldiers.  This to me seems realistic.  War makes all men equal.  When you are fighting for survival you work together.  A leader is required but he is not infallible and what this film does show is that it could just have been possible that some leaders could have used the  quot;human factor quot; to their advantage and won their troops over with respect rather than through fear.The characters themselves all have extremely complex psychologies as each is left to come up with his own, very individual, answer to the same questions.  We see joy, humility, fear, bereavement and pure adrenalin, each emotion tumbling over the next before the first has had time to expire.I was left with so much to think about, yet no conclusions.  So many complex answers to unasked questions - numb.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Should you watch it?~~~~~~~~~~~~~~I m glad that I did not see this film in the cinema.  It is one to watch on your own or with close family unless you are thoroughly hardened.  It is rated 15 which surprised me.  The violence is naturally strong and graphic, and it could be no other way.  I found some scenes quite distressing, not in an upsetting way but in a numbing way. ', '    I m not a huge fan of  War  Films although I ve watched a fair few over the years. It seems to me that there have been only a few that have done the subject matter justice. THE PLOTThe idea behind this film is simple and slightly improbable. During WW2 and four brothers go to war and three die in combat, the top rank of the US army come to know of this and decide to spare the family any further potential heartache and to send the remaining brother James Ryan, the youngest of the four home. Toward the end of the film there is a twist to the plot, which sets the film up for a momentous climax.CAST, PERFORMANCES AND OPINIONTom Hanks.... Captain John Miller Edward Burns.... Captain Fred Hamill Max Martini   Corporal Fred Henderson Dylan Bruno.... From the picture of an unknown American veteran in the present day kneeling in front of one of the hundreds of white crosses in a US serviceman s cemetery in Northern France we slowly zoom in to his eyes and then find ourselves transported to June 6th 1944 the day of the Normandy landings. Here we meet for the first time Captain Miller who has to lead his unit out of the amphibian craft up the beach in the face of heavy German defensive fire. The unit suffer huge losses and the slaughter is shown in horrific detail. Nothing is spared for the audience as we see soldiers have their limbs blown apart, others we see shot the head there is blood everywhere and in a very well constructed sequence the blood mixed with sea water is seen washing up on the beach around the bodies of the fallen soldier. We see the panic in the soldier s eyes but also there is a determination (or is it instinct) to survive and carry out their mission. These men are not portrayed as  heroes  at least not in the usual Hollywood way. There is no  Rambo  like figure that appears from the over the hill that with a godlike invincibility ready cut down the faceless enemy. These  heroes  are ordinary men doing what they can as best they can in an impossible situation.  We are left in no doubt after this uncompromising start that we are not going to be seeing a typical Hollywood war movie.  The initial battle scene last for about 25 minutes and it is totally riveting as the same time as being shocking. It is easy for anyone of my generation who has never experienced war first hand to forget what men and women just a little older than our parents went through and it certainly comes as shock when we are reminded of this in such graphic detail. The initial sequence in undoubtedly the most powerful of the whole film and in many ways you could argue that structurally the film suffers from this. The tension is never quite recaptured although there are other powerful, violent parts in the film. I can understand why the director chose to make the film in this way. The unexpected scenes of death and immense suffering that the audience are subjected to would not be as effective at the end of the film once we have been led through the story and when we have come to know the characters. The sight of these anonymous men dying before our eyes further reinforces the anonymity of war in general. This is an attempt to show us what really lies behind the bland statistics that are reported by war correspondent in short news experts.The performances are excellent by all involved. Tom Hank especially manages to play the key character of Capt Miller in a measured understated way and yet he is able to express clearly the underlying weight of duty he feels to his men and we can guess at the lack of confidence he has in his own ability to cope with the mission and to simply retain his sanity. Throughout the film he is left to make decision, which will affect the lives of men and it is clear that such immense responsibility is not easy to cope with despite his best effort to hide this. Only once in the course of the story do we see him, in a private moment, break down emotionally. Hanks always excels at playing the  ordinary guy  in an extraordinary situation and here again we see his great skill as an actor rather than a film star at taken on this everyman role. He certainly deserved an Oscar for this role more than for his performance in  Forrest Gump The supporting cast was in my opinion lead by the performances of Tom Sizemore as the hard noses sergeant of the unit and Edward Burns as the rebellious Private Rieben. Both actors again managed to inject a complexity in to their characters that added to the realism of the situation. A mention must also go to Jeremy Davies as the  cowardly  inexperienced Corporal Timothy Upham who is drafted in to the mission at the last minute for his ability to speak French and German not for his fighting skills. The rest of the cast including big names stars Matt Damon and Vin Diesel are fine in their roles but don t manage to compete in the acting stakes with some of their less well-known co-stars and are generally underused.The movie is beautifully filmed with great attention to detail and some wonderful reconstructions of partially destroyed French towns. John Williams a veteran of films composed the music and he certainly managed to produce a soundtrack that compounded the films  sombre tone throughout. ', '    War is hell and nowhere is that more apparent than the battle sequence Steven Spielberg uses to open  quot;Saving Private Ryan. quot; The much-lauded 20 minutes are brilliant and harrowing as we watch the terrified Allied soldiers push their way up Omaha Beach past a hail of German machine-gun fire. It  8217;s June 6, 1944  8212;D-Day  8212;and we  8217;re there in the thick of battle like we  8217;ve never been before at the movies.There have been good war movies ( quot;Wake Island, quot;  quot;The Bridge Over the River Kwai, quot;  quot;Platoon quot;) and there have been great war movies ( quot;Full Metal Jacket, quot;  quot;All Quiet on the Western Front, quot;  quot;Gallipoli quot;), but until now, there has never been a motion picture combat experience quite like  quot;Saving Private Ryan. quot; In the space of that beach assault, Spielberg re-invents the war genre, with a battle that is at once large-scale and intensely personal. I gripped the armrest with white knuckles as Spielberg showed me what great cinema technique is all about. With hand-held camera footage, slowed motion and sound effects so real I was ducking bullets, the battle is gut-wrenchingly real. Spielberg has created a miniature masterpiece here as we follow Capt. Miller (Tom Hanks) and his company of soldiers up the beach and their heroic assault on the German machine-gun bunker.But  quot;Saving Private Ryan quot; is not just about movie technique. It  8217;s about men and how they behave in combat, banding together despite their differences. In the eight men on this mission, we get a composite of the American soldier  8212;the bravado, the fear, the courage, the tenderness. Spielberg has set out to teach us not only about World War II, but also about ourselves and how we might think and feel when we  8217;re face-to-face with death.If  quot;Saving Private Ryan quot; had ended after the first 25 minutes, it would be a satisfying (albeit unsettling) motion picture experience. But there  8217;s more, much more, to this relatively simple story. A small, hand-picked group of soldiers is given the mission to go deep into enemy territory to find a paratrooper whose brothers have all been killed in combat. The Pentagon brass doesn  8217;t want Mrs. Ryan to get another black-edged telegram. And so, eight soldiers risk their lives for the sake of one person who may not even be alive or, if he is, may not even be worth saving. As one of Miller  8217;s men gripes,  quot;Seems to me, Cap n, this mission is a serious misallocation of valuable military resources. quot; The men understandably resent being sent on this public relations mission  8212;especially after what they  8217;ve just gone through back on Omaha Beach. They don  8217;t want to save Americans, they want to kill Germans.The film uses what appears to be conventional characters who barely dodge the stereotype bullets, thanks mainly to some of the best ensemble acting to come along in years. Spielberg put Hanks and the rest of the actors through a mini-boot camp prior to filming in an attempt to build esprit de corps between the crew. From the looks of it, he succeeds. I never doubted for one minute that these soldiers (actors) had dug foxholes together, shared C rations and maneuvered as a fighting team.Each of the young actors is great, but special praise goes to Jeremy Davies as Corporal Upham, the clerk who  8217;s requisitioned for the mission because he can speak German and French. Upham is a bundle of nervous chatter as he sets out with the rest of the squad, but by mission  8217;s end, he  8217;s come to know the true nature of his character. One of the most gripping scenes in the movie comes when Upham cowers in a stairwell, paralyzed with fright as one of his fellow soldiers meets a slow, agonizing death in the next room. Davies  8217; performance haunted me for weeks.And then there  8217;s Tom Hanks, the modern cinema  8217;s equivalent of Jimmy Stewart, Spencer Tracy and Gary Cooper  8212;the American Everyman. Hanks is so natural in this role you almost overlook the complexity of his Oscar-worthy performance here. As a soldier-by-proxy, you immediately put your trust in Capt. Miller, just by virtue of the fact that it  8217;s Hanks  8217; face under that helmet. Here is a true leader  8212;decisive, courageous and yet humanly vulnerable. Hanks  8217; greatest moment in  quot;Saving Private Ryan quot; comes after yet another of his soldiers has died. He walks away, finds a private spot behind an embankment and starts to cry, though he does his best not to allow his weakness show in front of his men. You can really see the struggle Hanks is going through as he tries to stifle his emotions.There are several small moments like that in  quot;Saving Private Ryan quot; (in fact, it  8217;s the little details that always add up to greatness in Spielberg  8217;s films):*Moments after securing Omaha Beach, First Sergeant Horvath (Tom Sizemore) scoops up a handful of the sand, dumps it into a tin and adds it to his knapsack which is full of other tins labeled  quot;Italy quot; and  quot;Africa. quot;*A bullet passes through a soldier  8217;s helmet. Stunned but unharmed, he takes it off, looks at the bullet hole, grins at his good luck, then  8212;BAM --another bullet hits his unprotected skull.*Soldiers take a break from preparing for the final bloody battle to listen to a recording of Edith Piaf. As the French chanteuse  8217;s voice floats through the streets of the village, the soldiers stop what they  8217;re doing to savor the opera aria. For some, it  8217;s the last music they  8217;ll ever hear.These are just a few of the threads woven into this great tapestry of war. To list more of them would be to risk destroying the powerful effect of this movie. quot;Saving Private Ryan quot; serves as a fine companion to Spielberg  8217;s other World War II masterpiece,  quot;Schindler  8217;s List. quot; In his earlier film, we see what the Allies were fighting for; in  quot;Ryan, quot; we get to see how they do it: with dignity and courage.(A note about the special limited edition of the video: the  quot;bonus footage quot; is just a 25-minute special about D-Day. It cobbles together interviews with the actors, historian Stephen Ambrose and World War II veterans. None of it really adds much to the  quot;Ryan quot; experience. Call it History Channel Lite. The most valuable footage of the special tape comes when we get to see clips from two of Spielberg  8217;s earliest films  8212;home movies he made when he was a teenager. Even at that age, when he was coercing the neighborhood boys into playacting Allies and Germans for his camera, it  8217;s possible to see the genesis of his genius.) ', '    When Steven Spielberg was an adolescent, his first home movie was a backyard war film. ', '    The top-grossing motion picture of 1998, Saving Private Ryan has had profound impact on the film industry and is rightly considered as one of the greatest film achievements in history. Directed by Steven Spielberg, Private Ryan was the winner of five academy awards, and captured numerous Oscars, including Cinematography, Sound and Film Editing. The story s opening scene, the historic D-Day invasion of World War Two (the biggest amphibious land invasion of all time), is one of the most important depictions of a real life event ever seen in film. Here, the true atrocities and brutal realities of war are recreated accurately, doing justice to the horrific events that occurred during the 1940 s, where other films have consistently failed.Following the Allied invasion of Normandy, two brothers lay dead in the wake of the onslaught and a third brother, fighting in New Guinea, was also killed in action. After the Army General Staff learns of the possibility that the fourth, and only remaining, brother may still be alive, a rescue mission is ordered to find the young soldier and return him home safely. The rescue effort, led by Captain John Miller (Tom Hanks), is the basis of the story that follows, with the soldiers assigned to the task well aware of the potential folly of their mission; risking the lives of their entire unit to save the life of one man. After numerous encounters with German forces, including a sniper attack and an assault on a machinegun nest, Miller and his men eventually find Private Ryan, albeit only after two members of their unit are killed whilst trying. When Ryan hears of the death of his brothers, he elects to remain with his company, which has been ordered to defend a bridge at any cost. Miller and his soldiers reluctantly agree to help the company, and what follows is a searing finale in which German and Allied forces fight an immense battle to establish control of the bridge. This is a gripping conclusion to the film, ensuring that the viewer is completely engaged and engrossed in the story until the very end. Even the biggest fan of Private Ryan would have to acknowledge, though, if he or she were honest, that the film does have somewhat of a limited appeal, given that s its subject matter may fail to grab the immediate attention or interest of a contemporary audience. Still, this is one of only a few aspects of the film which could be considered a weakness.  In keeping with its superb technical ability, Saving Private Ryan is showcased to perfection on the DVD release, which includes a short documentary ( quot;Into the Breach quot;) about the background and context of the film. A short, but interesting, interview with Spielberg himself is also featured here. It has been argued that this film could, if not should, have received a rating that is suitable only for persons of 18 years and over. That is not to suggest that Saving Private Ryan glorifies its depiction of World War Two in any way, though. Watch and learn how much pain mankind can inflict on itself. I recommend that everyone participate in this important history lesson. It is an unfortunate fact that we can secure peace only by preparing for war. Now I am 31, identify with the Julie Andrews character and still love the film as much.Although it is a long film, it never seems to drag. The plot is well written and it needs the time to tell the story so well.The main character, Maria (Julie Andrews) is a nun, who goes to be a nanny to a family of seven children headed by their stern father, played by Christopher Plummer. He runs his family as a tight military unit, but Maria suspects they need love and a little music to make their lives complete.The cast is excellent, including all the children. Angela Cartwright went on to act in  Lost In Space  and Nicholas Hammond became Spiderman, but all the actors and actresses in this film are superb.The songs are so well known now, they have become classics known by young and old alike. It is also nice to be able to sit down with your children and grandparents, who can all enjoy this film.      ', '     Three to Tango  is a quiet, unassuming and unpretentious romantic comedy, very much of the  quot;old school quot; of filmmaking, starring Matthew Perry (Friends) and Neve Campbell (Scream).The story itself is fairly simple - a couple of architects, one gay, one straight (Perry) are trying to secure a contract for work from a slick businessman who is cheating on his wife with an attractive young glass-blowing artist (Campbell).  Somewhat obsessed with her, and not wanting to lose her to another man he coaxes Perry s character - mistakenly thinking that he, like his partner, is gay - to spy on the girl and keep him informed of where she goes, who she sees etc.  Not wanting to lose the opportunity of pleasing the slick businessman, and thereby securing the contract, he agrees but slowly falls in love with the pretty young artist.All in all the story may sound rather twee but this film manages to engage you with its sheer simplicity and charm.  The on-screen relationship between Perry and Campbell really works and it s nice to see Perry applying his sharp wit and natural comic timing outside of  Friends .Although the film deals with what it s like to be thought of and treated as gay it does this in a very light-hearted and inoffensive manner, not for one minute pretending that it has any deeper subtext or social commentary on this matter.I had already gone to see this film in the cinema and I wondered if it would still hold the same appeal for me watching it for a second time on DVD but it did and, although the DVD itself is very sparse on additional features, if you re into light, easy going, romantic comedies then this is definitely one for your collection.     ', '    When this film came out years ago, it was the start of a whole new world. Now colourful graphics and animated characters maybe common but back then they weren  8217;t. I didn  8217;t really think this film was my age group but watch it since it was reviewed to be something   8216;very good  8217;. I can remember coming away quite satisfied and happy that I had been to watch it. It all begins in Andy  8217;s room when his toys come to life when he is not there. Woody is Andy  8217;s favourite, the voice over is by Tom Hanks. But there  8217;s also other toys like Potato Head who all have there own little character. When the new toy comes Buzz Lightyear who is a bright very modern sought of toys, flashing lights etc. Andy prefers him as every kid would. From here the story develops, you can watch the movie to find out what happens. The story is good but the graphics are quite something, they are very impressive and it really works well. You would think this film was suited just for kids but I enjoyed it and I am no kid.The voice overs are good and it  8217;s well directed, it  8217;s a good film and worth watching. I think it is much better than Toy Story 2, this is the original and the best.        ', '    I read this classic book by author Richard Adams when i was about 11 years old which took me 5 months, I guess i was not that good at reading back then. So when the film came out in 1979 i eagerly trotted off to the cinema with my older sister with these images in my head of different rabbit characters and a vision of a scenic settings of the fields at the back of our road. I was not disappointed and thought it was wonderful portrait of a brilliant book. If you have never seen the film i recommend that you get it out on video. The films amination is not of the highest quality and not of Disney standard but this does not matter because you will get compleatly lost in the story line.The film is about the lives of a community of rabbits which have to leave their Warren due to contractors building houses where they live. Most of them up and leave and some want to stay and are killed by the Bulldozers.The whole film is set around a rabbit called Fiver and his quest to find another home for the Doe s, He comes across many perils including other rabbits from other warrens which they were at war with and crossing the road which is always a hazard even for me.There are some really sad bits in the film which will make your girlfriend or wife defiantly cry and there are also some really funny bits too, Like the Seagull trying to fly.The voice overs are great especially John Hurt and his very distinctive voice. The soundtrack is the unforgetable Bright Eyes by Art Garfuncul which is played at the end, this will make you cry to.     ', '    Being a complete and utter scaredy cat (I am unable to watch 90  of the Jaws films and am almost brought to tears at the sight of a Scream mask... but that s another story), I reluctantly went to see What Lies Beneath with my beloved boyfriend...I must admit, for the first part of the film, I hid   I am unable to cope with any type of scary suspense, with the sheer possiblity that something s going to jump out at you at any second...  The cliche build up of music in the background only increased the tension.However, I found the story very slow and if I am honest, a little bit boring...  I soon guessed the plot (correctly- which i never do)and it kind of got a bit boring after that...  It IS a good little chiller, and I wont be able to go into a bathroom and look into a bath of water in the same way ever again (I almost died of shock and practically screamed at the end when Pfiffer is in the bath).  Although it did scare me, I cant help feeling that the story is missing something... a certain je n ai sais pas.  Watch it yourself to find out what Note: I wont give the film away for anyone who hasn t seen it- but personally, despite the tense moments, the ending was VERY predictable.       ', '    This has to be one of the funniest films I have seen in ages  Although it has a 12 certificate do not let that put you off  I was in a cinema with some kids sat next to me and they could not understand many of the jokes as they went straight over their heads, but the rest of us are crying with laughter.Nicky was brought up in Las Vegas in a Girlie show, but got a job in later years as a creative director. When the company needs to refocus its campaign Nicky (Gibson) is passed over for promotion in order of a woman, Darcy (Helen Hunt) to come in and bring in the female perspctive. Nicky has trouble at first but after a very very funny freak accident he gains the ability to read every woman s mind he comes into contact with  Human or Otherwise  And the story continues from there A fantastic cast with Mel Gibson truly brilliant as Nick, Helen Hunt as the creative director Darcy who has to gain a foothold in the company Nick as kind of ruled over for years.  Lauren Johnson is fantastic as the 15 year old daughter rebelling against the father she hardly knows.There are also wonderful appearances by Alan Alda(M*A*S*H) and Bette Midler (Beaches) as a psychiatrist A wonderful film that will have everyone crying with laughter, and I will never look at Mel Gibson in the same way again  His hero, macho image was completely blown as he tries to figure out  quot;What Women Want  quot;      ', '    I finally got around to watching this film recently. I picked up the video at Blockbuster and remembered  quot;Oh yeah that s the film where...... quot;Those of you that have seen it know what I m talking about. The sexy scene where Denise Richards (WOWWWW) and Neve Campbell (Double WOWWWW ) kiss in a semi lesbian  romp . Yes that s the thing that is universally remembered. But what s the film actually like?Well, it s not bad really. There is enough sauciness (watered down sex), suspense and actual plot to make it stand out just a bit above the average run of the mill  Lesbian Sex Romp  (and whats wrong with one of those I hear you ask).The film is full of visual treats, not just for the guys,  but also for you girls out there. As well as Denise and Neve, there is also Matt Dillon and Kevin Bacon, both have plenty of female admirers I m certain.Like the girls do, the film teases and tantalises you at every turn. Due credit should be given to the writer who justifies the use of tempting the viewers with those visual treats - only to twist your expectations.A decent script holds your attention, with enough surprises and twists to leave you wanting moregasping for breath. Everytime I thought I knew what was going on, the film would twist away again and leave me  on the verge . I won t reveal you any more, but I will say that it s a tempting little film - not just for the bodies involved, but it really is a clever twisty film and worth 90 minutes of your time.     ']

If you’re diving into *Saving Private Ryan* on DVD, you’re in for a cinematic experience that’s as intense as it is thought-provoking. Spielberg’s direction and the film’s impressive cinematography and special effects create an immersive, almost visceral portrayal of WWII, especially during the brutally realistic D-Day landing scenes. The sound design and music deserve a shout-out too—they don’t just accompany the action but amplify the emotional weight, pulling you deeper into the chaos and humanity of war.

Tom Hanks shines as Captain Miller, delivering a performance that’s both commanding and deeply human, anchoring the story’s moral complexity. The supporting cast, including Matt Damon, is excellent, with each character given enough individuality to avoid feeling like mere archetypes—even if some viewers find a few stereotypes creeping in. This nuanced character work fuels the film’s exploration of the central ethical dilemma: risking many lives to save one man, which invites plenty of reflection and debate.

While *Saving Private Ryan* is widely hailed as one of the most realistic and powerful war movies ever made, it’s worth noting that some suggest renting rather than buying, especially if you’re considering replay value. The film’s intense subject matter and graphic battle scenes might not be something you revisit frequently, but its cinematic achievements and emotional impact make it a must-see for any serious film enthusiast.

If you appreciate war films that combine gripping action with deep character-driven storytelling and moral questions, this DVD is a solid addition—just be prepared for a heavy, immersive ride that balances harrowing realism with moments of genuine humanity. And hey, if you’re like me, you might even find some dark humor in the camaraderie amidst the chaos, which adds a subtle but welcome layer to the experience.

', '    EMAEMA is money for students who go into further education.EMA stands for Education Maintenance Allowance.EMA is surposs to be for travel and to buy books and help with things at college or further education. Please let me know what you think.Please rate my other reviewsThanks Sarah     ', '    For most teenagers EMA is a godsend, but is it really fair? I know most of you are asking what the hell is EMA? It stands for Education Maintenance Allowance, and when you become a student and go into further education, EMA is there to help you buy books and get to and from school because now you have to start paying for your travel.It does have its downsides though, people who earn more than    30,000 a year are not entitled and in my opinion this is not fair. In a way, EMA is there to get teenagers to go into further education. My birthday s not until next July, so I m saving my EMA money to go towards my driving lessons and as I m doing a computing course I don t need to buy books. If you are below the    30,000 a year barrier you will either get    30,    20 or    10 a week depending on your parent s income. The closer you are to    30,000 the less you will get. If you do well on your course and you have over 95  attendance you will receive bonuses up to a hundred pounds.WHY DO YOU GET IT?The government understands the reason young people don t go into further education is because they struggle to pay for it, so by giving young people an allowance every week to keep them in school is a good way to keep the attendance high and the grades in the long run will be a lot better.HOW LONG DO YOU GET IT FOR?Three years is the maximum but it can be stretched over four years if you are in need of it. HOW DO YOU GET THE MONEY?It comes into the young person s bank account on the following week. Every Friday I hand mine in at reception and I receive it in my bank account the following week on the Thursday. HOW TO APPLY? Get an application form of the website or from a careers advisor at school and fill it in and send it off with the note of the parent s last years income.IS IT WORTH IT? God yes, as most of you know I was ill for 10 months before I started college. It mysteriously disappeared about two weeks before I started college, but in 9 weeks I have only had one day off and that was because I had been told specifically by the nurse to lay in bed. I think this is partially down to EMA; it s so easy to skip college/sixth form because the teachers don t really care, but if I miss a lesson I don t get my EMA for that day. DOES IT MATTER IF YOU VE GOT A PART TIME JOB?No, it doesn t affect you at all, it s an allowance and your job doesn t even get taken into account.DOES IT AFFECT MY PARENTS BENEFITS?No, your parents won t be affected at all. The money is for you and your parents don t get penalised at all.  WHAT YOU HAVE TO DO?I know that colleges and sixth forms are different. At college I have to get every lesson signed or I don t get my EMA, but at sixth form they only have to get theirs signed in the morning to prove that they were actually there.ANYTHING ELSE?If you are under the    30,000 a year barrier EMA is for you. I m quite smart with mine and am putting it into a savings account, so when I come to my driving lessons next year I won t have to worry as much. I m on a 2 year course so will only probably get it for two years, but in that time I ll probably make well over    1000. s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
EMA (Education Maintenance Allowance) is a well-intentioned scheme designed to support students aged 16-18 (sometimes up to 19) in further education by providing a weekly allowance of up to £30, based on household income. From my analysis, EMA effectively encourages higher attendance and achievement by linking payments and bonuses—such as £100 twice a year—to students’ attendance and performance. This incentive structure can be a strong motivator for young people to stay engaged in their studies, which is a definite positive for educational outcomes.

However, the scheme’s strict eligibility criteria, based solely on household income thresholds, present some challenges. For instance, families just above the income limit, especially larger ones with multiple children in education, may feel unfairly excluded despite genuine financial need. This rigid cutoff can disadvantage those who don’t quite qualify but still struggle to support education-related expenses. Moreover, EMA does not consider family size or the number of children in education, which seems like a missed opportunity to tailor support more equitably.

While EMA is intended to help with costs like travel and equipment, students have the freedom to spend the money as they wish. Many use it for personal expenses such as shopping or driving lessons, which reflects the reality of young people’s diverse needs but may raise questions about the allowance’s focus. Payments are made directly into students’ bank accounts and do not affect parents’ benefits, which helps maintain independence and avoids penalizing families.

The application process, involving multiple forms and annual re-application, can be confusing and repetitive, though staff are generally friendly and helpful—albeit sometimes strict about form errors. This administrative hurdle might discourage some eligible students from applying or continuing to receive EMA.

In summary, EMA offers valuable financial support and motivation for students, but its rigid income criteria and administrative complexity limit its accessibility and fairness. A more flexible approach considering family size and simplifying applications could enhance its impact, aligning better with the goal of supporting all students who genuinely need assistance to succeed in education.

product_reviews: ['    University College London (UCL) has risen in rankings in recent year, and currently ranks 4th in the world in the 2009 Times Higher Education rankings, and 3rd in Europe in the 2010 Academic Ranking of World Universities. A part of me thinks that s down to my having studied there for the last 3 years, but somehow I don t think that s the case. I will try to run through the facts and figures of UCL, and also some of my own personal experiences I ve had there; might I add, I enjoyed it so much I decided to stay on and study for my masters here (will begin in a months time).HistoryUCL was founded in 1826, and was the first university in the UK to be founded on a completely secular basis, and also the first to admit women on equal basis as men. That is truly something UCL students are proud of, which is why we like to mock Kings College London (KCL) as they were founded in response to UCL s secular activities. There is a gentle rivalry between us, which is often expressed in sporting matches; we have stopped the tradition of kidnapping each other s mascots now...As well as that, UCL is part of the University of London Union (ULU); this only really affects sporting activities (that I know of), and UCL have started awarding their own university degrees (for a while, graduates from UCL would only have a ULU degree; most of us now opt for a UCL degree, for personal reasons...)Another random fact is that we have Bentham s body on display in the main building at UCL; this was his wish, but unfortunately his head is now stored elsewhere as some trogladites at KCL stole it and (supposedly) threw it in the Thames.AccommodationAccommodation in Central London is expensive; that s part and parcel of living in London. There are far more students than university accommodation, so priority is given to those that live outside of the M25. You would expect to pay on average    110pw for a self catered room, although they can range from    70-   150pw (ones really far away, and other ones with ensuite rooms). The main UCL ones are Schafer, Astor, Ramsay and Ifor Evans. You don t get the campus feeling (what with it not being a campus university), but you are truly centrally located, and the first three are just off Tottenham Court Road. Cleaners are included (especially in communal areas), and they take the rubbish out for you (which is something we missed when we moved into private accommodation). Normally people only stay in halls in their first year; this is because it s hard to get a spot, and you are also likely to go out less and study more in your latter years. Private accomodation on average would be about    125pw including bills, although I paid    150pw for a double room including bills and mice. I moved out of that place shortly, unsurprisingly. ULU sends out a list of houses available to rent to students at the end of the academic year, so many people live with 3-5 friends          Pictures of London University College     ', '    I m in my second year of a 4 year degree at UCL, and since I ve been here I ve met so many different people, both within my department and at Ramsay Hall, my 1st year accommodation. Ramsay s central location (just off Tottenham Court Rd) was a big advantage, as was its proximity to UCL - just a few minutes  walk. There are two unions nearby - UCL union and ULU (university of London union), both selling cheap(er) drinks compared with usual London prices. The main disadvantage of studying at UCL is the cost of living in London, but I think it s worth it, and I would recommend it to anyone who s trying to make the difficult decision of which universities to apply for.     ', '    On Thursday the 11th of January 2001 UCL Union rejected the membership application of the Circle Pub Crawl Society. We were very bitter about the Union s decision as we thought we had much to contribute the the students Union and were eager to use the Union as a channel for publicity so those who would not normally know about our activities would be able to participate.The Union s reasons for rejecting the society included: It didn t want to be seen promoting a drinking culture that many people see as harmful and it didn t want to be involved if there was an accident or act of vandalism by a member of the society.Around half of the officers voted to reject the application, the rest abstained.Plans to issue a statement of protest have been considered  not worth it. --------Why we should have gained membership to the Union.Unfortunately after we d bothered to put in the effort to apply for membership to the Union they went and turned us down for a load of crap reasons.Our reasons for applying were solid and simple. By gaining the recognition of the union not only would our society gain a lot more initial respect from strangers but it would also be a hell of a lot easier to promote it.The Unions reasons for turning it down were not only crap but also seemed to go against the very Philosophy on which UCL was founded on. That is, to be forward moving by being radical and open minded.Starting with the most pathetic and working down was the qualm that drugs and alcohol awareness week was looming. Here is the Union, who offer a plethora of nights where one can get buckled for around a tenner sitting on their arse. Accusing our society, where the principle activity is to run madly around central London for a day stopping for the odd drink here and there, of promoting alcoholism. If anything we promote the opposite, we show how alcohol can be used to have fun as oppose to solving ones problems.Next. Heaven forbid someone on the crawl might trash a pub and, by the Union s rules, make me and Patrick, by being the organisers, responsible for it. A fairer point than the above. In real life however the person who trashes the pub pays. They chose to come on the crawl and they didn t realise their limits, drank too much and became rowdy. Along with this, during past pub crawls, nothing like this has come close to happening.There was a problem with advertising other establishments. The Union is obliged (probably by its fascist constitution again) to attract people to spend their money in its bars and shops. The thought of even suggesting they branch out a little bit and diversify into other bars and pubs is forbidden. The Union doesn t seem to realise that its lack of innovation already drives people from its establishments. The novelty of cocktails died a death before I even arrived at UCL. The only real reason people still go there is because London is expensive and the Union offers cheap beer. Then when it closes they all pile down Le Scandal, Los Locos, Hombres or in the past The Project for a bit more cheap binge drinking.Although we would have enjoyed their support for now we ll just have to accept the Union s decision to not recognise our society. The only people who will lose out are those who would have been interested but will not hear about it. We actually think the  Unofficial Circle Line Pub Crawl Society  has a nice ring to it This isn t a bitter stab at the Union but a polite way of making a point that they don t really seem to be sticking to the ideals on which UCL was founded. They also seemed to be looking only at the problems the society might cause and not at all the good things it could bring to the Union. Anyone who has ever done a Circle Line Pub Crawl will know that none of the Union s qualms apply to it at all. To prove our point we invite all the Sabb officers to join us on our next unofficial crawl which will be taking place at the end of this term.More information about the Cirlce Line Pub Crawl Society can be found at http://move.to/circleline     ', '    Having just completed my first yr in UCL, i have to say that UCL was extremely different from what i expected.  When i decided where to go for my uni education, i was torn between either LSE or UCL, i asked around and UCL had a far better reputation and my father also was more favorable towards this school.I was, to say the least, not prepared for anything this school had to offer me.  The lecturing was superb, with many reknowned professors, the library facilities were wonderful.  However, UCL is quite far behind on computer technology.  Im sure that if i was doing some sort of engineering that would not be the case, but in my instance, i was usually using 486s and windows 3.1.However, what UCL has going for it is that it is a campus university.  This is quite amazing simply because UCL is in central london, it is extremely fortunate that the students of UCL have this  plot  of land that is so greatly associated to them.The halls, are well... quite gd, comparitively.  There are many old halls but at the same time there are new ones, such as Schafer House, James Lighthill House, and even the old halls of residence are being revamped.. ie Astor College just this summer.All in all, this year in UCL has been a great experiece.  If u are looking for a challenging environment, with top rate teaching and warm friendly people, this is the place for you.     ', '    I am now in my second year at UCL. If you’re weighing up London University College (UCL) from a social and student union perspective, here’s a no-nonsense take grounded in what many students find noteworthy. The UCL Union’s approach to student societies has sparked some controversy—particularly their rejection of new groups like the Circle Pub Crawl Society. The Union’s official stance is a cautious one, citing concerns about promoting a drinking culture and potential liability issues. While understandable from a risk management angle, this decision rubs against UCL’s otherwise open-minded reputation, leaving some students feeling the Union is more gatekeeper than enabler.

Speaking of the Union’s social scene, the focus seems heavily skewed toward cheap alcohol rather than a diverse range of events. If you’re hoping for a vibrant calendar with innovative or varied activities, you might find the offerings a bit one-dimensional. The emphasis on budget-friendly drinks is a plus for those watching their wallets, but it comes at the cost of quality and variety in social experiences. For a student who values memorable nights out and fresh event ideas, this can feel like a letdown.

On the flip side, UCL’s academic side remains strong, with access to excellent libraries and renowned professors, which is a solid foundation for anyone prioritizing education. But when it comes to the student union’s role in fostering community and nightlife, there’s room for improvement. The Union’s cautious conservatism and narrow event focus clash with the social energy many students crave.

In short, if you’re after a university with top-tier academics and a student union that plays it safe—especially around drinking culture—you’ll find UCL fits the bill. But if you want a buzzing, varied social scene that pushes boundaries and embraces new ideas, you might have to look beyond the Union’s current offerings or push for change yourself.
