product_reviews: ['     Making a home.While browsing the site I came across this category for an opinion and I worked in a children  8217;s home many years ago and thought I would tell you about itThe home I worked in was a short stay home for children most of who were aged between 0 and 8. The children here were with us for a variety of reasons we has   8220;battered babies  8221; children waiting for custody battles to be won. Children  8217;s whose parents could not cope for one reason or another. The home in a large Victorian country house had 4   8220;family  8221; groups of about 6 children each group had two housemothers and two assistants who worked in the day.There was also night staff that came on duty when the children were in bed. There was a Matron and a deputy matron, cooks and other ancillary staff. I was a house mother in one group. To be a house mother you had to have N.N.E.B. qualifications or similar qualifications.Some staff were residential others lived out. I lived out I was newly married and  had just moved into the area when I started this job.As a housemother I would come on duty either at 7.30 o  8217;clock in the morning or 11 o  8217;clock and work till either 4 o  8217;clock or 7.30 in the evening. I would work one shift my co house mum would work the other each taking a lunch break at different times. Our assistants would similar shifts. When it was my co house mums day off I would work a long shift from 7.am till 7.30.pm with a couple of hours of in the middle of the day. We worked alternate weekends.Often when I arrived in the morning the children were ready dressed by night staff.In the morning we would serve and eat breakfast with the children. We would clear the breakfast and send any school children to a local school. I had 2 mentally disabled children in my group; they were collected by bus and went to a special school. The babies and preschoolers would stay with us. There was a nursery class in the mornings on site for those of nursery age (3).  During the mornings I would play with my children as any mum might. We would have a drink and biscuit maybe go for a walk.If I were working a long shift I would be off duty for a couple of hours from just before lunchLunch would be eaten by the children in their family groups family room .Those staff of duty would eat in the staff dining room with the   8220;mums from other groups  8221; Some of the children would perhaps have a nap after lunch, others watch TV or play. In the afternoon the children might get a visit from their real parents maybe go out them. In a few cases we would stay with the parent and child be watchful that the child was not   8220;snatched  8221; I felt quite sad for some of the parents and children.The parental visits would have been prearranged visits without arrangements were not allowed.If the parents were not visiting we would play together, go in the garden, go for walks activities you would do with your child at home.The children would arrive back from school at 3  8217;30 onwards the special needs children getting home about 4.30.When the children arrived home we would give then a drink and biscuit listen to their tales. Teatime would be at 5 o  8217;clock. After tea we would play a little or watch the TV. The day usually finished with a cuddle and a goodnight story. All the children would be in bed for half past seven when the night duty staff came on duty.It would also be my job to go shopping for new clothes for any child. I often wondered what became of those children, they will be adults now. I just hope the care we gave them helped them grow into happy emotionally sound adults. I left this job when my husband finished his teaching degree I was working while he was on a grant, the wages I earn were not much, work in the caring profession is not well paid. So we moved so he could get a job when he finished university I was just pregnant then anyway. I worked in this children  8217;s home about 18 yrs ago . I have not had the need to visit one since I wonder if the basic set up has changed much. Thanks for reading  Mary.      ', '    This review is on one of the most rewarding, yet most undervalued job that there can ever be. And I ve done some  First off, lets  take a look at the disadvantages. The work is not at all valued, which is shown in the number of hours that people work alonsgide the low rate of pay that is offered. Many care homes regardless of whether they are privately owned or are a part of a bigger company, will generally pay the national minimum wage or just slightly higher for health care assistants - a pittance for what they do, which I don t like one bit. However, council run establishments may pay more because after all what else can they do with our money. As noted, another downfall is that of having to do shift work. Starting times vary anything from around 7 in the morning, and finishing times normally at around 10 at night for day shifts. Night workers also find that times vary, and all that can cause difficulties for family life. School/ nursery start times; picking them up again; feeding, and so on. Some employers make allowances for this, and can arrange for your shifts to be in line with other committments. There is always the fear factor involved in care work - having to deal with awkward residents; having to carry out personal care for them, and of course the Big D - Death. As sad as it may seem, some people just can t deal with this for whatever reason, and so one would advise them not to go in for this line of work. But now, on to the advantages. These sadly do not outweigh the other side of the coin, but lets  just give it a go. First off, you get to meet a whole new bunch of people. New staff; residents, and their families are the main ones that you will have to deal with during your working hours. Yes, you will not get on with all of them but sadly that is life. If we were all to look for a job where we got on with everyone, then we would always be on the look out. Secondly, you also get the satisfaction of having done something for another person. Even if they are unable to thank you themselves, just imagine that you are doing for one person s elderly relative that another may just well be doing for yours - feeding them; clothing them; washing them, and ensuring their comfort and safety. Look at it like that, and it gives you a great sense of pride. Can I do this job? Ask yourself this  If you think that you could and don t mind the extra work that comes with it, then go for it. But if you are a bit prudish and think that this is for scum like me, then leave me your address and I will send a mob to your door. This is something that I am passionate about, and it is not beneath a single person just to at least try.     ', '    Overworked and underpaid, two descriptions which a  lot of people will attach to their own job but which is more than true in the field of residential home care assistants.  It is a job which requires less a wish for money than a desire to help people and make a difference in the twilight years of their lives.I worked in this field on and off for twenty years, both in England and in the US.  It is a hard job, both physically and emotionally draining, yet there is also joy from the smallest pleasures sometimes, and from knowing you are trying to do your bit to make these people lives somewhat more easy.When I began, there was no definite training.  You got hired, the people who had worked there a while showed you what to do, you worked with them and then you worked alone.  Nowadays, although a  lot of places will hire you with no formal training or qualifications, both in England and the US there is a  push for people to earn certification, to take classes and qualify.  Not only is the intention to upgrade the profession and to give credit to those in the field, but also to update knowledge and provide a more skilled workforce.  People who understand the needs and wants of the geriatric community, and who can provide a better standard of care for their residents.Nursing homes can no longer just be started by anyone with a couple of rooms to spare who decides that having a couple of old dears share a bedroom is an easy money-maker.  In England I think it is now the law that an owner have at least a nursing quslification or they must hire someone who does, and in America this has been the case in larger residential homes for a  long time.  So, if you are thinking   why would I want to get into a job like this that won t pay me enough and will work me to the bone?   My answer is,  To make a difference  For too long, nursing home neglect and abuse went on silently behind closed doors.  In the US, attempts to get people off welfare and into work meant they would go for interviews for these jobs, accept them, and then have to work them.  If they quit, they lost their welfare - it they were FIRED they kept it.  Thus they had only to  be laissez-faire in their attitude and could soon be back sitting on their rear ends and having to do nothing for their money.  Although different in England, this job has always had a greater need for care assistants and as such has been one of those which always managed to keep a steady flow of returning-to-work housewives and students passing through its realms.Some good people came in along the way.  Some just people, needing a job, to help pay the bills.The residential home attitude though, by its very nature, has been to institutionalize the individual.  It is no good for eighty year old Mrs Jones, who maybe fought in the war or taught children all her working life, to decide on Thursday that she fancies Chinese for dinner when the menu for that day is sausage and mash.  Her wishes are completely undermined, although now most places are attempting to at least provide options.  Is her wanting Chinese any different to yours and mine? No, but the confines of a residential home are not conducive to individual wants and needs.Likewise, most places usually have a tv lounge, and from what I ve seen, it is the assistants who decide what programme is being watched.  Some places do have tvs in the rooms for residents, but again there may be two or four people sharing that one room.  They have no place to escape for a  little solitude.I know there are also lots of activities planned now, anything from scrapbooking to having a piano player come in and having a good old singalong, to yoga classes, to crafts and poets like me going in to give readings, as I did in the Summers of 2000 and 2001.  These things give RESPECT to these people, an acknowledgement that they are indeed persons worthy of attention.So, to the person who is considering this career, I say, take a good look at yourself and be honest, can you do this job and be the best person at doing it?  Can you wipe someone s backside, whilst still managing to give them their dignity as you do so?  Do you care enough to snatch (and there s no time for idle chat, even though I feel we need to make it) time to have some kind of PERSONAL conversation with each of  your  people each day.  While brushing hair, making the bed, just grab that time and ask about THEIR lives, families, children, grandchildren, pets, the war, anything THEY want to talk about.  Something that shows that you CARE about them and that THEIR life has been valid.As you care for these people, think of the old adage  Do unto others  and apply it to everything you do, whether brushing hair (don t yank on tangles, for instance), to tiny observations of their personal options.  For instance, whilst bathing or bedwashing residents, I always gave them the option of washing and drying their own private area.  Not much of a consolation when they are in the bathing chair in the shower, naked as the day they were born, but a small piece of their dignity offered to them.For those who require feeding, do so gently and slowly.  You take your time eating your food, allow them to also do the same with theirs.  I know the clock keeps on running and you have a hundred other things to do.  Take the time to also give yourself a quick break in the midst of hustle.  Think that if this were YOU, how you would want someone to care for you.When moving people, do so slowly.  Although I always prided myself with being a gentle, conscientious person, since ill health entered my life, I realise the pain some people experience that is not visibly noticeable.  I remember a nurse telling me that someone who always complained of pain, as we touched her legs and ankles when we tried putting on her support stockings, was  imagining  it.  Well, that was one of the things I have now experienced and I ve told doctors, nurses and caregivers -  Believe it    The slightest pressure can be excruciating.  Don t think that just because these people are old they are imagining their pain, they are not.  It is real and it HURTS Lifting, turning someone in bed, helping someone to stand or sit, all of these also can be painful experiences for the elderly and infirm.  Do so carefully.  Recent years have propogated the use of a back brace to help the safety of the carer s back, we also need to consider the safety of the resident.  It is not just good enough that there is no bruising, we MUST try to make it as comfortable as possible when we do these things.  Although recently there has been an upsweep in the pay scale in the US, maybe one and a half times the minimum wage, this job is still way down on the list when it comes to monetary reward, and I think the case is much the same in England.  It does take a very special person to do this job and to do it well.There are days when you will want to come home and cry.  Do it.  Some days you will  lose  a person that you have interacted with closely for a while.  This will affect you, and so it should.  If it doesn t then you ve lost some of your humanity.  You will moan and complain about your back aching, the stress, the long hours, we all do, and it seems even having cushy jobs doesn t change that.What you will have is the knowledge that you are making a difference in somebody s life, at the end of that life.If I had my way (in my own version of Utopia)  there wouldn t be nursing and residential homes and the elderly would live out their lives at home surounded by families who love them;  sadly this is not something that a lot of families are capable of dealing with, so if nothing else, this career field offers job security.I feel that as time goes on, there will be more of a movement towards skilled qualifications (NVQ currently has 3 stages, I think, in England) and in the US each state requires licensing.  This is good and will enable carers to know more about how to provide good quality care.  But something they can t teach you, or quantify, is your empathy and in this job, that is one of the biggest skills required to do it with the individuals welfare at heart.Overworked and underpaid, underthanked.  This is a career that helps you appreciate your blessings, and well worthy of your consideration if you are up to it.     ', '    Introduction=========Since members are interested in the job I have taken I thought it might be a good idea to write a review about what I now do. However I would like to give you some background information on me first to better understand this review.I have done office work since I was 17 years old and have done various jobs within that from Telesales to Secretarial. I worked in an Accounts Department until October 2005 when I experienced a nervous breakdown, I won t go into the details but my doctor and I decided that my job was the cause and I should consider a career change when I was ready to go back to work.I am now 25 years old and in March 2006 I started my new career, my doctor was happy with my choice as it would help with my anxiety and shyness, as I have mentioned before I shy away from face to face contact.The Interview==========At the home the owner and the assistant manager interviewed me. I was told all about the history of the home and that this was only a small home that housed 18 residents many of which could do things for themselves. The home is also a freedom home and residents could come and go as they please, the residents also have a right to choose but more about that later.I was given a tour of the home and was shown various residents rooms to understand better how each room is decorated and furnished to the residents personal choice. I was told about some of my duties while touring the home but I ll explain more about that later. I was also introduced to some of the residents I assume to observe how I interacted with them and vice versa (I pushed through all my natural instincts to clam up and be friendly and talkative).They must have been very happy with me as I was asked to fill in an application form and CRB form so they could do the necessary checks before any employment started.The CRB check (Criminal Record Bureau Check) is to ensure that you do not have any convictions in the social care that you shall be working in. The home paid for this check and I would not be able to work in the home without it. However I was issued with a temporary permit to work as long I was being supervised for the safety of the residents. My CRB check took two weeks to come through, a copy is sent both to you and your employer, I had no issues with mine.Hours=====With this being a residential home the hours can be flexible but you also need to be flexible as well because sometimes you will be asked to cover for colleagues who are sick or on holiday.There are three shifts available. The morning shift, afternoon shift and night shift. My HoursMonday 2pm-8pmTuesday Day offWednesday 9am-12pmThursday 9am-12pmFriday 9am-12pmSaturday 2pm-8pmSunday 2pm-8pm (Saturday and Sunday are alternate weekend shifts)These are my set hours but I have been working more than this because of staff sickness.The Morning Shift 8am-2pm=====================Upon arrival all the staff are gathered together to listen to the report for the previous day and night because if something happened with one of the resident s overnight then the day staff need to be aware of this.On the morning shift there are four members of staff, two to work upstairs and two downstairs (at 12pm the Care Assistants is cut down to tow). The first job of the day is to serve everyone breakfast; there is a list as there is a choice of toast, cornflakes, bran flakes, porridge and weetabix. There is also a cup of tea or coffee as per the request of the resident.Everyday there is baths to be given on a rota for the residents, this is agreed with the residents as to there personal choice, i.e. number of times per week, morning/evening and bath or shower. The residents that are having a bath are dealt with first (there are four bathrooms in total) you take a wheelchair along to there room, assist them into the chair, gather clean clothes and toiletries and take them to the bathroom.While the bath is running you need to help them undress and support them into the bath hoist. The bath hoist allows you to lift the person without straining yourself, it is a chair that is connected to a pole that is drilled into the floor and on the pole you have a handle that is turned to lift and turn into the bath.If you a bathing someone who does not need to be supervised then you can leave the bathroom and return to there room to strip and remake their bed. Otherwise you have to stay in the bathroom and help them wash and dry themselves (you just have to do the bed afterwards).Once all the bathing is done it is time to get the rest up, which is literally helping them out of bed, helping them wash, getting them dressed, making there bed and either making them comfortable in their room or taking them down to the lounge.Some of the residents have catheters fitted to drain their urine away and you have to change the bag that is fitted from their night bag to their day bag. The difference is that the night bag is bigger and can hold more urine while the day bag is smaller and can be held against the leg with a stocking.After everyone is up it is then time to serve morning coffee, once that is served you sort the washing and start up the machines then get chance to have a sit down yourself and believe me you ll need it because it will now be about 11am.After you have finished your morning coffee the next job is to prepare the trays for lunch for those who eat in their room and also set the dining table for those residents that eat in the lounge. Before lunch is ready you will have just enough time to sort through the airing cupboard. Each piece of clothing is marked with a coloured dot, which corresponds to each resident. Sort into piles and put their clothes away in their room.The cook dishes up the lunchtime meal and the Care Assistants are responsible for delivering their food and ensuring that they take their medication. We only have two residents that need to be fed by Care Assistants and these are done last while everyone else is eating.Many of the residents take their time while eating so we go back to the laundry room and empty the washer into the tumble dryer and start that up, we also add another load into the washing machine.All the trays are wiped down and placed back on their selves. All plates and dishes are loaded into the dishwasher. Once the kitchen is back to being clean and tidy it is now time to help each resident to the toilet and clean them up from lunch as well.After everyone has been to the toilet (and emptied catheters bags) you need to start writing the report for each resident before your shift ends and the next staff comes on duty. Before you leave you always run through the report with the next staff just to bring them up to speed.The Afternoon Shift 2pm-8pm======================There is two Care Assistants on duty for this shift.Once again the first job is to receive the report about the previous events then you need to make afternoon tea for the residents. Before taking the cups of tea around you check what is for tea (4pm) so that you can ask the residents if they would like that or an alternative, this is always written down in the tea book.After you have spoken with all the residents and written down their choice for tea, you then need to prepare them. This can be anything from sandwiches and salads to spaghetti on toast to poached eggs.Once you have prepared the trays for teatime and done any preparation prior to serving you need to check the laundry room to ensure that the morning staff had enough time to complete all the washing. If there is washing left fold up and put into the airing cupboard.If you are lucky you might get to have a five or ten-minute break before the teatime starts. Tea is served on their trays with their choice of food plus a piece of cake and a cup of tea. The kitchen is always open so if any of the residents require any further food it can be done on request. You clear up after teatime and make the kitchen tidy and clean once again; you also need to set the trays up for breakfast (as per the list mentioned earlier).Since there is only one night nurse on duty per night the two Care Assistant s start to assist residents to bed as some need to be done by two Carer s. Many also want to go to bed early because the elderly do get tired very easily.Putting the residents to bed is a reserve from getting them up in the morning. You help them onto the toilet, wash them, undressed them and settle them into bed. Drain catheters and switch from the day bag to the night bag.You will put on another load for washing, which the night nurse will dry; the night nurse also deals with the ironing of sheets. The reports for each resident need to be done ready for when the night nurse comes on duty.The Night Shift 8pm-8am===================I have now done two night shifts so I now have that knowledge. The most scary part of this shift is that you are on your own, there is another member of staff on call should you need them in an emergency.At 8pm you receive the report from that evening and the past couple of days depending on when you were last on duty, then you are on your own. I was very nervous the first time but once an hour had passed by I was calm.The majority of the residents have already been put to bed and there are only about 3 residents that are still up. However there are about 8 residents that like a warm milk drink before going to sleep and for taking their bedtime tablets. These are done at 9pm. The other residents are helped to bed by 10pm; they will ask to go to bed.Other jobs you have to do are ironing sheets and shirts, preparing vegetables for tomorrow s lunch and kitchen jobs (there is a rota and I had to wipe the shelves on one night shift and wipe out cupboards on the other night).All these little things take you up to about 12am and that is without rushing. The only other job you have to do is rounds every hour. Rounds is basically walking around the home and checking on the residents. You then have the rest of the night to yourself (as long as no one gets up) which can be quite boring so just make sure you do not go to sleep.Once 5.30am hits you can start getting some of the residents up and dressed. The call bells will also start and it is a good idea to have a pot of tea at the ready, as many will want something to wet their mouths.Your final job is to write report about the night s activities or lack of them and inform the day staff when they arrive. In all I did not mind doing the night shift but I did find that between 11pm and 4am nothing really happened so I got very bored but that is where a good book comes in very handy.Skills====I think you need to have a certain type of character to be able to do a job like this. You have to be very patience with the residents as many of them are deaf and you have my have to repeat yourself many times before they are able to understand you. You also need to have a strong stomach, if you feel sick at the sight of bowel movements then I would not recommend this job as there is lots to be seen and believe me there can a be strong smell to go with it.A caring nature is also needed, you have to like doing things for people otherwise it will drive you insane because you are forever fetching drinks and taking them to the toilet.The care home that I work for will be putting me forward for NVQ qualifications after I have been working there 6 months. They have also paid to put me through my Food and Hygiene course and the Controlled Medication course. You need both of these before you can prepare food and give out medication.Overview=======Considering what I had done for the past seven years I can truly say that this is nothing like what I used to do at all and I do enjoy my job. It is such a pleasure to see the residents happy to see you.You cannot put into words the relationship you build up with the residents. Just the same as the social basis you will always have some that you like better but I can say that I get along well with all of the eighteen residents.Many of my family and friends have said,  I don t know how you can do that   and I have no reply for them. I am not going to pretend that wiping bottom is the best part of this job but having the resident say thank you for doing it is a reward in itself.Nobody goes into this type of work for the pay, my previous job paid me    21,000 per annum and I now get just over a quarter of that. It is also hard work and you are on your feet all the time, my feet killed me during the first two weeks I was there but I think they are now getting used to it. However the rewards you get from doing this type of work is wonderful and every time I am on duty I have many residents asking when I shall be on duty again. You can have a laugh and a joke with them and some even like to have a cuddle.I was provided with one uniform free of charge but if you want to have more than that you have to buy them yourself, they cost around    30 from new. I have four uniforms and have not paid for any because a friend who had given it up donated the other three.I now have a job that I enjoy and it has been helping me in dealing with people and over coming my shyness, which is not going to disappear overnight but hopefully over time it will.Thanks for reading.     ', '    After spending four and a half years working as a Care Assistant in a Residential EMI home, I feel qualified to give my opinion. I have often, after being asked what job I did, been met with,  I really don t know how you can do it  or  I admire you . Well, let s be thankful that there are care assistants as we may all need one at some time in our lives. *****What Does The Job Involve.The job can vary hugely depending on the place in which you are working and the needs of the clients there. The hours you work can also have an effect on the job that you will be required to do. In general you are offering assistance to clients where needed and helping them to remain as independent as possible. The word care can stretch a long way, it can mean so many things. Anyone in need of care and assistance could be your client, but the majority are the elderly. You will work under the guidance of a senior care assistant or a manager of a home. My job was in an EMI home, this means  Elderly Mentally Ill . Clients may suffer from Alzheimer s disease or have another form of Dementia. Duties carried out in this job are extensive, time spent chatting or playing a game with your client is just as valuable as nursing her while she is poorly. The tasks are basically mapped out to reflect the very individual needs of each person in your care. Washing, bathing and helping to dress, when needed and assisting with toileting. Changing a wet or soiled bed, applying ointment to a sore, giving out medicines. Going for walks, watching TV together, chatting to relatives, looking at old photo s. The list goes on and on   ..You have the opportunity to make a real difference to someone s life.*****Qualifications Required.At this moment in time anyone over 18 years old can work as a Care Assistant, providing you have had a CRB (Criminal Records Bureaux) check. This is to ensure that you are considered  safe  to work with vulnerable people. If your check is ok then you will be issued with a certificate. Most work places pay for the CRB, but I have heard that some expect you to. There are different types of CRB, according to what your job is, so don t just assume that if you already have one, you don t need another.In the near future it is the Government recommendation that anyone working as a Care Assistant should either have, or be working towards an NVQ level 2. For this reason most places offer or insist on you training for the NVQ, again they will pay as long as you don t leave within a certain period of your qualifying.You will have other on the job training tailored to suit your individual position, most if not all being compulsory because it is for your own and other peoples safety. It is also your employers duty to ensure that they have enabled you with adequate training to ensure safety. So look out for training in, Fire and Safety, Hygiene, advice on lifting and moving, abuse etc. Things that are not qualified by a piece of paper are also very useful for this job. A kind and caring nature, able to work as part of a team, and good social skills, will all be beneficial. Common sense is invaluable in situations where you can t just take the lead from a text book.*****Getting The JobThere is a high demand for Care Assistants in most area s. This can be seen just by scouring the local newspaper, where there are an abundance of advertisements. While there are some that prefer you to have experience, many will not. Normally you just have to telephone for an appointment, which will be quite soon, as they are in desperate need of your services. The interview is often an informal chat, then, subject to the CRB check, you can quickly start work. Obviously everyone isn t deemed suitable and some may not want to take the job once they have found out more about what is involved.*****Furthering Your Career.If you wish to further your career, you can do so by more training. You might choose to be a Care Assistant in a more senior position or you might like to manage a home or establishment. You could also regard this position as a stepping stone in the caring field, and even train as a nurse. Higher levels of NVQ are available and you will be expected to have gained some experience too. Obviously good references will also be needed.*****My Experiences.As already mentioned, I worked in an EMI residential home, and so a high level of care was required. Although it wasn t a Nursing home, a lot of nursing took place, for the simple reason that there are grey area s, you can t just automatically move a client when they deteoriate. Firstly it wouldn t be fair on the individual and secondly, there really are not the facilities available to do this.I went into the job with no experience or qualifications and it was quite a shock to me just how hard the job was. I have had good and bad experiences.My job involved assisting very confused and sometimes violent people of whom most were incontinent. I actually felt quite scared and intimidated at times when I first began doing this job, I didn t feel able to deal with all situations that I may be faced with. I had no knowledge of the clients that I was looking after. In time though things got easier and I was able to do my job with more confidence.On a practical level, my job was to help the residents with washing, bathing, dressing, getting into bed and saying goodnight. Giving them their medicine or something to eat. Helping out someone who may have had an accident and even spending the night down at casualty with them. Filling out reports and charts to make sure information was accurate and up to date. At night there was just two staff to ensure the safety and well being of 18 residents, we were very, very busy.Another part of the job was to speak to Health Care professionals, Doctors, Ambulance staff and Relatives etc. so good communication skills are very advantageous. Confidentiality is also extremely important.I was paid    5.30 an hour, a lot of places pay less   A few pay more.My holiday entitlement was the pretty standard four weeks and they offered an optional pension scheme.*****My Opinion.I believe that the Government are absolutely right to expect that all Care Assistants should have a qualification or be in training. This job comes with huge responsibilities and involves some of our most vulnerable members of society, human beings, not merchandise  The problem lies in the low and sometimes minimum wages that are being paid. Although there are very many dedicated carers throughout the country, the salary does not attract enough. This job is not the equivalent of being a chamber maid in your nearest hotel. It should be seen as a career, and a well paid respected one at that. All to often there are completely unqualified staff who are only doing the job because it  fits in  to their lifestyle, that s ok as long as they actually do care. I would class myself as a caring person who has good people skills, but admit that I found this job both physically and mentally draining at times. The sense of responsibility is great, I had never seen a dead person, if someone died during the shift, it had to be dealt with in a professional way. You could never guarantee what would greet you as you began a shift. If sickness and diarrhoea was going around the home, then so be it.My favourite part of the job was to see all the different characters, hear stories and look at photo s. These were fascinating people with great personalities and interesting stories and memories to share, (with EMI sufferers, it is their short term memory that is affected). Some residents genuinely thought that you were their friend just calling in on a visit. How nice that staff can be considered in that way.To sum up, this can be a very rewarding, worthwhile and satisfying job, if you choose to take this career path, be dedicated and train so that you are able to do your job to the best of your ability. Be prepared for hard work and know that you are able to deal with responsibility. Just think, what type of care would you like when you are old and frail.****And Finally.A manager in the home which I worked often overheard staff saying,  I wish I wasn t here , or  this is the last place I want to be, I d much rather be at home , with suitably miserable faces. At the next staff meeting, she quite rightly pointed out that this was infact HOME to 18 people, and why should THEY put up with such behaviour. How right she was.Thanks for reading. x     ', '    I have worked in the care industry for 32 years now and have worked myself up from an instructor in a day centre for disabled adults to being a manager of a day centre for disabled people.I had a career change31 years ago, when I decided teaching was not for me and I turned my talents to instructing crafts in a day centre.I have been trained through my employer - social services. I can say that I have had excellent training to equip me for my job.It was difficult at first to be put on training - it depends on whether you have a manager who is in favour of training- mine wasn t but I persisted and there were other managers higher up who saw my potential and mentored me.Nowadays - due to care standards attitudes to training are changing. Soon all care workers will have to be registered.You will need the appropriate training for your job to be able to register.In my county in Wales , where I work, all care workers will eventually have to be registered with Care Standards.Currently our county has the highest amount of employees trained to do thier job.The raining needed for the various jobs are-Care worker- home care, project worker, sessional worker- require NVQ Level 2 health and socail care.Instructor , home leader, senior care, care supervisor- require NVQ Level 3  Health and social careManagers-  NVQ Level 4 Health and social care or  NVQ Management Level 4Homes which are registered withthe care council will need a NVQ 4 Registered home manager qualification.As my qualification is social work I have had to be registered since 2003- I had to re-register this year as re-registration is every three years. I pay to register.I am NOT allowed to practice if I am NOT registered.  And now NO-ONE is allowed to call themseves a social worker if they are not qualified or registered. This point has caused some changes in job titles as Social work assistants cannot now be called that- the social work part of their job title has to be changed- currently this name change is happening in my county- no name has been settled on yet. (But it won t have social work in their title)  Registration is useful ( besided making more money for the government   ) as it demonstrates to those in receipt of our services, that the service is being delivered by proffessional people who have had to undergo training to gain the necessary skills to do their job.The main values of training in social care is to value the people we work with, respect the people we work with,to show no prejudice, equality and equal access for everyone we work with, to help people live as meaningful and independant a life as their are able to, and to be treated as we would wish to be treated ourselves. At times we need to be advocates for the people we support,And how many times have we seen social services in the news when something goes wrong??  THus the comment above that teh proffession can be seen as the  public whipping boy Training for NVQ Level 2 takes , on average, 18 months NVQ 3 2 years, NVQ 4 2 years.  Although you can fast track your training if you work hard and have the experience.Its  on the job  training, so youare not doing something you don t know about and even if you don t know there are always collegues who can guide you in the right direction.Social care work can be very rewarding for job satisfaction, can be very long hours and unsocial hours, but don t expect to get rich by it , its among the lowest paid jobs around.       ', '    I am employed as a care assistant, in a residential rest home. This entails, working on a rota system with other team members. The hours and shifts vary on a pattern of :-7am - 127.30 am - 2pm7.30am - 3pm3pm -9pmOn each shift there is a shift leader, who supervises the staff and informs us of any changes and events from the previous working shift. The shift leader is there for any questions or problems that may arise in the working hours.On entering the building, we have to gather together for a hand over meeting, this is when we are informed by the shift leader, of any events, i.e if a resident is ill, has fallen, needs a change of diet, is having visitors, or if the doctor or nurse is coming and anything else which is important for us to know, before we start work.We are responsible for the care of the residents, by way of personal hygiene, feeding the residents who are unable to feed themselves, assisting them to get up and dress themselves and assisting to put them to bed. Assist them to go to the bathroom and change them when necessary. Assist with baths and washing hair.We also have to assist in leisure activities, doing intervention where we can play board games, go for walks, read, play cards, paint and clean their nails and socialise with the residents.We also have to assist to transfer some of the residents from chairs to wheel chairs and vice versa with the aid of the hoists. As well, as doing their laundry, ironing, preparing meals at tea time - 5pm -6pm and taking the drinks trolley round with hot drinks at regular times during the day and before the residents bedtime.We also have to write input and output charts to monitor certain individual residents. We let visitors in and out, ask them to sign the visitors book, make them tea and take them to see their relatives.We are also responsible for the health and safety of residents, staff and visitors. This includes the wearing of gloves and aprons whilst assisting in getting the residents up washed and dressed, or put to bed. And regularly washing our hands.Checking that equipment is clean and safe to use, that the battery for the hoist is charged and that there are no spillages on the floor. That the air beds are in working order and that the rooms are stocked with toiletries, and clean clothing for the residents. We are regularly given a fire drill to time response of staff and meet in the hallway at the front door as required.We keep time sheets for our hours worked and are responsible for getting these signed at the end of a working week. We have to read the message book to see if there is anything written by the managers or shift leaders which is important for us to known and we have to write incident reports in the case of certain events.All files are kept in the cupboard where we have our hand over meetings, these include care plans, policy and procedures and message books, visitors books, time sheets and other files to refer to if needed.We are paid monthly at    6 an hour which is a low wage but the work is rewarding in other ways. I like my job and am at the moment training for an NVQ level 2 and will go on to do level 3 and other qualifications after. If your thinking about going into care work, then i d recommend it as a steady job, good fun and rewarding, even though it is hard work and can at times be challenging.     ', '    Whilst shopping today I had a sudden urge to write my next review and struggled to think of what the subject matter would be.... A tub of Jelly Beans maybe as I had munched through almost the whole tub whilst browsing in Boots the chemist.... Nah    I am only good at one thing ~~~ my job. So here we go me dears   The life of a care/ support worker part 2  THE BEGINNING. ~~~ You will all be aware of the fact that I work in my local town in a small privately owned care home for disabled adults.I help to look after 4 females and 4 males whose ages range from 35 to 60 years old. My eight spoonfulls of tonic and believe me, they are just that.From the moment I step foot in the home at 7.45 each morning they keep me entertained, busy, challenged,happy, sad,surprised... in fact the list of feelings/ experiences that they produce never ceases to amaze me.To be at the home they have been assessed by various medical,and psychological professionals and have been deemed suitable to receive residential care. They are then placed in a home that either their family or their social worker has agreed on and their life begins according to how they fit in and settle.The government agrees on the funding that the individual will need to be kept in the home and arrange payment to an account each week. At the moment I believe that the Disability Living Allowance ( DLA ) is in two components. 1. Care component and 2. Mobility component.Care component......... Highest rate is    67.00 per week                                         Middle rate is      44.85 per week                                         Low rate is          17.75  perweekMobility component ......High rate is    46.75                                          Lowest rate    17.75  paid weekly.When I first saw the rates over 6 years ago I was surprised at them thinking that they were quite good.... I have since changed my mind and now know what these wonderful unfortunate people have to fork out each week in order to try and have anything like a normal life. Everything has to be paid for, transport charges being the most costly.... If they attend a day centre ( which most of ours do ) they have to pay for every time the centre decided to take them off campus, even to pick up fish and chips as a special treat after working on the allotment for the morning. Me being a soft touch would like to offer to take them to the fish and chip shop for free. Not possible I m afraid as it would be difficult cramming twelve hungry people in my Shogun THE MIDDLE ~~~ Most of our residents have family that live close to the home and in all fairness some of them do try and visit from time to time. I have however caught one mother physically trying to limbo past our front gate so that I could not see her..... What she wouldn t know was that her son had been saying that morning how he would like to see his mummy... Yes a 36 year old calling his mother, mummy. It breaks ones heart to have to be that   pretend   mummy some times and to give the occasional hug to her son in her thoughtless absence. THE END ~~~ Do I enjoy what I do ? Oh yes indeed..... I work very long and sometimes demanding hours and would not swap my job for any other. I am lucky that I have a gaffer ( boss ) that really appreciates my input and although I earned just under     26,000  last year, I can truely say that I dont do the work for the money.... The residents are my second family and I love them all to pieces... One of them asks me on a daily basis if I will marry him and another one tells me that I am the best key worker that she has ever had ( I have also heard the same resident tell all the other staff the same thing so I wont get too big headed about it    )The eight residents that I look after have various conditions... We have three with Epilepsy ranging from mild to severe... One lady has Cerebral Palsy.... one gent who is now totally blind, two Downs Syndrome ladies with severe learning disabilities and one man with a crumbling spine and severe learning disabilities.WOULD I RECOMMEND ? ~~~ Yes I would... bear in mind that there will be days when you will be spat at, kicked, have things thrown at you ( and that is by the other staff    ) Look beyond those days and you will gain a wealth of experience from people who have been dealt bad luck in their sad but precious lives. Thanks for sharing my experience.Julie.xx     ', '    This is an opinion/review I can possibly write more from the heart than any, as I worked as a support worker, in residential settings for 7 years.  It wasn t an easy job, most people assumed it was just cleaning and wiping, but to me, it was a wonderful opportunity to inject a bit of myself into my job, I worked with and for some amazing people, had some great experiences, and ultimately, used my experience in the field to pursue a professional qualification in Social Work and now work from the other side of the fence, so to speak. As a support worker in a residential home, well, the work can be vastly different depending on who you work for (local authority, charity or private company) and the pay is invariably quite low (I was on    12,000 in London before I quit to do the social work training, 3 years ago- and I was possibly one of the better paid because I d been working there for so long and had wormed my way to the top of the pay scale). My direct experience was working with adults with learning disabilities, physical disabilities and mental health disorders. This is a vastly different experience from working with over 65s but as this is my experience it is what I will write about. As the larger long stay hospitals were closed down in the 80s, lots of people with learning disabilities and mental health disorders were moved into smaller  community  type homes, and it was in one of these where I first worked. The people I worked for had all lived in a hospital for 30 or 40 years, and although they had moderate learning disabilities, they were not able to function effectively in the society into which they had been thrown. That is why I use  support worker  rather than  carer . Our work did involve personal care, helping people to wash and dress, to cook (although some larger homes have designated  cooks  and domestics, ours didn t), to clean and to assist with medication, and make sure people got to where they needed to go and got back  We assisted with social activities, outings and even holidays and were the main contact, between us, for the people with whom we worked, more so than the social workers (who maybe visited once a year) even sometimes more than families (to whom their child with a learning disability was an  embarrassment , and yes, I did see that a lot ). We worked in shifts, covering the house for 24 hours a day, although other houses where I have worked have separate day and night staff. You are faced with challenges and situations on a daily basis, and that is what makes the job. In this job, possibly more than a million others which are more  high-powered , you really really are in a position to make a difference to someones  life on a day-in day-out basis. We had good times, and holidays (in the UK and overseas) and very difficult times, supporting residents through tougher periods, bereavements and illnesses (sometimes quite severe). It is a job unlike many others - the one thing we used to joke about a bit as staff though was that everyone said  oh, I could never do a job like that  or  you re so wonderful doing that  etc. It used to make us laugh, because, as I used to reply,  it s my job, I do it because I enjoy it, not because it makes me a better person, if I thought I would enjoy accountancy more, that s what I d do , it doesn t make you a better or worse person, working in a residential home, because you gain such a richness in being able to understand more about different people, and work in a great environment with great people, and that is ultimately, probably more important than the money. Saying that, the experience enabled me to go back to college and qualify as a social worker (2 years full time, hard work, but ultimately worth it ), so the prospects are there if you want to take them. My salary has literally doubled since I qualified (these bits of paper are remarkably useful ), but from time to time, when I m making my annual visits to my clients in their residential homes, I really really miss the contact I had and the opportunity I had to build relationships when I was a residential care worker. I fell into the work. It wasn t a vocation for me, it was just a job which I got because I d done a bit of voluntary work, and I ended up enjoying it and staying for probably longer than was good for me, but I d really recommend it as a career option, because you can go somewhere with it  It does really depend on your employers though, and check them out as thoroughly as you can. Local authorities tend to be good employers, but they are closing down a lot of their homes. Charities tend to be better than private profit-making companies, because they pay more and have some kind of basic ethos. I ve seen some quite heartbreakingly awful residential homes in my work as a social worker, and it just made me appreciate the wonderful place I worked even more       ']

s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
If you’re considering a role as a Residential Home Care Assistant, it’s important to recognize that this job demands more than just practical skills—it calls for a genuinely caring nature, patience, and emotional resilience. From my experience and what many have shared, forming close, almost family-like bonds with residents is one of the most rewarding aspects. These relationships provide deep emotional satisfaction, especially when you see the positive impact of your support on individuals who often face complex physical, mental, or learning disabilities.

Qualifications such as NVQ, Food and Hygiene, and Controlled Medication courses aren’t just bureaucratic hurdles—they’re essential for safely handling duties like personal care, meal assistance, and medication management. These certifications ensure you’re well-prepared to meet residents’ diverse needs, which can range widely and require both sensitivity and competence.

That said, the role isn’t without its challenges. The emotional toll can be significant, particularly when supporting residents through difficult health declines or end-of-life care. It’s a demanding environment that tests your resilience, but it also offers invaluable practical experience. For those passionate about social care, this position can be a meaningful stepping stone toward further career opportunities, such as social work or specialized caregiving roles.

In sum, if you value hands-on experience, emotional connection, and making a tangible difference in vulnerable lives, this role offers both challenges and profound rewards. Just be prepared for the emotional highs and lows, and ensure you pursue the necessary qualifications to provide the best care possible. It’s a path that requires heart and skill in equal measure—but for those who embrace it, the personal and professional growth can be truly transformative.

product_reviews: ['    NVQ In CareTrain and gain evidence of competenceThe awards to be achieved are:National Vocational Qualifications in Care. Levels 1, 2, 3, 4   5Mine is a City and Guilds qualification.For each unit there is a certificate then a certificate on completion with all units on.Work at a qualification while you earn at your place of employment. Gain relevant qualifications to gain promotion and better working practises.Level 2 is for Care Assistants/Support Workers and equivalent Level 3 is for Care Officers/ Senior Support Workers and equivalentLevel 4 is for Assistant Managers and equivalentLevel 5 is probably for Managers and equivalentThere are specialist subjects within the Care NVQ   s, such as independent living, mental health, and now possibly or in the future for supporting people with learning disabilities/difficulties.I have worked as a care assistant/support worker for 13 years now. I remember when NVQ first became available and was really interested. I completed NVQ level 2 in Care in April 2001 and have been chasing level 3 since then. Hopefully I will complete it by the middle of next year.NVQ In Care level 2 assesses the care that you deliver. We were told at our induction day that it would change the way we work. Well, for me I don   t think it changed the way I worked, but it did change the way I thought about the people I care for. It made me realise even more that they are individuals with rights and choices the same as anyone else.I completed 9 units, covering all knowledge criteria and performance criteria in less than 6 months. I had a very good enthusiastic assessor and an excellent internal verifier. This helped me achieve my award so quickly because I do know people who have taken a couple of years and got no where through no fault of their own but because assessors leave or work doesn   t get verified quickly.For each unit there was a set of questions, answered fully they covered all the knowledge criteria needed for that unit and some of it linked over into other units as well. This meant that by the time I had completed half the units I had most of the knowledge criteria and performance criteria for the other half and we only had to work on what else was needed to complete it.Each unit covers specific work areas. Some of these are: personal care, preparing food and drink, abuse, health and safety, confidentiality and communication.For each unit I needed two natural observations. This meant that my assessor came to work with me and watched how I completed set tasks. This was quite fun and by the end of it we knew each other well. At the end of each observation we sat and went through what was accomplished, how we thought it went and what improvements we could make for the future. This is where I started to think differently about the people who I supported/cared for.NVQ in Care is all about valuing people as individuals and offering choices to them and allowing them their rights to be themselves and to be cared/supported in the way that they want. It makes you think more about them as people and how you would like to be treated in a similar situation.Putting together my portfolio was great, I loved to see all the work building up and checking through each piece. I learned an awful lot through doing NVQ even though I had been working as a carer for a long time by then. My biggest panic was policies and legislation, what on earth were they? (well I was a bit thick) but once I knew all they were, were rules regulations I knew what I was looking for and what was expected. We actually bought our computer so that I could type all the work instead of hand writing it. Because I was experimenting with the computer each piece of work has a different coloured and shaped heading. I also included charts and clipart, which I thought looked quite professional. In the front of the portfolio we were told to include a piece about ourselves, a personal C.V. which I enjoyed writing. That gave the person checking through it on completion an idea of who the person was who had completed the portfolio.My portfolio went to the board on 25th April 2001 This meant that a board of people went through the portfolios that had been completed at that time. I don   t think they read all the way through each one but dipped in here and there to check the work was complete, assessed and verified. I spent the whole day on tenderhooks, what had I missed? Would it pass? I had worked comfortably with NVQ for almost six months and didn   t expect to feel so nervous that day.Well, I passed  Three of my units came back with Level 3 certificates which made me feel quite chuffed that I had included enough work for this to be.One thing I will say is that NVQ seems to be incredibly repetitive. I have looked back at the work that I did and so many of the questions are similar but about slightly different things so it was quite a task to vary the answers. I am typing Level 4 for someone at the moment and just doing the typing has highlighted that this is still so, very repetitive work.As far as I know by the end of 2005 the government wants all people who work within the care industry to be qualified to level 2 at least. I am not sure how achievable this is and whether it means that a good carer who hasn   t got an NVQ won   t get a job or not but I do feel that NVQ has standardised Care for all people who need it and means that carers are better trained. Being able to take the more specialised NVQ   s in Care means that people who work in specialised settings with people with specialised needs can get the training that they need to do their job properly. I work with people who have learning disabilities and have been working towards the LDAF programme, that is a whole nother story, and I think they are phasing that out anyway. There has been some talk of a new NVQ especially for people working with people who have learning disabilities but I am not sure yet if this is going ahead or not. Level 3, well I have been chasing it for three years now, I have applied twice where I work at the moment, twice because the first application form went no one knows where, but I am now in a position that I need this qualification so should at last be able to catch it. Do I recommend it? Yes, to anyone who wants to get on in work but didn   t get too many formal qualifications.      ', '    I was lucky enough to be enrolled on one of these by, my then employer as a gift  (The cost was    140).N.V.Q. or National Vocational Qualification in full, is a training method which allows the candidate to gain knowledge through use of observation, projects, oral and written questions, testimony of others, assessment of prior achievment and candidates own explanations at their place of employment. The course was to last for nine months.During this time I was allocated a Verifier(a person who marks my written work ),an assessor (someone who supervises my practical work ), Paper work and a resource pack.All the  work came from Regis Training.I was lucky enough for my boss to be my Assessor.  Although she had to go through a course to become one In the nine months that followed, I had to complete and get evidence of underpinning knowledge of nine different units pertaining to care.I had 4 compusory units, including Health and safety and fostering rights.The 5 others were of my choice, ranging from personal hygiene through to communication.I had the resource pack for guidance, very much like a text book.For each unit I had to do, I had to answer written and oral questions, obtain Witness testimonies ( outsiders to comment on my job ability in a certain scenario). I also had to write candidate explanationsfor certain topics that I have had to deal with in my job. ', '    Reading Stef1 s review on NVQ s I decided that I d give you my experience of this qualification as I have carried mine out at college for the last 2 years.What are NVQ s?Introduced in 1988. National Vocational Qualifications (NVQs) are work-related, competence-based qualifications. They reflect the skills and knowledge needed to do a job well , and show that the person is able in the area of work the NVQ represents.What NVQs can I do?There are NVQs for almost all jobs. NVQs cover general, industrial and commercial sectors. They are divided into eleven groups:  Tending animals, plants and land  Extracting and providing natural resources  Constructing  Engineering  Manufacturing  Transporting  Providing goods and services  Providing health, social care and protective services  Providing business services  Communicating  Developing and extending knowledge and skills                               ------------------------------------------NVQs are organised into five levels, based on the how competent you need to be on each level.Level 1 - Foundation skills in occupations Level 2 - Operative or semi-skilled occupations Level 3 - Technician, craft, skilled and supervisory occupations Level 4 - Technical and junior management occupations Level 5 - Chartered, professional and senior management occupations Levels 1-3 are most applicable to learners within the ages of 14-19 whilst 4 and 5 would be more applicable to older, more experienced workers.                                   -----------------------------BENEFITSNVQs can help you prepare for work or help your career development. Getting an NVQ shows you can do a job to national standards and have the up-to-date skills employers are looking for. In terms of work, a qualification which proves you can do a job well is a valuable possession and which makes it worthwhile. With NVQs the practice is as important as the theory - they show what you can do as well as what you know. You don t have to sit through hours, days, weeks or even years of a course, and there are no exams at the end. NVQs are about putting learning into practice. NVQs are flexible - you can do an NVQ as part of your normal job, work towards one at college or through open learning and private study, or a combination of these. There are no age limits and no special entry requirements. Who are NVQs designed for?NVQs are available to anyone at any age or stage of their career. NVQs are flexible and accessible - within reasonable limits, you can decide the pace, place and way in which you learn. Most people working towards an NVQ are in work but they are available to others through a number of different ways. My Experience with NVQ s====================After leaving school, I decided I wanted to carry on from my Food and Nutrition GSCE to a higher level. I enrolled at Swansea College on the NVQ Catering course but after a discussion with the tutor I as told to go on the BTEC course as this would give me both qualifications at the same time.Starting in September 2003 I was told there were 2 NVQ qualifications we would be studying for - Food and Beverage Service and Food and Beverage Preparation, at level 1 in the first year and onto level 2 in the second year.The qualifications each have around 10 units to be done over the 2 years. In the Service unit there would be for example a unit on taking payments at the till, serving food and drinks to customers and keeping the area clean and tidy.In the Food Preparation unit there are units with the titles like  Prepare and cook hot deserts ,  Prepare a pasta dish  and  Prepare a meat dish . These have to be seen to have been done at least 3 times in order for the assessor to know that you are competent in what you are doing. The course was full-time so every week, out of the 4 days in college, I would be in the college s own student  kitchen or cafe either preparing the dishes or serving them. The lecturers then observed what I had done and written an assessment. I think this has to be done for each unit around 4 times. I did have to spend    200 on the chefs uniform, serving uniform  and knives, but I got this back from the college a few weeks later after applying for a grant.A part of the NVQ requested that I do some assessments while on Work experience last month, so my lecturers came out an assessed me too, which completed all the units I hadn t finished.Once all the practical assessments are complete ,there are then question packs to be answered on each unit and also some additional questions asked by the assessor (which can get a little repetative at times). The only problem I had was not getting all the assessments done in the kitchen and cafe done in time. This meant a big rush at the end of the course, with me making 7 dishes in one day Having just finished the course, I have gained certificates in Food and Beverage Service and Food and Beverage Preparation both at Level 2 as well as my BTEC in Hospitality Supervision. CONCLUSION--------------------I think that the NVQ is a really worthwhile qualification to do. It has been set up by businesses by the standards that they want so you will be sure to know everything an employer wants and needs from an employee if they ask for an NVQ. They are very convienient as you can carry them out at work or college as part of your course or job with no time spent away. They are really easy to complete and the qualification you earn will look good on your CV.Employers should pay for the course so there are no costs for you. The only money I had to spend was on my uniform. But it was worth every penny.So in answer to the title.. Yes they are worth it.If there s anything I ve left out let me know please.Thanks for reading.Here s where I got my chefs uniform from as they are very well priced and deliver quickly. http://www.russums-shop.co.ukx-x-x sam x-x-x     ', '    Many people thought I was mad last September, when I decided to go back to the local College to do a Business Admin NVQ.  Even some of my tutors thought I was mad....  You ve got a degree, what do you need an NVQ for? You re going backwards, it s a Masters you re after    Actually, NO you re all wrong   So what if i ve got a degree. That only means I know the subject, not the practical side of things  My degree:  BA Modern Language Studies:  4 years at Leicester Uni doing French, German and supplemenatry Sociology. I had previous office experience, and now I had the languages, I wrongly thought it would be a doddle to get my good paying graduate job.  But no, down to Earth I fell with a massive BANG   I couldn t get my dream job, I had no qualifications in the office side of things.   I ve got prior experience, you could get a reference from them   didn t work with these interviewers. NVQ is short for National Vocational Qualification. This work placement is with a local company and is compulsary, as the focus of an NVQ is work-focused experience.  You get a big wad of paper which are called your  Standards  and these are the things that you have to prove that you can do to your teachers, your Internal Assessor and your Outside Verifier. Do this for every piece of paperwork, and you will find that it may or may not cover several different things in your standards.Once you ve ticked everything off in your standards, then your portfolio is ready to be assessed and examined.Well, i m off to pick up my certificate this week.  I think that the course has helped me in several ways:~it s given me the qualification I need (plus one in Book-keeping which I done alongside the Business Admin)~it s given me another reference to put on my CV, thanks to the work placement.~it s built up my confidence... now I know that I can do this~as a single parent, I ve had the chance to meet new peopleThis NVQ was more like a means to an end for me, which was why I chose it.  I have to admit that I did find it very boring initially, but I put this down to the fact that I had this idea in my head that it was going to be like I was back at Uni, when infact the teaching methods were totally different, you are just left to get on with it without much guidance.I would recommend this course, i ve found it very helpful.     ', '    The reasons for doing the National Vocational Qualifications or NVQ are vast and wide-ranging.  NVQ s are becoming a vital part of the workplace particularly in the manufacturing and service sectors were they are slowly becoming a prerequisite before starting work in such fields.  In my field, the health profession 50  of care assistants/nursing auxiliaries etc were supposed to have their NVQ 2 in care by the end of 2005.  There are several reasons why this became an impossibility and the date is being forever changed.  The NVQ is a relatively new qualification and was seen by the government as a long-term replacement for the BTEC and City and Guild qualifications.  However, the qualification has been and continues to be greeted with a mixture of apathy and scorn by both employees and employers and there are many reasons for this.The NVQ is described as a vocational qualification to be completed in the workplace.  You are assigned an assessor who can either be shipped in from an external body such as a college or has been trained as an NVQ assessor by the workplace.  The idea is that your assessor observes your work and documents how you behave, be it towards your clients/service users in the care sector, customers in the retail sector etc.  They also observe your working practices to ensure you carry out your designated tasks correctly and according to the procedures set out by your workplace and external bodies such as environmental health.  Examples of this in my case this would be observing me feed a resident or administer medication.  However, this element of the course is fine for most people but it is the  evidence  element that makes these work-based qualifications the scourge of many an employees and employers lives. The NVQ level 2 in Care is the perfect example of this.  Made up of four core units covering diversity and rights, communication, health and safety and abuse and a further five units of the employees own choosing from eating and drinking to continence control the employee is expected to write detailed accounts to cover the criteria of the units.  Not only are they expected to write step by step accounts of,  How they take Mrs X to the toilet ensuring privacy and dignity by shutting the door...  they must then mark their own work using the criteria supplied.  This is a ridiculously complicated process that takes longer than writing the actual piece or  reflective account  as they are called.  Add to this the need for  witness testimonies  from Supervisors or Line managers supporting your abilities and what you have is a vocational qualification that is bogged down in paperwork and bureaucracy.The problem with the NVQ is not the content that in my experience is relevant to the occupation but the way in which the pill is administered.  Imagine this.  You are a fifty-year-old care assistant who has been told they need to do an NVQ.  It has been a number of years since you have written anything approaching an essay style piece and you are confronted with this mound of paperwork and the possibility of needing to attend college for extra assistance.  Would you do it?  Where are the assessors in all this?  Now the success or failure of someone working towards an NVQ is largely down to how helpful an assessor they have.  As someone who assists those trying to get an NVQ and someone with an NVQ 3 in Care I am well aware of the importance of this.  The assessor is the person who is there to guide you through and help you.  It is they who decide whether you have completed a unit and indeed they who decide when you have completed your NVQ (after external verification).  Therefore, the importance of a good assessor cannot be stressed strongly enough.  A good assessor can get even the most non-academic employee through an NVQ 2 in twelve months whereas a bad one can make it a torturous process that lasts years.  My own NVQ lasted two and a half years not because I did not complete the work (as I completed that in less than six months) but because my assessor was like the Scarlet Pimpernel and when she was there gave little in the way of advice or guidance.  In contrast I know several colleagues who were guided through their NVQ with the assessor doing much of the supposed  self marking  for them.  This is one of the major advantages of having an assessor in the workplace rather than an external body.The employer also has a vital role as to your success o your NVQ course.  Occasionally you may be required to attend courses, spend days in college or have one on one time with your assessor in the workplace.  An employer s understanding of the need for this will largely affect whether you will spend six months or two years on your NVQ.  Many employers see the NVQ as a necessary nuisance and are reluctant to give time off or any assistance to employees pursuing it.So why on earth should I bother doing an NVQ?****************************************************In my personal opinion the NVQ in itself does not make you a better employee.  However, in many workplaces especially the care sector it is becoming something you have to do to continue in that field so many of you may consider it (like I do), a necessary evil.  It also can provides some benefits in that employers tend to pay that little bit more to employees who have an NVQ and indeed some workplaces have started to only accept employees with NVQ s.  An NVQ can also be used as a stepping stone to further your career as an NVQ 3 is classed in many universities as a viable qualification for access to many courses such as Nursing.  The advanced NVQ s such as NVQ 4 or the assessors NVQ may even provide an opportunity to become self-employed as a freelance assessor manager of a business.Congratulations to those who have completed an NVQ or are working towards one.  I know how difficult they are and have a respect for anyone who can get their head round this most complex of courses. ', '    I am currently doing an NVQ level 3 in customer service and thought i d write a little about it as i have found it really worthwile.Firstly, i heard through a recruitment company that if you are 25yrs or under your employer has to let you do an NVQ if you wish to do one. ', '    I am an NVQ Trainer/Assessor for a training provider. s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
For anyone considering NVQ qualifications, especially in healthcare or support roles, it’s important to recognize both the opportunities and challenges involved. Advanced NVQs can open doors to university courses and even self-employment, making them a valuable step for career progression. Many find that NVQs lead to higher pay and are sometimes essential for accessing certain jobs or climbing the career ladder.

One key factor influencing success is the support from employers. When employers provide time off and encouragement, candidates tend to complete their NVQs more smoothly. Conversely, lack of support can significantly delay progress. The role of the assessor is equally critical—quality mentorship and guidance can make or break the experience, so it’s worth seeking programs with strong assessor support.

NVQ courses are designed with flexibility in mind, which is a real boon for adults balancing family commitments. Some even offer childcare assistance, helping learners manage their responsibilities alongside study. The practical nature of NVQs, including required work placements, means candidates gain hands-on experience and can demonstrate real-world skills to employers. For example, the NVQ in Care covers essential units like personal care, health and safety, confidentiality, and communication—areas that build both competence and confidence.

However, it’s important to set realistic expectations: NVQs are not quick fixes. They typically take several months to complete, demanding resilience and commitment. But the payoff is meaningful—beyond qualifications, many report increased confidence and expanded professional references, which are invaluable in healthcare and support sectors.

In summary, NVQs offer a practical, flexible route to career development, especially when supported by good employers and assessors. They require patience and dedication but can significantly enhance both skills and job prospects, making them a worthwhile investment for those serious about growth in caregiving or office-related roles.
