product_reviews: ['    I studied for a BA degree in Russian and Soviet Studies at Portsmouth Polytechnic (now a University), but only stayed there a year and two terms, because I got married and had my daughter. It was a couple of years later that I decided to try to study with the Open University. My Aunt and my cousin both got degrees with the O.U., so I knew a lot about it and I was impressed.I was lucky enough to get a grant for my fees this time, which meant I did not have the huge handicap of expensive course fees to find. But you only get this once, so use it wisely. I ended up quitting again, which means I will have to pay my own fees, if I decide to study with them again.Unfortunately, the choice of courses offered by the O.U. is smaller than those offered at other universities. I had a background in languages, but finding nothing suitable in that field, I did D103, the Social Sciences foundation course.When you begin, you have to complete a year s foundation course, depending on the type of subject you want to study in. After this, you have to earn the rest of the credits necessary for a degree, including a mixture of first, second and third level courses. You have an exam every year, as well as a set number of assignments to complete.I found the courses very interesting and enjoyed being able to structure my studying around a pattern that suited me. I had no set times for lectures, just the odd seminar, which was voluntary, although it is better to attend if you can.Of course, I had a certain amount of work to do, my course requiring a number of TMAs (tutor marked assessments - essays to you and me  ) to be done over a period of time. These do take a lot of hard work, but are very rewarding and I had good tutors while I was studying with the O.U. They understood that sometimes I needed an extension for my TMA, because my kids had been ill or something. Being mature adults themselves, they have a good understanding of the  real world  and I found them more sympathetic than the tutors I had at Portsmouth University.The text books are of a high standard, plus you also work from tape cassettes and video cassettes, as well as the O.U. programmes being on TV. By now, I should think the computer aspect of the courses has began to play a greater focus too, but at the time I was studying, I did not own a computer.There are advantages and disadvantages to studying with the O.U. It is a very flexible approach to studying, which makes it highly convenient, but you might miss the camaraderie you get from attending regular lectures in a  normal  University. You have to be very disciplined and ensure that you get the work done, as you won t have a tutor breathing down your neck too much, they will leave it up to you to get everything finished. You owe it to yourself to do the best you can.      ', '    The World of Country Life is a family tourist attraction situated just outside Exmouth in Sandy Bay, East Devon.Easy to find by car, you just follow the brown tourist signs from Exmouth.  Its also accessible by bus, again from Exmouth.The park itself is sited in 40 acres with a good proportion of items undercover.  I like this attraction, as there is a vast variety of things to do from animals to museum exhibitions.It has it s own free car and coach park.  Admission prices maybe a little pricey:-**2004 PRICES**   7.50 for adults   6.50 for OAP s   6.50 for children up to 17 yearsFamily tickets are available (making a slight saving)at    26.00 for 2 adults and 2 kids or    30.00 for 2 adults and 3 children.  A group reduction will apply, for groups of 20 or more.If you intend to visit on a regular basis, as season ticket maybe of interest.  These are priced at -   27.00 per adult   23.00 per child or OAPThe park is open daily from 5th April until 29th October from 10am.  Dogs are not allowed in the attraction, although guide dogs are excepted.Once you ve got your tickets, the first thing you come to is the Exhibition Hall.  Here, you really do step back in time.  I think it s great to be able to teach the children of your party a little about our history, in such a fun way.  You walk down a Victorian Street, where you can visit a dress shop, public house, garage, Ironmongers shop or a cottage laid out exactly as it would have been in Victorian times.  Another interesting exhibition is the  100 year of brides , see wedding dress styles as they would have been through the decades, you can see how material was in a shortage just after the war and how fashions have changed.  Or you can see the old agricultural machinary used along with the life in the 20 s 30 s   40 s exhibitions.The Transport Hall, again takes you back in time, with vintage motorbikes, cars, fire engines and steam engines.The rest of the park is basically divided between animals and play zones.  For the cute and cuddly, there is a pet centre, animal nursery, farm yard animals including goat walking and animal paddocks.  A safari train takes you around the paddocks, although there is a extra charge for this.  From the train, you can see Llamas, deer, sheep, miniature ponies, wallabies (a favourite of our littl un), donkies and Rhea birds.Although these two mentioned aspects of this attraction can be very educational, the play aspect is probably the most exciting for any child.  Here, you will find trampolines (big enough for the adults too, as I found out on my trip  ), sand pits, swings, a Wendy House and new last year, was the addition of a large adventure pirate ship.  For younger children, there is a soft play area.  Some rides have an extra charge, these include the quad bikes (suitable for children between 8 and 12 years, although our 8 year old was disappointed with this ride, he pointed out he could cycle faster on his pushbike ), crazy golf, radio boats, electric cards and safari train.For food times, a picnic area is provided but this is outdoor or a restaurant provides anything from a snack to a three course meal.  For those with a sweet tooth, my favourite is the Ice Cream Parlour.This attraction probably gets busy in peak times, I ve mainly visited just out of season but I can t imagine it would get too overcrowded.To sum up, this attraction offers a balance between education and fun, catering for children of all ages from young at heart to very young.      ', '     I am in my second year of study with the Open University.  I found it really hard to find a college or university that could fit around my three children, a part-time job and obviously something within my financial range not ot mention creche facilities.  The OU give me all the above.Can anyone study with the OU?Yes, young, old and the disabled.  When I was at my summer school the youngest was 17 and the oldest was 93.  If you have a disability let the OU know when you register on a course and they will do their utmost to help you.The money bitEach course is differently priced, if like me finances are tight you can apply for a financial award, which means your course is paid for.  They will award a financial award on your personal finances, benefits you are recieving, number of kids you have etc, etc.  The form gives different circumstances and the financial threshold.  My threshold included married both working 16 hours or more recieving CTC/WTC and having three kids and a combined annual income of less than 18,500.Alternatively you can opt for a budget account were you spread the cost of the course over a few months or you can pay by direct debit.CoursesThere is a wide range of courses available:Business and management.Education and teacher training.Environment.Health and social careHealth studiesHumanities: Arts, languages and history.Information technology and computing.Law and criminology.Mathematics.Psychology, philosophy, politics and economics.Science.Social sciences.Technology, engineering and manufacturing.The point systemEach course is awarded points:10 points is equal to a few hours a week studying and is usually about 10 weeks long. 30 points is equal to around eight hours studying and is eight months long.60 points is 16 hours a week studying and is eight months long.  These points can be linked to your final qualification, whether that may be a certificate, diploma or BA or BA Hons.You need:60 points for a certificate.120 points for a Diploma at least 60 points from level 3.300 points for a BA without honours with at least 120 points from level 3.360 points for a BA with honours with at least 120 points from level 3. Levels of studyYou can start your studies with a level one course this enables you to learn and to get back into studying.  Then you can go up to different levels in the direction you wish to study.  The work load gets harder with each level.I am currently studying two courses this year, one is a 60 pointer at 2nd level and a 30 pointer at 2nd level. The highest amount of points you can study in one year is 120 this is classed as full time.  The courseEach course has blocks or units of study, after each unit you are asked to do a TMA, tutor marked assignment, which is graded by your alloted tutor (you get the name and addresses(plus e-mail) of your tutor when you get your materials and a letter for you to introduce yourself).  If you are really lucky you get to sit an exam at the end of the course.  SupportThe support from the OU is exceptional, you have a tutor, who is only a phone call or an e-mail away, the regional centre which can answer most queries and the best support you can get is from other students.  You can access other students who are on the same course as you on the internet in special conferencing sites.  All this information comes with your course materials.  Along with the course mateirals you get a study calender which guides to what you should be doing each week. Do I need to buy anything?Some courses get you to buy set texts, these are referred to often in your study and are easy to come buy in second hand book shops or from other students who are finished with them.Residential/summer schoolsIf you are really lucky, some courses have a residential school,  I can not stress enough the importance of an RS. These are usually held during the summer months and only a few Universities are picked to host the RS, so you have to be quick to book your place at the uni of your choice.  These schools are there to help you in your studies and also a great chance to put faces to the names you have met in your conferencing sites.  I was at Stirling uni last year and it was brill    These are obligatory, you need a very good reason to be excused from attending.  The attendance counted towards my course.Those with disabilities can attend summer school.  You must tell the host university what needs you have when you register.How to enrol on a course.You can send off for a prospectus, the address for this can be found on the OU website (see below).  Or you can enrol on a course online.I feel very lucky to have found the OU.  I can choose when and where I study, how I study and it fits in around my life instead of the other way round.You can get more information from;www.open.ac.uk and click on courses and qualifications.Go on give it a try.  It s as easy as ABC.     ', '    I wanted to tell you about my experiences, opinions and the education choices I have made. Although I could still be regarded of traditional university age (the grand old age of 22) and I have good UCAS points, I have chosen to study for a Social Policy degree through the Open University. There are many reasons why I chose this path and I believe bona fide distance learning providers are a real alternative to students put off by the expense of higher education and the difficulties involved with putting off entry into the jobs market. I have a young child (and another on the way) and the added flexibility and lesser cost of OU study means that I can cope with being a full time employee, a mum and a student. This was not the main reason however, in fact I enrolled before I became pregnant, and this is a rare situation for an HE student to be in. Being able to work full time while studying means that when I graduate I will be several years ahead, in terms of work experience, than most students. Distance learning also shows prospective employers that the graduate has the motivation and stamina to cope with deadlines, busy schedules and prioritising without the need of supervision. It can be no small coincidence that while average student debt reaches    9000 (Natwest Money Matters findings) the number of students under 24 learning with the OU has almost doubled in five years. The rise of under 21s learning with the OU I even steeper with some 4,313 in 2000/01 compared to only 1,543 in 1996/97. In fact the level of students of more traditional university age (18-24) studying with the OU (11,360 in 2000/01) is pretty similar to the student population of many UK Universities. (Figures courtesy of the OU). Courses available aren t just degrees. You can study a variety or professional courses (including an MBA - the OU Business School is one of the largest in Europe) and Diploma in Social Work. You can study just a couple of modules and achieve a Diploma. The basic way it works is modular. Modules can be worth 60 or 30 points. You need 360 points for a degree, 60 for a certificate and 120 for the diploma. I opted to take a degree in Social Policy but chose  strategically  so that my first year s course gave me a certificate and my next two gave me a diploma, that way I had a couple of additions for my CV along the way, good work  I am in my second year and although it s hard work juggling everything you still get a big break between courses which helps and it s definitly manageable. I believe that the Government s infamously controversial Education policies are misguided, exclusive and discouraging but the longer the system remains the same the harder it will be to either return to the previous grant system or have a complete overhaul and replace the loan system with a more progressive, affordable option. This is why I believe distance learning is a real alternative and should be enhanced and encouraged. Many young people are still unaware that they may be able claim a Part Time Student Loan for    500 a year for up to 6 years (which in many cases will cover the cost of an entire OU degree). Perhaps if this was more widely known more students, young and mature, would opt to take the OU route. Although part time student loans still need to be paid back (with few exceptions dependant on income and age) the sum total of debt for 6 years at    500 is    3000, a drop in the ocean compared to    9000, especially as concurrent full time work is possible. Although there are many negatives the current Education policies people should be made aware of the few positives that do exist and the OU is one of them. The OU has opened up so many opportunities for me and I feel passionately that everybody should have the chance to experience it. It is not just the realm of the retired and the stay-at-home mother, 18 year olds who are unsure if they wish to fork out the average debt and loss of earnings for a full time degree program would do well to consider it. You do not miss out on the student experience you just get a different experience.      ', '    I joined Open University last February after being out of education for the last 10 years. I started with a short 10 credits course on  writing essays skills ; that was extremely helpful and gave me a boost of confidence to carry on. I m currently studying a course called  Intoduction to Social Science , which is my first one towards a degree in Psychology.Open University has a very progressive way to get you back into education, starting with easier tasks, helping you getting the writting and studying skills you are going to need in further stages. Introductory courses and Level one courses are specially desingned to get you up and running, so don t be scared if you think you don t have the skills, it is a process achivable.The courses are well designed to help you organise your own time, and the materials and the tutors are very helpful. There are also pupil s forums in the ou web site and sometimes in facebook there are forums for students of determined courses. Those forums are of great help, I would say almost vital to succeed; in them you can find the support of people struggling with the same things as you. I have even made some friends I really recomend the Open University to all people that has no time for full time education but that want to learn.     ', '    I originally started out my universiy life at Manchester but after a year i knew it really wasnt for me. I passed the year but didnt want to go back. I didnt however want my hard years work to go to waste. I was told about the open niversity by a friend and it sounded quite interesting.At the open university you have the choice over many different couses in a range of subject. You can do it for fun if you like or to gain knowledge in a certain area but the main reason is to gain degree s or certificates of higher learning. Each course is worth an amount of points (typically 60). You need to get 120 points at each level of study which gives you a total of 360 points. When you have done this you recieve a degree with honours  Each level (levels 1 - 3) represents a year at university. For example level 3 would be your third year at uni and the couse material and difficulty will be harder than level 1. It may then mean you do two courses at level 1 each couse worth 60 points.This would give you your 120 points for level one. You could alterntalively do couses worth 30 points which take less time.The great thing is you can use points allready gained from other universities to put towards awhat is known as an open degree. This is most common degree at the open uni as it lets you pick couses from which ever subjects you like. Meaning you dont have to simply do a degree in geography or history. You could do a mix if you felt like it. In my case i had completed my first year at uni. This means I had 120 points at level one, so i dont have to do any couses with the open uni at level one. I decided for my first year to do just one 60 point couse at level 2. I have found it much easier than normal uni. The work is enjoyable and easy to work around every day life. The uni send you all the materials and books you need along with couse guides to help you plan your work. As an example I will use my couse. I recieved a DVD, a couse book (8 chapters - around 200 pages) a couse guide ( with timetable of which chapters to read in which weeks etc) and also some audio material. You also get a timetable showing your assignment deadlines and also a booklet with your assignment questions in. There are 6 assignments and one exam. The first project was based on the dvd. Over 4 weeks I had to watch the DVd and make notes on it. Then I had to answer a question based on subjects raised in the DVD using references to the DVD. Later assignemnts have been similar but I had to read around 4 chapters per question rather than the DVD. There would also be audio tracks to work from to gain quotes and information forthe questions. At the end of the year you nrmally will have an exam.Mine is 3 hours and involves me aswering 3 essay question. Not all courses have exams however. My first course involved  living in a globalised world  it wasnt too difficult and I have been averaging around 75  on assignments quite easily.Next I plan to chage subjects completely, im rather bored of geography and plan to go for something concerning history or astronomy. The cost isnt bad either. After one year f uni I was around    3000 in debt (lovely).However after one couse at the open uni I am around    250 better off (you heard me). If you earn under a certain amount (15000 a year i think) you are awrded a grant towards your couse fees and given some money to buy materials (which arnt really needed - i would guess its for a laptop) However dont worry if you dont fall into this group as you are only looking at between    500 -    700 for a 60 point couse. Meaning its alot cheaper than real uni.Also dont be put off thinking your degree doesnt mean anything. It means exactly the same as a degree from a university. The only difference is its may be a degree in a range of subjects  Employers take it just as seriously as any other degree I cannot reccomend the open unienough. I find it very easy to use and contact with tutors (yes you get a tutor) is only a phone call or e-mail away. If your still unsure go check the website. It has loads of info and full lists of all the courses available  note- this is from my dooyoo review     ', '    I know that some people think that the OPEN university is an easy option- if you think this then you are not suited to studying with them. Believe me, I should know- I have tried both regular university and the OPEN..and regular university is a breeze towards doing it with the Open. With regular university you have a lot of free time to do your assignments, and few lectures, and unlimited access to a massive number of textbooks in university libraries. If you don t get a good degree doing it this way, then you ve wasted your time. And got yourself into a lot of debt socialising as well, probably. There are cheaper ways to socialise. I enrolled with the Open University because I hated the course that I was doing at Nottingham- a very well respected university(the course was geography).The lecturers were really more interested in writing their books than teaching 18 year olds. SO ..older and wiser, I chose the Open University to do a course that at 18 I would never have had a clue how to deal with...PSYCHOLOGY.  I was able to bring up my babies( I enrolled in 1989 when I was about to have my second child) and study. I could take it at my own pace - one module a year. ..and did the courses I wanted to. This is almost certainly guaranteed to ensure that you pass- if a subject interests you, you do better at it. The courses are well presented and well taught. The subject matter and course material are of the highest quality- frankly much better than the  regular  university quality that I experienced. Each course is at a particular level of difficulty - 1,2,3 or postgraduate level, and each is is worth a number of points (60,30,15 or 10) which count towards your degree. For an ordinary degree you need 360 points, and 240 of them need to be at level 2 or 3 and for an honours degree, you need 360  points- 120 of which have to be at level 3. You can get credit for other study that you have done after leaving school- you have to contact the OU to get this transferred. I had the year at Nottingham University and I got credit for that study as well. When you apply to get onto a course, you will see how much it will cost for the year. Most cost just over    450, and if there s a summer school it costs alittle bit more, but if you want to do law it s    1400 a year. Quite a lot but still not as much as going to regular uni. If you are not well off, they take this into account -and there is a hardship fund with the OU that you can apply to for assistance. It does work- I was lucky enough to benefit from it after my ex was made redundant..it meant that I could continue with my studying. So..you send off for a booklet that lists all of the courses so that you can decide..they all look interesting but something you really have to take into account is the summer school requirement. Psychology that I did had several courses to make up an accredited psychology degree..and at least 2 had summer schools..so they are more or less compulsory for some study subjects. If you are not looking to do any subject speciality  in particular you ll be able to avoid them if you want to Summer schools are a legend..yes, things do go on- with a variety of people from all walks of life, there are bound to be attractions. The work is hard but fun, and for once, you are with fellow students - you could almost be a teenager again  Something I ll never forget, anyway. ', '    This is perhaps a slightly unusual review of the Open University, because I have actually been to University and the Open University. This may sound a little odd but I will explain. Having spent several years at University full time, and finishing without any formal qualification, that is to say a degree, the whole experience colud have been something of a waste of time. University is not for everbody and not everybody passes etc. but that is not the point of the story. some years later I became interested in some information I had recieved about the Open University and thought it may be worth looking at again as it is difficult to get anywhere these days without formal qualifications. I studied all the brochures etc and realised it could take up to six years to gain an Open University degree studying part time and it seemed like an awful long hill to climb considering  I have already been through a similar experiance to no avail. Hovever on further investigation I found that if you have already undertaken some formal education i.e University then you will be awarded credit points by the Open University for what amounts to up to two thirds of a degree, that is to say if you passed the first year or first two years of a degree course then the work you have done will be assessed and this will be deducted from the amount of work you will have to do to get an OU degree. It could be that a six year haul could be reduced to a couple  of years of part time study in the best scenario. You do however still have to complete at least 120 points with the OU themselves out of the 360 needed for a full degree.Most people complete a maximum of 60 points a year any more and the work load would become impractial, take it from me. I do not think many people are aware of this opportunity because there are many people who leave college without the full qualification and feel as though they may have wasted their time. It is inspiring to think that you could still get your degree, even now, if you are out their sitting on half a degree, and do not want to waste the time you have spent studying, it is not too late.My own personal experience with the OU was in the Arts and Humanities category. I took two units of History of Art to complete my degree, I was awarded the maximum of 240 points from previous full time study.240 points is the maximum they will award you from an exterior source. I think the reputation of the Open University has gained credibility over recent years it used to be considered as a bit second rate, by   8216;proper  8217; universities, but I think the balance has been redressed somewhat. Especially when there are so many distance learning courses available on the Internet and advertised in the press from other dubious sources the OU  has a great deal more credibility than most, or even all of them. An OU degree these days is certainly respected and if you knew how much work goes in to them you would know why.As an example the course I took, A316 Art and its Histories, Modern Practices and debates (no longer available, though it has been replaced with something similar) was divided into seven essay assignments each of 3000 words, you have to be within about 200 words max either way or loose marks, and a three hour written exam on the course work. The essays are marked on a continual assessment basis, send one in approximately once a month, when you receive a mark and some feedback from your personal tutor. This will tell you in what areas you need to improve, and also hopefully your good points .there are opportunities to attend focus groups during the year, a kind of group tutorial where you meet other people on the course doing the same work, which can be useful, and with this particular course there was a summer school where I went to a London University for a week during the summer holidays where I met other students on the course etc like the half day tutorials you get during the year but for a week. this does not happen for every course but the one I did was a level 3 course which is when these summer schools are most common. It was like being at university for a week, I suppose and the week was divided up into lectures,  field trips (trips to the national gallery, Tate Modern etc), and group tutorials and discussion. Most days would include and start with a group session a particular subject say expressionism and that would be the discussion for the morning. In the afternoon there would be a trip to say Tate Modern to look at some of the work that had been discussed where we were expected to make notes and answer questions in order to follow the subject up on return to the school. It was a fairly intensive week but worth it, and it put the whole years work in to perspective. Meeting other people doing the same work is very useful and interesting, especially when you spend so much time working on your own.    The part I did not look forward to or enjoy was the written exam at the end of the year. No one likes exams and this one is no different. There is a choice of about twenty essay titles, of which you need to answer three I think. The advice you are given is to be relevant stick to the point and don  8217;t wander off the subject, and write everything you know about an artist just to impress the examiner. Basically I ignored all of this advice, it is fine talk but when you get in there and find you can not answer any of the questions what else can you do. You have to write as much as you can as fast as you can and try to make what you know sound like the answer to the question by manipulating it ant way you can. This is what I did, and I did pass in case you were wondering, I do not know if I was inspired or just lucky. My advice would be, if you cant write anything you think is relevant, just start writing, you do not know what is going to given marks in the end, and you can not pass if there is nothing on the paper. I had to go through that ordeal twice as I did two units in two consecutive years and I was glad when they were over.I think despite all this it was enjoyable overall and it was worth it in the end as I got my degree. This review is really aimed at encouraging other people with half a degree to finish it off, though I hope it will be of some use to others as well.For the other unit I needed to complete my degree I took A216   8216;art and its histories  8217;. If I had taken another level 3 course I could have got an honours degree which is something I did not really take into account enough at the time, something I partially regret now but at the time I took a subject I knew something about rather than undertake an area of study I knew nothing about, and risk not passing at all, I did not want to spend another year chasing this degree. Also I did not know that if you want to go on to study an MA full time at a University you will need at least an Hons degree and preferably a good one. If you are on benefits the cost of the course need not be a barrier. These courses are expensive, A316 was around    700, for a years home study, group tutorials, and with that course a weeks summer school in London. I do not know if this scheme is still in operation, I seem to think that it was undergoing review just as I was finishing, if you were interested in this you would need to look into this, it would be worth it. There is also an OU students association were you can keep in contact with other students, wether they are doing your course or another, they have several services to offer, I do not know quite what they are as I did not bother with them much. When it is all over there is no need to feel excluded as there is an Alumni association you can join for free.When the study is over and hopefully you will have passed, there is the awards ceremony which is every bit as grand as the regular universities, you get to wear the robe etc, though peculiar to the OU they do not have the traditional mortar board (hat), it is not part of their ceremonial costume, though the robes are the same, a different colour for each subject. I think there are a lot of personal recommendations and experiences you can make, and I have tried to relate some, however if you intend to take up this kind of study you really need to talk to a professional advisor at the OU which is only a phone call away and it may prevent you from a lot of unseen pitfalls, and help you make the right choices. I would recommend this type of study to any one who finds themselves unable to go to a regular university, and would rate this above any of the other distance learning courses, not that I have much experience with others but this one is tried and tested, and at the end of the day an OU qualification is respected which is of the upmost importance. ', '    The Open University (OU) is the country   s largest provider of Higher Education courses but while it impacts directly or indirectly on many people for many more it remains a closed book. What does it have to offer at a time when there are so many opportunities for study?I graduated from the OU (2.1 since you asked...) after eight years although, as you will see, I have not been studying for all of that period. My main areas of study were electronics and computing.The OU provides courses to degree level and beyond using distance learning. The courses are open to all, regardless of previous qualification. Their degrees are fully accepted by industry and professional bodies, although some professional associations may require that particular combinations of courses be undertaken. All study is modular, that is the student chooses which courses to study year by year. Although advice is given on recommended prerequisite knowledge for courses, it is up to students to make their own decisions and there are no mandatory requirements for entry.Courses may be studied as stand alone units, or as part of various Certificates, Diplomas or Degrees. Degrees are either    generic    BA/BSc or named degrees (for example Social Science) if a prescribed selection of courses have been taken. Postgraduate courses are also available leading to taught masters. The OU also offers business courses through the Open Business School going via certificates and diplomas all the way to MBA. Be aware that since the government does not support the cost of business courses they are far more expensive than undergraduate courses. Typical undergraduate courses range up to about    250 for a 30 point course (more about points later). The courses can be paid for in monthly installments or you may be able to persuade your employer to provide sponsorship.Courses are classed by level: Level 1 are foundation courses and serve as introductions both to a subject area and to the methods of study employed by OU. These courses were formerly mandatory for all students but are now merely recommended. I would certainly recommend that a foundation course be taken in the first year of study, particularly if returning to education after some time or if you have never studied at higher levels. Level 2 courses are equivalent to the first or second year of a full time course and begin to develop specific areas of knowledge. Level 3 courses are equivalent to the level expected in the final year of study for a full time degree and are the most testing. Courses also have points values, most usually 30 or 60 points. These values relate to amount of material in a course. A minimum of 360 points are required for the award of a degree, although you may include up to 480 if you wish (you may have particular requirements for professional recognition, for example). A minimum number of Level 3 courses must be taken to qualify for Honours rather than Ordinary degree.30 point courses are said to require about 7 hours study per week, 60 point about 15 hours. The maximum number of points for which you can study in a single year is 120. This equates pretty much to full time study. If you can dedicate this amount of time it is possible to complete a degree in 3 years. My advice would be to proceed cautiously. It is very easy to overestimate the amount of work you can complete with the result that you fail to complete any of the courses.Courses are primarily distance learning which means that you get a set of notes and exercises and it is up to you to study in your own time and at your own pace. The study material is usually supplied as a set of books with supporting information and notes. Some have audio or video cassettes or associated televison programmes (usually broadcast at some strange hour of the early morning  - don t forget to set the VCR). You may be required to buy additional set books, this is detailed in the course information available from OU before the start of the course. Some units also include experimental equipment for your use at home. You are allocated a tutor who will be available to help by phone or email. The courses are well structured and are subject to continuous assessment by means of marked assignments. These are either Tutor Marked Assignments (TMAs) which are marked by your tutor (as you might have guessed) and provide good feedback on your progress or, on some courses, Computer Marked Assignments (CMAs) which are multiple choice papers marked centrally by computer. These TMAs and CMAs typically form 50  of the overall mark for a course and also help to keep your studies on track through out the year by giving definite points in your calendar.For those who wish to attend there will be tutorials offered somewhere relatively close to you. The actual distance will depend on how many people are studying the course; popular courses have many students, hence tutors, and will have more tutorial locations. These are a matter of choice, many people swear by them but I have yet to attend one. Tutorials offer the chance to get support from your tutor face to face and to work in a group.Some students also choose to work in self-organised study groups. These are groups of students who get together to discuss the course and provide some support and encouragement. Tutors will often help students to get in touch - another reason to attend tutorial sessions.Some courses have residential summer schools. These courses are compulsory and are an extra cost. The courses are one week in length, cost (last time I looked) in the region of    200 and are usually held on university campuses during the summer break. Bear in mind that the OU academic year runs from February to October, so the summer break for full time students is about 2/3 of the way through your year. Many students approach these courses with some trepidation but I found them a great opportunity to get a boost to my enthusiasm at a critical point in the course (usually starting to think about exam revision) as well as a chance to act like a real student for a week (beer...).Exams are in October and will be held at local venues, typically colleges although they can be anywhere - I sat a recent exam in the function room of a sports club. The exams normally form 50  of the overall mark for the course. They are usually three hours long. The atmosphere is made as relaxed as possible with many students bringing sweets or drinks with them into the examination room. For some students this is the only time the ever see anyone from the university. A few courses dispense with the examination in favour of an end of course project; this replaces the exam in the marking scheme. Results are normally received around Christmas (hopefully before).How effective is the OU? The course materials are excellent and, on the whole, the tutors are friendly and helpful. If you work throughout the course you should not have too many surprises in the exam. All the examination questions are based on the material you have covered. You can work at your own pace and in your own way, subject to meeting the deadlines for assignments. If you want to take part there are tutorials available. Some students can feel isolated, although it   s never bothered me. If this is a concern, there is an OU Student Association that has regular get-togethers in most towns and don   t forget that there is also an active on-line community on the OU   s  student web site.As I said at the beginning, I have been a student with OU for eight years, but I took two years out in the middle to get married and change job. If I had been more disciplined I could probably have studied through this period, but it was my choice. How many universities would give this flexibility? I have found the courses excellent value; the typical cost for a year   s course is less than I would pay for a single day course with telecoms training providers. Having compled my degree I am planning to continue my studies     it really can become addictive.If you want to find out more, see the OU web site at:www.open.ac.uk     ', '    I completed my degree at Glamorgan University in 1998, and decided last year that I wanted to complete further studies. I decided that studying from home (distance learning) was my best option this time round, some colleges and Universities offer this option but not to the extent the Open University does. I wasn t sure in what subject I would like to do further studies so sent for some information. Open University sent me comprehensive brochures and booklets, which not only listed the courses and modules offered but what they are worth and how you can build them together to form diplomas/degrees/postgrad. qualifications. I also found out that to study OU diploma and degree modules you do not need to have a certain level of educational qualifications, in fact, you don t need any at all. I opted for a Linguistics module (U210), as I had done some at Uni. and found it particularly interesting. I found out I could do four modules to complete a diploma or advanced diploma, then further modules to build it into a degree - but you are not obligated to decide at the start what you want to work towards, you can leave it at one module if you like, just as an interest. I chose to pay using the Open University Student Budget Account, which has meant I ve been paying a very manageable    51 a month. OU courses run from about February to October, and before the course started I was sent the first batch of course materials (you re sent the second batch midway through). OU courses (from my experience of one module ) are very self-contained, there is enough in the materials they provide to complete the course, and they seem to prefer it if you do not do lots of external research. They provide textbooks, videos, audio cassettes, guide books, study guides, all they ask is that you buy one text book (again, from my experience of this one module). You are given a calendar which marks the various stages of the course and significant dates - it tells you when your Tutor Marked Assignments are due, when the relevant OU TV programmes are broadcast (and their repeats), what chapters you should have read by when, at what stage of the course you should be, etc. It is all very structured and organised. You have one significant point of contact within the OU and that is your personal tutor. He advises you on and marks your assignments, and holds tutorials where you can discuss the course and course work and interact with fellow students. This can lead to further contact with other students, which can help greatly; you don t feel quite so isolated. There is an OU website (www.open.ac.uk), which gives course information and news, etc, and it also has a students section where you can check your essays marks  The course itself, I have found to be very interesting, very thought provoking, there is ample reading and research material. I have to complete one essay per month of approximately 2000 words, and they have, so far, been challenging but at the same time fascinating. With the demands of full-time work and the slight strain I ve felt since being pregnant, some of the latest essays have been late but, fortunately, I have a very sympathetic and, quite frankly, lenient tutor, who doesn t mind when they re handed in   Something that may be seen as a drawback for some is the fact that you do work entirely from your own initiative. You can seek help and advise from your tutor and other students, but if you are not motivated there is no one there to tell you to get on with it (except, perhaps, a concerned other half - concerned with the money he thinks you ll be earning when you ve finished  ). If you lack discipline and motivation this is probably not the way to study, unless your Mum/partner can cajole you into doing your homework      ', '    I left school during my sixth year and had no intentions of going to Uni, at that point I hated education. I went straight into full time employment. After a few years had gone on my attidtudes changed and I realised that a degree would help me progress further, problem was by this stage I had got far to used to having money and had the full range of commitments and a mortgage so going back to school was not an option.I was whinging about this at work to one of my employees and they must have got sick of me  next day they came in with a coupon filled out for me to send off for a prospectus I thought hey what do I have to lose.When it came through I felt a bit daunted, all these course at my fingertips. I have always loved biology so I plumped to do a bachelor of science in biology and duly registered of my first course. The registration was easy to fill out just some simple questions about your education level. There is a section that if you have done any study it might be able to be counted to your degree I didn t have this so mine was very easy to fill out.To get a degree you need 360 points. Courses are worth 10, 30 and 60 points each, And there are a list of courses which count towards each degree. they are also in levels, you have to start with level 1, and to get an honours degree you need 120 ponits at levels 3. If you are in doubt about if you can studt at home do a 10 point short course to try it out. My other half did one half way through my degree ( I think he thought if you cant beat them join them  )Then came the long wait. Courses run from January to October and registration for new students is early in the year so it seemed like months I had to wait.D-Day: a package came through the door- my life as I knew it was over    I gingerly opened the package and leafed through my first book - and it was so easy to follow. the books are laid out in a very easy format and have icons to guide you to what to do next. Also in the pack was some other paper work. Some forms, a timetable, CD-roms and a contents list. - A bit of advice here sit everything out and check you have everything on the list, I have learnt through experience that this saves a last minute panic when you have no form to send you assignments in with   . They also include details of your tutor for the year, this normally also ends up being your guidance tutor for the duration of your studies. You also get details for registering for First class, this is a great source of support and information.I found the first month not bad I studied the amount they recomended and I did all that was recommended. I then checked to see when my first assignment was due and realised I was not far enough into the course. I have found over the years that as a rule I needed to study about twice the lenght of time they advise to stay on track ( dont know If im just a bit slow    but bear this in mind) A lot of the courses have associated television programs which are viewed on the learning zone on BBC2 - remember when the say a date and time it s 2 am on that morning not the next ( I managed to do this a few times   ) Tutorials, these vary dependant on the course you are doing, unfortunately in my first year due to work and fear I didnt got to many - I was terrified that I would be the dunce at the back of the class. Please make the most of them, remember most people will be feeling exactly the same. Over the years I have found them to be invaluable not only for the tutors guidance but for meeting others. This is a great place to start up study groups even if it is just two of you a problem shared and all that  .As the months went on I got well into the swing of it and bored many people with my new knowledge. All the time I was dreading the summer school which was associated with my course - In my mind this was gong to be one whole week of humiliation.Summer Schools - not all courses have these, not all are compusary - please do them you will not regret it I promise. You normally get a pre summer school pack which gives information on what to read before you go. So with this prepared off I went bags packed ( pack fags if your a smoker as not all campus s have shopping facilities) I was bundled onto a train (this was a big enough experience as I had only been on one once before(sad but true ) )and went all the way to the other side of the world ( or so it felt like- Ok it was only Keele but hey Im Scottish  ) When I arrived there were signs everywhere guiding the terrified to the registration desks, I noticed a lot of hugging going on and I was petrified. We were all ushered into a big hall, clutching our packs which we had been given, in it is a timetable for the week, leaflets and a badge with a coloured dot on it. After the intro we are all told to go off in our groups ( blue spots together etc) the timetables are crammed full classes starting at 8.30am and optional tutorials going on to after 9pm. There are lists out up of these so you can sign up to them, I took advantage of everyone I could fit in and found  them to be a hugh benifit, often there are only a small group at them and you get an excellent chance to ask the questions you have been wondering about. There are always activities on in the evening, from quiz nights, Karaoke, Krypton factor and of course the last chance dance as it s known. These are a great opertunity to make a lot of great friends I have many still from this first school.  I was the one hugging friends on the next school I went to   Two of my friend are even married now after a Summer School romance During the school there are often exams or projects which you have to complete to pass the schools and quite often there is an assigment to complete afterwards. One thing I remember most clearly about my first chool is the enthusiasim that the tutor give. I came away thinking I want to be like that I also found a love for geology which I have never even thought about.Assigments: They are in two forms, TMA - or Tutor Marked Assingment and CMA - computer Marked Assignment.TMA s are normally a question and answer which you send to your tutor. They can also be in dissertaion form where you have to write a long thesis on a subject. CMA s are multiple guess, sorry choice, and are sent direct to Milton Keynes for computer marking. Courses have different amounts of assignmentsIn about September course choice for next year is due so not knowing if youve passed or failed you sign up to another year.End of year exam : This reminded me of why I hated School the hall all silent, everyone else scibbling while I looked blankly around......These are held in October and off you all go crammed upto the eyeballs with a year of study, fun and tears behind you. ( in certain circumstance these can be sat at home, one of my friends was a week away from giving birth so was allowed to do this, an invigulator came and sat with her).Then you have to wait, Normally in the week before Christmas the results come out, posted firstly on first class then you get it mailed. And you can enjoy the holidays in peace, knowing you have a couple of months off.Now I went though my degree in the minimum time allowed 4 years. I dont think I recommend this to anyone working full time as it was very, very hard work and I would often work full day and evening and come home and study through the night and staright off to work again (I was a bar restaurant manager and worked about 80hrs a week)The maximum points you can do in a year is 120 and in the first year I stringly (as they OU does) recommend only one course. My final year I did 3 level three cousres, 2 summer schools and a 10 point short course, went through a seperation and moved house - Oh and never had a nervous breakdown     So here I am Alison SInclair, Bsc (Hons) in natural Sciences with biology and earth science. I also hold a diploma in Biology and one in Earth Sciences and a certifictae in Natural sciences. And it was so worth it. Not only did I get the qualifications I got to see the pride in my parents faces when I graduated 6 days before my 30th birthday, I have a hold new group of lovely friends and a lot of skills which I never thought I had.Employers look very favourably at OU degrees - no longer are they thought of the easy option- they realise that to complete one you have to be self discipline, a good time manager and slef motivated.I am proud to be an OU graduate and am thinking about doing another one just for fun as I sorely miss the years of torture and fun I had.Good luck and remember you can do it          ', '    Hard going but well worth it  I have just finished my first exam with the Open University and am worn out  I did two degrees at University in Birmingham, which I completed in 1997. I have been sponsored by my company through a Quality module (history, gurus, theory, tools etc) with the Open University. I have always thought it s a wonderful opportunity to study without having to leave work, and had great admiration for anyone doing it whilst juggling a job and family. I never really realised just how much work it was though. I have been working pretty steadily since I started the postgrad module in May, and have enjoyed the content and being challenged by the assignments and even the exam, but my social life has been a bit on hold, or at least reduced, especially these last few weeks.You ve got to understand as well, everyone else you have relationships with aren t in the same boat, and they won t quite understand. Also their life doesn t stop whilst you re doing the course and there s not even necessarily someone to go to the pub with when you ve finished your exam like at Uni as they re all at work, however, the feeling having completed it is great         ', '    I am currently studying Exploring Education Issues, a level 2 course after doing DD100 last year and two years of maths before that.All in all I find the Open University a good professional organisation. Last year doing DD100 was a bit of a disaster for them, due to late books, tutors resigning, etc but they got over it.The current course I m doing is very good, and having a full time job, it fits in well.I always regretted going straight into employment and not in further education and this is where the OU stands out.  It recognises that some of its students havn t studied for a while, have full time employment, kids etc and caters for them.Try it, your ll enjoy it and get the learning bug     ', '    I am currently studying my first course with the Open University and i love it  i was at university full time last year and left for several reasons. I considered many othere universities and decided that the OU had the best course content. The other reasons also included i could work full time and fit my studies in when i had the time. The cost for my entire degree course is    200-300 more than what i paid for one year at uni  I have attended one day school so far and met other people on my course. The students communicate via an online forum board and there are assignments to complete. Your tutor is available to help you when you need it and the books have all the information that you need. I would highly recommend the OU to anyone considering a degree or any other qualifcaiton they may provide as you pick up qualifcations on the way to your degree. I will be gaining certificates and diplomas then finally my degree.     ', '    Well who d have thunk it  HotChef is ejukayted    The Open university is allowing me to further my  ejucashun , in a way that would otherwise be impossible. I have three children, and because of this lead a very hectic home-life. Having worked my way through the catering ranks...from the pits..to the pots.......to the TOPS(AWARD WINNING  8   P  ), and whilst doing so on average working ~70-90 hours per week, I decided that I was burning myself out and decided that there must be more to life....So I decided to teach I have 11 O levels, and 4 A levels but nothing else ...what could I do?I got a job working as a teaching assistant and project co-ordinator in a secondary school and signed up with the Open University....WOWIn my first year I studied two courses, humanities, and social welfare. These were great, the tutor support was really good, and courses incredibly interesting. The summer school was really helpful too.This year I am studying Literature and the history and future of the English language, and again they are rreeeeaaally interesting.Don t get me wrong, it s hard work... especialy doing two 60 point courses a year, but you ve got to think to the future.If you are happy in the position that you are presently in thats fine, just do a course for fun. You also meet new people at the regular tutorials.Don t have much time? That s OK too the Open University offer a ranch of courses at different intensities:- from 60 points(in my view ~18 hrs each per week) down through 30 point courses and then small 15 point couses.The range of courses is humungous, and there is probably something there to suit everyones needs.Not sur have a look at their web site -- www.open.ac.uk -- have a look around and see for yourself, all of the courses(with thorough descriptions are listed there, and you can also order a prospectus online.You don t know until you give it a try....Nb the comments below relating to accomodation, nightlife etcetera don t really apply to the open university, but I have referred to the summer school for this.HOTChef  xxx      ', '    I enrolled with the Open University this year, studying course DD100; social sciences for beginners, basically.When I first read through the literature before enrolling, it sounded like a very good idea. Study from home in your own time and learn at your own pace. The prices were very expensive, especially as the courses got into the higher qualifications, but I thought I d give the first course a go as it was only    150 and seemed quite reasonable for studying the way you would be. In January I started to get all the literature through, a few books, some audio cassettes and then I got the timetable through, I was shocked to learn that I was supposed to attend a tutorial every week. I thought the whole point of Open University was to more or less study the whole course from home otherwise you may as well go to night school where it s considerably cheaper.Needless to say, I cancelled my course for the year and next year will be enrolling in night school. I found the Open University to be misleading, highly priced and that the centres didn t cater for people without transport.      ', '    I left school at 15 long ago when it was allowed, without an O level to my name. I had always wanted to prove I wasn t as dumb as I looked so at 31 decided to enrol with the OU.It wasn t so daunting studying at home rather than being in a strange environment and it meant it could be done at any time to suit me. The tutors were helpful and always at the end of a phone and they gave helpful comments on the returned essays.The thought of summer school was a bit scary but it came at a time when I seemed to be losing interest and really spured me on again. It was great meeting people with the same interests and being there gave me confidence.The courses were interesting and it was useful if you wanted to study a few different subjects as you could chose from a wide range and encompass different subjects.I can thank my husband for supporting me and with all the confidence I have gained through the OU I have become much more assertive. My husband says he created a monster.     ', '    ******************************************************RESULT      Passed the last exam and will become the proud owner of a Certificate proclaiming my BSc (Hons) Natural Sciences with Biology and Environmental Science in June 2003  The only problem that I have now is...What do I do with all the spare time that has suddenly come my way   ******************************************************INTRODUCTIONI have been studying with the Open University (OU) since 1995 and should complete my BSc in Natural Sciences (Hons) this year (assuming a successful exam result).  I have thoroughly enjoyed my experience of the OU and thought that a synopsis of my experiences might be useful to anyone considering this route to Higher Education.WHY THE OU?As a teenager, I was predicted straight A  8217;s in my A Levels (Physics, Maths and Chemistry) unfortunately, I was distracted by new-found interests including part-time work, parties and the opposite sex and hence squandered my chances   My A Levels were nowhere near good enough to get a place on the courses that I wanted at a traditional university and so I left full-time education for the daily grind of the nine-to-five   8211; my first real lesson in the results of lack of prioritisation Some years later, I began to wonder whether I had it in me to study at undergraduate level and I began to research my options.  I found that the OU offered a number of attractive options.  There was flexibility of study - essential in my professional life, there were no pre-entry requirements other than commitment, and costs were reasonable.  The subjects on offer were closely aligned with my interests and student support seemed good; the reputation of the Summer Schools was legendary...And so my decision was made...COURSE ORGANISATIONA degree with the OU is awarded after earning a number of points   8211; 360 points is the minimum total currently required for a degree.  Each individual course counts towards that total, courses can be worth 60, 30 or 10 points.  Be aware that the number of points awarded is an indication of the amount of work/time required for that course, not the intellectual challenge involved, for example a 60-point course requires around 15 hours of study per week and a 30-point course 8   8211; 9 hours of study per week.  For convenience, OU students refer to a 60-point course as a Whole Credit and 30-point courses are Half Credits; lesser point awards tend to be given for attending Summer Schools.Courses are organised into Levels.  Level 1 courses are probably the equivalent of Foundation Courses in mainstream education and, broadly speaking, take you from GCSE Level to first-year degree level in pretty short order.  Level 2 courses equate to second year study at a traditional university and Level 3 courses equate to the final year of studies.  Courses may or may not have a 7-day Summer School associated with them   8211; some Summer Schools are compulsory, others are not.  As a general rule, attend them if you can   8211; they are invaluable as a learning aid, a good revision tool and an excellent social opportunity   8211; do be warned however that courses with summer schools are usually much more expensive (around double the cost) than courses without.I have found that the number of hours required per course is accurately reflected in the literature provided by the OU   8211; this was a shock as previously I had been used to the types of course where 5 hours work was crammed into 3 days   To succeed you must be self-disciplined, well organised and have a very understanding family   This last point cannot be over-emphasized   8211; 15 hours per week does not sound like much time but it is 2 hours per night, combine that with full-time work, a family and house-hold chores etc. and you begin to see the problems   8211; burning the midnight oil can be very common especially as deadlines approach.COURSE ASSESSMENTAssessment is generally by a combination of methods.  There are Computer Marked Assignments (CMA  8217;s), usually these are in the form of multiple choice question and answer sessions.  Tutor Marked Assignments (TMA  8217;s) are written assignments and, although structured, allow freedom to develop individual lines of thought and reasoning.  Lastly, there may be an end of course assessment, either in the form of a written examination or a project (or both) depending on the course.COURSE CHOICEThe choice of course subject available from the OU is vast and not all are at degree level, there are certificate and diploma courses as well as undergraduate courses.  In general, combining related subjects will result in a course profile that allows the award of a degree in a named subject   8211; useful if studying for professional or career reasons.  On the other hand, as long as you have the required number of points, a general degree can be awarded; this allows you to follow a course of study in subjects purely out of interest rather than with a defined goal.  This freedom of choice, I think, is one of the major advantages of OU study, but it is also one of the pitfalls.  There is a danger of ending-up with an eclectic mix of subjects that may not be of any practical use or that do connect or relate to each other in any way   8211; this connection is very useful, especially at higher levels where the intellectual demands may be more demanding.  There is professional advice available to assist in course choices should you require it.TEACHING / STUDENT SUPPORTWhilst I have no direct experience of traditional universities, many friends and colleagues have.  Drawing on their comments on what they have seen of the OU study materials and from what I have read or experienced, I feel that the standard of teaching is high within the OU environment.  Written material is very good, it is up to date and regularly reviewed; even the TV programmes are of high quality with hardly a beard, flares or open-toed sandal in sight   There are audio and video tapes available to enhance the learning experience and an increasing number of courses are embracing the internet as a medium for students and staff to get together in online conferences etc.  It is also worth pointing out that you are no longer denied the facility of an academic library since all students with internet access can utilise the OU s own library online.  You are assigned your own tutor who is never more than an e-mail or telephone call away.  You can be as sociable as you like   The only thing that I would say is that support is better during Level 1 courses than at higher levels   8211; presumeably part of the degree process is an increased independance.CONCLUSIONOn the whole, I have thoroughly enjoyed my studies with the OU.  I have studied courses that I wished to study and will be awarded the degree that I wanted to get.  The support and advice that I have received from the staff at the OU has been good.  I already have a great feeling of satisfaction from my studies and have picked-up a Certificate and Diploma along the way.  Hopefully, my positive experience will place me in a good position whent it comes to career and job hunting.  That said, studying with the OU requires dedication, commitment, persistence and discipline, it is easy to give up since no one badgers you for that late assignment or asks you to justify non-attendance at lectures.  Nevertheless, I thouroughly recommend the OU to anyone whether studying for reasons of enjoyment, career or challenge.     ', '    I have been studying with The Open University for a few years in order to obtain a degree as I would like to enter into teaching. I have 4 young children ranging from 7 months up to 11 years.  Studying with the OU not only fits in with my family, but allows me to choose which hours of the day I allow for studying.  I do not have to worry about childcare costs, or finding someone to take or collect my children from school.  I was also able to carry on working before I had my baby.There are lots of courses to choose from at different levels. You can decide to just do a course for fun or to gain a diploma or a degree.  A degree requires a total of 360 credits which can be completed in a minimum of 3 years - 120 credits a year.  Or you can take as long as you wish.There are courses in Maths, Computing, Psychology, Childcare, The Sciences, The Arts, languages and many more.  The cost is not too bad.  Some of the shorter courses (30 credits) are about    250 and the longer courses (60 credits) are from about    450. Most of the course materials are included although some of the courses require extra books.  Some of the courses are now online with computer conferencing.  I studied an IT course last year which was very interesting and some of the assignments were completed as a group.  This made it a bit more fun and was a good incentive to try and complete it on time.  The first year there is a lot of tutor contact if you need it.  After that, you are basically on your own but there are the occasional tutorials you can go to if you wish.  There is always someone to help on the end of a phone though.The assignments are good in helping you learn and if you fall behind, it is not a problem; the tutors are very understanding.  Some of the courses have a residential school, but if you have young children you may be excused from it. but I have heard it is lots of fun and very useful. Not all of the courses have exams but if they do there are various study guides to help.Overall, I am glad I joined the Open University and am looking forward to starting another course next year.     ', '    OU study is supported in the First Year on Foundation courses with a personal tutor, weekly seminars, radio and television programmes, plus audiovisual material of a very high standard. This is targeted at a widely divergent group of people, ranging from new school-leavers right through to mature students who have not written an essay for decades. Depending on how you feel about your fellow students, you can also be involved in discussion groups or self-help gatherings - sometimes held in pubs  If you get really lucky you might have a revision group like I once had where we actually discussed the very same painting that appeared on the exam paper - I couldn t believe my luck      ']

The points system lets you accumulate credits toward degrees or certificates at your own rhythm, which aligns well with a self-directed, resilient learner’s mindset.
