', '    The Sony MZ-R900 is my first venture into the world of the MiniDisc (MD) format, and let me say from the outset that I am impressed.  Thanks to the MiniDisc Long Play (MDLP) system and the supplied optical lead, you can record almost two-and-a-half hours of music in LP2 mode direct from CD onto a sturdy 74-minute disc costing less than a quid with no discernable loss of sound quality.  MDLP will in fact allow you to double that recording time again, but at the cost of poor rendition of high-frequency sounds (such as acoustic guitar) - therefore I would not recommend the use of that particular mode (LP4) for anything but voice recording.  Give it a go and judge for yourself if you decide to buy one of these little boxes of tricks, but remember that while recording it monitors the source - you will need to play your disc back to hear what has been laid down.The supplied headphones give remarkable performance, especially in the bass department.  My only niggle is that the cord length is ridiculously short - to listen without appearing to be committing a lewd act, you must wear the remote on your collar and thus look quite the prize idiot.  Be prepared to spend at least    20 on replacements of equal or better sound quality - cheaper ones will be badly exposed.The life of the custom battery is quite astounding.  Quoted at 60 hours  playback from a 3.5 hour charge (remember to press the stop/charge button after connecting the included power adaptor ), it will easily last out a whole week of arduous commuting; alternatively it will quite happily record an entire disc and play it back to you at full volume on the way to work the next day.While we re on the subject, I think it s worth pointing out that if you re used to recording a CD in seven or eight minutes, be it to hard drive or as a CD-R burn, going back to real-time, 1x speed transfer is going to come as a shock.  At least you don t have all that messing about with levels and timing that vinyl to tape requires - if you re recording digitally that is.  As I already mentioned, Sony provide an optical cable to facilitate this that would normally set you back    20 - but make sure that you have an optical output on your CD player.  This is sometimes labelled  TOSlink  and looks like a square hole and should be plugged with an angular dust exclusion peg.  Beware the output labelled  S/PDIF ,  digital coaxial out  or plain  digital out  and looks like the  TV out  on your video recorder - this produces an electrical signal that will require a trip down Tottenham Court Road to get    45 worth of digital coaxial cable and conversion equipment before you can record.  Any official Sony Centre will also be able to supply the converter bundled with the mains adaptor it requires, but chances are they will not keep it in stock and you will need to clearly state that you require a  digital coaxial in to optical out converter  - the direction is important as the reverse is also available.  Don t forget to buy a short length of digital coaxial cable to connect it to your CD player output.  If your CD player only has a coaxial output, or no digital output at all, remember that DVD players can also play audio CDs - so if you have one, check its outputs before setting off for central London.  Alternatively you could shun digital recording altogether and buy an analogue lead - these are available for    7.99 from the average high street electrical retailer.  If you re thinking of recording your old vinyl or tape collection onto MD then you will need one anyway, but by recording through an analogue lead from a digital source you will be losing some sound quality and the automatic track marks that are transferred with the format, plus you may need to adjust the recording level.The MZ-R900 is not cheap; the recommended selling price is    250, although you can pick one up from an internet retailer for    200 - and this figure will only go down as new models are introduced.  Apart from the cost, the only thing against this little box is that there is no integrated radio.  I don t think adding this extra would increase the size much and there is plenty of space on the fascia for base unit controls.  It would be a challenge to add the functionality to the already versatile remote, but I m sure it could be done with a little thought...There are a few gimmicks included such as the auto volume limiting system (AVLS) which makes sure sound output does not rise above a certain (for me, fairly low) level, and the ability to vary the speed of playback by steps (a bit playing a 7 , 45rpm single at 33 or 78rpm - fun for about 10 seconds).  Sony also include a leather pouch with a belt-clip to carry the unit in, but it does seem a shame to hide those beatiful metallic silver or blue looks away (other colours are available, but not in the UK for some reason).Overall, the MZ-R900 package is a fine offering, and if the lack of a radio is not a problem and you have the money to spare, I highly recommend it. The compression method is psycho acoustic masking, which basically means that much of the data which is deemed inaudible, is thrown away. The audio is then stored on the MiniDisc as an audio file(s).The data is stored on the disc using the magneto-optical writing technique, which uses both a laser and a magnetic head to record the data - the laser heats up the disc and the magnetic head then changes the properties of the surface of the disc according to the data to be recorded.MDLP2 and MDLP4 are extensions to ATRAC, which enable the user to record upto 160 or 320 minutes of audio.The antishock device used in MD is also different to CD antishock devices - as the music is stored as a compressed audio file, the memory just needs to hold the data from the disc - this is generally held 40 seconds in advance.The use of memory like this also aids battery life. As the disc isn t being read from constantly, battery life is greatly extended as motors take a lot of power to drive. Using the MDLP extensions also improves battery life as the memory holds the same amount of data, but can play back for two or four times as long.Now the stuff you want to know:The Sony device is an excellent solution - it has many features to aid recording and playback, and the MDLP system lets you record to MDLP2 at least without much noticeable quality loss. The 12 buttons consist of record mode, time mark, end search, record, enter, play, rewind, fast forward, stop, pause, and up and down volume buttons.  To the side of the player there is a plug for the remote, two jacks one for microphone, and one is for the optical cable.  And the battery cover is also housed here.The remote control has the same buttons on it allowing full use of it without having to touch the playing unit.  It is small and light weight and comes with a clip to allow you to attach it to your clothes.  The remote plugs into the side of the player, with a special looking plug.  I wouldn  8217;t like to think how much Sony would charge to replace it The rechargeable battery that comes with it isn  8217;t one of those ones you can only get from Sony and is really expensive.  It is a single AA battery.  Which means you only need to carry one with you.  With the battery fully charged, the unit will last ages and ages, as it is a very low power machine.  If you run out of battery you can replace it with any other AA battery that you may have, or you can use the mains charger.  The charger will also charger the battery, and this only takes a few hours, or like most things you can leave it over night.  It is recommended that you use the main lead when you are recording, as this will drain the battery a lot quickerI  8217;m sure you all know what headphones are by now, well if not look in the dictionary.  The pair you get with the MZ-R700 sound very clear and fit my ears nicely, but everyone is different so you might decide to change them for a different make.  The optical cable is a cable that can be used to record from CD to MD.  It uses light, and sends it down the cable.  This is a digital way of recording, and you must have an optical port on your CD player for this to work.  But don  8217;t worry if you don  8217;t have one yet, you can still use an analogue cable.  The sound quality is no different to me The instructions are packed with information on how to do everything on the unit, some may seem a little confusing, but its quick simple to get the hang of it The unit also has a great feature called MDLP, this is a long play facility, and you can record about 4 hours of music on one disc   BUT again the quality of the sound is reduced, but as I said earlier, I can  8217;t hear a difference.I bought this minidisc player at 179.00, last April.  This was when it was first released.  I was looking at minidiscs for ages, and i decided to wait until this one came out, as i felt it was the best one going (and it is).  It comes in 3 rather sexy colours green (which i have), blue and silver.      ', '    This is one sweet toy.... not an mp3 player so not very light with a disk in it, but many plusses with net minidisk players, you can store tons of music on one mdisk (approx. 70-80 tracks on one disk) and you don t need to delete the music you dont listen to, you can have many disks and change when you want. This player comes with a remote control on the headphone wire so you can change tracks easily with the player safely in your pocket, also comes in two colours; blue and silver, another good point is that it is strong and can sort tracks into numbers, authors, and albums if neccesary, the software that comes with this device enables the user to easily download music to the player from the computer using USB or you can real-time record, which isn t so good bu it gets the job done if you don t have a pc. overall a good buy for someone looking for a portable music player at a very good price (got mine for around    100 new six months ago from dixons, fallen reasonably in price.)     ', '    The Sony MD MZ-G750 Sony, the name just screams greatness.This like any other Sony product is great. I have friends that have other brands of MD s and they don t hold a candle to this one. Even though this MD is not top spec, it does all the things you need it to do.FacilitiesBuilt in digital FM/AM tuner.When you get bored of your mindisc s you can switch on the radio and listen to that. If you need to check the football results or even listen to the match it self.MDLP.Allows you to record up to 320 minutes of music. You can record digitally from a CD player, DVD player, etc. Via an optical cable (supplied), but the source must have an optical output.Up to 48 hours battery life.Depending on the mode you recorded it inLCD remote control.This comes in handy. When the MD player is in the belt clip you cant get to the buttons. The remote has volume and radio buttons. It has a switch for hold and a like roll switch for skip, play and pause functions.G Protection - jog proof.I have dropped, banged and shook my MD player but it is yet to skip. Analogue recording level control.It allows you to turn the volume of the recording up and down if recording using a phono to stereo lead. Digital mega bass.A good thing about all Sony personal stereo products I have bought the bass is amazing providing you have a good set of headphones (best to use in ear headphones).Monaural recording.This is the alternative to recording in stereo. I can t say much about it because I ve never used it.Repeat.Same as repeat on your home stereo. Repeat 1.Allow you to repeat just one track.Shuffle repeat.This plays tracks randomly and doesn t stop until you press stop. It will just keep repeating.Name editor function.Allows you to name your tracks. The track name shows up on the main unit and if you have a home MD system with MD editor function it displays it on it.Remaining battery indicator.Tells you how much battery is left. Personally I never pay any attention to it, but there again my battery I always running out on me.In ear fontopia headphones.Good quality headphones with a small length of wire that plugs into your remote.Rechargeable battery.This is a must it eats normal batteries (Panasonic) for breakfast.Carry case.Handy if you have small pockets or don t want to scratch it.Mains adapter.I do all my recording using the mains adapter because it run out your battery very fast.Enough with all the specs, all you need to know is that it is great and all you people out there that have cd players need to save up and go and buy a MD player/recorder.It s only right to point out its bad points.When recording in LP2 and LP4 the sound quality does suffer. The reception for the radio isn t too clever.If you use big headphones you loose the sharpness of the treble. If recording five hours you have to sit and wait for five hours.     ', '    I have tried almost every type of headphone/earphone and all have failed to satisfy. I tried over-head, they looked stupid, I tried street style ones which felt uncomfortable and i ve tried many so called  gel  earphones which also didn t fit my ears the way they should. Finally i stumbled accross these babies  (I must stress that my ear s are not abnormal, they just dont fit the ever so common standard shaped earphones supplied as standard).These earphones on the other hand fit like a dream and don t fall out if I run or do any other sort of physical activity. The earbuds supplied can be easily removed from the earphone s themselves and stay tightly on during use. They are so soft that I forget that they are actually in my ears sometimes Aesthetically these earphones look great and have many functions to their advantage.-The split wire socket enables people with sony walkman remotes (like me) to use them in conjuntion with it so that there is no excess wiring hanging around.-The supplied case is very handy for keeping the earphones shielded when the earphones are not in use.-The soft carry pouch for the wire extention and spare buds is also handy for when your travelling and you want to keep all accessories handy.-Gold wire connectors ensure the sound quality. The build of the connectors is also good and secure.-The very fact that they are in-ear mean that they also block out unwanted noise from the outside environment which means pure, louder sound.-The sound quality is second to none and the bass is real deep.All of these factors contribute to these great earphones success, and with sony you can mostly guarantee it s going to be well built.The only draw back is that I paid    34.99 for mine which was a lot of money for a pair of earphones. But the way I saw it i had no other choice due to fitting problems and at the end of the day you pay for what you get, these are a quality set. I now finally have some great headphones which will undoubtedly last a very long time. One word of warning, clean your ears before use, because remember that in-ear means right in your ears After many months of use of these headphones I have found that everything has remained satisfactory apart from the loss of sound in one earphone. This is due to layers of dirt and wax that inevitably build up over time on the actual earphone surface which needs to be cleaned now and again. These earphones are more at risk of becoming dirty due to their exposed surfaces beneath the earbuds. Another problem is I do not know how to clean them or what to clean them with so I still experience a decrease in volume when using them...but i m sure i will find out how to clean them sooner or later.With the online price  currently so cheap, why wait?      ', '    I was excited at the prospect of downloading music onto mini-disc, but I m afraid Sony has ruined the experience for me.  Maybe I m just not that technically minded.  The instructions which came with this model might as well have been shredded for hampster cages.  After deleting a couple of mini-discs, and having a nervous breakdown, I then got the hang of it.  I don t even bother entering the names of the discs or tracks because it takes so long.  The sound quality is fine, but the volume could be better.  Maybe they make it so quiet so you can t hear the quality...?  This model is hard to use, and a bit clumsy.  Let s just say I wouldn t recommend it to my granny.     ', '    This Mini -Disc recorder is pretty simple to use, which can help if you are technologically challenged. It  is very small and is suitable to fit into a pocket, the downside of that being it can easily get scratched and it is also very fragile, this meaning that if it is dropped it is likely that it will get broken.I bought my Sony Net MZ -N510 Christmas 2003 and I have found it to be a very good mini disc player I did drop it at one stage which made it stop working for about 1 week. I did find  though that the Net MD function was very useful as it was very easy to record music off of CDs and your PC very easily simply with a few clicks of the mouse.The remote that comes fixed into the headphones supplied with the player is very useful, I found it to be very helpful if the player was in my pocket. I did find that the remote weighed down the earphones making it harder for the earphones to stay in my ear Overall I would recommend this player as it is very easy to use and is great value for money being at around    100, although it can be quite easily damaged mine still plays even though it has received a bit of a battering. I think that the Net MD function is very good and for that price and the security of Sony you can t go wrong.     ', '    Having dropped my ye olde faithful MZ-R30 on the floor, shattering the LCD to pieces, I set about looking for another Sony portable recording MD walkman.  I knew from a MD mailing list that the latest batch of Sony gear were sporting features such as long play modes or USB connectivity but unfotunately to date, no model encompassed entirely what I was looking for - the R700 was prolly about the closest to what I needed.The main used for my MD unit is recording sound bites and/or rough demo tracks for the band I manage (see profile for more blurb on that) and we needed online editing and ideally a shock proof recorder given some of the SPL s we deal with tend to vibrate the entire immediate neighbourhood My only gripe with the R700 over having used the older R30 for several years is that most of the R700 functions are now buried under several layers of menu s instead of being immediately accessible on the front panel with a button. Still, you get used to this after a while although I dearly miss my old  Display  button - always nice to know how much time is remaining per track as well as initially know how far through the track you are...While the R700 is supplied with a charger and NiMH cell, I run the unit of alkaline cells, dunno why, just find it easier to pop a fresh cell in every once in a while instead of going through the rigmarole of finding the charger and then  activating  the charge mode to top up the NiMH cell.     ']

product_reviews: ['    One of the best pieces of running kit I ever bought was not an expensive pair of running shoes, nor one of those fancy running vests that supposedly help keep you dry and cook when you sweat. Not, it was a tiny little 1GB iPod Shuffle. Strangely, at the time I had a cheap pair of running shoes and no special running vest, so at    44.00 it was also the most expensive piece of running equipment I had ever bought, but it soon proved to be well worth the cost, especially as it s proved the most durable piece of running kit I have - even more so than my legs, on occasion.You see, whilst I enjoy my running, I m not a particularly good self-motivator. As long as I can run on the shoulder of someone, I can go for miles, but when I m on my own I tend to do fewer miles and at a slower pace - assuming I make it out of the house at all. However, research has shown that running to music can be a powerful motivating force, both in terms of increasing distance and speed and several people I knew often ran with music playing. At the time, however, the only music player I had was a mobile phone which would have been a little too cumbersome to carry (I hate running with something in my hands) and wouldn t be secured anywhere about my person. An iPod shuffle was the only obvious answer.What I ended up with was a blue, 1GB, second generation iPod Shuffle. I wanted the silver, but it was out of stock and I turned down the chance to spend an extra    15 on the 2GB version, as I knew the 1GB would store about 9 hours of music and I didn t anticipate running any longer than that. The design is simplicity itself, a rectangle of brushed aluminium about 4 cm long by 2.5 cm wide and maybe half a centimetre thick with a large clip on the back, with the whole thing weighing something like 15 g. The buttons were minimal, with an on and off switch and a selector to either shuffle the songs or not on the top, plus the play and volume levels in the traditional Apple circular theme on the front, with volume up and down on the up and down parts of the circle and skip forward and back on right and left, with play/pause in the middle.When I first got the Shuffle home, I found setting it up to be really simple, although it did help that I m not entirely inexperienced with gadgets and already had iTunes installed on my PC. For those without iTunes, this will need to be downloaded, as Apple s iPods only seem to allow songs to be uploaded to them from other Apple products, although other mp3 players may be compatible with other music software if that s what you use. However, for me, set up was almost pathetically easy. I just took the Shuffle out of the box, connected it to the charging stand and plugged that into my PC with the USB attachment and off it went. Setting it up to sync in with my iTunes was a matter of minutes and I was ready to put my music onto my new iPod.This is where I started to have a few problems with the iPod Shuffle. Not that putting the music on it was difficult. There are several ways in which this can be achieved. You can either drag or drop directly from iTunes into the iPod when it s connected to your PC, or you can ask it to automatically fill itself either from your entire library or from individual play lists you may have set up on your iTunes. The problem comes when you re as big a music fan as I am, yet horribly indecisive. I currently have more than 8000 songs on my iTunes and the Shuffle would accept only around 100 of these. It is at times like this that the Autofill feature comes in handy and even on the first set up, it doesn t take more than a few minutes to add all the songs to the iPod, even if you re filling it up more or less completely. What does take a fair amount of time is fully charging the battery.There are two play options on the Shuffle, which are selected from a switch at the top of the unit. You can opt to either play the songs in the order you have placed them on the Shuffle, or play them in a random mode which Apple call  quot;shuffle quot; mode, hence the name of the unit. I never used the play in order mode, as I always used the Autofill mode on my Shuffle, which selects songs from the play list in a fairly random order and thus made the play in order slightly redundant, as I was effectively always going to get the songs in a relatively random order no matter which option I had selected. However, if you placed whole albums on the Shuffle deliberately to play them as a whole, I can see how this option would have been useful, but that wasn t something I ever did.I found the Shuffle to be perfect for my needs. The clip was very strong and it clipped securely to the pocket of my running shorts and the earphone cable was long enough to reach from there to my ears without affecting my running position, but wasn t so long it was flap about all over the place and potentially get caught up with anything I may have been running past. The Shuffle, being a hard drive player, played without skipping, regardless of how quickly I was moving and the clip was strong enough that it rarely slipped, putting strain on my ears as the cable moved or becoming loose and unclipping from my shorts. Even now, having had the Shuffle for near enough 3 years and running countless miles with it, the spring on the clip is still strong enough to keep it in place.Unlike some, I also found that the headphones were suitable for me. Admittedly, they are fairly low quality and after several years, some of the plastic bits around the connector and the earphones themselves are showing some wear, but they generally retain position in my ears fairly well and the sound quality, whilst a little tinny, is suitable to listening to whilst I m running, walking or travelling. They re not sound-blocking, but the volume on the Shuffle is adjustable enough and goes high enough that I found I could shut out many of the sounds around me. Fortunately, for those people who don t like the earphones, the headphone connection is a standard one, so replacing them with your own choice of earphones or headphones is easily achieved, but not something I have ever needed to do.There were a couple of minor annoyances I found with my Shuffle, however. The first was that the battery indicator wasn t particularly clear. There was a tiny LED on the top that lights up in various colours when you turn the Shuffle on to indicate whether the Shuffle was fully charged, or how low the battery was getting. However, this gives no indication of exactly how long you had left on the battery and there was also no idea given by that little light as to how much charge had gone into the Shuffle whilst connected to the PC. Several times I was mislead by the light stopping flashing whilst I had it connected to my PC, which I thought meant it had stopped charging and was full, when it actually only meant that it had finished adding all the music to the Shuffle.This meant that I would occasionally get part way through a day s commute and find my battery had run out and on one particularly annoying occasion, the Shuffle went flat 9 miles into a Half Marathon in which I d been doing rather well and disrupted my rhythm. But for this to happen on few occasions in several years isn t too bad and, fortunately, it wasn t often a problem as the Shuffle battery life is immense. With the very simple functionality of the Shuffle, it doesn t place a lot of strain on the battery and so it seems to last forever, so it s unusual to find yourself getting caught out with regards to the battery running down at an inopportune moment.The other minor annoyance I had with the Shuffle was that it there was no way of knowing what song you were listening to at any point, apart from waiting until you got home and trying to trace it from the play order on your iTunes. Again, this wasn t often a problem, but with adding songs to the Shuffle completely at random as I did, you do sometimes come across a song from an album you hadn t listened to often or recently and so I didn t recognise the song, yet having enjoyed it had no way of easily finding it again to listen to the CD in full later on at home.Fortunately, I ve been pleased to note recently, these issues have been fixed in the new 4th generation iPod Shuffle. There is now a little button on the top of the new Shuffle which apparently can be used to check both the battery life and to find out the details of the song you are listening to. I thought my old 2nd generation Shuffle was a decent enough machine, but with a couple of minor things that could be improved. The 4th generation Shuffle appears to have solved the minor issues I had and is available for less money than I paid for my Shuffle 2 years ago and for more space, with the new 2GB Shuffle being priced at around    39.For those who want to listen to music whilst exercising or travelling, I thoroughly recommend the iPod Shuffle for those who already have all their music on iTunes. For those who don t, there are cheaper alternatives out there and if you re going to have to mess around putting music onto your PC before you do anything, you have little to lose by going for a different version. But for sheer ease for those who already have all their music on iTunes as I had, the Shuffle is hard to beat. It s simple to put music on, plays wonderfully and the clip and the weight of the Shuffle are perfect to be able to conceal or hold it in position well whilst exercising, which is exactly what I was looking for from an mp3 player. My little 1GB 2nd generation iPod Shuffle was ideal for my needs and I love it. If you re a keen runner, I can t help but feel from what I ve heard about it, the 2GB 4th Generation sounds even better, perhaps pretty close to perfect for me needs and good enough to tempt me into considering an upgrade, which is something I rarely, if ever, do when the old piece of machinery is still in perfect working order.      ', '    If your after a small mp3 player with the ability to hold your favourite tunes the iPod Shuffle is what your looking at right now. Although it costs more than its competitors it seems to be very stylish and seems to be a cool product to have but is it all its cracked up to be.It can hold about 250 songs which is good as you can put your favourite music on it. It s not the sort of mp3 player that would be your main one but it s ideal for usage in the gym or when your jogging or in any place where you can t put stuff in pockets or hold onto anything big. ', '    What if five years ago you told somebody that they could ditch their portable cd player and have over 100 tracks in something the size of a chewing gum packet. They probably would have laughed at you and carried on ruining their hearing whilst annoying the other passengers on the bus.Well portable MP3 players are now all the range and at the top of the pile is the iPod from apple. Backed by some funky advertising it s safe to say that this is one of the in gadgets to have at your disposal. But for those on the go and liking to be discrete they may favour something more inconspicuous. For those spy s among us Apple has brought out the  Shuffle . A small portable MP3 player that you can fit into your pocket or sling around your neck, either it won t trouble you, you probably won t even know it s there. The shuffle comes in 512mb and 1GB flavours. For the computer illiterate that just means that one holds about twice as much as the other but obviously at a greater cost. The device is meant for people on the go, those that just need a musical distraction rather than worrying what track is where.Everything is about it is minimal. There is no display screen, there is only one control button and there is only one switch. As far as options go it is incredibly limited, you can either play your songs in order or simply select the  shuffle  mode and listen to tracks at random. The control button simply give s you volume and back/forward track selection. To put your tunes on, you take off the end that unveils a USB connection; plug it into your computer and using the itunes software transfer your tracks via the USB port on your computer. As for charging, this is also done by the USB port. Seeing as it s a really a storage device you can also use it to do just that but then you may as well just spend a tenner on a USB pen drive instead.The headphones supplied give a good sound quality, purists may wish to upgrade them but then they probably wouldn t be going for this model anyway. Now for the downside, the shuffle is a smart little thing but I have to say for    69 (512mb version) it doesn t really offer a tremendous amount of value. 512mb usb storage drives are around    20 and I m sure the mass production of electronics means that the additional audio components inside don t add up to a great cost. Of course Ipod s are the Armani of the MP3 world. You re paying partly for name and prestige as well as supposed reliability. Aside from the software and the shuffle itself all you get extra for your money is a bit of string to put the shuffle around your neck. I m sure a lot of people will be amazed should you show them this and then cough at the retail price. For something so small I have to say it also feels breakable. But then the smaller things get the more care you feel you have to take.Obviously the other big drawback is not having a visible track list. You can select your tracks with your PC but then I m sure no-one memorizes their order of tracks. This means that you can be sitting there flicking through quite often. But then the name  shuffle  says that Apple didn t intend for this to be nothing more than a small, effective way of storing tunes as a way to pass the time. For around the    70 mark this is worth considering but you really have to weigh up the pros and cons against other brands before purchasing.My experience of this product has been good, it s a family members and I would have to say I personally wouldn t  have paid the money for it. Hopefully we can share the Ipod love and dominate the world one day       ', '    This 512 mb extremly small new ipod shuffle is a spectaculer piece of technology.  it is simple to use and all you have to do is plug in straight into your computer via the usb.you can charge the mp3 via your computer usb socket. the songs can be easily downloaded off of itunes for 79p each.in my opinion i love this ipod becuase it is simple to use, quite cheep at only    30. however you can get these a lot cheeper on ebay like i did. seeing as the already brought out ipod shuffle 2nd gen is out i think this is not one for the future.it has a bit of an ugly shape and is slightly unconfortable to hold.however it is easy to use and is very good if you want to go on a run. in my opinion it is simple to use and is briliant for someone who is quite simple. however watch out ofr the 2nd gen it is a lot cooler and better designed. maybe a bit small        ', '    From chewing gum to jeans clip, the Apple iPod Shuffle has redefined how the ultra compact mp3 player should look like. Up until now, monochrome LCD screens were a standard feature of any mp3 player. With their last iPod Shuffle, they decided that people could be pleased with a stylish mp3 player that could randomly or sequentially play their favorite songs, as long as you had a way of putting music on it. Since then, Apple has even replaced the USB connector on the Shuffle with a docking station that cannot be easily replaced, but makes it so that the earphone jack also acts as the charging/connecting interface between the Shuffle and the computer.If you are using an old version of iTunes, you will be forced to update and possibly upgrade your shuffle with new firmware. The features are fairly barebones, with a play/pause charge LED light and the standard controls. Even the earphones have been kept the same since the last iPod (not the newer type shipped with the iPod Video). At 55 pounds (now available for even less), it is quite expensive for a small box like that. For me, the docking station cable broke after 3 months, so I had to really make sure that there was a connection for the Shuffle to charge.Due to its size, it s fairly easy to use and you only know that the battery has run out when it doesn t play anymore (although it lasts quite long) for its size).If you have the money, I d rather go for the iPod Video 30GB, because of the video functionality. The nano on the other hand is just a music player with menu functionality.This is quite a good birthday present if they haven t already got one, or as a marketing gift for your customers. If you order it from the Apple website, you can also have it custom engraved with your company logo or so.Finally, don t expect the world in terms of sound quality. The sound quality is not as good as the iPod video, obviously, but prolonged hearing brings out the uncomfortable feeling caused by the iPod earphones (a bit tight for me).     ', '    The iPod shuffle many people would say that it is a step back for Apple as it doesn t include a screen and it has a lot less memory than its other larger iPod brothers. It is small (about the size of a packet of chewing gum) it is sleek and looks cool, up to 12hrs play time on one charge cycle, perfect for people on the go and don t like chunky MP3 Players, it is about the weight of a car key. One of the best things is that it charges when you put it into your USB port and it will charge when you are putting music on it.It has an easy to use slider switch on the back (Off, Play in order or Shuffle) also a battery light, all you have to do is press it and if the light is green (full battery), Orange (Roughly half full) or Red (Almost Empty).  The Shuffle which will cost approx.    90+ is a good buy compared to the more expensive iPod or iPod mini which would cost    130+ although they have screens and a superior amount of memory. The Shuffle with 1Gigabyte (1024 megabytes) compared to the other iPods which start from 4Gb and go up to 60Gb. The iPod shuffle will hold 240 songs about 4 minutes in length which from my point of view is enough but it also can store videos, pictures, documents etc. It comes with headphones, another cap so you can carry it around your neck and a CD holding iTunes music player where you can put your songs and then carry them onto your iPod Shuffle.     The downside is that it can only play the songs in order, in a random Shuffle (hence where the name came from) and change the volume up or down. It s simple but still can compete with all the other MP3 Players.This is a definite step up for Apple.     ']

', '    Ive owned this from new which means i have probably had it for almost 8 years or so and in this time it has never let me down.It is black in colour so matches my black panasonic tv i bought it to be used with.It is a NICAM vcr so when i play videos which have digital surround sound it sounds great as i have it all wired through my hifi surround sound system.It still records and plays back as well as the day it was bought.In the box you get the VCR itself, a manual, a coaxial cable, aremote contro with batteries and a manual. ', '     I was apprehensive about buying this Sony Walkman MP3 player after reading the complaints about the SonicStage software, but I took a chance because the 2GB version is now on offer for under    50. If you’re after a compact, no-nonsense music player that punches above its weight, the Apple iPod shuffle 1 GB is worth a close look. Its standout feature is portability: this little device is so light and slim, you might forget it’s even clipped on during your run or gym session. The design is stylish yet rugged enough to handle everyday bumps and drops, making it a solid companion for active lifestyles.

Battery life impresses too, delivering up to 12 hours of continuous playback—enough to power through a full day of workouts or commutes without hunting for a charger. Compatibility is another plus: it works seamlessly with both PC and Mac, and supports a variety of audio formats like MP3, AAC, WAV, and Audible files, which is great if you like mixing music with audiobooks.

Sound quality is surprisingly clear and crisp for such a tiny device, which is no small feat given its size and price point. The simple control pad and button interface keep things straightforward, so you won’t waste time fumbling with complicated menus. Plus, it doubles as a flash drive, letting you transfer files easily—a practical bonus.

That said, the lack of a screen is a double-edged sword. While it keeps the device minimal and lightweight, it means you can’t see or select specific songs on the fly. If you’re someone who likes to curate playlists on the go, this might feel limiting.

Overall, the iPod shuffle 1 GB offers excellent value for money, especially if you prioritize portability, durability, and ease of use over flashy features. It’s a pragmatic choice for music lovers who want a reliable, skip-free player without breaking the bank. Just don’t expect it to replace your smartphone or more advanced players when it comes to browsing your music library.

product_reviews: ['    As a rule, I m not a devotee of the glossy magazine but I do bend this rule from time to time if I have a long train ride/ flight or something and always when some of my kind colleagues leave finished with copies in the office break room. What attracts me mainly is the small  handbag  size, kind of a tabloid version of a magazine, so easy to slip in your handbag rather than have to get a carrier bag for it or fold it five times to get it in  Glamour was, I believe, the first to with the A5 format and it has been this way since the magazine was first launched in the summer of 2002.I have the October 2005 issue in front of me; this was a freebie issue that I found on a train. I will now go through it in more detail to give you a general idea of what to expect from a typical issue.  The cover this month features a naked Cat Deeley, but don t get too excited boys all her  interesting bits  are neatly covered up by a silver flash banner promoting the celebrity bodies  special issue . This would probably have put be off actually buying the issue since I hate the media s obsession with celebrity figures and faces but it does actually include a few vaguely interesting articles and interviews on how celebrities I don t give a fig about keep their impossibly thin shapes. I only wonder how desperate you have to be to get your picture in a magazine if you re prepared to have your sex life analysed and pulled to pieces in front of everyone you know. If that had happened to me, I think I d still be trying to recover my power of speech, let alone ringing round magazines to find someone to pick up my tragic wedding story. Still, it s not up to me to judge and best of luck to the girl in question; it was a very moving story.Then there s a article entitled  date me, love me, marry me - Glamour s guide to achieving this in three years  - you can imagine what that s all about and it s the type of article that makes me ashamed to read this type of magazine. Get a life people and take life how it comes Our 7/7 heroes is a real eye dampener, the kind of article that makes me think actually women s magazines aren t always fluffy and frivolous    It describes the experiences of a number of passengers, passers by and emergency services staff on that dreadful day in July. However, I did by the French version when I was in France last year and this was only    1.50 so it no longer seems quite such a bargain. Anyway, as with most magazines a subscription offers a much better deal with a 40  discount (a mere    13.60 for 12 issues) and each month there s a different free gift on offer to boot. October s offer was a set of 3 L Oreal hair care products (worth over    24) - shampoo, conditioner and intensive hair softening mask, all in all not a bad deal at all. You can subscribe on line for the same price for a year, or an even cheaper    23.60 but I don t think you get the free gift if you do it that way.All in all I think Glamour has a very wide-ranging scope, offering something to interest almost all women (and quite possibly a lot of men if they keep up the vice women articles). I remember the lyrics of a certain Savage Garden song contained the words  I ve learnt that beauty magazines only make you feel ugly  and I ve often felt that to be oh so very true, but this one isn t that bad (though perhaps I was just having a good day )     ', '    Womens Magazines... chunky, heavy and expensive.Not if you re a glamour reader    This dinky little read will set you back just    1.50 (Eat yer heart out cosmo ) and WON T leave your arms aching as you clutch it while running for the bus  Better still, it doesn t assume that all it s readers are city slicker chicks earning    60k a year, who think nothing of shelling out    200 for a gucci handbag    It s written for normal, bright young women who fancy something fun to flick through on their way to work.It s got a nice blend of all those  flick through lookin  at the pictures  essentials; fashion, beauty, the odd  makes you think  article, and my personal favourite, readers embarrassing stories  (Well, it s nice to know that I m not the only one stuid things happen to  )You ll find all the usual celeb gossip, but this mag also finds fun in laughing at the rich and famous and particuarly their  fashion blunders   (nice to know that Posh doesn t look oh so perfect ALL the time, isn t it ) Generally, it s written in a sort of care-free, what you see is what yu get sort of way, which I think is what we all need during our coffee breaks (save the hard hitting journalism for bedtime, LOL )So, if you wanna keep up on what s hot   what s not WITHOUT spending the best part of    5, you can t go wrong with a copy of Glamour      ', '    About time for a small magazine   Having seen this invention in France a couple of years back, I wondered when it would be our turn. Have a nice reading all  Hope you will enjoy it as much as I do      ', '    When Glamour first hit the shelves (with Kate Winslet on the cover) I loved it. It was small enough to fit into my bag, had a good fashion section with a nice mix of clothes I coveted but couldn t afford, and cheap versions I could try myself. It had the celebrities I loved and pretty great beauty writing. The only thing it lacked that I like to see was decent lifestyle features, but this was never a magazine that was big on journalism. There was the odd nod to relationships and sex, an interview or two, but all-in-all this is a glitter, glamour and shopping magazine for people who like to dip in and out without taxing their brains too much. Which is fine, to a point.However, there s only so long we can stare at pretty pictures of the same lipgloss we were being sold this time last year. Because I m a fashion journalism student, magazines are pretty much my textbooks, and I buy a LOT each month. I only have subscriptions to two, but I can safely say Glamour isn t one of them. Because of its jam-packed look, it s glossy fashion and beauty spreads, it s handy size and (most importantly) its cheap    1.80 cover price, (over    1 cheaper than most of its rivals) Glamour is the best selling women s mag on the British market. By about 200,000, in fact. It out-sells Cosmo by a huge majority.What pisses me off more than anything about Glamour though, is that the more popular it s gotten, the more advertising and advertorial (you know that  glamour promotion  crap when you realise every item on the page is from Dotty P s or New Look?) they ve sold. If it s not an advert anyway, every other page is sponsored by something or in association with something or promoting something. But there has to be a line drawn somewhere. s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
If you’re on the lookout for a magazine that’s both a breeze to carry and easy on the wallet, Glamour ticks those boxes nicely. Its compact A5 size means it slips effortlessly into your handbag—perfect for those moments when you want a quick, stylish read on the go without lugging around a bulky mag. Plus, at a price point lower than many competitors, Glamour offers solid value, especially if you’re considering a subscription. The deals often come with free gifts, which is a nice bonus, though fair warning: the delivery of those freebies can sometimes test your patience.

Content-wise, Glamour keeps things light and lively with short, digestible articles spanning fashion, beauty, celebrity gossip, relationships, and lifestyle. The fashion and beauty pages stand out with sharp photography and clear info, making it easy to spot trends or products worth trying. If you’re someone who enjoys a bit of variety without diving into heavy reads, this magazine’s mix hits the sweet spot. It’s entertaining and covers a broad spectrum—from real-life stories to advice—without feeling like a relentless ad fest.

On the interactive front, Glamour spices things up with regular competitions and reader discounts, which add a fun, engaging layer for readers who like a bit of participation beyond just flipping pages.

That said, if you’re craving in-depth features or investigative pieces, Glamour might feel a bit surface-level. It’s designed for quick consumption rather than deep dives, so it’s best suited for readers who want a stylish, practical, and affordable companion rather than a heavyweight cultural critique.

In sum, Glamour is a handy, budget-friendly choice for those who appreciate a well-photographed, varied, and entertaining read—just don’t expect it to replace your go-to serious fashion or lifestyle journals.

product_reviews: ['     For 20 years when it comes to television entertainment breakthrough s Sky Television has been at the forefront. Over the last 12 months Sky have been battling for a bigger control of the population, there biggest desire to become a what is known in the business as a triple play contender. But then late in 2006 Richard Branson stepped out of the shadows making himself a quad play contender, and with firm plans to take up another three services the battle between Virgin Media and Sky has just begun, but is the battle over before its begun for one contender?First things first, Virgin Media is the formation of two companies the first being Virgin Mobile, the second being NTL:Telewest. Over the past five years NTL and Telewest have both been in trouble, jobs were lost all over the country and the services for both suffered. Richard Branson was keen to get involved in the television business with the desire to end the monopoly Sky have across the nation. As we move ever closer to a digital television revolution, some people in pockets of the UK will be left without any television at all. Sky have the most solid solution being able to accommodate 99  of the population, but not everyone wants a Satellite dish on their house.  Virgin Media s aim is to try to get 100  availability across the UK by 2010 and the only way to do this is to ensure that they offer the best deals around.I had been a Telewest customer for a short amount of time when I heard that Virgin Media was taking over the service. I came to pick Telewest when we moved to our new home, we could only get abysmal television pictures through an external aerial. Like I always had before I contacted Sky who told me that I could have installation in just over a month. We were entering the time of year where you did not want to be without television so I made the move to contact Telewest who installed not only the digital television, but the telephone and internet too saving me    10 -    20 a month off separate Sky, BT, and AOL bills. I found the service pretty good, my bills to be pretty much bang on each month and a level of freedom I had not experienced with television before. Then in February Telewest passed over the reigns and Virgin Media took over.Virgin Media offer what initially seems to be a far limited package compared to Sky, but when you look a little further you find that the service far outweighs what Sky offers. In respect of standard television Virgin offers three packages Medium, Large, and Extra Large. Medium comes free providing you have the Telephone package.  This is basically Freeview television (39 channels) with the addition of some ON DEMAND services (explained later), and Sky One which you do not get with Freeview. For as long as cable television and telephony has been about this has always been a way into people homes  Free TV  sounds great. The next level is Large this gives you 83 channels and costs    11 per month highly noticeable additions are all the UK TV channels, Discovery Channel, Living and Eurosport. Finally there is the XL (extra Large) option giving you 129 channels, which includes full access to ON DEMAND services as well as the Disney Channels, FX, Zone Horror, and National Geographic. There are also a variety of options for film and sports channels at an additional cost.The lynchpin as I see it for Virgin over Sky is ON DEMAND, this option is split into two.1) Catch Up TV - This takes about 50 of the most popular channels each day (excluding ITV channels) and makes them available for you to watch at any time of the day and night for 7 days from the date of original screening. Whether it be an episode of Eastenders, Panorama, Shameless or the latest must have TV show of the moment its all stored up here for viewing later. This was a real gem recently when I arrived in work to hear about this great TV show called Five Days already on its third night, as is often the case I hear about these things as they are nearly finished. Thanks to ON DEMAND however I was able to see the previous two episodes as and when I wanted over the next few days2) ON DEMAND TV - This is the saviour in our house, and its about to become much bigger. This offers a selection of approximately 500 TV shows (many of which are multi part) that you can simply watch as and when you wish. You simply select the show you want to watch, enter your pin (if its before the 8pm watershed) and the show starts instantly minus any adverts that may have originally been there. Everything taste is catered for, whether you an action junkie wanting to watch Alias, to a comedy freak who loves Friends. Shows from across the world and across the decades are available for you to watch as and when you please. Last month we watched all three series of Channel Four s popular comedy show Peepshow.  We also watch a large amount of documentaries from over the years, there is a great one on at the moment about Sharks in Cornwall. But the other big plus for Virgin is their V+ service. This is pretty much identical to Sky s Sky + service but dramatically enhanced. All V+ boxes come High Definition ready where as Sky + boxes don t and Sky will charge you    300 for the privilege of getting HDTV. Also each box comes with 80 hours of recording space where as Sky+ boxes start with just 20 hours.Basically V+ allows you to record shows or movies on to your actual receiver box, there these shows will stay until your ready to watch them. You can either then record the programme to Video, or DVD or just watch and delete it. But the use does not end there if your watching live television and the phone rings or the door goes you can simply press pause until your ready to return to the programme, or of course you can just record it instantly. Where Virgin wins over Sky is that with Sky you can record two programmes on separate channels at the same time, however one of the two if you were sat at home you would have to watch. With Virgin you can record two different shows and watch a third.The quality of picture you receive on either standard TV, V+ or ON DEMAND services is excellent, the service does not have the same issues as Sky in respect to signal outages either. With Virgin the cables are underground so the weather will not influence the picture, unlike it often does with Sky. Neither do you need to call engineers to reposition your equipment when the wind has been strong.An important thing to point out as well is that the V+ equiptment is either free or costs a maximum of    10 per month to use. Where as Sky will make you pay for a box, and if you dont have an almost full package will charge you for their Sky+ services.This is a TV review but I feel it unfair not to briefly touch on the other services and in doing so explaining the quad play brilliance of Virgin.Telephone - A variety of packages from    11 (including line rental and free calls) to    40 per month with all inclusive call options. Where Virgin really pick up that BT do not is that on the    20-   40 packages each month the cost of a call to any overseas country is the same as a call to your neighbour, and you ll get a load of free calls thrown in to boot.Broadband - From    14.99 -    35 per month dependant on speed and requirements. Your Modem comes Free as does Internet Security. With the larger packages there are no limits to the amount of downloading unlike certain other providers. You ll also get 55MB of webspace to play with.Television - We have already discussed.Mobile - There are a variety of options here, but for me the best deal is a Sim card only option that will work in any existing mobile phone. This costs    10 per month and comes with 300 minutes of calls and 300 text messages, this is probably the cheapest deal around.Richard Branson s Virgin Media is now seeking approval to offer Gas, Electric and Water to its customers. This is going to be a big plus for users of Virgin Media because it means that they will be able to budget easier with one direct debit payment going out on a day selected by the customer each month. Also the added bonus that Virgin Media are claiming that they will be able to beat the current provider of the services when its available. With one service being approved the good news for non Virgin Media Customers is that by providing all services Virgin will be able to offer Television, Telephone, and Broadband to places that previously assumed they would never get them. For example Polperro in Cornwall that when the big switch over of television happens in 2010 otherwise would not get a thing.The future is looking  golden for Virgin who for the first time in history have actually been able to secure some channels and ON DEMAND services away from Sky. HBO for example looking to set up a TV presence in the UK will offer a fantastic range of 200 TV shows on demand through Virgin. Its not just HBO, other major players are all boarding Virgin s entertainment train Discovery Channel, Disney, Warner, and Showtime are all signing exclusive deals with Virgin. If you can I d strongly advise you to as well.  UPDATEAs of March 1st 2007 Sky pulled Sky One, Sky Sports News, And Sky News from the Virgin Network. As I see this its a temporary glitch as the massive price hike Sky are emposing on these channels is unrealistic; and pulling the channels from Virgin has cost Sky 60 million pounds. Virgin have promised Virgin Prime a channel to equal Sky One giving the viewer better shows. As well as increasing the ON DEMAND selection by over 100 additional slots by the end of March.      ', '       Formally Telewest and subsequently Telewest/NTL and now Virgin Media in whatever name they have attempted over the last decade or so to provided me with the services for which I signed up. ', '    When my partner and I made the leap to move in together we knew we needed to get some sort of internet connection and landline set up as we weren t fond of mobiles but very fond of the internet. If you’re weighing up Virgin Media for your entertainment and broadband needs, here’s the lowdown—served with a side of my usual cheeky honesty.

Virgin Media scores well on value with its competitive bundles combining TV, broadband, and phone. They sweeten the deal with special discounts—especially if you’re savvy enough to call and negotiate (yes, a little charm goes a long way). The V+ HD box is a neat bonus in higher packages, letting you pause and record live TV, which is a lifesaver when your favorite reality show hits a cliffhanger mid-dinner. Plus, their Video On Demand library is pretty solid, boasting HBO and Warner content, free for XL package users—perfect for binge-watchers craving quality drama and celeb gossip.

Broadband fans will appreciate Virgin’s fast, reliable service with no download caps, a rarity these days. Bills are clear and itemized, with perks like discounts for direct debit—no nasty surprises there.

But it’s not all roses. Virgin’s TV channel lineup can feel a bit stingy compared to Sky, especially after losing Sky channels during that contract spat (cue collective groan from fans). Although they’ve restored some Sky channels to higher packages, the catch-up TV service disappoints by missing popular channels like ITV and Channel Five. And if you’re a stickler for flawless tech, the V+ box can be a bit temperamental—program info sometimes vanishes, and installation isn’t always a walk in the park.

Customer service? It’s a mixed bag. Sometimes you get quick, helpful support (especially via their special internet/email lines), but other times you’re stuck on hold forever or dealing with overseas call centers where communication feels like a game of charades. Equipment returns and billing issues can add to the headache.

In short, Virgin Media offers decent bang for your buck with some clever perks and solid broadband, but be prepared for occasional channel frustrations and a customer service rollercoaster. If you like a bit of negotiation and patience, it can be a worthwhile ride. Otherwise, keep your remote handy—you might need it.

product_reviews: ['    Researching the market for selling my short stories, I recently bought a few magazines to see what the standard was like. One of these magazines was That s Life  which comes out weekly and is priced at 65p. This is one of several almost identical looking magazines aimed at women from around 20 to 60. Whilst being one of the cheapest, I m afraid the look of it suffers from the obvious cost-cutting measures they have employed, as the paper itself is low quality and feels almost greasy to the touch.The magazine is 48 pages long and seems very crowded, with photos and texts fighting for space and your eyes unsure as to what to focus on next. The cover itself is bright and cheerful but again full and this feeling of trying to cram in too much continues from start to finish. With a weekly magazine, I am sure it would be possible to de-clutter the pages somewhat. It looks like the editor is frightened of any unused space The magazine doesn t take long to read, maybe half an hour, so it is ideal for a doctor s waiting room or a quick tea break at work. If you want a more substantial read, you need a different magazine. Even when talking about serious issues like the true life stories, the magazine manages to give an impression of being lightweight and disposable.As you would expect from a woman s magazine, there are regular sections on beauty, fashion, the home, health and cooking. Whether I am unusual or whether the idea of what a woman is interested in is very wrong, I m not sure, but none of these subjects interest me much at all, except health, so I am unlikely to spend long on these particular features.At least with these kinds of magazines, things are reasonably priced and attainable. The fashion items in this issue (18 August 2005) are available in sizes 6 to 20, which covers a wide range of society (though sadly, I m a 22-24 ) and can be bought from stores such as Tesco, Next and Primark. The fashion here is practical and modern, without being outrageous or you needing to be stick-like to carry off the look. Similarly, the suggestions for beauty products, meals to cook and home improvement ideas are reasonably priced. You re not expected to be a designer brand snob if you read this magazine and everyday shops like Argos and John Lewis are used as examples of places to buy furnishings from, with make up products covering a slightly wider range but still only costing between    2 to    21 in this issue. The regular features include horoscopes, letters pages, an advice column and  rude jokes of the week  (where the rudest thing I saw was the word  arse  so it s hardly X-rated stuff ). But the main part of the magazine is devoted to true life stories submitted by the readers and a wide variety of prize puzzles to enter.The competitions include crosswords and word searches and you can enter all of them on the entry form printed in each issue, so it only costs you the price of one stamp. The prizes are good - holidays, shopping vouchers and generous amounts of cash. I was also quite impressed with the standard of the puzzles as they aren t too difficult, but they do make you think.The true stories are often sad ones, with this issue including a young girl who was badly burned in a petrol bomb attack and a woman whose husband was violent. They are written in the first person with colour photos to illustrate the article and they are written in a chatty, conversational style. I found them fairly interesting, but nothing more.If you have your own true tales to share, you can make some money from the magazine too. In fact, this must be where its entire budget goes to, as there seems to be a money-making opportunity on every page. They pay    500 for a true life story,    200 for your true secrets,    200 for a mini-feature true story and    250 for a health-related article. Even if you don t want to expose your innermost horrors to the nation, you can earn between    20 and    50 by having a letter published or contributing to the awfully named (and sexist)  Aren t Men Daft?  regular column. I found the fiction to be rather bland and far too easy a read. There is only one story per issue though, so it is easy to avoid if you would prefer something more challenging.Overall, the magazine passes a few minutes and you can make some money from it in various ways, but overall, I found it disappointing and insubstantial. But it s popular and has a wide readership, so it must be doing something right.      ', '    ***Intro - TRASH***Now s here s a review I didn t think I d find myself writing when I joined Ciao   Put quite simply,  that s life   magazine is TRASH.  It is NOT the sort of magazine I would buy (or at least admit to buying ) out of choice - and certainly not a magazine I would want to see myself appearing in.  I just want to clear that up before we go any further Trashiness aside, there does seem to be something about the human mind (at least for many women) which draws us to this trash if it happens to be lying around   ..or (in my case anyway, please tell me it s not just me, please?) makes me feel the need to read it over the shoulder of someone next to me on the train and get really frustrated when they cotton onto me and turn the page before I ve finished, and as a result I never get to find out whether Tracey s baby twins were Wayne s or Gary s   ..or one of each   I hope I m not offending any avid readers of the magazine   .even if you like the magazine (and I respect anyone who will admit that) I m 99  sure you ll agree that it is trash  *A note to readers*:If you are reading this review (as many if not most of you will be) purely to get an idea of what the magazine is like, rather than hearing my personal experience of featuring in it, I suggest you skip the next paragraph, read the background information, and then skip to the part where I give detailed information about an issue of the magazine.I would also like to apologise for the length of the review (this is becoming a bit of a theme for me).  However, in order to talk about my personal experiences AND give an adequate review of the magazine I felt it had to be this length.  I really hope that you do find it interesting and worthwhile to read.***So after that intro you might be wondering, why am I writing a review on this magazine?***  Well, my relationship with the magazine started in December when a fellow director of the self-injury charity (LifeSIGNS - www.lifesigns.org.uk) I m involved with forwarded me an e-mail from a researcher (we get a lot of media requests).  The researcher was looking for a woman between 25 and 44 to be in a magazine - at this point all we knew was that it was one of the magazines in the  Bella  group.  I would assume that most women in the UK will at least have heard of Bella - for the benefit of men, it is a weekly women s magazine.My fellow trustee Sarah appeared in  New Woman  magazine in January (a far more young and classy magazine I must say (not that I read that trash either) as Sarah is younger and much classier than myself). ', '    In Style is a magazine that I have repeatedly bought since it was first released. ', '    Match of the Day 2 takes a look at Sunday s football fixtures, and witty punditry from Adrian Chiles makes it much the superior to Match of the Day, shown on a Saturday.Sunday usually gets quite important games fixtured from the Premier League, and the fact that there are less games played on a Sunday lets a more detailed look be taken upon the events.There is also a look on all the goals of Saturday, with humurous moments from managers or fans being commentated by Adrian Chiles, which is worth the watch in itself.The punditry is a lot better than that of Match of the Day. If you’re after a light, budget-friendly read that’s perfect for killing time during hospital stays, long journeys, or just casual downtime, *That’s Life!* fits the bill—think of it as the cheeky, tabloid cousin of high-end women’s magazines. It covers a broad range of everyday topics like health, beauty, fashion, and cookery, but don’t expect deep dives; the articles are pretty surface-level and often feel a bit flashy or trashy, much like those guilty-pleasure reality TV shows we all secretly enjoy mocking.

On the plus side, the health pages stand out by offering genuinely useful advice on various issues, including men’s health, which adds a touch of substance amid the fluff. The cooking section delivers easy-to-follow recipes that change each issue, so it’s handy if you want simple meal ideas without the fuss. Puzzles are another highlight—numerous, varied, and engaging without being brain-busters, plus there are plenty of chances to win decent prizes like holidays or cash, which is a nice bonus for a magazine that won’t break the bank.

The magazine’s conversational, chatty style—especially in the true stories and letters pages—makes it an entertaining read, though the tales tend to be on the sadder side and sometimes veer into the bizarre. If you enjoy a bit of light-hearted humor, the “Aren’t Men Daft?” column and mild rude jokes add some cheeky fun. Plus, readers can submit their own stories, jokes, or photos and even get paid if published, which is a neat interactive touch.

However, don’t expect quality paper or sophisticated fiction; the pages feel thin and greasy, and the single fiction story per issue is bland and forgettable. Also, while the magazine has fewer adverts than some competitors, its overall vibe leans heavily into throwaway entertainment rather than meaningful content. So, if you’re after something substantial or thought-provoking, look elsewhere—but if you want a cheap, entertaining, and occasionally amusing read that’s perfect for group laughs or salon waiting rooms, *That’s Life!* delivers just that.
