Customer service is wonderful, the staff could not be more pleasant and helpful.3)After you have made six payments to your loan account, you can a repayment holiday of up to three months - a good option for over the Christmas period perhaps?4)You can make additional payments to your loan whenever you like - this can be done by bank transfer or cheque. ', '    Providian National Bank are an American company relatively new in the UK, but by no means naive when it comes to issuing credit cards. product_reviews: ['    The rather splendid Easter egg which I was presented with, was of the Nestle Smartie variety, and in being so it was therefore filled with two of the new funky shaped packets of  Smarties. It had been a while since my taste buds had been tingled by the small crispy beans of chocolate, and in fact it had been as equally long since I d even seen them around. The packaging although now of a hexagonal nature, was none too different from the one s I used to purchase some years ago. It did however have one added ingredient, a bold set of lettering declaring that the BLUE Smartie was back. I can vaguely recall it s disappearance some while back, but put little significance on it s return, but could see how certain children might well be pleased at it s re-introduction. One thing that does strike you straight away on seeing the packet of Smartie s is that Why did they never think of the Hexagon shape before            it makes so much sense when you consider how unstable the old packaging was when left on a perhaps uneven surface.          Well having now two packets of the sweets I could indulge a little more than perhaps I might have done, There is a very ingenious lid on one end of the hexagonal tube which once opened would appear to be so for good, but a clever little catch system enable it to be shut quite securely again. On opening it you can clearly see that the tube has a cardboard hexagon covering the end to stop the sweets from falling out. This hexagon has a semi-circular hole cut out from one of it s edges. The hole is just big enough for the smarty s to come through and prevents them ALL from falling out at once, which might be OK for some but I do like to have a decent few smarty s in my mouth at once so I was forced to tilt the packaging a few times until I had the desired amount of sweets in my hand.          It was here that memories came flooding back, the sweets apart from a slightly less bright colouring were the same as they have always been, small half inch beans of crispy coated chocolate. The colours although recognisable as red, yellow green etc did look a bit dull and less bright than I remembered, but I could just as easily be mistaken in this fact. Looks aside the small beans were of the same delicious quality as those of my memories. It did also seem that the crispy candy coating was just a fraction thicker than memory would have me believe. There is a different flavour to the different colours, but it s resemblance to anything has me baffled and amused at the same time. It is a quite sweet taste and is probably best described as fruity although as to which fruit I am once again baffled. The good news is that there are NO E numbers contained within these beans.          The chocolate is the usual high Nestle standard, which is unfortunate since Cadbury s chocolate would have made the beans so much more enjoyable, that is not to say they are not, they most certainly are. The contrast in textures between the crispy shell and the soft chocolate makes for a sweet strange experience which is one you will not get with make confections these days. As I understand it the Smartie s currently retail at around the 50p mark which I cannot vouch for since mine came with a rather tasty Easter Egg. If 50p is the going rate for a packet of these then by my reckoning they are indeed pretty good value for money. One of the nicest things I discovered is that is it so refreshing these days to find something that hasn t been tampered with, and is just as it has been for many a year. I m also going to join the kids here in welcoming back the blue Smartie whatever flavour it is supposed to be.     ', '    Over the years the tube to smarties have changed alot from being in a thin round tube with a lid and under the lid was a letter of the alphabet now it is in a thicker octangular tube and the lid with the alphabet letter has gone.The smarties tube is blue in colour with smarties printed all around and bubbly writing saying smarties. The smarties themselves come in different colours such as pink, blue, green and orange.The price of smarties have gone up over the years and are probably around 50p but they are a good tasting sweet chocolate coated with a shell.Smarties are great for kids as they can be kept in the tube and won t melt all over there hands and if you have more than one child you can share them out equally without too much fighting and arguing going on.     ', '    When I was little, I used to absolutely adore Smarties.  They were colourful and the sugar shells and chocolate tasted absolutely wonderful.  I used to have a lot of fun dividing them into groups of colours and then eating them colour by colour.  I then used to have hours of fun with the tube (taking the top on and off, popping out the bottom of the tube and looking through the tube, putting a little paper ball inside the tube and blowing it out to try to hit someone/thing, etc).I recently tried a Smartie when my friend offered me one.  Having not had a Smartie in a few years, I decided to have a try.  I put the Smartie in my mouth and I was absolutely disgusted by the way the sugar shell tasted.  The only thing I can compare it to was when you get perfume or hairspray in your mouth accidentally - it was horribly bitter.  I couldn t bear to keep it in my mouth.A few weeks after that event, I decided to buy a tube of Smarties for myself to see whether or not I just tasted one bad Smartie.  So I got my tube and ate a couple, which weren t bad - not as good as I remembered them, but still not too bad.  I then put another one in my mouth and found the same disgusting taste as the one from a few weeks before.  I figured then that it must be a colour-related thing and got my brother to try one of the same colour (I think it was purple or brown, but I can t remember, because they all seem to be a bit dull, colour-wise, now).  He also had to dispose of his because the taste was so foul.I am supposing that this all happened when they decided to take away artificial colour because it was (supposedly) making kids crazy.  Now, I simply don t believe that because I don t know of anyone, nor have I ever hear of anyone who went all crazy and hyper after eating Smarties when I was a child.But I honestly think that they ve taken the fun out of Smarties - some of the colours taste like they could poison you, all of the colours are less vibrant than in the past, the tube is not really a tube any more, and once you ve opened the pack it doesn t stay sealed very well because there isn t any actual lid - just a flap.     ', '    Everyone loves Smarties, don t they? They have been around for 78 years so there me something pretty great about them  I love Smarties, I used to like collecting the little plastic lids with letters on, when I was very young I used to get very excited when I came across an L (the first letter in my name ) lol. Unfortunately they have stopped producing Smarties in the thick cardboard tubes with plastic lids. They now produce them in hexagonal tubes with a plastic flip top lid. They have however, started printing a letter on the lid of the tube again. The letter is now part of a question, the answer of which can be found under the lid. Smarties come in red, green, pink, lilac, yellow, brown, orange and blue. They are around 1.5cm diameter and around 3mm thick. They are discs of milk chocolate with a crunchy, crisp sugar shell. They are also very yummy  They now contain no artificial colours or flavours and have 174 calories per tube so are not too bad for you and are suitable for children every now and again. If you like chocolate, you will love Smarties - buy them, buy them now  You can find them in most shops for between 35-55p or in packs of 5 for between    1 and    2, depending on where you shop.      ', '    **Originally posted on dooyoo in 2008**Nestle SmartiesIt had been ages since I had bought a tube of these Nestle Smarties so I thought I would try them out again as they used to be a firm favourite of mine. They cost a little more than they used to at nearly 50 pence for the tube inflation hits hard in the confectionary world. The tube seemed smaller than I remembered but still contained a fair few of these multi coloured discs. Which is what Smarties basically are. Small discs of chocolate covered in an outer crispy sugar coating dyed all different colours. If you hold the Smarties too long in your hand the colourful dye will tend to come off of the Smarties and onto your hand but I don t think I hold them long enough any more for this to happen. Again, like the size of the tube the Smarties inside the tube seemed slightly smaller than I remember but their bright colours still looked the same. On a taste test, however I was rather disappointed at how different I remembered them tasting. The Smarties tasted rather cheap and as though the chocolate was not real (you know the cheap fake sort of chocolate). I can honestly say I did not enjoy eating these Smarties at all (although I did still make myself eat the whole packet - they cost nearly 50p ). The outer sugar shell was rather nice to crunch through and had a slight Minstrel way about them but just because the chocolate tasted so cheap and awful I certainly will not be buying these Nestle Smarties again My taste buds must have matured within the last few years or else I have just eaten too much nice chocolate. I did give a couple to ~Jack though and he did not seem bothered by the cheap taste at all. In my view though these only deserve a 2 star rating. NOT RECOMENDED      ', '    I used to eat smarties all the time when I was younger  I don t eat them very often any more, but as I received a smarties easter egg for easter this year, I have got addicted to them  There are many ways you can buy smarties these days, when I was a kid you just got the usually tube with has lid on, but now you can get mini smarties, sharing bags of smarties, smarties in a box etc. You can even get smarties cake bars and ice creams now  They are in cookies too which I also love  These smarties are aimed at children obviously with all the bright colours. They have brown, green, orange, pink, red, yellow purple and blue coloured smarties. In case you didn t know, smarties are little counters of nestle milk chocolate, covered in an outer sugar shell, which are different colours. They are a bit like minstrels but with nestle chocolate and they are a lot smaller. I love making brownies, fairy cakes or muffins and crushing smarties up and throwing them in, they are gorgeous, or go great in home made cookies. We crush them up and put them on our ice cream too. Nestle have added no artificial colours of flavourings to these smarties. Per 100g of smarties there are 457 calories  So like any other chocolates they are not good for you, I can easily get through a sharing bag to myself  These are 150g so that s about 600 + calories I m consuming  They are gorgeous though and once you have one you just end up eating the whole lot, as they are so small you don t really realise how many your eating  I highly recommend these smarties by nestle, they are great for kids and adults too  Just beware of the calorie content in them       ', '    ~~~~~~~Smarties~~~~~~~Smarties are sugar coated chocolate sweets that come in 8 different colours - Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Lilac, Pink, Brown   Blue.  Personally as I m a girlie girl pink was always my favourite, and although all the Smarties taste the same, I used to stay away from  boy  colours like green and blue, which my mum was thankful for    The blue smarties used to contain a high amount of additives and used to send children into hyperactive mode, they were removed for a short amount of time, but have now returned and all the colours and now additive free.  307 tubes eaten per minute in the UK, proving they are very popular, and still ever as popular as they used to be.~~~~~~~~~~About Nestle~~~~~~~~~~Smarties are made by Nestle, famous for NESCAF    and Kit Kat which are the two main brands of the UK company, but this is not all they do, they have a huge variety of products they manufactor - Nestle is the second largest company in the UK s yogurt and fromage frais sector, with brands such as Ski and Munch Bunch. They also have Nestl    businesses of milks and creams, pasta, Herta and Maggi. Henri Nestl    was the man behind Nestle, originating in Switzerland but now has factories all over the world, thanks to its great popularity with its consumers.  The UK headquaters is situated in Croydon, Surrey, which I interestingly found out the other day when driving through East Croydon train station on a train to London, as it clearly displays it under the sign for East Croydon.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Invention of the Hexatube~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~The famous Smarties tube has been given a contemporary new look with the launch of the six sided Hexatube. This is the first ever change to the traditional Smarties tube since the product hit the shops 67 years ago.  Hexatube has now been available in the shops since 2005.Nestle recognise that the round Smarties tube was an icon in packaging design and has had an array of fun uses for generations. Along with washing up bottles, baking foil and egg cartons, the Smarties tube has always been an essential part of every kid s DIY modeling kit, used to create all manner of things from space rockets to castles - a true Blue Peter essential  They now think that, with the development of the Hexatube, a new chapter has begun for Smarties and along with it a whole new range of possibilities for the tube. I just can t quite see this, children don t get as excited as they used to over little things like a cardboard tube.  They have bigger, better and more expensive things so why would they want a cardboard box, that they could just throw in the bin   I m not sure about Nestles theory on this, but only time will tell, we will just have to see The packaging of the Hexatube is the colouring to the original packaging which contains a dark blue background with smarties erupting everywhere, like a Smartie volcanic eruption and the word Smarties largely and clearly written over this eruption in white with a chocolate brown outline.   The packaging is bright and stands out and is clear to see.  It stands out from other brands, with it s multicoloured Smarties.One thing I do miss about the old cylindrical tube was the plastic coloured lid has gone, it is now purely a 6 sided  Hexagon  cardboard tube which does up at the ends.  I can t see this been quite as secure as the plastic lid though, especially been carried around by excitable children   Although I did used to squeeze the tube for the plastic lid to pop out and hit my friends, maybe a reason for them changing it   The plastic coloured lid used to have letters on, and me and my friends used to collect them to spell out our names, it was just another little novelty of the product when you were younger   The  lid  on the Hexatube, instead of having the novelty coloured letter, now contains stickers, images or quirky phrases.  I suppose this is a lot more exciting to a child these days, but for us adults still eating Smarties, a plastic lid with a letter satisfied us more than enough   The tube is also now bigger, although it is now recycable, it just doesn t quite have the same feel, memories and fun as the original one. At least you can still do the same things you used to with the Smarties, spelling out words with the colours, eating them colour by colour or picking out the ones you don t like and kindly giving them to your parents   Although the tube appears larger, it still only contains the same amount of Smarties as the previous tube - 48, which is a reasonable amount for the price.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Who are they suitable for?~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 84 per cent of SMARTIES packs are bought by adults on behalf of children,  according to Nestle.  Smarties are suitable for both children and adults, but I think now due to their change in tube, they won t be quite as popular with adults as they were, the old tube was a reminder of their childhood and brough great memories, now it seems like it is just a new product, even though Smarties have the same look and taste, without the packaging it just doesn t seem the same.  I don t think this will change children s opinions, it is just now good to know that they don t contain any artificial colourings now, so you can safely give them to your children without the worry of them turning hyperactive ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Taste, Texture   Smell~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Smarties are small milk chocolate discs, covered in a brightly-coloured crisp sugar shell. Smarties are by far the best tasting sugar coated chocolate sweets available, some supermarkets sell their own brand versions, but they just taste plain and a bit too sugary   So it is good to know that there is no change in flavour or even the colouring from the old full of artificial colourings Smarties, they are just the same as they always were, just alot better for you and now not able to send your childen crazy from all the E numbers  I find all the colours taste the same, but this is not everyones opinion, although I do find some of them for example the deeper colours do taste a bit stronger  Orange Smarties are special in that they contain orange-flavoured chocolate but I don t really find I can taste a difference in this to the other colours. In appearance they are a more colourful yet flatter version of an M M, but have a completely different inside, only pure chocolate.  They are easy to eat, you can crunch them, chew them or suck them to get the sugar coated layer off them enjoy the chocolate. The shell crunches in your mouth, then the chocolate melts satisfyingly leaving you with a warm, smooth sensation in your mouth.  The chocolate is tasty, it is not too creamy, nor is it too bitter.  The only aroma I get is a chocolately smell, but not really anything significant that stands out.  If you have too many Smarties though, I do tend to find they start to get a bit much a due to the sugar content can make you feel a bit sick and start to feel them at the back of your throat.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Free from Artificial Colouring~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~In June 2006 Smarties become free from artificial colourings.  This came around due to consumer wants for healthier lifestyles, it also makes the product alot more suitable for children, as it will no longer make your childen hyperactive.  In the first year since Smarties become free from artificial colours sales increased by 9 , proving that this descision was a wise one.The  no artificial colours  message is featured widely on packs, and special displays will be mounted in-store to make sure that parents are well informed of the choices available to them.~~~~~~~~~~~Blue Is Back ~~~~~~~~~~~Many people seem to be confused on this and do not think that Smarties any longer contain that overly artificial filled blue colour, but luckily they are wrong  The blue was removed several years ago, due to its content of way too many E numbers, but recently, and since Nestles change to all its Smarties being free from artificial colours due to popular demand the ever loved blue Smartie has returned and like all the other colours, it is also free from artificial colours as the colouring is now taken from a natural substitute from the seaweed Spirulina so now you can enjoy as many blue smarties as you want ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Nutritional Information~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~For a 38g standard Hexatube of Smarties - Calories - 174 kcal Protein 1.6g Carbohydrate - 26.9gof which:sugars 24.8gFat - 6.5gof which:saturates 3.7gFibre 1.0g Sodium 0.0228g Salt Equivalent 0.057g175 calories are 10  of a child between 5 and 10 year old s Daily Recommended Allowance of Calorie intake.  It is over 60  of the sugar and 25  of the fat Daily Recommended Allowance.  10  of the calories doesn t seem extortionate, but when you look at how much   of the daily allowance of carbs and fat are taken up by one tube of Smarties, it is quite worrying. Although this is a fair amount, it is to be expected from a product such as Smarties, you can t expect  sugar coated chocolate  to have little fat and sugars in   I wouldn t recommend letting your child have too much of these, just as an occasional treat.For adults the Daily Allowance is different, for a woman 174 calories is under 10  of their Daily Allowance, sugar content it is about 25  and the fat content is under 10 .  For a man, it would be even less than this.  When you look at it for an adult compared to for a child, it seems that the product is much more suited to adults.~~~~~~~~~~Ingredients~~~~~~~~~~For those that like to know what they re eating, here s a list of ingredients:Milk chocolate (58 ), Sugar, Wheat flour, Modified starch, Flavouring, Glazing agent (carnauba wax).  They used to contain many E numbers but these have now been removed.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Other Smarties Products~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Smarties Hexatube - single and 4 packSmarties CartonSmarties Mini CartonsSmarties Hanging Bags~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Price   Availability~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Smarties Hexatube can be purchased for 36p as a single and as a 4 pack for    1.31.  In a single tube you 48 smarties.  Hexatube is the cheapest pack of Smarties you can purchase.  Both single and 4 packs can be purchased from a wide variety of stores, such as supermarkets including Tesco, Sainsbury s (where I purchased mine from), Asda, Morrisions, they can also be purchased from stores like Woolworths and WHSmiths and also petrol and service stations.  Majority of stores that supply a range of chocolate bars will stock this, so it is not hard to find.~~~~~~~~~~Contact Info.~~~~~~~~~~NestlePOBOX 203, York England. YO9 1XY 0800 63785385 www.smarties.co.uk~~~~~~~~~~Conclusion~~~~~~~~~~Still a popular choice of sweet/chocolate for both adults and children.  Hexatube is a reasonable price to pay, and the quality of the Smarties are still the same, just without artifical colours, making them more suitable for children.  The only downer is the new packaging, but as I said I don t think this would matter to children      ', '    Milk chocolate in a crisp sugar shell - This about sums up what smarties are, but now they are good for kids?  This is such a well know chocolate that I will not bore you with the history of the company, just get straight onto my opinions of the sweets Smarties are now made with no artificial colours or flavours so shouldn t make children hyperactive.  I do know quite a few people who had problems when they used to give their kids smarties, and to be honest I am not sure if the new recipe has made any difference, although in theory it should Due to the change in ingredients the colours are a lot less vibrant than they used to be, and for a very long time blue smarties completely disappeared as they could not find natural colourings to make blue.  This Easter they are very pleased to announce that  Blue is Back , but this time as a very pale duck egg blue.I must admit that I am not a big fan of smarties and as far as I can tell from what I remember them being like as a child, they taste the same as they did when they were full of artificial goodness My kids do however love these, and Grandma is well known for keeping a constant supply of these.  Now that the tubes no longer have the plastic caps that you could shoot off by squeezing the tube I find that I feel more confident giving them to my kids knowing that there are no accidents waiting to happen  (If you exclude the younger one stealing all the sweets and the older one pinching him for his troubles )Sometimes the colours do come off onto the hands of my kids, but luckily the chocolate is contained within the shell so at least there is very little chocolate to smear everywhere The new style tubes as previously mentioned are not as much fun, but safer  The all cardboard design does seem to work well with the lid closing better than I expected, if the packs get really squashed they will not close, but then neither did the old style   Also it means that packaging is 100  recyclable.At around 40p per 38g tube I think that they are good value for money, knowing that there are no hidden additives does make me feel better about giving them to my kids, and 174 kcal per tube isn t too bad either      ', '    Just bought one of the new hexagonal shaped packs of Smartie, they call it a hexatube. It was 39p in Morrisons but may be available for less elsewhere.Opening it I found more difficult that the origianl type that had a plastic top. With those you could squeeze the tube and it would just pop off. I remember having fun seeing how far you could pop it. There is also no letter on the new type tops like the old ones.The tube is made of a thin cardboard and you open it along the perforations. Once opened it folds back on a hinge and reseals but not as well as the original. Upon opening you discover the open package has a restriction in, so when you try to pour the smarties out you only normally manage to get one out at a time. I remember with the old ones you could pour the contents out very easily.My tube is emblazoned with the words blue is back and it also says no artificial colours or flavours. They still taste the same but the colours are more subdued. The crisp shell cracks as you bite into them to get at the tasty chocolate contents.I have emptied the tube and the contents are 33 Smarties in total meaning a cost of over 1p each. Still not expensive but i wpould have liked there to have been 39 in total. The tube being all cardboard now means it is easier to recycle.The breakdown of colours of the 33 is as follows,6 Blue5 Brown6 Green6 Pink5 Yellow1 Red1 Orange 3 Purple.The subdued colours mean that any children eating them are less likely to get hyperactive from any E numbers.If you eat a whole tube you will obtain 174 calories. The pack gives the nutritional information for 100 grams of product but the tube doesnt appear to have a weight on.I thoroughly recommend the product but dont eat too many of them, i still prefer the old style tube but the new tube doesnt stop me eating them.     ', '    Ok, so I have finally bitten the bullet and decided to have a go at the product of the week, mind you this is the first POTW that I have actually fancied writing about The product (in case you have had your head in the sand ), is the new and may I add improved hexagonal tube of Smarties.The first thing I wish to say is I may be one of a very small majority that really appreciates the new design. Not so much the fact that the tube is hexagonal, in truth I could care less about the shape of the tube, admittedly it is aesthetically pleasing to the eye, but I am more pleased with the now lack of plastic lid.Ok I will elaborate. As a child, well I was 12 years old at the time I had the misfortune of viewing a casualty of these somewhat dangerous lids.I will never get out of my mind the sight of one of the older girls in my school being rushed into the back of an ambulance chocking on one of these unassuming pieces of plastic, so anyone that dislikes the new cardboard flip lid on these tubes, tough   I would rather see my children struggle to open the tubes than watch them choke to death   (The older girl by the way was alright, but unfortunately at about the same time another child in England did die from inhaling one of the lids, hence the reason they were then banned from my school).So now onto another improvement I wish to mention, the reduction of additives and colourings. Again back to my childhood there were two sorts of sweets that were categorically banned for children by parents, these were    of course Smarties and Opal fruits.Both contained an incredible amount of E numbers and were proven to increase hyper activity in children, the one thing I (as a parent of  two young children), worry about.So in  2006 Nestle (the makers of  Smarties ), decided to remove all artificial colourings. According to them after all the years we have been eating them, they were only now concerned of the effects of the chemical dyes used, on children s health, oh well better late than never I suppose  Unfortunately the only colour they couldn t source was the blue, so took it out and replaced it with the white ones, which were later removed from the range.Then in 2008 (NOW ),  a natural dye was found to  bring back blue  , the colour is now derived from a type of seaweed called spirulina.Can I also mention, that out of the remaining 7 colours,( red, orange, yellow, green, mauve, pink and brown), only mauves natural dye is mentioned, due to the fact it is made from cochineal, which I was unaware is a derivative from the cochineal insect, (yuk  ), making Smarties neither suitable for vegetarians or kosher.NOW FINALLY         . Now I have got that off my chest may I say that even after all of that, I still enjoy them as much as I did as a child, admittedly with a few less side effects   The extreme sweetness as you shove a handful into your mouth, never one at a time, not anywhere near ladylike enough for that  The delectable crunch and grittyness of the sugar shell, as you wait for the chocolate hit. Then the soft, smooth taste of chocolate making all your taste buds stand to attention      .. Thanks anyway      ', '    Easter has come and gone but my house is still dominated by brightly coloured boxes containing shiny foil wrapped eggs, we ended up with a staggering 17 eggs this year not to mention all the sweets and extra s on top of all that, now many Ciao members will know I have 2 young children, Elsa is almost 2 and Christopher is almost 4, so alongside a stack of Cadbury Buttons eggs stood an equal stack of Smarties eggs. s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
Nestlé Smarties Hexatube offers a colorful blast of nostalgia with its small, sugar-coated milk chocolate discs that delight both kids and adults alike. The classic crisp shell cracks satisfyingly to reveal smooth, sweet chocolate—though, fun fact, the orange Smarties sneak in a subtle citrus twist, while the rest keep to the familiar chocolate flavor. This sensory experience remains largely unchanged, preserving the joyful treat many grew up loving.

The packaging has undergone a notable makeover: the new hexagonal cardboard tube is sturdier and fully recyclable, a definite win for eco-conscious snackers. However, this flip lid isn’t as secure or easy to open as the old plastic lids, which many—including myself—fondly remember for their collectibility and playful reuse in games. It’s a bit of a trade-off between sustainability and that tactile, nostalgic charm.

Health-wise, Smarties have stepped up by ditching artificial colors and E numbers, making them a smarter choice for children prone to hyperactivity. The blue Smartie’s comeback, now colored naturally with spirulina, has been warmly welcomed, though the overall hues are more muted than the vibrant shades of yesteryear. Still, this shift aligns well with a growing preference for cleaner ingredients, even if it means the colors aren’t quite as eye-popping.

Of course, these treats are still high in sugar and fat—packing around 174-184 calories per tube—so they’re best enjoyed as an occasional indulgence rather than a daily snack. For those who cherish the playful rituals of sorting colors or savoring favorites first, Smarties remain a fun, nostalgic delight, balancing tradition with thoughtful updates in health and sustainability.

product_reviews: ['      Give us a twirl.Its Friday night just finished a busy week at work. My friend and I tired, worn out frazzled by the kids went to tesco   s for our shopping.   Standing by the till wilting, I spot the chocolate. Tempted I cautiously picked up a twirl and put it in the shopping trolley.I paid for the shopping the twirl cost 38p I think or there abouts. I got in my friends car to go home. I could wait no longer I had to have it and now. I opened the bright Cadbury blue wrapper with twirl emblazoned in yellow across the pkt .the foil paper tore easily to reveal 2 fingers of chocolate I offered on to my friend and I bit into mine. I bit through the chocolate coating into a crumbly flake of chocolate. In fact it is a flake dipped in chocolate I think. Mmmmmm the taste was divine smooth creamy chocolaty. It gave me that buzz I needed, I bit again I savoured the taste then bit again hungry now for more I demolished the last small bite savouring the chocolaty sensation. Although I would have liked more the one finger was just enough to satisfy me.Still feeling work weary we arrived at my home where we went it for a remedy of a cup of tea. Refreshed I sat down and read the wrapper The 1 finger I had just consumed contained 115 k cal     6.6 g fat. 12.3g carbohydrates. 1.8g proteins. But I really did want/ need that chocolate. Maybe I should have resisted I will admit it I no longer have the slim body of my younger days, its not grossly podgy but will become so if I succumb to my chocolate cravings.Thanks for reading best wishes Mary     ', '    I ve always liked Cadbury as a chocolate brand, and am particularly found of one of their bars that s been around for a while now, but still seems to be as popular as ever. How can I verify this..............well since I m a vending supervisor and am responsible for 87 machines I think I can judge by my sales whether or not a product is popular or not. Twirl is by no means the most popular bar but in my job it certainly rates as one of the top five along with Mars bars and Kit Kats.The blue packaging with the bold yellow Twirl logo printed across it s front, is perhaps not the most impressive wrapping I ve came across, but it is eye-catching in it s own right. Wrappings however are superficial it is the contents within that shall determine whether your confection is going to withstand the test of time. So many only last a short while and are never seen again.Twirls are pure Cadbury chocolate created in a similar mould to that of a flake but with less flakiness. Like several twirls of chocolate twirled together and then covered in more delicious chocolate. There are two such fingers in each pack and they retail at around the 55p mark. Each finger is just over 5 inches in length and about half an inch in diameter being a kind of irregular circular shape. So there is a substantial amount of chocolate here for those who like me enjoying a choccy hit mid morning or afternoon or better still both.The first bite tells the whole tale and sets the trend for the rest of the eating experience, smooth yet sort of crumbly sweet and delicious chocolate breaking into ting pieces on your tongue and teasing those little taste buds. The fact that it breaks into small parts merely increases the pleasure since they all melt simultaneously sparking an explosion of chocolatiness that is pure heaven.Easily worth the purchase price and well worth trying if you have never had one before. Once tried I think you will like me find yourself returning to sample this delight on numerous occasions.     ', '       Only the crumbliest, flakiest chocolate, tastes like chocolate never tasted beforrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrre     All right, that was how the Cadburys Flake used to be advertised and indeed it had a monopoly on the whipped up crumbly chocolate bar for a long while. That is, until some genius decided to take a successful idea and make it better.The first difference that people with an IQ above 3 will notice is that there are two sticks instead of one. This is great, as anyone with a partner will appreciate. Many a time I would trudge around to the shops, having first asked my beloved if she wanted me to get her anything while I was there. I was always met with a definite    no    and like a fool I always fell for this trick. Having made the trek through wind and rain I would open the front door, clutching my Flake knowing that I had earned my reward. Thirty seconds later, my wonderful partner would ask for a    taste    and promptly eat it all, cleverly mimicking the Flake girls on television to distract me from the fact that she was eating all my chocolate. So, the first improvement over    ye olde Cadbury   s Flake   , two sticks of chocolate, one for you and one for your fat bloater of a partner The second benefit the Twirl has over it   s rival, is of course the fact that it is covered in a layer of chocolate. Many a time I would sit in my car and munch on a flake (only place I could hide it from my girlfriend ). Crumbly chocolate is great but unless you are prone to wearing a bib it gets everywhere (and let   s face it not many adults use one, I did say most  What you get up to in your own home is your business ). No matter how careful you are, chocolate crumbs always manage to fall on to your seat. This in turn leads to the chocolate melting on to the back of your trousers and ultimately accusing stares from passers by when you exit your vehicle. So, benefit number two is that the Twirl is coated in chocolate preventing the flakes from spilling everywhere. It therefore saves on embarrassment and a stained bottom   Last but by no means least it tastes better  For some reason, many a flake bar seems to taste just that little bit stale. Gorgeous yummy Twirls taste fresh at all times So having compared the two bars, what does the Twirl bar taste like? Well, as you sink your teeth in to a Twirl bar there is a light crunch as you bite through the outer coating of chocolate. Slowly you sink your teeth through gorgeous ripples of flaky chocolate that crumbles and melts away in your mouth in to a sweet chocolaty goo paste. The chocolate tastes creamier than the average Cadbury   s chocolate bar and has that taste that makes you want to keep eating it until it   s finished and then get another one  (Special warning, even though it makes you want to eat more bars, DO NOT EAT MORE THAN 12 bars on the trot as this can lead to repeat vomiting of a very nasty colour  (Yes I have tried it and as they say, never again ))The closest comparison and leading competitor against to Twirl is the Galaxy Ripple. This to me is far superior to even the great Twirl bar. Being Sweeter and smoother, it tastes great. However, the mad fools only provide you with one stick, like the humble flake so The Twirl just has to win on amount more than anything else Packaging, blue with yellow writing and that   s all I have to say about that .     ', '    On a recent trip to B+M I decided I was going to get my self a large stash of of chocolate bars, including: Fudges (6 of), Curly Wurly s (5 of), Daim (4 of), Twirls (7 of), all for less than    5, which lets be honest, was wonderfully brilliant, gotta love the budget stores in this time of financial hardhsip.This review in particular is for the Twirl s, that was 5 multipack bars with 2 free (so 7 bars), each is double fingered but shorter than the normal twirls (I think...or at least hope, as these look tiny).Although they aren t particularly cheap when bought singularly, the multi-pack options as always is considerably cheaper, in fact, I think there were about    1.49, they were certainly not much than that anyway. Which means about 21.2ish P each. a bargain for a chocolate bar in this day and age. In fact about 10.5P a finger, it s no wonder that there wasn t many left on the shelf.The bar was first released in the 1970 s in just Ireland as a single bar similar in size to the flake before becoming a two fingered bar in the 1980 s and being released to mainland UK in the 1990 s. The bar is made by Cadbury s who personally I feel make better chocolate than the Mars owned Galaxay, which do a similar bar called the Galaxy Ripple. Though saying that, lets actually get on to the bar, which for those familiar with Flakes will be considerably familiar, just, less messy. The bar comes in a purple foil wrapper with large yellow print    Twirl    and the Cadbury logo.The Twirl is for all purposes, a flake with a solid chocolate cover, which, in turn keeps the flakey bits inside and stops the regular waste of chocolate that we all know happens with the wonderful flakes. The almost legendary well known Cadbury taste is at the forefront when you put one of the fingers inside your mouth, long before you bite into the thin chocolate coat and notice the two tone texture, of solid chocolate and chocolate flake. If your like me and just want to shovel it down you gullet, you may miss some of the intricate details of the bar, the fact that the flake effectively melts in your mouth after breaking up when you break the coating in your mouth seemingly giving an even sweeter and more pleasing taste. The immediate comparisons to flake are obvious, yet despite the similarities the bars are different, the solid coating gives the bar a tougher feel, a more wonderful taste to be honest, the two different chocolate consistencies work brilliantly together to  give your mouth a sensation of taste that s just brilliant.Now some will prefer the Ripple, it does appear to be better, personally I d rather have a Cadbury s rather than a Galaxy s bar, but I know some folk are different. So the taste is a personal thing, in regards to the chocolate type, the Galaxy bar seems to be softer in the mouth than the Cadbury, so this takes a little something away from the bar.The ingredients are very simple:MilkSugarCocoa ButterCocoa MassVegetable FatEmulsifier and FlavouringsThe 180 Calories per 2 finger pack is 180, which is quite excessive, but the bar is nice enough to deserve having as a treat every so often. About 3 inches long by     an inch or so across and a lil bit shorter, so for those that like a filling bar, you won t really enjoy this fully, as it s a little on the short side, not like a filling Snickers, or Yorkie. A tip for eating these is to NOT put them in the refrigerator, as the chocolate    flake    becomes more solid and the bar seems to lose a lot of its appeal. A better alternative is to leave them in a cool room, where the bar maintains it s uniqueness in it s multi-textured character. A bar that despite being different and tasting nice, seems a little bit small and is a bit flawed in a    there s something different here, but I don t know what    type thing. The bars immediate rival is worth a try, but I feel the Galaxy chocolate is just a little bit too rich to eat much of.     ', '    Cadbury Twirl: Being my Second Favourite chocolate bar in the world I thought I would have a go at reviewing it.The Cadburys twirl is all chocolate no biscuits or wafers    just chocolate (which is a good thing)So just 2 plain milk chocolate fingers 43g of nice mouth watering chocolate. It should cost around 50p or less (I don t really take much notice I just want the chocolate)     ', '    *** this review first appeared on dooyoo.co.uk ***The Cadbury Twirl is Cadburys best shot at beating the Gaaxy Ripple. Basically, the Twirl is a Flake which has been covered with smooth milk chocolate. In every packet there are 2 fingers, I suppose this is probably the best way of doing it as one long bar tends to be to big. The Twirl has been out for quite a few years now, and it has always remained one of Cadburys best products. Well, in my opinion. Taste There is literally nothing to fault the Twirl with on the taste front. The only problem I had with the Flake was that it is too crumbly and the chocolate was to dense. With the Twirl, both of these problems have been resolved. Now there is a smooth layer of chocolate over the flaky centre. Personally, I think its the inner part of the Twirl that makes it so good. This part is quite soft and melts very easily, since the chocolate melts in your mouth. You get a much better taste off of it. So the Twirl is exceptionally good on the taste side of things. Again, typical of Cadburys, the actual item itself isn t made bigger but instead they are sold in multipacks. These multipacks will cost around    1.80 for 5. I think this is quite a good deal, as you are effectively getting more than one bar free. So to round the review up, I personally strongly recommend the Cadbury Twirl. Its far better than normal chocolate and it tastes fantastic.      ', '    In my constant quest to review as many different Chocolate Bars and Sweets that I can possibly lay my hands on today I return not only to another of my favourite Chocolate Bars but also to yet another product from Cadbury s, today it is the turn of the Twirl.THE PRODUCTCadbury s launched their Twirls back in 1987 and since that time this brand as established itself as a popular product, albeit it is outside the companies list of leading brands, but it has always been up there with sales that have remained constant.They are usually sold singly in a 43g Bar which costs around 42p, but they are also available in multi-packs of four which I have seen in Asda for    1.09.THE PACKAGINGTwirls come in a shiny, metallic looking wrapper which is predominantly purple in colour. The word  twirl  is written across the front of the packet in large yellow letters so it stands out amongst the other confectionaries on the shelf.APPEARANCE   TASTEOn tearing open the wrapper you are greeted with the sweet smell of the Milk Chocolate which is nice and pleasant and reassures you that this Bar is of the usual Cadbury s standard, but lets face it I haven t bought this to sit and sniff at it all night.The product inside consists of two individual fingers of Chocolate which at around five inches long I consider to be a reasonable size. The Milk Chocolate coating on each finger is the rich brown colour that I always associate with Milk Chocolate and it has a textured, rippled effect.Biting into one of the pieces the initial taste is of the Milk Chocolate and the taste is very rich and creamy. I would describe the taste as being similar to that of a Cadbury s Flake, which is about the purest, finest Chocolate that you can buy. The texture is nice and soft and quite gentle on the teeth which is a bit of a rarity these days, and the Chocolate melts quickly in your mouth.If you look at the side profile of the finger once you have bitten into it you will notice that the inside of the Bar comprises of lots of thin layers of Chocolate folded over on top of each other. This clever layering of the Chocolate is not unlike that of a Cadbury s Flake and leads to a lighter taste than you tend to experience with most other Chocolate Bars.Overall I find the taste of Twirl to be very nice but it is a little bit rich and I do sometimes find that it can also be a lit bit sickly. If you like the taste of Cadbury s Flake then the chances are that you will love these too and they are nowhere near as crumbly or as messy.THE NUTRITIONAL INFORMATIONEach finger contains 115 calories which doesn t sound too drastic but let s face it you re going to eat two of these aren t you so you will have to double this. ', '    Imagine, if you will, some future world devoid of cocoa trees. Imagine an archaeologist picking over a landfill site and uncovering a sweet wrapper or two. ', '    1987 is not a year that I remember a whole lot about, I was too young at the time to remember much.  However it was a year with some significance in the confectionary world. Lastly you can find mini-Twirls inside boxes of Cadbury Heroes.I have to say that I have always admired the Twirl   s wrapper.  For such a new chocolate bar the wrapper is really quite classy. Along the side of the wrapper is the phrase    The intense chocolate hit   .  The word    intense    is red as is the word    hit    the other words are white. The outer coating of chocolate also gives a slightly more intense chocolate taste than that of the folded centre.Overall I rather enjoyed my Twirl, it is a very, very nice chocolate bar.  I would recommend it to anyone who likes Cadbury   s chocolate but in particular fans of the Flake may quite enjoy it when they fancy something more substantial or less messy than a Flake. s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
If you’re on the hunt for a chocolate that’s both a treat and a tiny mystery wrapped in shiny purple, Cadbury Twirl might just tickle your taste buds—and your curiosity. Picture this: two slender fingers of crumbly, flake-like chocolate center, cloaked in a smooth, creamy milk chocolate jacket that melts luxuriously in your mouth. It’s like a chocolate hug that’s less messy than its flaky cousin, the Cadbury Flake, making it perfect for those on-the-go moments when you want indulgence without the chocolate dust explosion.

Now, here’s where it gets interesting—some folks swear Twirl has a secret ingredient giving it a distinctive tang, a little “je ne sais quoi” that elevates its flavor beyond your average bar. Whether that’s true or just chocolate folklore, the taste is undeniably rich and sweet, so much so that one finger can satisfy a serious chocolate craving. But beware: it’s a high-calorie delight (115 calories and 6.6g fat per finger), and eating too many might leave you feeling a bit overwhelmed by its sugary richness. Think of it as a special occasion treat rather than your daily snack buddy.

The packaging deserves a shout-out too—its shiny purple wrapper with bold yellow lettering is eye-catching and screams “pick me up!” on the shelf. Plus, Twirl is suitable for vegetarians, though it does contain E numbers and flavorings, so if you’re ingredient-conscious, that’s worth noting.

Value-wise, Twirl often comes in multipacks or on special offer, making it a wallet-friendly indulgence. Just a heads-up: the chocolate melts quickly in your hands, so eat promptly unless you want a sticky situation. And if you’re like me, saving the second finger for later is a heroic challenge—Twirl’s moreish nature makes it hard to resist devouring both in one go.

In short, Cadbury Twirl is a playful, rich, and convenient chocolate treat that balances indulgence with practicality—perfect for those moments when you want a little luxury without the mess. Just don’t say I didn’t warn you about its addictive charm!

product_reviews: ['    First of all a coffee time quiz:(All answers can be found in the review)(Do not go to the end and look at the answers - that s cheating  )1 - What company is Nescafe part of?2 - What decade was Nescafe born?3 - How many species of coffee are there?4 - Can you name the two most commercial beans?5 - How many cups of Nescafe are drunk every minute in Britain?``````````````````````I never used to like drinking coffee, but after I had my son Toby, I found myself drinking the odd cup at friends houses, and now I regularly drink one with my breakfast and another mid morning, I don t feel I can get through the day without them. I ve always liked the smell of coffee, but was happier drinking fruit juices or water. Since drinking it I have spent a bit of time trying different brands and types, I have also learnt loads about where it came from, and felt that whilst I have a cup in front of me, I would tell you what I have found out, and let you all know which has become my favourite jar I reach for, when I want a cup.Why NESCAF   ? ``````````````````````My husband always drinks Nescafe Gold Blend coffee, which I must say I do like, but I felt that I wanted to try other varieties, so went to the supermarket and found their own brand, Kenco, Douwe Egberts and a huge range from Nescafe. I avoided the supermarket brand, as I wanted a bit of quality, and tried the standard Kenco and Douwe Egberts, but was not overly keen on the taste, one I found to be quite bitter, but cannot remember now which one it was. I tried my husbands Nescafe and was happy with the taste, providing I made it wit the right amount of milk. There was another problem though; I now found that I couldn t sleep at night, so I need to reduce the amount of caffeine in my diet, I found that Nescafe made a Gold Blend Decaff coffee, I bought a small jar, tried it, and liked it. I still drink a couple of cups a day, and now sleep well at night. NESCAF    - The Beginning ```````````````````````````````NESCAF    has been traced back to the 1930 s, when the Brazilian government challenged Nestl    to create a drink that could be made simply by mixing water to coffee beans, but which retained the coffee s natural flavours. After seven years of development by a coffee guru Max Morgenthaler and his Swiss research team, NESCAF    was born and the breakthrough was introduced to the world on April 1st 1938. During World War II, it became the staple drink of the United States armed forces and, from then on, its popularity really took off. In 1941 the entire production of NESCAF    s US plant, about a million cases a year, was reserved solely for the boys in uniform. By the 1950s, coffee was the  in  drink for the young rock n roll generation who flocked to the new coffee bars. NESCAF    was not the first coffee drink introduced; A Japanese chemist called Kato patented a process for making soluble coffee powder in 1903 in Chicago. He was followed in 1909 by the Englishman, George C Washington, who made instant coffee powder commercially available for the first time. It was the Brazilian Coffee Institute in the 1930 s who decided that a good instant coffee that would retain its flavour would stimulate demand and help reduce Brazil s huge coffee surplus. NESCAF    today`````````````````````Since then, the NESCAF    range has continued to grow. When you go into the supermarket, there is such a large selection of coffees to choose from, Mild blends to strong premium, full-bodied coffees to after-dinner, and decaffeinated.NESCAF    continues to innovate, launching different varieties, including their Fairtrade certified coffee. They have a long-term commitment to develop sustainable agricultural practices, specifically in Ethiopia and El Salvador. The coffee process``````````````````````Your coffee starts life on a small, evergreen tree that grows across South and Central America, Africa and Asia. The young coffee tree needs exactly the right amount of shaded sunlight, regular watering, fertilising, and pest and weed control, as well as constant attention, but it will take four years in these conditions before the plant starts producing beans. A well managed plant could carry on producing beans for almost 40 years.Although there are about 60 species of coffee, the main two which are grown commercially are Arabica and Robusta. Only 100  pure coffee goes into NESCAF   , they use a blend of both of these beans, to guarantee a consistent quality of flavour and aroma. The Robusta bean is characterized by strong flavours and a low acidity, while the Arabica is more delicate, with a pleasant acidityDo coffee beans grow on trees?``````````````````````````````````Coffee beans actually grow inside a red coffee  cherry . The cherry takes about nine months to ripen, they are then picked by hand, left to dry out and sorted. Only the quality beans are packed and shipped around the world. Those that are imperfect are thrown away.How do make a perfect cuppa?``````````````````````````````````I m sure if you speak to a selection of different people; they will each tell you different ways of making their perfect cup of coffee, whether it is instant, cafetiere, white, black, cappuccino, espresso, with or without sugar. You can always be sure of a quality cup of coffee from NESCAF   . They roast the beans to release that familiar coffee aroma and flavour, it is then ground, and specially dried so that when you add the hot water, you are left with a perfect cup every time.Did you know that we British drink a massive 15000 cups of NESCAF    coffee every minute  (Source IRI 52 w/e 24 March 2007). My Nescafe decaf coffee``````````````````````````````The jar of coffee I have in my cupboard at the moment is a 100g jar. It has a light blue lid, (I ve always bought it with the blue lid, I m not sure when the colour changed, but the picture above is the old design) The label on the front is a mixture of gold, blue and silver, With the Nescafe title/logo running vertically down the left side, in white font. There is a picture of a bean in the background with a wispy bit of steam coming from the top. In gold writing there are the words Gold Blend and rich aroma. In clear brown writing at the bottom of the label is the word DECAFF. This has to be written clearly, as some people can only drink decaff, and some people can t, so to have this clearly labeled is a must.There is all sorts of information written on the back, including contacts, best before date, and promotion details about Pick me ups, which I ll explain later.All Nescafe jars are glass, and have a distinctive hour glass shape, which makes it easy to hold onto when you are taking out the coffee with a spoon or pouring straight into a cup.When you unscrew the lid, you find a foil seal across the top of the jar, locking all the flavours and aromas inside, you can peel the top off, but I personally love to give it a good stab then tear the foil off. When you do this the strong coffee aroma fills the air instantly.The granules are brown in colour and look like fine gravel. If you hold a piece between finger and thumb it crumbles easily into a powder. I scoop a teaspoon of coffee into my mug, and add a small amount of milk to it, whilst I wait for the water to boil. The milk instantly reacts with the granules and dissolves them, turning the milk a brown colour.Once the water has boiled I pour water into the mug and watch the water turn brown with the coffee and milk mix. All the granules have dissolved and I m left with a light brown medium strength coffee. Depending on your preference you can add more of less coffee and milk and also sugar if desired.Having a coffee gives me the energy I need to get on with jobs for the day, most days I have another late morning, but all depends on what I m doing and where I am; recently my son got a cup of coffee spilt over his arm at a toddler group. Thankfully the drink had cooled enough not to do any damage, but I will not drink any hot drinks around children, as the effects on their skin can last a lifetime.I can t drink coffee as soon as it s made, I have to allow at least 5 - 10 minutes for it to cool slightly, but when it gets too cool then I have to start again, my mother-in-law re- heats her cold coffee in the microwave, but I find this makes it taste funny. As stated earlier, I find that drinking coffee, too late in the day means that I can t sleep at night; this is still the case with decaff coffee.  Did you know that, decaff coffee still contains some caffeine. Due to the processes used, not all caffeine is removed so you would expect to find about 2 - 4 milligrams of caffeine in each cup. I m glad that coffee makers have given us the option of buying a standard coffee or a decaff variety, just recently Nescafe bought out the half caff variety too, so there s no excuse now, you should be able to find something that suits you.Answers to coffee quiz````````````````````````````1 -  Nestle2 - 1930 s3 - 60 species4 - Arabica   Robusta5 - 15000Totals - How did you score?``````````````````````````````````1-2 You need another cup of coffee and read the review again 3-4 Well done, but could do better5    Go to the top of the class, you deserve a choccy biscuit. Just in case you have enjoyed learning about coffee - Did you know:```````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````` ```````````````(taken from Nescafe website)~ Coffee is a great natural source of antioxidants, with even more than green tea or fruit juices. Antioxidants matter because they  soak up  free radicals, the nasty waste products of exposure to tobacco smoke, radiation and other pollution. Free radicals are also a major contributor to ageing. ~ If you re on a diet or like to keep an eye on your weight, you ll be glad to learn that black coffee contains virtually no calories. There s one less thing to worry about. ~ We all need to stay hydrated and most people think that means drinking lots of water. In fact, coffee is just as good and counts towards your 6-8 glasses a day. Go onto the website:http://www.nescafe-pickmeups.co.uk You have to register, but you ll be given a free bean to start you off, and you ll need to print off a collector card, but then get collecting, you can then exchange them for gifts, for example:6 beans - Book or DVD rental10 beans - Eco bag15 beans - pamper set or 2 for 1 theatre ticketThere are several other choices, depending what you want, you may have to pay a little towards p p. I used to tell him he was addicted to caffine and he would nt believe me until one morning we had no coffee and he had to have tea which he didnt like in the first place but after this he still wasnt happy and started to get grouchy.  I started to mention decafinated coffee and he was very adimant that you can tell the differance between them and I was sure that you cant.So what I did was go to the shops and buy a jar of decafinated coffee, but my trick was to swap jars (tip the decaf into a normal coffee jar) which I did with success and when my partner had a cup of coffee that day nothing was mentioned so I let him carry on until the jar was completely empty and to this day he dont know it was decaf coffee and unto this day he has not moaned or mentioned it.So honestly can you?....can you tell the differance?I also like this decafinated coffee as its cheaper in price a normal jar of coffe is priced around    1.99 upwards  and decafe is around about    1.20 so its value for money and like I said undetectable and better for you.     ', '    I love coffee, it  8217;s a drink that always gives me a lift and even though I really enjoy the taste, I guess primarily I drank it for the for the buzz it gave me from being loaded with caffeine. But as I got older, and since the M.E. in particular, the buzz started to get a bit out of control, friends refused to meet me for coffee because they knew just how loopy I became after my caffeine fix, high just wasn  8217;t the word  After my good pal Debs had to scrape me off the ceiling just one time too many at our favourite coffee house, we decided I  8217;d better switch to caffeine free before I was locked up once and for all What a disaster  What I found with most brands is that caffeine-free normally translates to flavour-free  Most brands of caffeine free coffee that I tried were completely lacking in any sort of flavour. Well, that  8217;s not strictly true, they had flavour, you just couldn  8217;t compare it to the taste of coffee. Most were bland and completely unappetising. Until I hit upon Nescafe Gold Blend  I had always avoided Nescafe in the past, feeling that it was too strong and it left a bitter aftertaste that lingered for hours. But not so with the decaff version, this stuff is wonderful  It still has a good rich coffee taste but without being too strong, and no aftertaste  And even though this is an instant coffee, it  8217;s incredibly full flavoured without a trace of bitterness and could be a rival for most espresso brands. I  8217;ve even used it in my coffee machine and still achieved a good flavour with a delicious aroma wafting through the house The coffee itself comes in a nice newly designed jar, clear glass with a nice curved feel to it, and a big bold red lid. The granules are a nice dark rich colour and dissolve very quickly when you add boiling water, none of those annoying blobby bits floating around the top  An average jar (100g) costs around    2.60. A 300g jar works out at far better value, around    6.20.Nescafe have been making coffee for over 60 years and the Gold Blend brand was nine years in the making until they were confident that the blend they created was the most aromatic and flavoursome possible from a simple instant coffee. They are certainly one of the biggest and best known instant coffee brands and according to their website, they estimate that, on average, some 3,000 cups of their coffee are drunk every second. I guess that says something about their success  The UK website is fascinating, it gives the history of the company, lots of interesting coffee details and for anybody who is interested, they offer a holiday prize draw for playing their   8216;Bean Game  8217; and you can also try your luck at winning an Internet Survival Kit, with some great coffee prizes. Check out the site for more details at www.nescafe.co.uk.     ', '           NESCAFE GOLD BLEND DECAFF COFFEE.                                                                  Nescafe is the world s favourite coffee, as a nation we  drink a staggering 15000 cups of Nescafe every minute.                                                                                                        DECAFFEINATED COFFEE IS IT FOR YOUThe word decaffeinated conjures up thoughts to me, of a coffee which has had the the main strength taken out. Surely it s the ingredient caffeine, which gives coffee it s rich, distinctive flavour. It also gives it  The Kick , which we associate with coffee when drinking it. Coffee is for most people one of the simple pleasures of the day. Drunk In moderate amounts it can be  a treat for the taste buds. Many people start their working day with an espresso. This small concentrated,  strong, coffee gives them an immediate  kick  of energy; a  Rush , to prepare them for their busy day ahead. Coffee houses are rife nowadays selling many different forms of coffee. It is very much a part of our culture. However coffee however taken in large quantities throughout the day can lead to your body reacting in a strange way. The key to coffee drinking is therefore is to limit  the quantity which you consume. If you exceed more than three or four coffees per day this can result in the  coffee jitters , and these are caused by an over consumption of caffeine. Caffeine is associated with addiction. How many times have we caught ourselves saying  I NEED a cup of coffee   It is a definite boost to the energy levels, it works on the central nervous system, by stimulating the stress handling hormone, Adrenalin, and increases our cortisol out-put, which brings with it a heightened awareness, increase in energy levels, and alertness. It also increases intellectual activity. Coffee brings with it some health risks, and over an extended time caffeine taken in large amounts during pregnancy has been linked to a high increase in stillbirths, miscarriages, birth defects, and low birth weight. So coffee is definitely not to be consumed whilst pregnant, or if nursing. - There are also many people who are allergic to the caffeine in coffee, or they may have a  medical condition from which they are suffering which may be aggravated by the consumption of caffeine. Also over consumption of caffeine can result in adrenal exhaustion.- So after looking at the facts, I think safety wise that decaff is by far the wiser option, though I am yet to find out if it is the tastier option. Coffee is a great kick-start to the day, and to eliminate it from our diets completely would not be the answer. So would removing caffeine from our coffee be the sensible solution I wonder.~    NESCAFE GOLD BLEND DECAFF COFFEE.   I have the 100g bottle which cost    3.27 - There is also a 200g jar which costs    4.35 Both prices quoted from the Co-op.  Now this is a little dearer than normal coffee, but considering there is going to less health risks attached , I don t feel this is too high a  price  to pay. Prices may vary, and you may want to shop around for this product, and possibly find a better deal elsewhere. Check on the Internet for best available pricing on Nescafe Gold Blend Decaff, as you never know, some sites may offer a special deal. But considering how many cups you will actually get from the 100g jar of Nescafe coffee, I feel it is still good value for the price I paid. ~ The Jar.The Nescafe Gold Blend Decaff coffee is housed in an attractive, shaped glass jar tapered at the waist for easy handling. It has a bright blue lid with Nescafe embossed upon it. There is a blue/brown/   silver foil label to the front with a large coffee bean upon it, and stamped upon the bean, in the format of Gold Hallmarking, is a cup, some steam, and a smaller coffee bean. The word Decaff is placed to the bottom of the jar, and running up the side of the jar is the word Nescafe written in White lettering, and Gold Blend,  Rich Aroma to the top. There is also a bean tied with a ribbon, which is  promoting the gifts that the bean tokens provide. To the reverse we have the expiry date, which is one year, various other information, and a free coffee bean token, with a website address, and freephone number, where you can check what rewards can be gained from collecting the tokens. ~ The Coffee.The decaff coffee is freeze dried soluble coffee. The granules are light brown in colour, and quite large. As I crumble the freeze dried coffee between my fingers, it crumbles to a fine powder and releases a welcoming deeper  smell of coffee . s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
If you’re like me—someone who loves the ritual and flavor of coffee but wants to dodge caffeine’s jittery side effects—Nescafe Gold Blend Decaffeinated is worth a close look. This blend uses a freeze-drying process that does a solid job preserving the inviting aroma and rich flavor you expect from a good cup of coffee. Made from a mix of Arabica and Robusta beans, it delivers consistent quality that’s surprisingly close to the regular caffeinated version. Honestly, it’s tricky to tell them apart by taste alone, which is a big plus if you want the coffee experience without the caffeine kick.

From a health perspective, switching to this decaf can help avoid common caffeine-related issues like sleep disruption, dependency, or sensitivity reactions—something I appreciate, especially when I want a late afternoon pick-me-up without sacrificing my night’s rest. Plus, it’s a smarter choice for pregnant folks or anyone advised to limit caffeine. Just a heads-up: it still contains a tiny bit of caffeine, so if you’re super sensitive, late-day cups might still affect your sleep.

On the downside, Nescafe Gold Blend Decaf is pricier than some other brands, which might make you pause if you’re hunting for bargains. However, considering the quality and smooth, bitterness-free flavor, I’d say it’s good value for what you get. It’s also super convenient—easy to prepare and customizable with milk or sugar to suit your taste.

Lastly, if you’re watching calories or antioxidants, this coffee fits the bill nicely—virtually zero calories black and a decent antioxidant boost. Widely available in various jar sizes, it’s easy to find and stock up on.

In summary, if you want a reliable, tasty decaf that respects your health goals without compromising on flavor, Nescafe Gold Blend Decaffeinated is a solid contender—just be ready to pay a bit more for that quality experience.

Well, it was basically Burger King - which is actually situated within The Big W itself   8211; or McDonald  8217;s which is on the other side of the car park.The final decision seemed to come down to me, so   8211; after considering the excellent reviews of both places written by hpoulton (which I read only this morning on Ciao)   8211; I chose Burger King. The fact that I have already written an opinion on McDonald  8217;s was only a tiny factor, honest.We have eaten fairly regularly at McDonald  8217;s over the past year or so, mainly because of the TY beanie promotions they do. The cost was certainly comparable to McDonald  8217;s. We bought a Veggie Whopper meal for the five vegetarians amongst us, the solitary meat-eater ate a Chicken Royale meal. The toilet facilities were handy and clean, although they smelled rather too fragrant, the lavender smell catching in my throat a bit.Burger King itself is arranged in rows of seats and tables, with a long counter running the length of the area. The staff seemed friendly, pleasant and helpful too. They were doing a Simpsons promotion, but the toys weren  8217;t very prominent, except on a poster, which meant the children didn  8217;t even ask for them  So the food arrived -  I noticed they use much less packaging than McDonald  8217;s, the burgers wrapped in strong tissue-type paper rather than those plastic boxes. This seems much better than all the waste its rivals must throw away. The straws were sturdy, the serviettes much thicker and overall, I was impressed with this aspect of Burger King.But let  8217;s face it, restaurants and cafes are basically about the food itself. While the cokes were comparable, the burgers and chips (oh okay, fries, whatever) weren  8217;t as nice as those served by McDonald  8217;s. Burger King  8217;s fries are much less greasy, bigger and crispier, but they just didn  8217;t taste as yummy.The Veggie Whopper was quite filling with a generous sized burger and quite a lot of salad   8211; not just the obligatory soggy lettuce, but also discernible pieces of gherkins and tomato, plus a lovely mayonnaise dressing. The bun was fairly tasty, but the burger was a bit strange   8211; admittedly, it wasn  8217;t mushy vegetables, but I  8217;m not quite sure what it was. It didn  8217;t taste meaty (thankfully ), but it was slightly nutty and I spotted some mushrooms in there. Once again though, the McDonald  8217;s veggie burger wins hands down on taste.It wasn  8217;t just my fussy palate either. The kids weren  8217;t as enthusiastic about their food than they usually are, if we go to McDonald  8217;s. My five year old ended up complaining of a tummy ache. My meat-eating partner enjoyed his Chicken burger, but wasn  8217;t so impressed with the fries.Overall then, it was certainly nice enough, but the food didn  8217;t seem as tasty as McDonald  8217;s. If I were out somewhere and there wasn  8217;t a McDonald  8217;s around (Silly idea, I know ), I would be happy to eat at Burger King   8211; but next time I have a choice, I  8217;m going back to the old favourite, sorry.     ', '    It has to be said that Burger King beats all the high street burger bars in my book. If you’re weighing up Burger King against the usual fast food suspects, here’s the lowdown from someone who’s tasted and tested with a critical eye (and a hungry belly). First off, Burger King’s flame-grilled burgers genuinely pack more flavor and a meatier punch than McDonald’s. That smoky char isn’t just a gimmick—it adds real substance, making the slightly higher price tag (around £3.50–£4.00 per meal) feel somewhat justified. You’re paying for taste, not just convenience.

Now, about those fries—or chips, as some might call them. Burger King’s chips are chunkier and less salty than McDonald’s fries, which is a double-edged sword. On the plus side, they avoid the salt overload, but beware: consistency can be hit or miss. Sometimes they come out a bit hard, lacking that soft, fluffy middle we all secretly crave. So, if you’re a fries purist, this might be a sticking point.

Service-wise, Burger King scores well. Staff are generally polite and patient, especially during those late-night rushes when everyone’s a bit hangry and less charming. The restaurants themselves maintain good hygiene standards with frequent cleaning, which is always reassuring when you’re grabbing a quick bite.

In summary, if you’re after a fast food burger with genuine flavor and don’t mind paying a bit extra, Burger King is a solid choice. Just temper your expectations on the fries—they’re decent but not consistently great. And kudos to the staff for keeping things professional even when the clock strikes midnight and the crowd gets rowdy. It’s a tasty, if slightly pricey, option for your casual dining fix.
