Final Straw   , the album they put together, turned out to be an incredible, flowing piece of work, fixed around the central theme of the break up of a relationship. Lightbody   s dark and bitter lyrics are matched by snarling, angry guitars that bite into each song and rip it apart, dissecting everything except Lightbody   s voice, which stands up. It   s not the greatest voice ever, but it   s emotive. He sounds like a man with only one more song in him before he gives up, because life   s overwhelmed him. His lyrics don   t really focus on big themes, but it   s the way he   s exploring small things, such as finding the sweater his ex accidentally left in his room, small things that ultimately become the main memories taken from broken relationships, that gives his songs an everyman feel. I played it constantly for three years or so, and over that time I started to explore other music, I got into other music. So really, for me, Final Straw is the album that started it all off for me. But I   ll try to stay neutral, and keep away from praising it constantly. If I can. I listen to it rarely now, because it   s an important record for me, because along with Aimee Mann   s Magnolia soundtrack, it what really introduced me to music. Nobody ever seems to realise that Snow Patrol shouldn   t be lumped in with the Coldplay/Travis group of artists who create soft melodic music capable of bringing grown men to tears twixt their eyes. Sure, they have their moments of quiet, but more often than not they grunge out with heavy guitars. They   re totally different from Coldplay. Snow Patrol are not, and I shall repeat this now Snow Patrol are NOT, soft-rockers. They are dark, and they are disturbing, and their music critically and lyrically dissects love in all it   s forms. They don   t swoon. If Snow Patrol were a person, they   d be the guy who wears a hoodie, listens to Nirvana, and never contributes at University until the day you accidentally walk into their room and find their book of poetry and see drawings and sketches plastered across the walls. And then they catch you in the midst of thievery and throw you out. That is who Snow Patrol are.What   s great is that I can look at the album now, and still enjoy it. There   s an edge to it that carries it along, and the record feels complete, like a journey almost. Starting off with the final words of a relationship (How To Be Dead) and ending with the energy release of Half The Fun, it carries you along right from the start, gripping you with it   s sense of desperate urgency. The record is split into four distinct parts, and kicks off with    How To Be Dead   , which fails the first time it tries for a guitar melody, and then falls back onto xylophone, which then gives the guitars a chance to return. Acoustic-driven for the first half, the song is an argument between two people as their relationship cracks up. After each have said their piece, the record pauses briefly, and then breaks into a heavy guitar riff, dominated by the drum beat. After, the conversation closes and the argument ends, with the couple splitting up. It   s a heavy way to start the album, but the song, with it   s bittersweet message and spindling pieces of electronica, is a gem. It segues into    Wow    (Snow Patrol rarely have their song titles appear as lyrics) and the guitars roll around, until a drum beat comes in, and heavy, heavy guitars struggle to drown out Lightbody   s muffled and distorted vocals. In turn,    Gleaming Auction    and    Whatever   s Left    follow straight on respectively from the last song, in essence creating a four-song-suite - although with guitars, not with Nancy philharmonic nonsense. Gleaming Auction is a song which struggles to keep away from the guitars, which sound dangerous and are always on the edge of breaking out and taking the song - Whatever   s Left, on the other hand, starts off dark and grows darker and heavier as it goes on. Yet there   s a strange sense of melody creeping throughout the four songs which holds them together, and keeps them on the right side of grunge.One feature of the album is the way that the producers have inserted    cracks    in the music. A little like antiquing the album, throughout are little glitches (intentional ones, promise) which break up and distort the sound briefly. Crackles of static, things like that. It all builds up, much like the singles    Spitting Games    and    Chocolate   , which come next. Spitting Games is the closest the band come to glorifying heavy metal, with multiple guitars screaming out at once and thudding drums announcing Lightbody as he sings    I broke into your house last night/and left a note at your bedside    It   s all about being unable to find the words to say (shout-out to an earlier Snow Patrol song there) to a crush you have, about finding it hard to ask someone out because of the fear of rejection, and works rather well. Chocolate, on the other hand, is one of the more melodic touches on the album. Controlled by a restrained guitar, and some rhymic drumming, it   s also one of Lightbody   s best vocal performances. He sounds muffled throughout the album by vocoders and distortion, but here he sings clearly, and the track is a moment of clarity lost amongst bitterness, jealousy, anger. As such, it   s made all the more poignant.    What have I done? It   s too late for that/What have I become? Truth is, nothing yet.    He sings.    Run    closes the second section of music. A downbeat anthem which caught the nation   s attention, I   d be surprised if you haven   t heard of it. Lightbody   s attempt at creating an anthem starts off slowly, each verse sounding slow and deliberate. Then, from nowhere, comes the crashing chorus        Light up, Light up     as if you have a choice    , and guitars and keyboards and drums mash into cacophony, and suddenly everything   s alright. It   s an astonishing tune.   Grazed Knees    is a slow, thoughtful song, with slow guitar melodies and a plaintive call for help from Lightbody as he deals with the aftermath of returning to an old girlfriend for a rebound fling     always a bad idea. Keyboards come in, and announce the appearance of    Ways   Means   , another song with crashing guitars and hard drums. It   s one of my favourites, actually, because the chorus is totally a singalong, even if it is distorted quite heavily at times. Everything seems to be building up, and the chorus doesn   t disappoint. Neither does the short two minute track    Tiny Little Fractures   , which sails along quickly with fast vocals, fast guitars    strong drumming, and a    whoa-owa-whoa-owa-whoa, yeah    chorus which begs you to join in. But all this is just a set-up, so the guitars can exhaust themselves in time for    Somewhere A Clock Is Ticking   , the best song I   ve yet heard about the Iraq war. It   s sung from the viewpoint of a scared new recruit trying to make sense of his position and stay alive. It   s a slow-burner of a song, held back remarkable-well by the band, who refuse to release the full force of the guitars until the song is ready for them. It   s a masterpiece of timing, a highlight of the album, and a stunning song in it   s own right. It   s the sort of song that can send goosebumps up every part of your body at the same time, and make you feel like you   re totally still. The third section of the album closes with    Same   , which deals with the fallout of the extreme ending of    Somewhere       A piano, surprisingly, is the lead for the song, and it closes everything off, the themes of a broken relationship, trying to get over troubles, everything is dealt with and wrapped up here.Which just leaves us with time for the two bonus tracks we Brits get as a reward for being born in the right place at the right time.    We Can Run Away Now They re All Dead and Gone    is a song dying out to be played during a romantic drama, when the young couple decide to make a go of it whilst sat in a trendy caf    having coffees. The bouncy rock/pop mixture keeps the song going, and the chorus    you are all I really want, in this world    says it all, really. It   s the start of a new relationship after the failure of the last one, and a positive way to finish        cept, as    Half The Fun    points out, the future isn   t clear (or orange), it   s kinda dark    and unknown. It   s what I can only describe as a release of all the pent-up anger, leaping onto the guitars which furiously vent their rage during the last minute or so, which is completely dominated by a wall of thrash-guitar. Every track is important. Every melody, lyric or piece of static have their place, and everything clicks together to make the album a whole. If you’re diving into Snow Patrol’s *Final Straw*, you’re in for a well-crafted journey that balances energetic rock with introspective calm—something that should resonate well if you appreciate albums with thoughtful pacing and emotional depth. The album’s structure is a highlight: it skillfully alternates between upbeat tracks like “Gleaming Auction” and “Whatever’s Left,” which showcase sharp guitar work and a driving rock energy, and slower, more reflective pieces such as “Ways & Means” and “Somewhere A Clock Is Ticking.” This ebb and flow keeps the listening experience engaging without ever feeling disjointed.

“Run” stands out as the emotional centerpiece—haunting and beautiful, it’s a track that lingers long after the music stops, much like those nostalgic songs from the 80s and 90s that evoke a deep sense of feeling. On the quieter side, “Grazed Knees” offers a delicate blend of finger-picked guitar and violins, creating an achingly beautiful moment that contrasts nicely with the album’s more upbeat numbers like “Spitting Games,” which features a catchy, memorable riff that’s light and infectious.

While *Final Straw* may not break new ground in originality, its consistent quality across all tracks makes it a solid breakthrough album for Snow Patrol. There are no weak links here, which is a refreshing rarity and makes it a worthwhile addition to any collector’s shelf—especially if you value albums that maintain cohesion while exploring different moods.

In sum, *Final Straw* is a dependable blend of rock vigor and melodic introspection. It’s not just a nostalgic nod but a well-rounded listen that rewards those who appreciate both technical musicianship and emotional storytelling. If you’re after an album that flows smoothly from energetic riffs to heartfelt ballads, this one fits the bill nicely.

Tenacious D’s self-titled album is a fascinating blend of rock, comedy, and folk metal that offers a unique listening experience—perfect for those who appreciate originality and humor wrapped in solid musicianship. Jack Black’s versatile vocals shine throughout, complemented by Kyle Gass’s impressive guitar work, creating a dynamic duo that balances musical skill with comedic flair. Tracks like “F**k Her Gently” stand out as ballad-style gems that are both hilariously witty and musically well-crafted, showcasing the duo’s ability to blend emotional resonance with humor. product_reviews: ['    A little bit of Lidl historyLidl is the last name of the man who founded the store, Ludwig Lidl. The company was founded in the 1930 s by a member of the Schwarz family. Although most of Lidl s products are their own brand they also sell alot of well known brands such as walkers crisps, barr lemonade, lurpak butter, heinz soups etc. I also love the lidl juices, the fizzy juice tastes very like what it is supposed to and is very cheap aswell. The fresh juices are great aswell, my kids and i love the carrot and orange juice. The cheap prices may put some people off but personally i love this store.I hope my review has been useful, thanks for reading. x Summary: A cheap and cheerful store     ', '    The first Lidl shop opened in my area approximately 3years ago (Dorset) and I didn t think much of it. The etiquite is to dump all the stuff back into the trolley then go to the packing table to bag it up     ', '    After slating Kwik save, I thought its only fair to give my opinion on the another   cheap   supermarket, so here it is. ', '    Anyone who   s used a Lidl supermarket will know what to expect even before they read this; those who haven   t may find it a surprising experience for a number of reasons.Lidl is a German-owned company with supermarkets all over Europe; its philosophy is of the Pile-It-High, Sell-It-Cheap, Keep-   Em-Waiting variety.And there we could leave it     but that would be only half the story and anyway, Ciao expects so much more than that for an op The company   s main characteristic is that it sells almost everything much more cheaply than comparable goods in any other supermarket.  Much of their food stock is own-brand, i.e. of German origin and may not always suit British palates, though their fruit and vegetables, always labelled as being at    half price    are often local.(Lidl philosophical aside: How can anything be called half price if it   s ALWAYS sold at that price?  It doesn   t make sense to be permanently half price because that becomes its normal, i.e. full, price.  Doesn   t it? Or not? Or should I have had that brandy   ?).The range of foodstuffs is much more restricted than in other supermarkets     no Organic section, no Vegetarian Range.  However, what they sell is generally of reasonable quality and ocasionally outstanding.  Their biscuits and cakes, being largely German in origin, are usually interesting and really good.  The wines, spirits and ales are similarly of unknown brands but certainly in my limited experience (Cognac ) of good quality and remarkably good value.However, I suspect that most of their customers use the place for goods other than foodstuffs.  Every Monday and Thursday they display the week   s Special Offers for sale.  These may be anything from clothes to computers; from watches to whisks    you get the picture   This week I bought a phone which features caller I.D. (you know, the number of the person ringing is displayed on the screen so you can decide to be OUT), hands free operation (you can talk to the phone without lifting the receiver and listen through its speaker), a phone book that automatically dials the number you select     and it cost just under a Pavarotti (oh, all right then, a tenner).Being a gadget-lover I just had to take home a digital pedometer (go and look it up in the dictionary     you don   t expect me to explain everything, do you?) at    4.99; while their computer peripherals (don   t snigger ) have to be seen to be believed: cordless optical mouse with rechargeable batteries and charging unit,    9.99, USB 4-port mini-hub,    5.99, six-in-one Memory Card Reader (for digital photographers who keep changing their minds and their memory formats) at    12.99.  PC World can eat its heart out The point about these bargain items is that you never know until the week before what   s going to be on offer, and they   re only on offer for a week at a time, so I nip in at least once a week (usually on a Thursday) to pick up the Offers leaflet for the following week.  At various times I   ve seen on sale there televisions, hi-fi systems, toasters, shoes, school bags, watches, pine drawer cabinets, coats, ladies    underwear (please stop sniggering  It   s so childish ), garden strimmers, radio-controlled plugs (to go in the mains in awkard places so you don   t have to crawl under the table to switch them on and off     but why am I telling you this?)    The list goes on.A Lidl word of warning: make sure you check whether the items you want are to be sold on the following Monday or Thursday.  Twice recently I turned up on the wrong days and found that they   d sold out of the things I wanted.While you   re in Lidl you can play Spot The Assistants (not counting the harassed-looking girl on the checkout). To be fair, I did once spot one and gave her a mini-breakdown by asking her a question. All I said was,    Does this mouse come with a PS2 adapter or is it USB only?     An innocent enough question, I   d have thought, and not one normally calculated to cause a Freak Out.  Ah well   The Joke Checkouts are interesting.  I   m not actually sure what they   re there for and when I asked the checkout girl about them, SHE seemed to have a mini-freak-out, too.  There are two branches of Lidl in Lincoln and one has four checkouts, the other (I think, from memory) six. Yet I   ve NEVER seen even two at a time working, so I   m sure the others are some obscure kind of joke.  When I   ve figured it out, I   m sure I   ll laugh till I stop.I   ll add that you won   t find nice, helpful baskets to carry your shopping round in and that if you want a trolley you   ll have to insert a pound coin in its hungry maw, returnable when you re-park it.  They accept cash or debit card but not cheques.  If you want a carrier bag there   s a charge.  And if you want to phone the manager, hard luck     they don   t have a number for the public to phone in on.But if you want a bargain and love queuing, you   ll really warm to Lidl.  Just a Lidl.Update, about 24 hours after I wrote the above: I ve just returned from another quick excursion to Lidl.  I suddenly realised I m out of Cognac and fancied a drop or two or three.  It goes under the name of Vieux Gar   on and is even better than I remember it, equally as good as any other supermarket s own brand and, at    9.99 for a 70 cl. bottle, about    2 cheaper...But that s not why I m writing this update.  I m writing it because I ve beaten the ONE open checkout record and found the NO open checkout   The checkout girl was mopping the floor (it was about 7.30p.m.) and there were two of us waiting for about three minutes before she spotted us and apologetically logged in.  And, on a chilly, late October evening, it was colder in the store than outside.  There was no heating on (the checkout girl said they are very strict about when it goes on - probably when the milk goes stiff and chunky) and, as far as I could tell, only two staff in the entire place.  No wonder they can afford to cut prices Oh, and I forgot to mention earlier the range of packet fuit juices which ia quite extensive and very good indeed, especially the Citrus And Carrot drink, known as ACE (presumably the vitamins it contains) at 99p for two litres.For those who are interested, the current offers include an orbital sander at    14.99 (for anyone who wants to smooth down the M25, I suppose), a wooden bird-house (no, not for wooden birds) at    2.99 and  quot;wax jackets quot; (they must mean waxed I guess, unless they re designed to melt in the sunshine) at    29.99.  From Thursday (23rd October) you can choose between a 28 quot; television (   179.99) with a three year guarantee (including a pickup and repair service), assorted kids  fleeces (for assorted kids -    3.99) and a two-speed micro-cassette dictation machine (3.99) - plus all sorts of other oddser nends.  You pays your money and you joins your queue (or vice-versa).Happy queuing      ', '    I ask you a simple question, what do manners cost nowadays? I ask you is ths the way to treat customers?Then when i finally got to the check out i was orderd for my money with not a sign of a please or a than you. I ask you is this the way to run a business? well maybe it is but the only place the manager is going to run this branch is into the ground.     ', '    I used to live in London and we were surrounded by supermarkets and food shops: Tesco, Sainsbury, Safeway, Waitrose, M S - you name them; we had them.  Our nearest supermarket was Lidl.  I only ever went there on about two or three occasions. It was awful It was a fairly new store but seemed so run-down and badly managed that the times I didshop there I left feeling depressed.  OK, so it was cheap - but it was definitely not cheerful These days I live on the west coast of Scotland, we have a Tesco, a Co-op - and a newly-opened branch of Lidl. When word first got out that    some funny sounding supermarket    was going to open here I did my best to spread the word.    Oh, no    I said, in my best Frankie Howerd voice,    you won   t want to shop there    I assured everyone that I would certainly never step foot in the place............well, of course I had to go and have a quick look, just to confirm my prejudices You   ve probably guessed the rest  I was really impressed. The store has been open for about a month now and I just can   t find fault with it (well, maybe a few little niggles, but more of those in a minute)  It is spotlessly clean, well laid out and the staff are pleasant, helpful and enthusiastic. The aisles are wide and the shelves are heaving with goods.Lidl are a German company and a lot of the goods they sell are more    European    than those that we are used to seeing on our supermarket shelves. If you are into proper pickled cucumbers (which are sweet, not vinegary) or vacuum- packed salami or iced gingerbread biscuits this is the place to come. Many supermarkets would classify such items as    deli    goods and charge accordingly. At Lidl they, and almost everything else they sell are cheap.Almost all of Lidl   s goods are own-brand. There is a huge amount of choice; everything from tinned vegetables through to pet food and household products. Rather than beingpackaged in dull, corporate own-brand packets and tins, each product is attractively packed with a picture of the contents. Actually the picture is a big help as many of the goods have their contents written in the language of origin. (without the picture to help me I would never have known that Fagioli bianchi di Spagna was Italian for butterbeans )  You will need a magnifying glass to read the small print on the label that states that the product was    Specially produced for Lidl   . So far, all the own-brands that I have bought from Lidl have been as good as named brands or other supermarket brands - the difference is that they are cheaper. I have managed to wean my dogs onto Lidl   s own-brand take on Winalot biscuits at 69p a box compared to over    1.00 for the    real    thing. Admittedly they look a bit    rough    (the biscuits, not the dogs) compared to the genuine article but they have definitely had theJack Russell seal of approval from my two. I   ve bought tinned sardines, very tasty andexcellent value at 27p a tin, tinned sweetcorn for 21p, litre cartons of orange juice for 46p which was excellent - not    cheap    tasting at all. The only time I   ve been caught out has been with chopped tinned tomatoes at 19p a tin they are 1p dearer than the Tesco Value ones - but they seem better quality and come in a far more attractive-looking can than the Tesco tomatoes that have    cheap    written all over them Because I   d tried to forget my London Lidl shopping experience I was surprised to see the range of fresh vegetables available at Lidl. The only down-side is that they are mostly pre-packed and in large quantities. I prefer to buy my veggies little and often and don   t really want or need catering pack amounts. Having said that,  the vegetables look very fresh and good quality - big bunches of carrots with their green tops still on and lovely wooden crates of satsumas.I had also forgotten that Lidl do sell some named brands - such as Weetabix , Pepsi and Hovis. They also have    specials    for sale - amongst the one-off offers have been Wellington boots (very popular in this part of the world) and SatNav systems which sold out almost straight away (easy to get lost round here ) Another very big plus for Lidl is that they have a policy of charging the same price for goods throughout their UK stores. This may not seem like any big deal but, although I live in a town, we are quite remote and supplying shops here is expensive and at times difficult.  Tesco, for example, is dearer here than in a lot of their other stores because of the logistics of  bringing the goods in.  Another policy which gets my vote is that (I have been reliably informed) Lidl will never    re-arrange    the store -the same goods will always be on the same shelves - and the layout is the same throughout all their shops. Lastly, praise for their sell-by policy. When goods are coming up to their sell-by date they are reduced to half price. If after a day they have still not sold they give them away  I   ll repeat that: THEY GIVE THEM AWAY   Once past the check-out there is a big trolley full of    freebies    - and the staff  practically beg you to help yourself   It must be a British thing but I actually felt embarrassed taking stuff  - but thankyou anyway, I   ve now got afreezer full of bread that I   ve accumulated over several visits.It seems a bit churlish now to have a moan  The one thing that really bugs me is that there are no baskets - only    1.00 in-the-slot trolleys.  Because I usually pop in to buy just a few things,  I need a basket. I don   t want to push a trolley round neither do I want to juggle things in my arms. Also, trolleys are difficult for people in wheelchairs. On my first visit I was with someone in an electric wheelchair - she had no problems getting into the shop, there   s a ramp, she found the wide aisles easy to navigate but for her to push a trolley around would be impossible.Lidl   s you lost a customer that day.Err - that   s it really, I suppose I was initially a bit annoyed to pay 9p for a plastic carrier bag, and then I told myself that it made sense as it encourages people to re-use bags. Which can only be a good thing.So really, not much to moan about at all On balance, I think I   ll probably stick to Tesco for    the big shop    but I am genuinely veryimpressed with Lidl and I   m glad that I didn   t  heed my own advice not to go there  (My thanks to the girl on the check-out who was so enthusiastic about Lidl s policies and told me all about pricing, layout etc  She was a real star )     ', '    I had never been into a Lidl store before, up until a few weeks ago. I pass one every day on my way to work and just recently we have been receiving leaflets full of vouchers and offers currently on in the store. These make great reading whilst eating breakfast  I decided to go and see what all the fuss was about. I have always thought of Lidl as being a cheap and cheerful supermarket, and that s exactly what it is, even the sign above the door looks cheap, blue, yellow and red showing just the word Lidl. Lidl stores always seem to have a good sized car park without the potholes and rubbish you would find in more British supermarkets. When I first went into the store I was surprised how clean everything felt, the floors were shinning and the trolley didn t have any wonky wheels. The size of the store is much smaller than that of other supermarkets, e.g Tesco or Asda. It s surprised me how much they sell, food, gardening products, motoring products, power tools, always totally random  If you go in there regularly I am sure you could really find some bargains. The choice of food is pretty limited compared to a usual supermarket, this is a good thing if you are looking to save money, there is nothing that you would buy off instinct. You are not lured into buying more than you need either. The food that we have tried has always been of good quality, the garlic bread is delicious and many of the ice creams they offer are lovely. I actually picked up a huge jar of peanut butter in there for 60pence which was just as good as Sunpat at     of the price  Their own range of bread rolls is also good, costing about 33p for six nice sized rolls, they are nice and soft and last ages before going dry. When you get to the till, something very strange happens. I have never known checkout staff who scan items so quickly, before you know it everything is at the other end of the till waiting to be bagged up. Unfortunately there are no free carriers, you can pick them up for 3p so it s not too bad. You re not given any space at the end of the checkout to bag up, so many people put it all back into their trolley and then bag it all up at the packing bench at the front of the store. I have only ever picked up a few bits so hasn t bothered me. Another strange thing, is that they do not accept credit cards, only cash or debit. Make sure you have the right means of payment or you could face leaving empty handed  I wouldn t think twice about using Lidl again, it is far from the cheap and nasty shop I expected it to be, I would say you would struggle to do your weekly shop here every week, purely because of the lack of choice. Overall though, it is well worth a look, give it a try       ', '    Our Germanic friends have invaded these shores with various no-frills, budget-tastic supermarkets. One of these, Lidl, sprouted a brand new branch near me so I decided to investigate it after getting fatigued with the usual fare from Tesco. This was a good move as after visiting Lidl a few times I really enjoyed it as an alternative to the mainstream run of supermarkets. In my opinion Lidl has seemed to have achieved its low cost status by cutting costs to the core as I witnessed :Low staffing levels     they always seem to be busy in a number of roles going from stacking shelves one minute to serving on a checkout the next.Products are simply stacked on minimal or no shelfing. If you’re looking for a budget-friendly supermarket that balances cost savings with decent quality, Lidl is definitely worth considering. From my detailed observations, Lidl consistently offers lower shopping bills—often saving shoppers £10-15 weekly compared to other supermarkets—thanks to its focus on non-branded and imported products. This approach keeps prices very low without sacrificing too much on quality.

Lidl’s product range is deliberately limited, concentrating on basic essentials rather than luxury or specialty items. For example, their bakery goods, like white sliced bread, are not only cheap but also tend to last longer than typical value breads elsewhere. Similarly, their cleaning products and dishwasher tablets perform well and come at a fraction of the cost you’d pay at bigger chains. Household goods and packaged meats also offer excellent value, often matching the quality of supermarket own brands. Even their tinned products stand out as both inexpensive and high quality compared to other value brands.

On the flip side, the selection of fresh fruit and vegetables is minimal and only average in quality, so you might want to supplement your shop elsewhere if produce variety is a priority. Also, Lidl’s payment options are somewhat restrictive—they don’t accept cheques or credit cards, only cash or debit cards, which can be inconvenient if you prefer other methods.

Accessibility-wise, Lidl stores are thoughtfully designed with wide gangways, making navigation easier for disabled customers, though they don’t provide wheelchair trolleys, which is a notable gap. The stores tend to be quiet with minimal queues, creating a pleasant shopping atmosphere, and staff are generally friendly and helpful, albeit few in number.

Lidl’s appeal extends to foreign shoppers too, thanks to its range of imported products from various countries. Overall, if you’re pragmatic about your shopping—prioritizing value and decent quality over extensive choice or luxury items—Lidl offers a solid, no-nonsense option that can stretch your budget without too many compromises.

I am ashamed to say that today I am as bad as she is.  If I am ever in need of an item of clothing, the charity shop is my first stop.  You cannot always find what you want on the first visit - for example one week I needed some white blouses for work and could I find any?  Not a chance.  A few weeks later however, white blouses were almost coming out of the shops to greet me   This is quite frustrating and I do find myself getting quite annoyed these days if I have to buy anything new   I don t look for clothes for myself so much anymore, but rather clothes for my toddler.  I could almost go so far as to say that I haven t bought her a full price new item of clothing since she was born (apart from a few vests and pairs of socks).  The charity shops in our town always have an amazing selection of children s clothes and many of them are brand names.  Holly has clothes from Gap, Next, Laura Ashley and none of them cost me more than 79p.  Last year she had a choice of 3 winter coats to wear and all of them bought from charity shops.  This year I went shopping for a new coat for her and found a Marks and Sparks one in the first charity shop I went into.My favourite charity shop is Oxfam Supersaver.  We have a large one of these in Bognor Regis, which always has an excellent range of clothing.  All children s clothing on hangers are priced at 79p an item, with smaller items in baskets at 49p.  Ladies trousers are    1.49 and shirts/jumpers are    1.29.  I have been so spoilt with this shop that whenever I have to pay    2+ for an item in another charity shop, I feel robbed I could go on and on about charity shops, but you will be glad to hear that I won t.  Only to say that these shops have a range of other items for sale like books, nik naks (not sure how to spell that ), shoes, handbags, children s toys etc and all at exceptional prices.  If you have never been to a charity shop, give it a go.  I have a sister who will not go into one because of the stigma attached.  I think this is a real shame because not only do you benefit but so do the people who the charity shop is there to support.   After all, that is what it is all about at the end of the day.     ', '    I have been buying goods from Charity shops for about 10 years now. At first, it was mostly curiosity that took me through their doors, but since my divorce and return to the UK, I have found that these are THE shops to buy from.Living off benefits of just    53 per week was very hard, especially if I needed to buy new clothes or something for the house. But now - well, now - just about all my furniture has come from charity shops, 95  of my clothes too. There are many people who would just  die  at the thought of having to set foot in Oxfam or Shelter etc -  Oh my God  I could never wear/use something that s been used by someone else , I would often hear. But I felt that I was killing two birds with one stone. I was spending what little I could afford on things that I really needed, and at the same time, helping those even less fortunate than myself. It gave me a feeling of self-worth and pride  I have found some fantastic bargains in one of my local charity shops. A suite - 3 seater, 2 seater, chair and footstool - for only    90. (It was originally    120, but because I shop there so often, I got discount. Can t be bad, eh)? A hoover for    10 and a pine kitchen table and 4 chairs for    40 - all in excellent condition  BRAND NEW clothes at just    3 for trousers/skirts and    1.50 for jumpers. So think about it, WHY pay    10 on one item when you can get 3 for the same price? Everyone loves a bargain.I have converted so many of my friends to shopping in charity shops - the same ones who said they would never set foot in them. They have bought CD s, lamps (Electrical items are always checked for safety before being put on sale), crockery, pictures....the list is endless. Once, I even bought a brand new pair of  Next  shoes for just    3  (I would be wary of buying 2nd hand shoes though, as you don t know if the previous wearer had any foot problems, and NEVER buy 2nd hand shoes for children).I don t think that there is as much stigma attached to shopping in Charity shops, but my kids always prefer to wait outside the shop next door instead of coming in with me - just in case one of their schoolmates walk past  Having said that, my son was delighted when I bought him a brand new FUBU top that I found in Oxfam and my daughter a GENUINE  MISS SIXTY  mini skirt - both were just    2.50. (The price of the Miss Sixty skirt in the High Street Shop is    65).Ha Ha  Who s laughing now, kids? (Love  em really).So, go ahead, bag yourself some REAL bargains and visit your local charity shop. Ok, some of them might be a bit whiffy when you go in, but you can always wash the stuff again when you get home, although, nearly ALL charity shops will wash the items before putting them out for sale.     ', '    I have heard from people that they would never go into charity shops as it is embarassing but then again these are mostly young people who say this. When I left school I started working in a charity shop and it was hard work. People may think it is easy but it isn t, all the customer sees is you working on the till but there is work behind the scene that they never see.People find unwanted items in their home eg. clothes, toys etc and then they decide what to do with them. When they finish deciding on where to take them they bring them to the charity shop.When people bring clothes into the shops they have to be sorted through to check that they are any good, if they are they then get sorted through for cleaniness, then age/sizes. If clothes are in good condition but need washing then someone usually takes them home to get them washed. But it isn t only clothes that can be taken in, its books, clothes,toys, shoes, bags, almost anything apart from electricals as most shops don t have someone to check them. When I was pregnant with my daughter I couldn t afford brand new clothes for her so I went into charity shops to get clothes for both me and her. As well as buying clothes from there I also got some toys for her (for when she older) and even though they are cheap items they are in good condition to be sold second hand. I have picked up some bargains while shopping in charity shops and even though I have had my daughter I still go into the shops from time to time.When I have finished with clothes or any items that I don t want anymore I give them to charity shops but because there are so many I usually have trouble deciding who to give them to.Even though Oxfam is the longest one to be standing over the years it has managed to survive the other charity shops that have built up over the years like St John s, Barnados. All the profit the shops make it all goes to the charity the shop is representing.All you people who have old items that you don t want anymore get them out, put them bags and take them down to any charity shops.     ', '    Charity shops are where most of my book collection come from.  There is a good selection and they are usually cheap, so I can buy books which I m not sure if I will like without wasting too much money.  I used to get books from the library but always used to forget to take them back in time.  The fines soon mounted up so I looked for a new source of reading material and happened upon charity shops.  They don t have the latest releases, but they do have a lot of classics and there have been enough good books written in the past for it not to matter.I also like to buy second hand records from charity shops.  As with books there are a lot of classic albums to be found for not much money.   I have found some quite collectable albums and CDs which if I did want to sell I could probably make quite a lot of cash from.The main bulk of the merchandise on sale in charity shops are clothes.  If you have a good sense of style, you can pick out items of clothing for a fraction of the price they charge at high street stores and look really cool wearing them.  I, not having much sense of style, buy something which seems alright in the shop, which actually makes me look about 50, so I gave up on buying clothes from them except for perhaps things like t-shirts which you can t really go far wrong with.Charity shops are run by volunteers and are a great way of giving to good causes and also getting something you want.  They support many charities such as Oxfam, Barnardos, Help the Aged, Cancer Research and more.  Buying second-hand goods is more environmentally friendly than buying new so you can feel very good about yourself if you shop there.In the town where I live there are lots of charity shops and bargain basement type shops.  Not very many other businesses survive.  I was quite surprised to read in other peoples opinions that some people find charity shops embarrassing as I don t think they are and I don t anyone who does.  The worst thing about them is that some of them smell of wee.     ', '    I have become an avid charidee shopper - amazing my friends with my prowress in these places   Over the years I have bought fantastic items and have been lucky enough to create a small fortune out of them myself.I do like adapting things for my own style and feel that charity shops are the best place to do this on the cheap.  Here are a few hints I live by when charity shopping.1. Take care when you go.  Different times give you different bargains.  If you try to go at the end of the January Sales, you will come across a lot of brand new things that have not been sold in the sales.  Quite a few high street shops pass on their  quot;no-sales quot; to charity shops - soo keep an eye out.  At the end of spring, after everybody has had their  quot;spring clean quot; you may come across summer bargains (due to the  quot;I ll never lose the 20lbs to fit into that dress by July quot; syndrome2. Be open-minded    Don t go into these shops expecting to find a Dolce   Gabbana Suit for the knock-down price of    5.  Just like any other shop, you will pay for quality.  Also don t look at things as they are at the moment, but how you can adapt it to your own style (i.e - a pair of white stilletoes you might be able to buy for 50p can benefit from a splash of colour from the cheap jewellery counter, using a pair of Pat Butcher earings.)  3. Invest in a good pair of scissors - This will really help you with point 2 - obviously only snip what you buy    Cut a long skirt into a funky short one, improve on a plain T-shirt with the removal of collars, cut the ugly motif of an otherwise funky jumper.  If you see a coat or something you like, but v. naff buttons, change them - if you get a bargain, a couple of quid extra will enhance it.4. Make time - don t go in on 5pm on a Saturday afternoon - you will be hard pushed to find anything as you ll be rushing.  Comparing Charity Shopping to High Street shopping is like comparing Football to Rugby - both same principal but different game altogether   Normal shopping you can see everything already and it s easy and acceptable to walk in buzz around and decide nothing is for you, as charity shops only have one of everything, a good trowl is needed through the rails.5. Be nice - Get on friendly terms with the volunteers, and if your lucky, like I am, they will actually keep things you may be interested to the side untill you call in (size 7 shoes are all kept in one certain shop to the side until I ve called in on a Saturday for my pick)6. No cards please   Have ready cash.  Not many charity shops take cards, and those who do tend to ask for    10 or more to be spent as they get charged for using the machines.  It s less embarrasing for everyone.7.  Check the item - no point buying a  quot;bargain quot; only for it to fall at the seams first wear.8.  Be careful with electrical equipment.  Yes it might be cheap, but funerals aren t   If you do buy any electical equipment, please get it checked out   Most electrical stores could do this for you for a small fee.9.  Think of long term cost - the whole point of Charity shopping is bargain hunting - if you buy a coat or jacket that needs a completely new lining - it ain t gonna be cheap  10. Different Areas Different Quality.  If you go to Charity shops in better off areas, you tend to get a better buy, that hasn t been worn as often   Ohhh how it is to have money  11.  Last of all - HAVE FUN     There are so many things to find in these places it can t be nothing but intersting   Go with a group before a fancy dress party, or take your kids to buy something for them to personalise - it s all good fun that leaves you with a warm fuzzy glow inside    Remember situations are what you make them to be      ', '    I like books. I like to read them. Own them stack them up in big piles and lend them. I decorate in books. I think with out my books my house might fall down. They hold up the walls. But I don  8217;t like to spend money. Call me a spendthrift, cheapskate, tightwad, spend shy, miserly young chap if you will. But really today  8217;s prices on books are very expensive. With a decent size paperback going for about    7.99. But pop along to your local charity shop and find piles and piles of decent books often priced at less than    1 even sometimes as low as 25 pence. Oxfam and Amnesty operate shops dedicated to books. These are not always the cheapest shops to try, but have a much more comprehensive range of literature. Usually properly categorised and in good condition.  Some of the cheapest places to find books are   8220;local  8221; charity shops that support a charity in your area such as Air Ambulance or local Hospices. My best charity book shopping experiences include the   8220;Imperial Cancer Research  8221; shop in Grantham Lincolnshire where they had fill a carrier bag with books for    1. And also the   8220;RSPCA  8221; shop in Middlesborough where they let me into the stock room to look at all the titles then let me take a box full for about 50p. On a general note if you are giving books to charity or running a charity shop never sell or give books with missing or torn pages or covers. It  8217;s not fair on the buyer. And they are especially junk. When making up a parcel for the local shop think   8220;This is still good, I don  8217;t want it but someone will.  8221; Don  8217;t use it as a way of palming off rubbish you can  8217;t bear to throw out. Another added extra that I get from charity book shopping is the little things I find in the books. These have included newspaper cuttings, old cinema tickets, love letters, shopping lists and much more. I tend to leave these things in the book as they give them a character of their own. I particularly like books that have at one time been given as gifts with a personal message in them. But that just the way I am.      ', '         Im writing this opinion to let you know theres absolutely no shame in shopping in charity shops.  As more and more of them spring up in towns everywhere the quality of the goods found in them go up and up.     I live in a small town, and cant help but get lured into the charity shops, in fact nearly other shop is a Charity Shop, theres more of them in the town I live I think than actually new clothes shops.     Im beginning to become a bit of a Charity Shop  quot;conosseuir quot; now, and find the best one locally is the British Heart Foundation Shop.  Although you cant have a good  quot;rummage quot; in there, as you can in some charity shops the layout and goods they sell are of very high quality, in fact most of their stuff is designer label stuff.  I also like the way they put everything in size order in there, some charity shops tend to put their clothes in  quot;colour quot; order, which looks very pretty but makes for much more searching to find goods in your required size.     In Hastings we also have a Shelter Charity shop, this stocks a lot of Richard Shops seconds all new with slight flaws but they always state on the ticket exactly whats wrong like hem needs attention or button missing, but for new trendy clothes at about half price its well worth spending a little time repairing the garment.    Im not sure what the Charity shops do with the all the goods they dont actually sell in the shops, they must select them out, I dont know whether they pass them round, send them for recycling or what.     Books are a really good hit in the charity shops, ok youre not going to find the very latest publications, but they usually have a good selection and perfect for reference books.     The shops like the YMCA and we have a local Hospice shop are more  quot;rummagie quot; where you can sift through boxes of stuff which adds to the fun because youre not sure what you might find.     Accessories like scarves and belts and things I have found sometimes you can find things that are a little more unusual than you would by in a chain store.     Oxfam and a few of the others sell some quite nice new goods, so if you were buying anyway its nice to know that some of the money will go to charity.     I dont know whether youve noticed but some of the Charity shops smell really nice, I think thats what puts people off sometimes, because some of them can smell very  quot;fusty quot; I tend to hurry out of those shops.     I must admit now that about half the clothes I buy are from charity shops, some of the best dressed women around locally use charity shops   i know this sounds awful but Id rather wear a designer t-shirt from a charity shop than a naf t-shirt from QS theyre going to cost around the same.     Recently I have never entered an empty charity shop, there are always people browsing, but i have been in Etams and BHS lately and there hasnt been another soul in there.  Maybe people are wising up at last.     I think its a great idea when someone has got fed up with something or made a bad purchase that someone else can have the benefit of it, but sometimes I look and think its criminal what people throw away in this consumer society.    Anyway I shall continue to scour the Charity Shops for a bargain knowing i might be doing someone else some good somewhere.          .          ', '    The first charity shop was opened on Broad Street, Oxford in February 1948 by Oxfam.  The shop remains but today it is accompanied by thousands of others all over the country and each shop with a needy cause.I along with many other people am in favour of charity shops and feel they do a great deal of good, not just for the charities they support but how they influence a variety of peoples life   s in many ways.  In this opinion, I intend to tell you how.HELP OTHERS IN NEEDEvery time you visit a charity shop and make a purchase the majority of that money will go to the charity.  For example if you purchased two shirts from Oxfam for    6.99 that, money could buy 36 fruit trees that could be planted in Burkino Faso.  Just imagine how that could make a village prosper.  It would produce more food and more jobs.Therefore, from just a small purchase you really could affect many people   s life   s including your own.BARGAINSOf course, another reason why some people love charity shops is getting a bargain.  The buzz of finding a top you want or the book you have been looking for is satisfying.  I bought a brand new dress from a charity shop last year.  I had numerous compliments from friends asking where I had it from and how much it was, when I told them they were very surprised.  Some people have a misconception that clothes in charity shops are scruffy and old and it is just not true   Clothes in charity shops are checked thoroughly for marks and holes before sale. Any old clothes are thrown away.People who do not have very much money can also benefit greatly from charity shops as they can afford clothes and shoes for their family at a much cheaper price than clothes stores.VOLUNTEERSCharity shops would not be here at all, if there was not enough volunteers to run them.  The people who work in charity shops put a great deal of effort and hard work into their jobs and should be highly commended.The People who choose to be a volunteer worker in a charity shop often find it gives them a new lease of life, more confidence and a chance to meet new people.  The charities are very accommodating to whom they employ.  They often invite the elderly and people with learning difficulties to work for them as well as many other volunteers.  To me this is wonderful as these people are often discriminated against in other areas of work and are now being given more of a chance.As you can see from just one visit or donation to a charity shop you can help yourself and so many other people from all areas of life.  So when you are out shopping on Saturday go and have a look inside.  There might be a bargain with your name on it      ', '    One of my favourite shops in the world is Oxfam. I totally adore it. I regularly visit the Chester store on Frodgham Street. In this store I find a wide range of clothes, with many different sizes and styles to suit any tastes. I have recently bought a gorgeous long black coat from the shop which was made by Warehouse. It s absolutely stunning and the quality is amazing. I bought it for just a snippet at four pounds and twenty-five pence  What a bargain  I have also recently picked up a few nice tops from the Chester store which have been of great use for going out to clubs and pubs, and also for everyday ware. Another fantastic thing about Oxfam is that you can get some great collectors items in there at a very low price. About a month ago I bought an old LP from there which turned out to be a collector s item and I sold it for more than fifty pounds- I bought it originally for fifty pence   Oxfam also does a great range of food goods. Ranging from coffee, to lentils, to chocolate  And what s more they all come direct from the people who make them in poorer countries. The food is not over priced, and is delicious. It s worth every penny for the taste and the help you re giving to thousands of people in poverty. I would highly recommend CafeDirect. It s a gorgeous blend if coffee beans with a rich aroma. Far better than any of the other brand names you ll find, which all exploit the people who grow the beans. And of course the main reason you should shop there: IT S ALL FOR CHARITY. The cause is fantastic. With you, the  consumers, help, Oxfam  does so much work for needy people. So there s no reason not to shop there   Happy shopping      ', '    Imagine wearing dead people s clothes? I always thought when people told me they went to a charity shop. A little while ago, I d have never even dreamt of setting foot inside a charity shop. I had a vision of some old spinster behing a MFI table with odds and sods which would have looked bad even on Madonna (and would be about the only place she wouln t shop fot that  new image ).However, it was only when I had to do something for charity in college, and not being the type to run half way around the earth or make a fool of myself in public, I decided (reluctantly) to help out in the local Heart Foundation shop. This is itself, was one of the most embarasing things to do in the name of charity, but I had to do something.And so at 9.30 Monday morning I tramped into the shop. My first of many suprises was how bright and freindly it was. Sure, there are a few old dears who came in buying tweed skirts, but they were actually reall friendly and a good laugh. I also found a book donated that dated from 1933, which was found to be able to fetch the charity a lot of money.But my biggest suprise was when my best friend came to the till with a few odd coursework books and a armful of new-looking clothes. She always looked so carefully dressed. Anyway, she nearly died of shame when she saw me, and i learnt she bought a lot of stuff (not only clothes, but books, home things ect.) at charity shops.And so that is what gave me some confience to go and shop in them. i have been in a few which where a big yucky, but the majourity of them cater for all tastes, budgets and needs at such great value. It also makes you feel good knowing that some little kid in Africa has survived another day because of you.It s simply a glourified way of recycling. When I don t need anything any more, I donate it to the shop. When I do, I can buy a lot of things ona  much smaller budget. I m certainly not ashamed, and for any of you who don t like the idea of wearing dirty clothes, when I was helping out I saw the amazing amount of work that went on. All clotes are washed twice, ironed, checked and steamed before sale, and if they don t meet a set standard are thrown away.So please, whether it s donating time to help out, old stuff to sell or your custom, give your local Oxfam a try. It s not as glamouros as Harvey Nicks (and you don t get a posh bag), but you can be assured to be able to spare some cash to enjoy on a Friday night.     ', '    I m a big fan of charity shops, and lucky for me my high street is full of them. I regularly pop in to see if there are any bargains to be had. My favourite shops are Save The Children, Drink Sense and Oxfam. Obviously some times there is nothing to be had and yet other times you will see an absolute bargain. I mainly look out for ornaments especially brass, I ve picked up loads of beautiful pieces of brass over the years. They are the type of things you would never see in the shops. My favourite piece is two elephants copulating I picked this up for only 50p. I also get books for my daughter as she is a big book fan, she has been delighted with some of the stuff I pick up, I ve got educational text books, and horror books which she loves, charity shops seem to be especially good for old education books and car maintance books.In addition I ve picked up all most new clothes for next to nothing, and it s not rubbish it s all modern stuff. I also get teddies for my two dogs, and if I see a decent board game I get it for my grandchildren. When you shop in a charity shop, you get stuff at bargain basement prices, and best of all you are helping charities.      ', '    Advantage; It is quick and easy.Disadvantage; No time to prepare.I really like this book as it has some fantastic recipes in. It has different sections in for different types of food for example my favourite sections are pasta, rice and noodles, puddings and drinks and starters. Other sections in the book are vegetarian and side dishes, fish and seafood, poultry and meat, pizza and bread and the basics. Each section is good and most recipes even have a picture which i think makes it look more presentable and helps me choose which  one i d rather choose. I really enjoy cooking and this book really helps me to do that.  I would really recommend this book especially if you like to eat healthy and dont have a lot of time on your hands   Try it and let me know what you think of it its great for me, and sometimes when i get a bit more time on my hands i blend in a few recipes together.      ']

s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
If you’re into sustainable shopping and love the thrill of a good bargain, charity shops are absolute gold mines—especially in wealthier neighborhoods where the quality tends to be noticeably better. Don’t be discouraged if you don’t find your dream item on the first visit; stock rotates frequently, so persistence really pays off. Plus, the variety is impressive—from clothes and handbags to books, toys, and homeware, there’s always something unique waiting to be discovered.

One of the best parts? Charity shops often have well-organized, clean items, with clothes checked for quality and cleanliness before hitting the shelves. Still, a careful eye is essential—inspect everything for wear or damage to avoid surprises later. This patience is part of the fun and makes the eventual find all the more rewarding.

If you’re like me and enjoy putting your own spin on things, charity shop finds are perfect canvases for customization. Whether it’s tweaking a vintage jacket or upcycling a handbag, these pieces let you express your individuality while keeping fashion ethical and sustainable.

Beyond the bargains and creativity, shopping at charity shops feels good on a deeper level. You’re supporting causes that matter and helping people in need, all while avoiding the wastefulness of fast fashion. The friendly volunteers running these shops often go above and beyond, making the experience welcoming and community-driven.

In short, charity shopping is a win-win: affordable, eco-friendly, and full of potential for unique style. Just bring your patience, a sharp eye, and a bit of DIY spirit—you’ll walk away with treasures that are as meaningful as they are stylish.

product_reviews: ['    My local Co-Op  Swift shop  opened a couple of years ago. Before this it was an Alldays, the chain was taken over by the Co-Op. ', '    Our local Co-op store has a great advantage over our Somerfield, it is nearer and larger.The staff aren t too bad, some are a bit grumpy but you can get a smile out of some of them. spend all the money on petrol and busses, to go to the supermarkets.P.S. i have put the address in there, come say hello to me on the butchery counter, you will see how lovely and polite i really am LOL :):)     ', '    The co-operative movement has its roots in the 19th Century when the industrial revolution resulted in widespread exploitation and misery for many working people.The first retail outlet was accredited to pioneers in Rochdale in 1844, although there had been earlier attempts.The Pioneers opened a shop in Toad lane Rochdale, selling unadulterated goods at a reasonable price.In 1860 the Rochdale Pioneers drafted their values with which they would trade, and these included:    Open and voluntary membership     Democratic control (one member one vote)     Fixed and limited interest on share capital     Surplus allocated in proportion to members  purchases     Provision for education     Co-operation amongst co-operatives     Political neutrality     No credit     Quality goods and serviceDuring the last century however, the co-operative movement has undergone many changes in order to meet the challenge posed by other retailers, including combining to create larger and more efficient organisations. Today, there are about 48 retail co-operative societies in the United Kingdom ranging in size from small  one shop  society s to giants with sales of over    3 billionThe company supposedly retain the values they set in the early days even today (so they say). I expect by now your thinking wow what a wonderful store?Well it did used to be a good efficient store in my hometown of Haverhill, which has had a co-op for as long as I can remember. They maybe lead the way with the buy one get one free offers. But the store in the town lacks many things. It is dull and dismal for a start. When I complained about the lack of disabled trolleys initially over two years ago, they assured me they were on order. After over two years of waiting and complaining, they still have not materialised.Of course this may not be the norm in all stores, but in our local HAVERHILL store bad management has filtered all the way through, and staff are disgruntled and unhappy.The co-op avoid it  8230;  8230;  8230;  8230;.     ', '    Many people who criticise the co-op are probably unaware of just how socially responsible this organisation is. While I agree with many people that it is nothing special as a shop I do think more consideration should be given to its aims and policies when making an evaluation.The Co-op food and retail stores are just part of a much wider co-operative network which is actually worldwide.The roots of the Co-operative movement go back to the 19th century when the industrial revolution caused hardship and suffering for many workers. Social reformers introduced trade unions to assist workers but it is the Rochdale Pioneers who were responsible for starting the first co-op in 1844 to stop the exploitation and adulteration of foodstuffs also prevalent at the time. The values and policies, which they established, form the basis for most co-ops now, found throughout the world.All co-ops are businesses but with a difference. A co-operative is   8220;an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social and cultural needs and aspirations though a jointly owned and democratically controlled enterprise.  8221;Now it would be possible to argue that co-ops are no longer needed in this day and age. People aren  8217;t exploited and food isn  8217;t adulterated, at least in this country. But more so today than ever this is highly debatable   8211; food is constantly tampered with in one way and another. But the co-op has always quietly but continuously been concerned and involved in actively ensuring that consumer  8217;s needs are met. Not only does it have its own ethical policies on all the areas which affect the consumer it also actively campaigns to challenge injustice and bad practice.The co-ops Webster contains detailed information on the co-op  8217;s policies on consumer issues. It contains very detailed explanations of the current law and general practice followed by the co-op  8217;s own policy and any action they are taking. With regard to irradiation, for example, it states that the co-op does not sell any irradiated foods.Another way the co-op shows its social concern is the way it continues to operate shops in local communities. As more and more local supermarkets close as a result of competition from the large out of town supermarkets it is the co-op which seems to take them on. This is a deliberate policy.Finally, the co-op tries wherever possible to support other co-operatives. Some of the co-ops in our area stock excellent ranges of whole-foods supplied by local co-operatives packed in very simple packaging, and other similar products. I have never found these in any of the major supermarkets. Fair trade produce is also stocked as a matter of policy.So in many ways I think it is unfair to compare the co-op with the more popular superstores because its aims are quite different. Big stores like Tesco  8217;s and Sainsbury  8217;s have national and local initiatives to support schools and other projects but the co-op have always had a genuine interest in the community and continue to do so but does not make such a big deal of it.Our village has a small co-op which is probably typical. It is nothing special but the most important thing is that it is there. For those without transport it offers a good selection of products at reasonable prices. It usually has all the BOGOF offers which are available in the bigger stores and it certainly has far better prices than other local stores. If there is something which you want regularly that they do not stock they will order it for you and I have always found the staff very friendly and helpful.I have recently been in two larger local co-op supermarkets and was pleasantly surprised at the range of foods on offer. The larger stores at least seem to be making some effort to change their old fashioned image. The deli counters, fresh ready meals and in-store French bread and patisserie are particularly good. One quirky little thing I have found in nearly all Co-op supermarkets is the way they display small household gadgets, toys and other odds and ends all around the store hanging from the shelves. I don  8217;t know if this is local to the area where I live or is common elsewhere. It reminds me of homely, old fashioned general store and maybe I am old fashioned too but I think its rather fun.If you are interested why not take a look at http://www.co-op.co.uk/     ', '    Everything you could possibly need last minute under one roof. From bottle openers to Roald Dahl s  quot;George s Marvellous Medicine quot;. I love the Co-op. The store itself is clean and well stocked and the late opening times are ideal (From 8am til 10pm ). Although the store is more expensive than a larger chain store such as Sainsburys, if you do not want to travel far, then this is the place to go. Unfortunately, I have yet to witness another store in my local area so I guess I m just lucky that my town is blessed with a Co-op Furthermore, being a smaller shop, queues are often during peak times, which is a huge disadvantage when you ve been standing up on the tube for an hour and just want to get home and put your feet up  In saying this, the queues are never huge and you should never expect a wait longer that 15 minutes. ', '    There has been a motion.  Or perhaps I should say a commotion as the Co-op has finally got its act together and had a shuffle at the top.  Put simply they ve done away with the old fuddy duddies and brought in some bright new sparks who still maintain the old Co-op ideals.  What this means for us lucky Co-op shoppers is a new approach to the way the Co-op is working.  One such instance (and I apologise that I am only referring to the Oxford Swindon and Gloucester Co-op here) is the introduction of what they have called village stores.  These are a new style of the old Co-op small store and is usually involving revamping old stores with new interiors and a rather neat looking blue exterior.  These stores also carry a larger range than previously with more shelf fillers to keep the stocks up.  The first store in my area opened recently in Evesham (a nearby village) and generated much interest from the press aswell as from customers and seems to have taken well with the punters as takings have increased almost 40  since the same time last year.Does this bode well for us in general though?  The Co-op also has major relaunch plans for other stores, most notably their superstore in Swindon which has seen a massive revamp in the last few months which has made the store even more accessable to diabled customers aswell as making it look really fantastic for all the rest of us.That brings me rather swiftly onto the difference between the Co-op and other food retailers.  The main point is that they are run by the people, for the people.  The customers are often share holders and they are free to run for election in any of the societies key positions if they like.  If the customers don t like what they see, they can vote at a monthly meeting and have it changed.  They also get the reward of monthly reduced rates so for one day in this month for instance they gave out 3  off vouchers to all members.  Not a bad deal really.The Co-op is also driven by community and not by profit.  This doesnt mean they dont want to make money, but you will find that a large percentage of their income actually goes to local causes.  In their own internal newsletter they detail awards of    400 to a school for a new pond area,    350 to a community project for the blind and    700 to a project for deaf children.  They support far more in small ways and donate so much money to good causes it would be impossible for me to list them all here.This means that purchasing your goods at the Co-op is supporting your local area and the charities and schemes within that area.  Another good point and one that probably keeps about 50  of their customers there.The Co-op actually works as a coallition of many small stores.  The idea was that 5 greengrocers wanted to order goods in the beginning.  By order a sack of potatoes each they paid about 20p - meaning    1 in total.  But when they asked the price of buying 5 bags, they found it was 80p.  They soon realised that by joining together they could save money on their spuds so they all grouped together and paid a set amount to a nominated driver who then went and got their 5 sacks and dished them out accordingly.  Obviously it was more complicated than that but this advantage gained from  bulk buying  was the humble beginnings of the Co-op movement.  It now has so many stores its scary to count and the main trading office is in Manchester, where all goods are ordered collectively.  Each Co-op places their order at Manchester which then makes one large order and distributes it fairly between the stores.  The movement was made mainly of local workers and people who cared about their community and so it all began.Today the Co-op is struggling to match the prices of Tesco and Asda who have outpriced them by a large margin in their price wars, but their prices are by no means unreasonable. Of course you will always get the bad egg in the bunch but on the whole the staff are good people.The shops are often centred around making money in the same ways as Tesco and Sainsbury s but you will notice a huge difference when you go to look at some of the stock.  They have all the brand named goods and they are the same as anywhere else, but if you look closely at their own label goods you will notice something.As the Co-op is so dedicated to the community and being fair to all, you will notice a large amount of fair trades food, often far greater than Sainsbury s and Tesco.  Be it wine, lager, peas or tea you will no doubt find a fair trade product on it, and if you want to look at Co-ops own brand (which isnt tested on animals ) then you will also notice that they are similar in their fair trade values. If you care to peruse the plastic cased products such as cleaning fluids and bleach you will notice that the labels all have braille on them to help the blind.  Another sign of their attention to detail.IF you do manage to spot anything that could be improved and have a suggestion on how to improve it then they have a freephone helpline you can call or you can simply speak to the store manager.  If your problem is at store level (you feel shelves are too high or a matter wasnt dealt with well by the staff) then there are new books you can write in.  Not only do you get to write in their small box but within a week a response from the store manager is promised.  I have seen some of these responses and they are usually quite helpful. You might want to worry about the milk which arrives about 4 hours before many of the stores open, so it may have been standing outside a while before it goes on the shelves.  This isnt a problem in Winter when its cold outside anyway but in the summer you might want to watch out for floating black bits   Its the same at any supermarket though, its just the way life is.You will usually find that if you ask a memeber of staff something they will be able to answer and if not then they will try to find someone who can help.
