product_reviews: ['     A week off of University and online travel agents, what a great combination  Thoroughly fed up with London transport and the traumas of reading Chaucer I was desperate for a break, and whilst my budget wouldn   t stretch to faraway shores and winter sun, a hop across the channel with my boyfriend seemed a great idea. Two weeks before departure we booked our trip with www.expedia.co.uk; three nights (mid-week) in a 5 star Amsterdam hotel with flights from London Heathrow cost us just    145 each. I highly recommend Expedia for ease of booking and great service, as well as offering astounding value getaways to destinations all over the world; and if you want to organise your accommodation yourself, Expedia offers flights from less than    60 return including all taxes. We flew with bMi but many other operators fly to Amsterdam including easyjet and British Airways. The reputation of Amsterdam is a somewhat seedy one, characterised by its liberal approach to soft drugs (epitomised in the renowned    coffee    shops) and its sprawling legal red light district, where the prostitutes even have their own union,    The Red Thread   . Whilst many people visit the city simply to sample the    menus    of cannabis available in the (unsurprisingly, when you think about it) laid-back brown cafes, there is plenty more on offer for the tourist apart from the smell of hash that haunts Dutch streets and British halls of residence alike.  Amsterdam itself combines the charm of a compact centre with the busy and vibrant lifestyle of a cosmopolitan city. You can easily travel across the centre on foot or using the vast tram network. We found the trams very easy to use; you can either buy single tickets on most trams or a money-saving strip from transport offices; for 6euros you get a strip of fifteen tickets, with most single journeys within the city costing two tickets. Another way to get about is via the canals, with tours taking you around the city on a boat costing from    5 per person. Amsterdam is famous for its canals, lined by houseboats and streets of tall narrow houses, many dating back from the 17th century. One particular stretch of canal is lined by a vast flower market popular with tourists and locals alike where you can buy both fresh and artificial flowers and souvenirs to suit every budget     it   s definitely the place to go to buy something for your mum  Wherever you are in Amsterdam be very alert as you walk along     not because of pickpockets, which are not a particularly common problem in the city, but because of the leagues of manic cyclists that show very little concern for any unsuspecting tourist who dares to cross their path  Amsterdam and Holland in general are ideal for the cyclist as they are very flat and have many cycle lanes, and if you want to hire a bicycle then they are available very cheaply from numerous agents.Amsterdam is home to many museums great and small, with its art galleries being particularly popular with tourists. The Rijksmuseum is home to works by all of the Dutch masters, and if you ever studied art at school then you   re bound to recognise some the paintings  The same applies to the Van Gogh Museum; when we went here it was very very busy with parties of school children so is perhaps better to visit off-peak. Entrance to these museums costs approximately    6 each. Having had our cultural fix, we decided to pay a visit to one of Amsterdam   s top attractions;    The Heineken Experience   . This was fantastic value; for    5 you got to tour the old Heineken factories and enjoy some    interactive    exhibitions which included a simulator ride emulating travelling on a horse over cobbled streets; a bit sore on the rear if you know what I mean  The best parts of the experience however surely had to be the three free glasses of Heineken you got as you proceeded through the tour, and at the end you were given a free Heineken glass in a souvenir tin so you could relive the Heineken experience in the comfort of your own home. I recommend    The Heineken Experience    even if you   re not a lager fan as soft drinks are available and it was a fun way of passing a couple of hours. Just outside of the Heineken factory is a pancake restaurant where we ate some delicious pancakes (a Dutch delicacy) smothered in sweet fillings including cherries and cointreau     yum yum  Pancakes and sweet treats of every kind are available on every street in Amsterdam, and I dare you to resist a sweet, sticky waffle  Eating out in Amsterdam isn   t particularly cheap, but if you look around then it is possible to have a three course meal and drinks for under    20 per head. Thanks to the Lonely Planet guide we found a fantastic restaurant where for only 40euros (less than    30) we had an Indian feast including naan, poppadums, a mixed plate of starters and vast portions of garlic chicken, vegetable curry and delicious delicately flavoured rice. If you enjoy Indian food then I urge you to check out    Shiva    at Reguliersdwarsstraat 72, just off of the Rembrandtsplein     it is a truly divine eating experience, but be sure to arrive early as seating is limited and when we ate there the restaurant was full by about 7pm. Visiting mid-week we didn   t really get to experience Amsterdam   s notorious nightlife, but I have been told that Melkweg and Sinners in Heaven are some of the most popular and fashionable clubs in the city. I personally found alcohol to be quite expensive     in one bar on the Rembrandtsplein, a well known area for nightlife, a Malibu and coke cost about    5.50, a little steep by any standards, and to a student on a tight budget, shocking  Beer is the cheapest drink by far, but be warned standard Dutch drinks are about the size of a half pint; for a pint be sure to ask for a large beer.  As Amsterdam is well known for both its attitudes to sex and drugs and its cultural museums, it seems only natural that there are museums devotes to both Sex and Hash. We couldn   t resist visiting the Erotic Museum    Venustemple    on the Damrak; the main street that leads from Centraal Station to Dam Square. For only 2.50euros you get to explore three floors of exhibits relating to everything sexual; pornographic photos from throughout history prove that the Victorians were far more randy than their prim and proper image suggests, whilst clips of early pornographic movies show that anyone who says    it wasn   t like this in the old days    is obviously lying  There is a moving figure of a flasher and other animated figures carry out acts of a varying level of obscenity, whilst a slightly more cultural feel is provided by phallic artefacts from the Roman age and Ancient Egypt. Most of the Museum isn   t really that offensive, but for those of a sensitive disposition the most explicit exhibits are confined to a room at the back marked out by a warning sign. We stayed in the 5 star Hotel Barbizon Palace; this had an ideal location right opposite Centraal Station and only a 5 minute walk from the very centre of the city. Walking through the town at night it   s impossible to avoid the Red Light District, where women dressed in bikinis stand in large windows lit by a red light, displaying their wares for all to see. Surprisingly its not as seedy as you would imagine; in Holland prostitution is supported by the government and the women pay taxes just the same as any other worker.  Amsterdam is a great destination for a mini-break no matter what your tastes or interests; from high culture to non-stop partying, the city has it all. With fantastic value deals on flights / accommodation available via the internet, then it really is the ideal place to get away on a tight budget. If you   ve got a little more disposable income then Amsterdam is also the ideal destination for a shopping extravaganza, with several streets lined with every kind of retailer varying from huge department stores and exclusive designer boutiques to cheap and cheerful fashion shops and more shoes, jewellery and accessories than you could wear in a lifetime. Some say that if you remember too much about Amsterdam then you haven   t really seen it at all  Whether or not you agree with this its certainly worth a visit whether for your first or fiftieth time     there   s so much to explore by day and by night, and its only an hour from London by air.       ', '    I went to Amsterdam in February half-term with my mother - I m 31, and she s 60.  We re not interested in drugs, sex shops or loud nightclubs, so if you re interested in a review of those, then you may as well stop reading.  All I can give is my perspective of a short stay in a city I loved, and reviews of some of the things we saw and did.Firstly, arrival in Schipol Airport: the airport seemed much less crowded and bewildering than Heathrow, but then, most places do.  It was the only time my suitcase has been waiting for me on the carousel by the time I got off the plane and into the baggage hall.  We went from plane to outside the airport in about fifteen minutes.  We had chosen to pre-book a transfer by car to our hotel, which was a really pleasant extra. We were met by a very friendly Dutch guy, who carried our luggage and drove us in luxury to our hotel with 20 minutes.  Having said that, there is a train station directly within the airport, and the link to Central Station in Amsterdam seems very quick and easy.The centre of Amsterdam was laid out pre-1600, and the Singel canal was the boundary of the city. However, the growing population needed more space, and they dug three more canals in a horseshoe-shape around the centre. The Herengracht, which is where our hotel was situated,  was the first of these, and was financed by wealthy merchants who built stunning houses along the length of the canal.  Our hotel was converted from two of these 17th Century houses.  There were very high ceilings, large windows overlooking the canals, oak beams and beautiful marble floors.Most of the streets are fairly narrow, but feel much wider and more open than they would otherwise do, because of the canals. None of the buildings are higher than five storeys, because the soft ground won t support the weight. Because of this, most of the buildings have very narrow fronts (most around 9 feet), although the real sign of wealth in the 17th and 18th Centuries was to have a double-width house.  I was surprised that there was very little in the way of a barrier to stop cars, bikes, or drunks falling in the canals: there is a rail about ten inches from the ground, but no walls or fences that I could see, other than on the bridges. We spent a lot of time just ambling around the streets, looking at the buildings and discovering quirky little side-streets and unusual shops. As many other reviewers have said though: beware of the bicycles   We found it very easy to avoid the drugs and sleaze. Maybe we weren t in the wrong (right?) areas, but the women in windows are easily avoided, and we didn t see any obvious drug dealers or dodgy looking characters. On the whole, I felt much safer than I do in London or Glasgow.  As for some of the main things I d recommend, let me describe a few:***Rijksmuseum***The Rijksmuseum is listed in every guidebook as an essential. However, if you are one of those people who likes a decent painting, but isn t so keen that you want to spend all day looking at every single thing in detail, then I definitely recommend the Rijksmuseum before the end of 2004.  We were warned that they are currently refurbishing the museum, and that most of the collection is not viewable. However, until January 2005 there is a smaller  Highlights of the Rijksmuseum  exhibition in a wing of the building, which I think was actually much better.  We got to see all the most well-known and beautiful paintings, without having to trek around miles of gallery space and seeing every single thing. I find that an hour and a half is quite enough for me in a gallery - more than that and I start to get lost or bored.  As it was, the cut-down Rijksmuseum was perfect.  And at a fraction of the cost of the normal entry, it was a bargain. (I think adult entry was 5 Euros.)My favourite part of the Rijksmuseum were the Vermeer paintings - much smaller than I d expected, but the colours and impression of light were awesome.  Worth the entry just for those.***Van Gogh Museum***The Van Gogh Museum is worth getting to early - we arrived at 10 am and there was no queue at all. When we left there was a long queue around the building. Entry was 9 Euros for adults.The building is modern and very spacious. There were 140 primary school children in when we visited (which the museum helpfully pointed out to us before we paid, so we could come back later if we d wanted to), but we hardly noticed them on the way round.The exhibitions feature hundreds of Van Gogh s paintings and drawings. It really is stunning to see so many famous paintings all in one room, and the colour and movement in his work is just out of this world.***Anne Frank House***Many others have reviewed this in detail, so I won t start repeating them. Suffice to say that it is an essential and very worthwhile visit - very moving and extremely well done.  Entry was about 9 Euros, and we spent about an hour and a half going round.***Canal Bus***We paid 15 Euros for a day ticket, which meant we could use the Canal Bus as often as we wanted all day, and up to 12.00 the following day.  There are three routes that circle the canals, and cover most of the main places of interest.  The boats were warm and comfortable, and the glass roof meant that we got a great view of the canal houses, which was an interesting change from the view from street level.***Metz   Co***I can recommend the cafe on the top floor of Metz   Co, a department store on the corner of Leidsestraat and the Keizersgracht.  Excellent, reasonably priced food, and wonderful views over Amsterdam.  Just don t be tempted to look at their very expensive handbags on your way out of the shop ***Flower Market***I assumed that there would be very little in the way of flowers in February, but I was pleasantly surprised by the Bloemenmarkt.  Easily found, located on the Singel and between Koningsplein and Muntplein, the flower market had huge displays of tulips at ridiculously cheap prices. Sadly there was no point buying any, but I did buy some tulip bulbs. Again, the choice was huge, and the prices extremely low. The stall I bought mine from had an enormous range of pick n mix tulip bulbs, with 30 bulbs costing only 5 Euros. There were types I had never seen before in England, including a pure black tulip, bright blue ones, and frilly purple ones, as well as the more traditional colours.Finding places to eat was easy - there are loads of restaurants to suit all budgets and tastes. We had some excellent meals, one very reasonably priced, one mid-range, and one that was wickedly expensive but worth every penny.On thing I would recommend more than anything else, if you decide to go to Amsterdam in winter - take a scarf   When that wind whistles down the canals, it can get VERY cold.  Be warned Overall, I think Amsterdam was one of the nicest cities I ve visited, and I m dying to go back. ', '    As luck would have it, a few weeks before my birthday, we got the news that we had won a mini-cruise from Newcastle upon Tyne to Amsterdam. This solved the dilemma of how to celebrate my birthday and we decided to extend the trip to include a night in Amsterdam. If we had just gone for the straight package as offered in the prize, we would have had only 6 hours in the city before sailing back home again.I will not give full details of the crossings either way (the review is about Amsterdam after all), suffice it to say that I will never be a sailor and that if I ever mention going on a boat trip again, you have my permission to shoot me We were deposited opposite the central station and decided to head straight for the hotel to drop off our bags. A one-day ticket costs around 7 Euros and gives you unlimited travel on buses, underground and trams. Trams are an especially good way to travel because the next station is announced by the driver and also on a small screen. The trams and buses are clean and frequent - we didn t use the underground - and a pleasure to use. You must remember to validate your ticket when you make the first journey by stamping it in one of the machines on the vehicle.If you want to do as the natives do, then there are plenty of cylce rental shops and there are literally thousands of cycle racks to secure them. Do be careful with regards to crossing roads and the combination of cars, trams and cyclists can be quite confusing and trams do have a tendency to creep up quietly from behind Our hotel, the Quentin England (Roemer Visscherstraat) was situated in a quiet mixed residential/hotel area near the Leidsplein and within easy walking distance of the Museum Quarter and the main shopping area.We were greeted warmly and checked in quickly with minimal fuss. All the Dutch people we met were friendly and helpful and genuinely keen to provide a high level of hospitality. (Again I am talking about the city as a whole so will not dwell on the hotel, except to say it was comfortable, clean and not too expensive at around 45 Euros for a double room for one night, with private facilities).First stop was for refreshment and food and, as the heavens had opened, we dived into the nearest place which happened to be an  English style  pub, The Three Sisters, on the Leidsplein. All these themed places tend to serve the same food- sandwiches, toasties, etc and are fairly expensive ( around 7 Euros for a toastie) but you have to remember you are in a capital city.  If you prefer something more trditional there are loads of coffee shops and cafes serving various light meals and snacks which are usually a bit cheaper than the themed places.Amsterdam has culture in abundance. It s a really arty city - not only are there the famous museums and galleries but there are also  art restaurants and cafes  where you can view works and even buy if you wish, not to mention the smaller galleries on every street and lane.The Dutch are very proud of the artistic heritage, nowhere more so than in the Rijksmuseum and the Van Gogh Museum. The Rijksmuseum is about to close for a long time just before the end of 2003 for major works and some of the galleries are already closed. If you are going befoer the end of December 2003 check with the Museum for details. Even if you cannot go to the Rijksmuseum it is worth going along to see the building itself: it is immense and truly impressive with intricate spires and turrets and fantaastic carvings. In the centre are two huge vaulted arches/walkways and this is a good way to get to the Van Gogh Museum.  Emerging from the arches, cut through the scenic park follow the signs for the VG Museum, turning right for the entrance.The Van Gogh Museum is a very modern building with very light and modern exhibition spaces which suit VGs work well.  The ground floor is dedicated to the life of VG and includes exhibits relating to his family, etc. The next floor is a chronological exhibition of his works including well-known pieces such as  The Potato Eaters  and  Bedroom at Arles . The top floor includes more works by VG and contemporaries who were influenced by his work. When we visited it was very busy - partly, I think because of the bad weather - but I get the impression that it is always fairly busy. This can be quite frustrating becuase it can result in big queues to see the more well-known works and the pace does not always move as you would like. Entry is around  9 Euros  but there are various discounts for Amsterdam card holders and students, etc. Another top attraction is Anne Frank s House on Prinsengracht near the Westkerke. You enter through the new visitors centre which is very informative. This is a very moving place, especially when you go into Anne s own room and see the pictures on the wall which Anne  cut out of magazines and pasted to the wall. Again, delays do build up so make sure you leave enough time to do the place justice. I would advise around 90 minutes. Entry here is 6 Euros 50 for adults.Amsterdam is great for shopaholics and shops tend to be grouped according to content. The main shopping area has all the international chains (H M, Shoe Locker, etc) and lots of shoe shops - several have a few branches of the same chain on just one street.Utrechtstraat is the place to go for quirky gifts and unusual kitchen equipment/plates,etc.Just past here is Waterlooplein where a flea market is held most days which sells all manner of goods and includes good second hand clothing stalls.Near the Heineken Brewery is the Albert Cuyp Market which is similar to the one on the Waterlooplein but in addtion there are some fantastic shops in this area. In particular there are sevral vintage clothing shops and super antique/kitsch collectibles emporia.Not everything has to cost money in Amsterdam however. It is very enjoyable simply to walk around the streets along the canals taking in the atmosphere. The houses are beautiful and although built in the typical Dutch townhouse style, each one has it  s own quirks. Some of the houses look as if they are about to topple into the canal or fall aginst a neighbour. When evening falls the most popular attraction is probably the red-light district. I thought I wouldn t bother but then curiosity got the better of me.  I would say keep to the main street where it is more sanitised and be careful if you go off into any of the narrow alleys, where there seem to be lots of dubious looking men hanging around, either to sell drugs or to lure punters away from the security of the legalised sex industry into something more seedy.Basically you walk from one end of the street to the other and look at bored-looking young women sitting in red-lit windows. Some were even chatting on their mobile phones  Much more fun are the sex shops and even if you re not comfortable going in, they have such good window displays you don t need to. Really...the mind boggles Restaurants of every kind abound in Amsterdam and like the shops, they are arranged according to type of cuisine so in the Leidsplein for example you will find one street lined with Argentinian and Uruguayan steakhouses and another with several Mexican joints.Another very popular cuisine is Indonesian with one such cafe or restaurant on every street.  However, we plumped for seafood and chose the Oysterbar on the Leidsplein. However there were no tables downstairs and we were advised to try upstairs. This seemed to be OK but when we were given the meuns for the sister restuarant  At Night  we soon found out that it is much more expensive than it s more casual counterpart beneath. However, the food was wonderful and it was my birhday after all. A meal for two with starters (a dozen oysters ) and a bottle of house white cost just under 90 Euros. Well, you re only 32 once Alas we did not get as far as any clubs on this occasion - we were far too tired after the slap-up meal but we did have a few drinks before turning in.  Amsterdam pubs and bars are friendly places and there doesn t seem to be any trouble. Everyone is welcome and you can find something to suit everyone in this cosmopolitan city. It seems to me that although it is quite a youthful city, older people will not feel that they are squeezed out like in some cities as far as nightlife is concerned. I would recommend a visit to Amsterdam to anyone. It is a friendly and convivial place, just the right size to navigate and has activities and attractions to suit all tatse and budgets.     ', '    I ve been to Amsterdam Airport more times than I can remember.  Living in Cardiff, taking the KLM flight to Schiphol and changing was quicker than going all the way to London.  But I d never actually left the airport, I was always just there in transit.  To be honest, I d never felt any great pull to leave the airport and look around the city.  I love culture but I d never thought of Amsterdam as having lots of old churches and museums for me to look around.  I d always associated it more with the Red Light District and  coffeeshops  which didn t really interest me.Then I got a call from a friend saying that she was planning a girls trip to Amsterdam.   How do I get out of this one  I thought.  Another friend persuaded me, saying that she would accompany me to the  boring  parts while the rest of them drank to their hearts content GETTING THERE:Amsterdam is a hub for connecting flights and therefore lots of UK airports fly there.  I looked for a flight from Cardiff with KLM (to get my airmiles ) but it was over    100.  I checked with Easyjet from Bristol and they only charged    70 return - that s better   The airlines and airports which fly there are too numerous to list but shop around and you can find good bargains.  Remember that using KLM to connect from Amsterdam may be cheaper, but a ticket just to Amsterdam can sometimes almost be as expensive as one that will take you all the way to New York via Schphol.TRANSPORT ONCE THERE:I found the transport very good.  The odd train was delayed slightly but living in Britain I expect nothing less   The trains from the airport go every 10 minutes and cost 3.60 Euros one way. Remember to have it stamped or validate it yourself in the yellow machines when you board the tram.THE EXPERIENCE AND WHAT TO SEE:We arrived on Monday afternoon. When the others arrived we went for food and then, as one had been before, we walked around.  I enjoyed walking around and did not feel unsafe.  We went to the Red Light District, which did not bother me, in fact I found it very tacky, with big neon signs depicting all sorts of things   We went into a  coffeeshop  which I was uncomfortable with as I don t really agree with any type of drugs. To be honest, I would rather have watched a sex show, it would have offended me less The next day my friend and I were the only ones awake in the morning.  As we were the ones who wanted to see the sights we invested in the I Amsterdam Card.  This is a fantastic investment if you plan to see a few things in Amsterdam.  We paid 51 Euros for a 72 hour card, which entitles you to free public transport, free entrance to many attractions and discounts on other attractions and restaurants.  Among the attractions included on the pass are the Oude Kerk (old church) Neuwie Kerk (new church), the Amsterdam Historical Museum, the Van Goch Museum and the Rijksmuseum.  The card can be bought from all tourist offices, where we found the staff extremely helpful.On the first day we did some shopping.  Many of the shops were the same as those in Britain, H M, Zara etc.  The prices were about the same for clothes.  The prices for cosmetics were sometimes cheaper, but buying in the airport was cheaper again.We also visited the Old Church, which is in the middle of the Red Light District.  The Church was very bare, but interesting.  It contains the grave of Rembrandt s wife.  If you go in the winter, take your thermals, we were absolutely freezing in there   We also went to the New Church, which I was very disappointed with as it is no longer used as a church but as an exibition centre.  These on their own would have cost nearly 20 Euros, so the pass really is worth it.That night (when the others finally woke up  ) we went to Boom Chicago, a comedy show in a theatre located in Leidseplein.  This was hilarious.  We also had dinner before the show in the theatre.  The cost was 36 Euros which included a 2 course dinner, which was very tasty, a drink and the show.  I found this to be a very good deal.The next day we went on a boat tour (again included in our pass).  This takes you on a tour of the canals and out to the harbour, and gives a commentary in Dutch and English as you go round.  The boats are covered in so don t worry if its raining.  There are many companies offering this, we chose on near Leidseplein and found it very informative.  It did get a little choppy in the harbour though We then went to Anne Frank s House, which I recommend as a must to anyone going to Amsterdam.  The atmosphere and the exibits were very moving and seeing how small an area the 8 people who were hiding lived in will really make you think.  It costs 7.50 Euros to get in but it is worth every penny and I spent a good hour and a half in there.   Be warned, if you want to avoid the Red Light District, be careful where you wander.  We were walking in an area which we didn t think was marked as the RLD on the map, only to be comfronted by a host of women pressing their...assets?....up against the window.  This didn t bother me, in fact I found it quite funny, but for people that go to Amsterdam with children, be careful were you go That evening we went out to a bar in Leidseplein called the Bulldog. The drinks were about the same prices as you would pay in this country (about    2-2.50 per pint).  This place closed at 1pm.The following day, after a light night by all except me, I headed out on my own.  I felt very safe walking round by myself and ventured into parts that we hadn t seen before.  I went to the main Catholic Church, St Nicholas, which is near the station.  It was spectacular.  Not very big, but very ornate and beautifully decorated.  A definate must if you like looking round churches like me.  I then went to the Amsterdam Historical Museum, which was fascinating, but there is a lot to see in there and I can see children becomming bored quite quickly.  The museum tells the story of the city from its beginnings in the 13th century right up to the modern day.  The exibits include artifacts, paintings, videos and more.  One very interesting exibit was a video in the World War Two section.  This is not really highlighted but is so fascinating.  The video shows a group of people who went into hiding during the war.  Its nowhere near as famous as Anne Frank, but really adds to the overall story of those hiding.  If you ve got the I Amsterdam card then I would definately say to make time for a quick walk around here as its included and parts were very interesting.  If you ve only got a short time or have children who find most museums a drag, then perhaps this isn t the place for you.The afternoon saw visits to the Rijksmuseum and the Van Goch Museum, both on our passes.  I loved the Rijksmuseum.  At the moment only around 12 rooms are open while they rebuilt other areas.  In these rooms they have put the most viewed items, those which people would come to the museum to see.  These include artifacts in the first couple of rooms, from the Dutch Golden Age.  Then there are rooms of paintings, including a room for Rembrandt, one for Vermeer and one for Frans Hals.  The most famous painting was the Night Watch by Rembrandt, which was enormous.  The museum building was absolutely huge so I m quite glad that I didn t have to walk through all of it in the time we were there.  However, I would like to go back there if I had more time.  The Van Goch Museum was interesting, but to be honest I m more of an Old Master person   It was interesting to learn about his life, although his ear, or lack thereof, was not mentioned   There were many of his paintings on display, included one version of his Sunflowers.The next morning we headed back to the shops to rid ourselves of some Euros, and then to the airport.  The shops in the airport are great, you could buy almost anything.  I ended up with some cosmetics and some famous Dutch cheese - yummy CONCLUSION:Would I go back to Amsterdam?  Well I would, but it wouldn t be top of my list.  Would I recommend it?  Again, yes, but with reservations.  I really didn t find it a family orientated place.  There were places, such as Madame Tussaudes and the Amsterdam Dungeon, but you would definately have to pick and chose carefully where you walked with children.  You can avoid the RLD fairly easily, but the  coffeeshops  are everywhere.  Another thing to bear in mind with youngsters are the roads, which seem to have no set pattern and trams, bikes and cars come at you from all directions   If you offend easily then this may not be the place for you.  However, it can also be a cultural experience.  It is a fascinating place to go.  There are lots of museums and churches to visit and even just walking around the canals is a pleasant experience.  Remember that it gets very cold in winter because there are no hills blocking the wind, and I ve heard that the flys can be bad in the summer becuase of all the water.  Another tip is to make sure you change you money before you go as the rate they give you is terrible, as with changing in most places when you get there.  Unless you have a Nationwide account your bank will charge for ATM use but this is probably less than the exchange rate will do you out of.So overall, I would recommend it if you re looking for a cultural trip, or if you re looking for somewhere for a weekend with friends or a stag or hen do.  If you like the idea of going somewhere with very relaxed attitudes then Amsterdam is ideal.  I enjoyed the trip very much, but I won t be hurrying back. ', '    I have just returned from my twentieth visit to Amsterdam, this includes the year and a half that I lived there and the countless summer holidays that I spent there. After a year and a half, I decided that my education would be a lot better in England and moved back, spending most school holidays in Amsterdam. I feel like Amsterdam is partly my home and have spent enough time there as both a child and an adult to write a comprehensive review of the do s and don t of Amsterdam. I m going to begin with the basics and move on to places that I specifically recommend that you should visit when in Amsterdam. This is by no means a weeks worth as I have been visiting the city for 13 years and to do it all would take a while Anyway, enough of the introduction as to why I think I m qualified to write this, on to the review itself The basics:Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands, located in the province of North Holland (The Netherlands or Holland is split up into provinces as England is split up into counties) Many people didn t know this, but Amsterdam is situated only an hours drive from the coast (albeit the north sea). I think that answers the question  Another factor is that it cost s us nearly exactly the same, if not cheaper for me because of the soaring price of petrol I live in Manchester and until this year I ve had to travel to Liverpool for cheap airfares. Once you re off the plane and have your luggage, getting from the airport to the city is incredibly easy.  Train tickets can be purchased from machines at the airport and the journey only takes about half an hour to Central Station. Literally everyone speaks English and all the signs and directions are in English. It is impossible to go wrong. ****Be warned: KLM and Amsterdam airport in general have the WORST record of any airport world wide for lost luggage.*****It is also possible to get the ferry from Newcastle on DFDS. I looked in to this however and found that it was actually more expensive than flying in addition to taking much longer.   Once in Amsterdam you will find that the city is very compact and there is little need for public transport.  You can cross the city by foot in about an hour which adds to its appeal. If you want to explore further a field, bicycles are the way to go.  These are abundant in Amsterdam and the flat land and numerous cycle paths make it a perfect city for cycling. There are numerous shops across the city from which to hire bikes and it won t set you back too much.  If cycling really isn t your thing then Amsterdam also has a good network of trams which are reasonably priced and easy to use. Things To Do and See.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~The Canals. Spending some time wandering the picturesque canals and cobble-stoned side streets, exploring shops packed with knick-knacks and enjoying a coffee or a beer in the sun by the side of the canal is just an ideal way to spend an afternoon and this is an essential part of any trip to Amsterdam.  The Prinsengracht  is one area I would particularly recommend, this is the area where all of the  posh  houseboats are and believe me they are really worth a look, the boats have amazing roof gardens and some are just stunning.  Canal trips are also a common and I am sure relaxing way to view Amsterdam although sadly this is something I did not have the time to do on this occasion. Markets. There are numerous markets in Amsterdam and these are a great way to waste a lazy afternoon and to pick up some bargains. The Albert Cuypmarkt, located in the Pijp district, is the best-known and busiest outdoor market in Europe, attracting thousands of visitors who come to browse the 300 odd stalls. The Waterlooplein Flea Market is also one of the most popular and is worth a look and there are many others for those who are serious about their bargain hunting. The Red Light District. Everyone has heard of the red light district and I am going to be blunt about what s there.  The red light district is a haven for tourists for a number of reasons.  Firstly, because there is an abundance of cheap accommodation, youth hostels, bars and eateries to be found in the area.  The other reasons are more illicit.  There are many  coffee shops  in the red light district in which one can enjoy more than just a coffee and cookies or a fruit smoothie.  Each of the coffee shops has a menu on the wall from which the customer can select the type of ganja they would like to smoke which is then keyed into the till, just like you were paying for milk. You are then free to sit and get stoned at your leisure.  The other reason that the red light district is famous is of course for the sex.  There are many scantily dressed women on display in window fronts and this is very blatant. In addition the red light district is home to many porn shops and theatres, gay bars and clubs, a condom museum and a marijuana museum.  It really isn t an area for those who are easily offended but it is fascinating and frankly I d be amazed at anyone who couldn t resist having a look  It is a busy area and I never felt unsafe there at any point. The Van Gough Gallery.Situated on the edge of the city centre in huge park called the Vondelpark this is an absolute must if you have any artistic inclination at all   There are a great deal of masterpieces housed here. At EURO15 it is pricey to get in and we had to queue for a good 45 minutes but it was definitely worth it.  The gallery also has a large area housing temporary exhibitions, while we were there this featured the works of Monet and Manet, which was also exceptional. Rembrandt s house.  Situated adjacent to a particularly pretty cane,l on Jodenbreestraat and near to one of the larger markets of Amsterdam, Rembrandts House, which became a museum in 1911, was also interesting and worth the trip. Rembrandt collected many old classics by other artists and a whole host of other knick-knacks including stuffed animals and foreign objects of interest.  These are on display along with over 250 etchings, works which Rembrandt completed relatively early on in his career and which are relatively unknown. The highlight was a workshop we attended on the makings of these etchings, using all of his old, original equipment, although this massive and grandeur house is worth a look just in itself.  Admission was EURO7.50   Anne Frank s House.   Anne Frank s House, located on Prinsengracht, is essential part of any trip to Amsterdam. If you do want to go, then expect to wait in line, I had to queue for about an hour to get in and it was raining to top it off.  The admission price is EURO7.50 for adults, which is reasonable and I d say you should expect to spend a couple of hours here at the most. I presume that everyone knows the story of Anne Frank and her family, who hid from the Nazis, for two years in this tiny annex at the back of the bookcase. I found the visit very sobering although utterly fascinating. The house itself and the accompanying museum is a shocking and moving account of the power of the Nazi s and the misery they brought to ordinary citizens. This is a must visit attraction and was definitely one of the highlights of my trip.   The Magic Mushroom Museum.This small and very modern museum, located on Spuistraat, presents an introduction to the world of legal herbs and there uses, which I found totally fascinating. You can buy magic mushrooms here complete with advice about how to use them and what to expect alongside just about any other legal stimulate you can think of, what s more it is completely free so theres no excuse for not popping in. Just down the road there is also some great graffiti which is worth a look. Other Places of Interest.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~In addition to the places outlined above there are many attractions which I did not have the pleasure to visit during my stay. These include the Artis Zoo, the oldest zoo in Holland, the diamond cutting and polishing factory, Madame Tussauds, The Royal Palaces, The Modern Art Gallery, The Heineken Brewery, and the Amsterdam History Museum. Further information about all of these attractions is available on the web. Places to Stay.~~~~~~~~~~There is something for everyone in Amsterdam from plush five star hotels to basic hostels in the red light district, which is where we stayed.  The advantage of staying in the red light district is that this is just a five minute walk from Central Station but the disadvantage is the noise at night. The red light district is after all famous for it s night life. Money. ~~~~~The Dutch Guilder was exchanged for the Euro back in 2002 and prices are generally similar to those observed in the UK. There are ATM cash machines everywhere and you can pay by card in most places. Summary. ~~~~~~~~I would recommend Amsterdam as a city break to anyone, regardless of interests   It is a perfect city for art lovers with a wealth of galleries and some wonderful architecture to admire. It is a great place for couples and is a truly romantic and picturesque City. In addition Amsterdam is known as a top destination for British stag and hen dos and it has a great party and night life but it also has a sophisticated edge and had many attractions for the more mature traveler. I loved Amsterdam and I am sure that I will return at some point to sample some more of the night life and to see some of the things I didn t have time to enjoy on my first trip. The fact that it is such a compact city and just a stones throw away from the UK make it an ideal destination for a weekend break and if you haven t been already you should definitely consider a trip. Five stars for this beautiful and cosmopolitan city which truly does have something to offer everyone. We finally decided not to have desserts as it was so difficult to get the attention of the waiters, so we paid and left.     ', '     well where do i start i want to tell the truth this hotel is the best around leeds i have seen in a long time  from the moment you walk into this hotel you are treated like you you are royalty   me and my girlfriend walked and instantly they asked for any luggage. i happily said no  i was over the limit for driving but not that drunk  they showed us to our room. it wasa double bed room over looking the park and the grounds of the hotel. the bed was so comfortable and i slept well. in the morning we ordered room service and had a good sized very tasty breakfast. we both enjoyed it  we got freshened up and i went down to pay the bill, ihad to pay    159, it was steep but it was good for what i had and we also had the cance to test the gym nad the spa and even the swimming pool, my girlfriend but i just slept untill my hangover was gone  all in all a good hotel and a nice night and good food      ', '    I recently visited Monkey World, Dorset.I have seen the programme Monkey Business lots of times and really wanted to visit and see the likes of Charlie and Rodney the chimps.  I wasn t disappointed. The cost was    8.00 per adults and    6.00 for children/oap s.There are various enclosures with various monkey s although there are more chimpanzees than any other monkey s.   There is the Chimpanzee nursery with all of the young chimps that is very lively and noisy and also the batchelor pad with the older male monkeys and the rest of the chimp enclosure having a mixture of chimps.   They are all very well cared for and in very natural environments and were even enjoying ice lollies on the day I visited.There is a large orang-utan enclosure and we also got to see a baby orang-utan being cared for by the staff.There are various other monkey s including squirrel monkey s, ring tailed lemars and gibbons.There is also a small enclosure with donkeys and small animal like rabbits, guinea pigs and chickens.The facilities are very clean and well maintained and there is a good cafeteria with a good menu at reasonable prices.There is also a very good gift shop which is  reasonably priced.Monkey world is very well signposted and there is very adequate parking.If you are interested in adopting a monkey, you can do when you are there and it costs    25 for a picture, certificate, updates on your monkey and also free entry to monkey world for one year.This was a great day out and I would definately recommend it and I would be certain to  visit again.     ', '    I have been shopping at Marks and Spencer for about thirty years.  Its always the first place I go to for clothes.  I think its a really great store not only because of the good quality but they take so seriously any complaints.  I especially like their bed linen and it has outlasted just about every other I have bought.  I went into their new coffee shop in Glasgow recently and that was just fantastic.  The coffee was gorgeous and so was the cake to go with it.So I am a Marks and Spencer fan but I have been a bit disappointed with their clothes of late. I want non-fussy clothes that are good quality. They seem to be trying to please everyone but succeeding with no one, not even me. They are doing a large size range - and most of the clothes looked baggy and big.  I bumped into a friend recently and we were both searching for a smart suit but Marks seemed to be giving way to the tatty look and anything with a reasonable style looked creased.  The quality of Marks clothes also seems to have fallen somewhat.  I bought a pair of black trousers and the seams split before I had even washed them but no doubt they will replace them.However, I have bought a couple of T-shirts that have kept their shape and feel comfortable after washing, so all is not lost.  Hopefully Marks will get back on track soon.      ', '    If I am in the town centre in Manchester I just have to visit Pizza Hut, I love pizza  8217;s but I also like the service provided by Pizza Hut. They can be fairly busy at times and rushed off their feet but they try to be quick as possible wit your orders. The place is clean and decorated well, it  8217;s nice and cosy and a good place to eat and talk. The prices are really good and there  8217;s a good range of pizza  8217;s available and in different sizes. They are happy to change your order so it suits you and if you want more or less cheese just say so. They also serve side salads and have a good selection of cold dishes. If you are taking your children then they have a special fun packed menu for them, and they are given some activity sets.   The drinks are reasonable and you can have an ice cream to finish off your meal.It  8217;s a good place to eat out if you  8217;re with some friends, affordable and much better than Macdonald  8217;s.       ', '    On a recent trip to the new West Quay shopping centre in Southampton we decided to have a late lunch at the Pizza Hut restaurant.    We being myself, my husband, my 4 sons aged between 15 and 23 and the oldest sons fiancee.   Like most boys of their age pizzas are always a favourite and normally good value.However not one aspect of this visit was any where near up to standard.    When we tried to place an order several standard items were not available.    Although the others went for pizza I opted for a pasta dish.After a wait of over 40 minutes food started to be brought to our table but they did not have any large pizzas so they brought medium instead.   Have you ever tried feeding males of that age range - they eat a lot - if you order large it is because they need large.   However having waited so long we could not wait any longer to wait for more to be cooked.   The food was also brought out in stages about 5 minutes apart.   In fact by the time my pasta arrived they had finished all their pizzas and were waiting to leave.I would also comment that the state of the restaurant could only be described as disgraceful.   There was rubish all over the floor, tables were not cleared etc.   In fact it almost became a bit of a joke because one waitress dropped a cup and saucer on the floor in the walkway between the tables.   For over 15 minutes it was left on the floor - waiters/waitresses stepped over it, round it etc but nobody picked it up.   In fact it was still there when we left.I would normally have given Pizza Hut a good report but standards are obviously slipping drastically.     ', '    My partner and I have recently returned from Santa Ponsa after a one week break.We stayed in the Parasol Apartments which is just a few minutes walk from the main cetre of Santa Ponsa.There is a very good atmosphere here.  The town has a whole range of different bars and restaurants.  There is a very Irish feel in Santa Ponsa with a great deal of the bars being Irish run.     Everyone is very friendly and although it was very busy there it was not as hectic as places like Magaluf and Palmanova.   The beach is superb and very clean.  There are lots of boat trips around the beach and these are very good value for money.It is very easy to travel around to local attractions and the bus service is excellent.  Closeby there are three very large water parks.  There is Aquacity, Aquapark and western world.  These are very good value for money and around 15 Euros for Adults and 8 Euros for children.An excellent evening is the Pirates evening which is on the outskirts of Magaluf, which is approximately 3 km from Santa Ponsa. There are excursions here.  We went on the adults only night which was 55 Euros but this does include all food and drink.  It also include you return travel to the venue and it is a magnificent night.  I would say that this was the highlight of my holiday so definately recommend it.Although we went as a couple and we had plenty to do, it is a very good place for familes.     ', '    The Red Lion can be found on a corner just off the road running between Liverpool Street and Moorgate, near South Place making it a very handy place for a sneaky pint during work hours if you work in the City.Although it s quite a small pub it does have two floors and, tardis-like, seems able to house quite a few people at any one time.The usual selection of beers are on offer here aswell as some good food at good prices.  I d recommend the burger and chips which is just    3.50 and is very filling - better than a McDonalds any day.It s mainly filled with City bods most of the time and as a result is pretty heaving after 5:00 every weekday.It s a pretty traditional-looking pub, but one small problem is that you feel a bit like you re in a goldfish bowl with the two street-facing walls being dominated by large windows as they are.The other problem is that there s often no table-space for eating.     ', '    My first cruise on the Topaz was July 1998 The holiday began by flying to Orlando Florida on a Tuesday. Arriving in Orlando late afternoon. I chose not to have a car but transfers which were very good. We were transfered from Sanford airport to our hotel on International Drive where we were to stay until Saturday morning before our transfer to Port Canaveral, for our seven day fully inclusive cruise on the Topaz. The first four days in Orlando were great, with visits to all the Disney parks, the hotel provided a shuttle bus service which was excellant and justified our decision not to take the hire car. Our transfer to the Topaz was very easy and our first impressions of the ship was that it seemed a little old, we had paid extra for an outside cabin with seaview, but the porthole was to high to see out of and the cabin was rather basic and not too brightly decorated. Our exploration of the ship was quite good and has the next seven days came and went, we had a great time, the ships staff and crew were fabulous,and very helpful, indeed at the end of the cruise we were sad to leave the friends we had made aboard. The ports of call included Bahamas (Nassua) Key West Cozumal(Mexico) and Port Lucaya (Bahamas) we swam with Dolphins and had a fantastic time The free drinks and more than enough food made the holiday great. AT the end of the cruise we returned for a further three days in Orlando Visiting Sea World and Universal Studios. Since then I have been on two more Topaz cruises, they are without doubt, excelent value although not five star they are well worth the experience.     ']

s5_annotated_personalized_summaries:
If you’re planning a trip to Amsterdam, here’s a practical and honest rundown to help you make the most of your visit. Accommodation options span from budget-friendly hostels to upscale hotels, but a heads-up: during peak seasons, snagging a room without advance booking can be tricky. So, book early to avoid last-minute stress.

Food lovers will appreciate Amsterdam’s diverse culinary scene. Beyond the international fare, don’t miss out on local treats like Dutch pancakes and desserts—they’re delightful and worth seeking out. Dining spots generally offer good service, with friendly staff adding to the welcoming atmosphere.

Getting around is a breeze. The city’s compact layout means you can explore on foot or rent a bike for that authentic Amsterdam vibe. Public transport—trams and buses—is efficient, affordable, and easy to navigate, especially with multi-ride tickets.

Culture buffs will find plenty to dive into: the Van Gogh Museum, Rijksmuseum, and Anne Frank House are must-visits that richly reward your curiosity. For a quieter day, consider a trip to nearby villages like Volendam or countryside tours, which offer a peaceful contrast to the city’s buzz.

Amsterdam’s liberal and open-minded spirit shines through in areas like the Red Light District and its cannabis cafes. While generally safe, it’s wise to stay alert—especially at night and in crowded spots—since pickpockets and drug dealers can be a nuisance. Stick to groups and keep valuables secure to enjoy the city worry-free.

Weather-wise, winters can be chilly, but the city’s charm and lively vibe persist year-round. And for a scenic treat, a canal boat ride offers a unique perspective on Amsterdam’s historic architecture.

In short, Amsterdam blends rich culture, culinary delights, and a friendly atmosphere, but a bit of planning and caution will ensure your adventure is smooth and memorable.

product_reviews: ['    Having lived here for 25 years now, this should be the most detailed, if not opinionated, review you will ever read from me. Leicester has a little bit of everything and something to interest almost anyone. Two of the country s best universities are here, there are two fine shopping centres that are both soon to be extended and re-developed, the world s oldest outdoor market is here , historical links to the Romans and Richard III, successful sports teams in football, rugby, cricket and basketball are based in Leicester,  it s the home of the National Space Centre, the nightlife features dozens of absolutely outstanding bars and restaurants. Add to that attractions like Twycross Zoo, DeMontfort Hall, the annual Comedy Festival, some stunning countryside views and scenery and possibly the UK s biggest mix of ethnic backgrounds, colours and creeds and you can see that Leicester has more to it than most people realise.Located 90 miles south of Leeds and 105 miles north of London, Leicester sits halfway up the M1 motorway at the heart of the East Midlands. It is served by both bus and coach stations and also has, within it s county boundaries, (Nottingham) East Midlands airport. Popular in earlier years for the shoe and textile industry, Leicester is now trying to establish itself in the top ten cities in the UK and with the range of people visiting the area and moving here, has every chance of doing just that. It s that multi-cultural, cosmopolitan make up that I mentioned that Leicester is becoming more famous for these days. Recent surveys have showed that ethnic minorities will outnumber white people in Leicester for the first time in any UK city, possibly by 2010. Leicester has such a diversity of temples, churches, mosques and other areas of congregation that anyone from any  religious background will find themselves at home here. The celebration of Diwali - the Indian festival of Lights - is a classic example of the cosmopolitan nature of the town andis greeted nowhere more than in Leicester. It brings together the whole Indian community and attracts many tourists from across the globe into the city to witness the unique celebrations. The suburbs around Belgrave, Melton Road and Evington come to life especially at that time of year.After the cultural diversity, Leicester is widely known for some of it s sporting successes. In football, Leicester City have been one of the Premiership s most consistent teams of recent seasons, renowned for their battling qualities and winning the league cup twice in three years along the way. Leicester Tigers have been even more successful, winning the Premiership title in rugby 4 times in succession and following on that success with triumphs in Europe. Leicestershire County Cricket club are well established as a hotbed of young cricketing talent and won the county championship four years ago. Outside          Pictures of Leicester in General     ', '    We decided to catch a train to try Leicester for a day. If we liked it, we d go again, but for perhaps a few days.We left Cambridge train station and arrived at Leciseter within a few hours.When we got off the train, the station looked rather dull and unfriendly. As I went to the toilet (No disabled toilet), There was litter on the ground, and it was not pleasant at all.Leaving the station we hoped for better things. We walked into the city centre, it wasn t that far. The streets never had any of the litter or dirt of the station. But what it lacked in litter and dirt it made up for  in people  I m not saying the peop[le were dirty and grubby, but there WAS a lot of them  A real lot  The streets were absolutely packed, in fact rather uncomfrotably so. There were masses of shops, but not too many cafes, and what there was - they were full   I expect if you don t mind mass crowds, then maybe you should visit, but otherwise stay weel clear. We didn t find it very wheelchair friendly, or people friendly. i expect that the reason being there ar ejust too many stressed people However in its defence  it was a Saturday. All in all, a day we were gald to get home from.     ', '    It is strange that having lived in Leicester all of my life I am quite comfortable in criticising the city, but if anyone I know from outside Leicester criticises it, I suddenly feel quite protective.  Admittedly, if you are looking for a day trip in the Midlands you are probably better off going to Nottingham or Lincoln, but Leicester certainly has some charms (mostly well-hidden).Shopping-wise I quite like Leicester - the city centre is compact and has all the big chain stores you would expect as well as some more interesting independent retailers.  The main shopping centre is  The Shires , and is quite modern and much better than either of the two shopping centres in Nottingham.  Leicester also has the largest covered market in Europe with the famous Lineker (as in Gary) stall.One annoying thing about Leicester city centre is the number of people trying to get you to fill in surveys or take flyers or sign up to a charity etc. - it is really getting out of control   Add this to the Christmas shopping rush and the centre can get very packed and claustrophobic.One of Leicester s strong points is the true multicultural mix of it s population, and if you are prepared to go a bit further out from the city centre you can go to  The Golden Mile  where you can sample food from one of the many curry houses and delicatessens or perhaps buy some jewellery.Leicester also has a good theatre (the Haymarket) - every year they put on a big musical, last year it was a cleverly-adapted Wizard of Oz.  There is also a small cinema in the city centre and a larger Odeon complex a couple of miles outside.Leicester s cricket, football and rugby teams are all performing well, but the actual sports facilities for the public in Leicester are very poor - the main swimming pool has been demolished, as has the basketball court at Granby Halls.  There is no ice rink.Leicester does not have a great appearance - there is a horrible ring road running right past some of the nice churches, and there is no photogenic castle (like Nottingham) or cathedral (like Lincoln).  You can see Roman remains at the Jewry wall museum, and areas along the canal have also been redeveloped and are worth seeing.The best news for Leicester is the opening of the National Space Centre in June, the UK s only attraction dedicated to space, with interactive exhibits and all sorts.  The building for the centre looks fantastic and this should really help Leicester develop.  In the meantime, I don t think it s worth coming out of your way to go to Leicester, but try in June and you may be pleasantly surprised.     ', '    Twycross zoo is in Leicestershire near a little village called Twycross. This is one of the biggest and best zoos around. It opened in 1963 and covers about 50 acres of land. Currently it averages about 400,000 visitors a year, which proves how popular it is.I must admit I`d never heard of it until my father-in-law took us there, but it is a day out all our family will always remember.The zoo became a charitable trust in 1972 and receives no government funding, in spite of this it is still relatively cheap. Prices: Adults -    6.50, Children -    4.50, Senior Citizens -    5.00It also offers a membership option. Membership runs from 1st April to 31st March.Membership Prices: Adult -    25.00, Joint Adult -     42.00, Junior(3-16) or full time student -    12.00.Membership includes free entrance for the whole membership year, and free admission to most monthly organised events. These events include treasure hunts, primate and reptile evenings and a grotto construction and decorating day towards christmas.The zoo opens from 10am till around 6pm every day except christmas day. At the moments it currently houses over 1000 animals of nearly 200 different species. Of these, 3/4 are classed as endangered species. It is because of this that the zoo takes part in many captive breeding programmes. I m afraid to say that I can t tell you much about either of them because I don t go to either, but I m sure that you can find out a lot by going to their websites.At the moment Leicester has three public libraries for your learning pleasure, the Central Lending Library, The Goldsmith Music and Drama Library, and the Reference Library. From here you ll be able to get to anywhere in the Leicester City area. Campo de  Fiori means  Field of Flowers . Definitely magical, although not altogether accurate. There is no field of flowers here, well, not any more. What you do have is a bustling and thriving, vibrantly colourful market.Just south of the Piazza Navona, this market boasts a range of fresh goods for sale. Fish, Fruit, Vegetables, Meat, Flowers, everything looks of good quality and very tempting, espcially the fruit. It also doubles up as something else very traditional for this historical city. Come the afternoons and political speakers spout forth below the statue of a philospher, Giordano Bruno. (He was a monk who was burned alive in the 15th century during the Inquisition, for the forehead-slappingly stupid idea that the earth existed within an infinite universe, with many more galaxies than just ours. I mean. Kuh  How dumb is that...). As long as you are fluent in passionate Italian, then I m sure it makes for interesting listening.Anyway, this little treasure can be found off the Corso Vittorio, and is but a short stroll from the River Tiber, the Pantheon, and the Palazzo Farnese.      ', '    The Circus Maximus is best viewed from one of Rome s great hills, the Palantine. From here you can see down onto the immense stretch of grass, where crowds of just under a quarter of a million people would come to watch the chariot racing.They used to do it in a bit more splendour than you can now see. Back then, there would have been row upon row of marble seats, where as now there are just the raised and grassy banks remaining.It takes a bit more work on your imagination here to try and drum up the sounds of neighing horses, clashing metal and bloodthirsty cries from a hyped up crowd, but if you manage to chuck the odd bottle of Vino down your neck, it does make it a bit easier. Oh, and do that once you ve made the journey DOWN from the Palantine Hill and are standing at the side of the arena.There used to be an obelisk, dating back to the times of Egypt s Rameses II (circa 13th century BC) that was brought back to Rome by the Emperor Augustus and erected in the Circus Maximus. But they moved it. It s not there now. You ve got to go the Piazza del Popolo to see that.So there you have it. Not one of the most stunning sights you ll see in Rome, which, let s face it, is spoiled for them, but just try and imagine what went on here all those thousands of years ago, and it does get a bit more impressive.Sadly, no signs of any statues to Charlton Heston..     ', '    Go For ITI think a gap year is an excellent idea, I took two and I think I really appreciated from them, now their more opportunities than ever to do what you want. There are some excellent ideas, and they cover the majority of areas people want to go in when they decide they need a break from studyingI went to India and spent six months teaching English, it was great, I learnt so much, I had some really good times, and some bad times,, all of which I believe have made me a better person. I think if I didn  8217;t have the break I wouldn  8217;t have appreciated my university degree. You come back with so much more ideas. The downside is that you don  8217;t always think you should go back, you live the easy life, working and earning and having a good time, that you think what is the point. That is when reality hits home, and you realise that you can  8217;t live like that forever. Whether you take your gap year after your alevels or when you have finished your degree I really recommend it, you should get as much information about what you want to do and go for it. You only live once. You will definitely find a lot about yourself that you didn  8217;t know before.     ', '    We decided to catch a train to try Leicester for a day. If we liked it, we d go again, but for perhaps a few days.We left Cambridge train station and arrived at Leciseter within a few hours.When we got off the train, the station looked rather dull and unfriendly. As I went to the toilet (No disabled toilet), There was litter on the ground, and it was not pleasant at all.Leaving the station we hoped for better things. We walked into the city centre, it wasn t that far. The streets never had any of the litter or dirt of the station. But what it lacked in litter and dirt it made up for  in people  I m not saying the peop[le were dirty and grubby, but there WAS a lot of them  A real lot  The streets were absolutely packed, in fact rather uncomfrotably so. There were masses of shops, but not too many cafes, and what there was - they were full   I expect if you don t mind mass crowds, then maybe you should visit, but otherwise stay weel clear. We didn t find it very wheelchair friendly, or people friendly. i expect that the reason being there ar ejust too many stressed people However in its defence  it was a Saturday. All in all, a day we were gald to get home from.     ', '    Leicester is a pleasant city with a nice atmosphere and good environment, but as a tourist you need something to occupy your time.Unfortunatly Leicester hasn t really got much.Although there are some tourist attractions the fact is that there are more in other places and for that reason I would recommend putting Leicester near the bottom of your list of places to visit.If you fancy a bit of a stroll and some decent shopping Leicester does the job however.The citys sports facilities may be of interest, and in most respects are the cities big attraction. Leicester Racecourse, Leicestershire County Cricket Ground, Leicester City Football Club and Leicester Tigers Rugby Club all puill in the crowds.     ', '    I flew EasyJet On January to London. EasyJet usually land in Luton Airport which is really interesting for the company, for this airport and for customers.Before landing once you see the Vauxhall factories, some roof and that s it you land, no time to be scared...Then you just drop off the plane, 5, 10 walks and you arrive into the airport building, not really busy as it could be in Heathrow or even Nice-C   te d Azur Airport. And that s perfect, a real friendly atmosphere.No time to lose.You are looking for a bus going London Center, there are some waiting for you immediatly outside.
