What a good bargain For the people who like shopping and dutyfreetaxing not so many boutiques but there are some...The decoration is to be improved, it seems cheap at least.There unless a negative point that I want to set up.When I came back from London center to Luton Airport there was such a traffic on the road (stocked 1 hour on the motorway and it was a thursday evening on January ) that I though missing my fly but fortunatelly and that is the final positive point for Luton Airport, you can easily come at last minute, check-in is quick and most of the employees are very helpful. No long and never ending corridors, gates are easy to find and finally you are prepared for another fly.So if Luton Airport stay as it is, I feel confident to come to London...     ', '       McSorley s is located on 8th Street in the East Village.  It sits on the same block as Burp Castle and Brewskis which are two other beer havens on the Lower East Side of Manhattan.  McSorley s is an Irish style pub which serves two beers on draught.  There is a pale ale and a dark beer.  They are both tasty beers but neither will really curdle the toes of a serious beer lover.  This bar is a place to go when you want to quaff a few beers among friends.   It is always crowded but the staff is pretty friendly.  They seem well adapted to handling a large influx of patrons.  A visit to McSorleys is essential for any beer lover making a trip to the Lower East Side.  It has become an institution in New York City.  While I can t honestly rave about the quality of the McSorley beers, I would state that they do have bottled beers and a full liquor bar.  This is a fun place to go to have a few and let your hair down.       ', '    Travelling from Nice, Monaco is only a half an hour train journey away.  You arrive into the very modern train station and are then only about a 15 minute walk from the harbour.  If you re a Formula 1 fan then it is simply wonderful to be able to walk around the actual circuit, and you ll never be able to watch the Monaco Grand Prix on the telly again without getting goosebumps.  The circuit isn t particularly long and it s no bother to walk it.  It also gives you the opportunity to admire the many expensive road cars which drive on these streets.The Harbour is in itself beautiful, and the yachts are very eyecatching.  Monaco also has an artificial sandy beach, so if you re tired of the pebbled beaches of the south of France this is a welcome relief.Unfortunately if you go at the time of the Grand Prix itself you will not get to walk the circuit and the huge crowds mean it is a totally different experience.  So my advice - go twice - once before a GP weekend and once during       ', '    So new york,i go back to 1996 january i was on my way to new york on a trip i had won on local radio for two people.I realised the wifw wouldnt let me take the girlfriend so i took her.I recall driving in to Manhatten for the first time,the buildings just shut out the light and it just overpowers you.The people in Manhatten are not the nicest and the traffic was 24 hours,tooting and shouting,it was just crazy.but on the plus side what a place,the buildings and the shops are just made for the shop browser and i have to say i put my hand to my wallet a few times and bought a few things.The cds,clothes and food were very cheap but was tok back by how easy it is to get lost in new york,and if you are thinking of going dont go in January because the cold is so bad it split my lips.Anyway the hotels are not as good as on television and the service is very poor,the customer in Manhatten is treated very poorly in the shops and not looked after at all.My final verdict on new york is if you have dreamed of going there well ok Times square,Statue of liberty,Empire state,they are all great to look at but for an overall verdict on Manhatten,dont go..put your money to a holiday in the sun because i think like me the dream of New york is nothing like the real thing...     ', '    The idea is great: a chain sandwich bar selling freshly prepared sandwiches guaranteed additive-free, with a range of coffees, soft drinks (inc smoothies) and cookies on the side. The reality isn   t: the sandwiches are expensive (starting at    2.59) even if they are very fresh and packed with ingredients, and don t taste as good as they look. Consume them in-store - not a comfy option, the steel stools and mini-tables look good but are uncomfortable - and you   ll be charged an additional 17.5 . And friendly staff aren t compensation enough.(This is cheating slightly, but I feel I have to explain: someone laid down the challenge of writing a VH op in exactly 90 words, I d never normally write something so short but it seemed like quite a challenge: I d love to see if anyone can do it. Comments please )     ', '    Last year, my family and myself decided to go on holiday to Cyprus.  My mum had heard good things about it, so we decided to go to Protaras.  We stayed in a smaller town about 1 mile from Protaras centre, called Penera.  It is a lovely town, which is quiet and relaxing.  There is a long road with all the bars and restaurants on it, then from our hotel it took about 5 minutes to get to Penera Beach.  The beach is clean and not as busy as the main beaches nearby, such as Fig Tree Bay, although very nice, when we went, we couldn t find any space   The weather is absolutely beautiful and very warm.  It is a perfect location, because everywhere is just a taxi ride away.  It doesn t take long to get around, because it s quite a small island.  I d have to warn people about the scooters, because a lot of people find this way fun to travel, so they can come speeding from any direction.  I would say it is quite a safe place to be and people there are really friendly.  It s mostly British and Germans.There is a water park in Agia Napa, which has a Greek theme to it, it is very enjoyable, although, because you walk around with nothing on your feet, the floor can really burn your feet    This is an ideal day out for families with either teenagers or small children, most hotels run trips each week.  It can get quite busy, but if you pre-book, you can get in more quickly.  The parts of the island which i visited, were extremely nice, and mostly quite busy, but full of shops, cafes, bars and restaurants.  Cyprus deffinitely caters for everybody, old or young.      ', '    Somebody says to me Rockies I autotomaticaly think strippers or drag queens just the mental image I have of the bar it has always seemed to be a seedy little bar.  But last time I was in I was quiet pleasently surprised It must be coming up a bit in the world, or was it just a one off (more than likely). Always seems really busy as it is so small and always clutered.  Situated at the Newcastle end of the Redheugh bridge, is where Newcastles gay scene begins or is it ends am not quite sure how it works Depends on which way you come into town, it is very handy to the New powerhouse so come last orders you will find everbody will be heading here to be six deep at the bar. Lets hope they cater for this eh  Bank holidays is always busy (totally different crowd to your normal week nights) but as the scene is so small you will find most of the bars are anyway. But if your out on the bank holiday and wanna see a stripper or drag act and sometimes a kareoke this is definatly the place to go       ', '    Selfridges is located in the heart of London along the ever busy Oxford Street. They sell practically everything you could ever want here and the prices aren t particularly extortionate. The service is also good as the members of staff are always on hand to help you out and they are also very polite, it was only the other day when i went and seeing i had a lot to carry a helpful member of staff rushed to the door and even offered to help me hail a cab. Service or what? Recently they also had a Tokyo Life...well, exhibition i guess where by they were celebrating all things japanese. They sold all manner of japanese food and drink and many people were bold enough to try the sushi, which i declined (raw fish never really tempts me. There was also a japanese band playing in the centre and it had attracted quite a crowd. Anyway back to the shop itself. Selfridges is fun and fresh and you know if you are looking for something they are sure to have it here. One could spend hours merely roaming around aimlessly lost in a maze of products. No wonder the place is always busy      ', '    The museum is situated in the city centre, it is quite easy to miss though, with a small door on the main street.  The admission price was roughly    4.  The museum takes you through the history of sex with loads of pictures.  It is a great place to go for a laugh, although not as good as we expected.There are lots of photo opportunities, to record some of the unbelievable sights (including a model of an enormous penis )   There was too much emphasis on animal sex for my liking   It was an eye-opening experience though  The museum itself was quite small.  Its the sort of place you visit, and is very funny but you wouldn t go to it again.  It was jammed packed when we were there.        ', '    We have had our Border Collie, Ben for 5 years now.He is a cheeky male dog that always wants attention.This breed of dog is mainly a working one used on farms to herd sheep.You need to have plenty of energy as they never tire out  Requirements.Stainless steel bowls are preferable to plastic ones.This is because they can t be chewed.Heavy glazed earthenware bowls are also suitable with the added advantage that they are less likely to be tipped over.A collar and lead can be bought straight away.Although a puppy can t safely go out until it s had it s vacinations.Vacination.I recomend that you have the dog vacinated reguarly for worms etc at least once a year.This is mainly as a prevention.Grooming and Bathing.Bathing should be done aprox  once a month and the dog needs brushing daily.This should be done with a metal comb, as it will remove much of the loose hair.A flea comb is a valuable acquistion, while a hopund or grooming glove is also useful for giving the coat an attractive finish.The directions for using medicated shampoos must be followed closely, and the contents kept out of the eyes.Our Dog, loves going for a run on the beach at least once a day.Feeding.We feed Ben Pedigree Chum, Pal and Win-alot.He also gets a daily allowance of chews.Play Time.Ben also loves playing with various toys.His favorites are: Hedgehog, Football and my softtoys.He loves Teletubbies       ', '    What can i say? Stunning gals with sweet arses, cheapish beer, table dancing and its courtesy to put your head between the barmaids breasts Teasers is conveniantly opposite the red light district   within reach of Dam Square (i think that is what it is called ). The service is  friendly  with the emphasis on buying  bodyshots . For those bodyshot virgins out there... this is a process where salt is rubbed into a quite often ample cleavage, the remaining flesh is doused in lemon juice (fresh), and a welcoming tequila shot is held in the waitresses mouth  Youve guessed it. Lick the salt, suck the lemon (its good practice and only polite to take your time during this part)and somehow rescue your shot   Don t ask me prices, for obvious reasons i have little recolection of the experiences (but enough ). There are a few down sides to this joint however. Firstly the music is sub standard club/pop clap trap- but this is only a minor disadvantage. It costs a fortune to go to the loo, and trust me- one will need to go a lot in this place  Oh yeh...there are live web cams situated in every corner, so dont let the G.friend catch you in the act.As a final comment if you really can t get the place out of your mind, you could always start your own teasers franchise- but i can t remember the website 4 this- sorry. Go there, get the t-shirt   do not let the naughty lil gals pull your pants down in a private table dance      ', '    If you have read the first op i did on this then, this is it but i have improved it, so read on and see  I first went to see this with my mum and dad about a year ago and i am hoping to be going again soon.Before i went to see The Lion King i saw Saturady Night Fever, that was very good but i personally think that The Lion King was better. Dont get me wrong Saturday Night Fever was very good but there was something about The Lion King that was very good, i cant really say what it was but it had that thing about it that made it very good  I thought that the costumes that the actors and actresses were wearing were brillant. The costumes werent totally animal like, you could still see there faces but they had animal hats on if you know what i mean. I thought that the lion mask was the best becuase it looked so real. Their makeup was very very good. Their voices were so good and they could all sing very well. You could every word that they said even if you were at the back. I thought that the price was good as it was a west end show. Our tickets cost us about    15 -    25 because we got them from the little ticket box in the main part of london. If you gte your tickets from there you get them cheaper than you would if you ordered them from the theatre.The story hasnt changed from the disney film, so if u have seen that it is the same story, but you need to see the musical for the experience and to say that you have been to a london show        ', '    Softair is a way of having a paintballing experience, but with replica weapons. You can organize your own skirmishes, and have battle re-enactments. You choose your own weapon, and you can find a Softair version of it on the internet. Softair guns normally shoot 6mm Plastic Balls to distances of up to 30-40 metres in length. They do sting a bit when you are hit, but not as much as with paintballs. The power that is exerted cannot legally be over 1 Joule of energy. This means that you can have a realistic battle, and NOT get hurt. If you are interested in playing this game, just do a search on http://www.uk.yahoo.com for softair and find a nice place to have an ENJOYABLE battle.Thank you for your time      ', '    I m not saying that I m not a fan of McDonalds as I do call in from time to time.  However, the service sometimes leaves a lot to be desired   I ve lost count of the number of times I ve stood in a queue of about 10 people with one person behind the counter serving and about 6 others just wandering about trying to look busy   I suppose this largely depends on which branch you go into....you d never catch that happening at Marble Arch in London but it s a frequent occurence at the branch next to my local cinema.Another complaint I have concerns their drive thru service....why are they never capable of giving me the right drink (just cos I tend to be picky and ask for fresh orange juice.....since when did this become either still or fizzy fanta?????)  I always end up having to get out of the car and change my drink thus defeating the object of the whole drive thru thing You may now be thinking that with all these complaints, why do I still go there....well.....it does have some redeeming features.....On the positive side, it s cheap, clean and friendly with a quite a good variety of food on offer. Plus, the happy meal toys are excellent....and I don t mean for the kids either   I have a collection of Whinnie the Pooh and Toy Story toys from happy meals that are really cool....okay, so I m just a big kid at heart      ', '    The odeon cinema is situated in the centre of sheffield and so, is really, really easy to get to.  However, its one of the strangest places I have been to.  This is the only cinema that I have ever been to, where there is a break for icecreams and drinks between the trailers and the film  The lights go on and the odeon light starts zooming around the ceiling again.  There is usually a instantaneous round of applause for the swirly light.  During the well-renowned  break  there is  quality  music played -, usually 70 s stuff or soundtracks from movies,  they once played  ferry across the mersey  repeatedly The refreshments are obviously ridiculously expensive, but they do have quality pick-a-mix  (including  fizzy chips  )It is always a good place to go on a Tuesday, as it will only cost    2   The rest of the time the odeon is reasonably cheap, with student discounts available, which are always good The cinema is always crowded and full of screaming kids   This gets particularly bad during the school holidays, so avoid like the plague There is absolutely no room for your legs, although the posh seats do allow for a midget  (they used to charge you more for the posh seats, but they seem to have given up now )The screens are on lots of different levels and access may be difficult for diabled people.  The staff however, are very helpful.They usually get the latest releases, although they don t show indie films very often - the showroom is the best place in sheffield for alternative films.     ', '    A superb city that has something for everyone. The most attractive aspect of the city is the tourism. So many different people from different cultures visit Strasbourg every year and add to the already existent culture. The large number of museums means that no-one goes away with an empty mind. For example, the  Mus   e Alsacien  covers the history of life in the region, the characteristics of the region, the crafts and much more. The city is supported by a mayor who is very ecologically minded and as a result, an electric tram system was setup, running very frequently through the city from a park and ride area. The city itself is of great beauty, the wonderful medieval cathedral and many interesting monuments. The added charm comes from the quaint caf   s and restaurants that line some of the cobbled streets, in between the boutiques. As you would expect from a large city, the full array of high street shops are present. Another important reason for visiting Strasbourg is the link with Germany. German culture is evident and a short drive leads to the German border. Strasbourg is one of the most attractive cities in France and with the European Parliament residing in the city, the city has a strong business aspect too.  With an airport that serves 18 major international airlines, as can be expected froma  central point in Europe, access to the city is excellent. From the limited time I spent in Strasbourg I was enthralled and very much attracted to the city. I even considered going to university in the city such was the appeal. As I have mentioned above, the sheer number of mixed communities withi the city provides something for everyone and Srtrasbourg is certainly a city not to be missed.      ', '    Amazing is exactly how I found Times Square   There was so much life there, and it s such a great atmosphere   The biggest Virgin Megastore is situated here, and it s a must to visit for any music fan.  It has everything you could possible think of Theres alot of places to eat around here, including the 24 hour McDonalds.   You ll never go hungry there   If your looking for tickets for Broadway shows, the TKTS booth (just underneath the famous Coca-Cola sign) sells off the days tickets normally at 50 .  Theres always big ques for this, but is worth it when your saving 50 .  To stand underneath the Coca-Cola sign is a must also   You ll never be able to see it on t.v. again without shouting out  I stood there      Just next door to the 24 hour McDonalds is a Tourist Information Office.  This is very handy, and has information on just about anything you d need to know about New York.  You can also buy tickets for bus tours etc. here.  One thing they will be able to provide here, is information on stand-by-tickets for T.V. shows.  If your interested in being in the audience of a T.V. show such as Ricki Lake (I went, and it s deff recommended ), Who Wants To Be A Millionnaire, Good Morning America etc. then they ll be able to provide you with the full list.The bus terminal is just a few blocks up (about a 10 minute walk), and Times Square is an amazing place to see lit up a night.  It s really is amazing to see.       ']

Using a mixture of phrase book, dictionary and common sense I managed to book two tickets for the Juve match, total charge    49. In addition they had found a nearby bar that would be showing the Modena v AC Milan game live on TV. What a way to spend a mild Spring Sunday afternoon in Milan, sitting in a bar packed full of locals watching football while knocking back the beers. It was awesome, bearing in mind that kick off wasn t due for ninety minutes. Each set of supporters had a cheer leader armed with a megaphone, organising and conducting the chanting and singing  while hanging dangerously over the parapet. Amazing.As the ground began to fill up, seats around us were being taken by a number of English lads who looked very shaken. I would recommend going at this time if you are not bothered about a bit of cold because it costs so much less  We woke up one morning and there was snow  covering the ground that had fallen overnight, but none fell during the day, it wasn t much colder and it looked quite pretty on the buildings. MetroI would recommend you ask the hotel staff about the local metro ticket service if you don t know about it as we couldnt understand it at all. There were no English instructions on the ticket machines and nobody around seemed to know a word of English. So we were having to buy a ticket for almost every journey which was a pain, we were trying to find out how to get a ticket to hop on and off all day. The tickets seemed very reasonably priced though. Also the metro stops are often and there isn t really anywhere you could want to go where there isn t a metro right outside. In the stations there is a lot of grafitti and we got tiny children coming over asking for money sent by their parents which wasn t very nice. Also there are a lot of people on a night setting up stalls of hangbags, sunglasses, hats etc. They don t harass you to buy stuff though. AccomodationWe stayed at the Hotel Adam, this was only a metro ride away from everywhere and luckily the metro is right outside the door which is very good. It was    97 for both of us for 3 nights at this hotel. It was a 4* and very nice. We booked this through expedia.co.uk.It didn t have everything stated on the website but was good. If you are on a budget we found expedia a good option. Food and DrinkWhen we arrived at the hotel we were hungry and wanted a beer, we had a wander around and after walking half of Milans ground found a restaurant - it looked very quiet and it was 11.30 so we thought we d get a take away - we got 2 pizzas for 11 euro and found in the town the pizzas were 6 to 7 euro each so not badly prices at all and they are yummy. The drinks are very cheap in supermarkets, so if you are likely to be drinking at your hotel, I would suggest buying from a supermarket rather than an off license, mini bar or hotel bar. We paid 24 euro for 4 small bottles of budweiser at the hotel bar - how silly are we. There are Macdonald s everywhere  I had to try the real italian version of my favourite dish ever - Spaghetti Carbonara, bu was disappointed to find the pasta quite hard and stodgy. I thought maybe it was a crappy restaurant but a few people I ve spoke to said it was all over Italy like that.There are quite a few chinese restaurants that I heard were nice thought we didn t visit any.One restaurant we did go to was Ajoblanco. It was very nice and served traditional spanish dihes and tapas. It was reasonably priced and the setting was lovely. Would definitely recommend the paella. Well that s about it. I would say couples and sightseeing lovers, or very rich shoppers are the people who would appreciate Milan most. I don t think children would be that interested as there isn t that much for them to do  We got a bargain with accomodation and flights with both and insurance for less than    100 per person. The flights were booked with ryanair and expedia for the accomodation. This price included airport transfers we booked through Ryanair at    9 each return which was good as the coach was regular and easy to get off the plane and straight onto. Insurance was also included in the price so can t moan. Once you re there if travelling on the metro and you can figure out how to use the machine, travel is cheap. Food is reasonably priced unless you visit the v. posh restaurants.Most of the best attractions don t have entrance charges and if they do, they are very small. For the daily budget at the bottom I don t know what to put because that depends on what you are going to do, where you are eating and drinking and shopping  I would say about    30-   40 a day. Things that we didn t do and you may want to are - go go-karting, go to the motorbike museum, art galleries and see The Last Supper painting which you have to book to visit. I think it was about 6 euro per person and you book  at most newspaper kiosks. I don t think I would go back as I have been and seen all of the things I would want to see but I would recommend it. If you go 3 nights is probably best - if you plan to do a lot a week is the most you could probably stay.One thing I would definitely say is to take a guide book and brush up on a bit of Italiano because it ll help a lot  Thanks for reading. x     ', '    The first time I went to Milan, I hated it. Then I went back. Then I went back again, and I grew increasingly fond of the place. Milan isn t the first place that immediately springs to mind (my mind anyway ) when it comes to picking places to visit. It is the industrial and financial centre of Italy and it leans far more towards the lifestyle of northern Europeans than Italian cities further south. Most famous for it s shops, fashion industry and a whopping great cathedral, it is also quite a young city. As for the shops and the fashion, I can t really comment because I didn t have much money to spare when I was there. They certainly looked good from the window and even the most un-shopping person has to take a walk down the Via della Spiga which is where many of the top designer shops are, and it is a great  people-watching  spot, possibly one of the best in Europe. You can smell the wealth dripping off these people, and the shop assistants look so snooty you almost feel obliged to laugh at them  At the other end of the scale there are many  outlet  shops of the designers which sell last season s fashion at knock down prices. The Piazza del Duomo is the heart of the city, in more senses than simply geography. The Duomo is possibly the main  must-see  in Milan, and it is worth going up to the roof (there s a lift ) because the views from the top are great (and there s a cute security guard at the top ). Next to the Duomo is the Galleria, which I think is the oldest  shopping arcade  and is certainly one of the most beautiful. It has a mosaiced floor and a glass ceiling and there s even a McDonalds in there if you can t afford the prices of some of the upmarket cafes  In the Castle Sforzesco lies next to a park (the only park in the city, not particularly pleasant place to stroll, I managed to wander into the part where loads of young kids were busy injecting themselves with all sorts of substances (and I doubt it was treatment for diabetes.. )). The Castle itself is worth a visit, not least because it s free, but there is a museum inside which you pay to go into and is quite impressive. Lots of paintings and sculpture. Milan is also home to  The Last Supper  which is in Chiesa della Maria Santa delle Grazie, but I didn t see it as the queues were too long. La Scala, the fine opera house has also recently emerged from scaffolding and is back to her former glory. The area of Navagli around the canals is a great spot which comes to life at night with many clubs, pubs and bars. In an attempt to draw italians out, earlier in the evening, many of the pubs and bars offer free food, and it isn t bad food either, usually a buffet-type deal with finger food, but enough to keep you going, and the drinks aren t overly expensive either. There are some markets which appear over the weekend as well, on the banks of the canals and you can find just about anything you want to. Milan is probably more fun than I expected it to be. I thought it would be more staid and stuffy, but like most places, it depends where you head when it gets dark  And one last word of warning.. beware the mosquitoes       ', '    One of the most striking things about Milan is the traffic. It s terrible - people drive like maniacs, park like lunatics and lean on the horn at any opportunity. For this reason it is always better to avoid the stress of trying to drive anywhere at every opportunity. OK, you cuold take a taxi, but with a public transport system as good as Milan s you d be a fool to do so. . . . Public transport in Miln is completely integrated - the buses, trams and tube trains are all run by the same company, so a single ticket can get use any or all of these methods to get you where you want to go. If you have a bus pass (enquire at the offices, near the tube station Zara at the end of the yellow line) then it s even better value for money. . . .  most people though, just buy un biglietto for 1500lira (about 50p) at any one of the little newsagent booths in the city. Once stamped on the train platform or aboard the bus/ tram it is valid for an hour, so you can hop off your bus and catch another one if necessary. This is enough time to get you at least half way across the city, if not more, although different rates apply if you want to use the metro to explore some of Milan s outlying towns (it s worth travelling northwards on the Green tube line for a while - it takes you right out of the city.) . . . . the tube stations are great for short journeys between busy locations and not at all claustrophobic, although they do suffer from dodgy smells and grafitti, but the authorities do try and these things can hardly be avoided. The trams are better for less heavily frequented routes, they are generally clean and prompt and some of the older ones must date back to the 1930s but are still in perfect working order. They often have their own lanes on the roads and so are less affected than buses by traffic conditions.The buses are convenient, modern and comfortable, but perhaps a little less prompt than the other forms of transport, due to their vulnerability to traffic jams.     ', '    I spent 3 months living as a student in Milan and, to be honest, I didn t like it. I found it dirty, ugly, unfriendly and oppressive, and expensive to boot. This did at least give me the motivation to seek out the best places to drown my sorrows, and I will be sharing some of that knowledge later. I ve since returned though, and have learned to appreciate some of the good things this sprawling city has to offer.Milan is an industrial city in the North of Italy, easily accessible by Malpensa Airport and then a short bus ride. It is also well connected to the rest of Italy and the countries to the north by train, and so however you arrive you will probably wind up at the stazione centrale. It s worth looking at this building, which is an incredible example of the fascist/futurist architecture favoured by Mussolini. Keep a tight hold on your wallet, pickpockets abound here.The most famous building in Milan though, has to be the Cathedral in Piazza del Duomo. Take a tram or underground train (public transport in Milan is excellent, don t even try to use a car or taxi.) to  Duomo   and spend some time soaking up the cosmopolitan atmos - Milan draws tourists and fashion industry professionals from all over the world, and a large (by Italian standards anyway) immigrant population . On the whole, Milan seen from ground level is not particularly pretty, so walk round to the left of the cathedral where you wil find stairs (and a lift) to the roof where, for a few thousand lira, you can take in the most spectacular views in the city.You are now on the outskirts of Milan s fashion district. Keep wandering away from the piazza and sooner or later you will find little side streets crammed with designer outlets, each more exclusive than the last. Unless you are planning to really impress someone with the size of your wallet, don t buy anything to eat or drink within half a mile of the cathedral - you are unlikely to find anything really worth eating. If you really must eat go to the AutoGrill or (If desperate) one of the dozens of McDonalds in this area. While the food is no better than anywhere else locally, at least the prices are acceptable.For really good food, there are only two restaurants I can recommend - and sadly I can t remember the name of either - however they are both on the same street and easy to find: Go to Parc Solari to the South and West of Duomo, and head for Via Montevideo. Before long you ought to stumble upon an excellent pub called Murphy s Law. Stop here for a pint and a chat with the (Irish) landlord, then head into one of the two restaurants on the same street. You will pay a fair bit of money at either one, but the food is truly magnificent.If you prefer to cook your own food, the market near Piazzale Piemonte and Piazza Sicilia is unmissable. You can get all your genuine italian speciality meats and cheeses at market prices. For clothes and other goodies at market prices, try the Monday morning market along the South bank of Milan s main Canal. This canal, and the canals around it are all about 15 minutes walk south of Piazzale Duomo, and is the real heart of Milan s nightlife. There are more pubs and bars along here than you could care to mention, all of various quality. I recommend you try as many as you can and pick your own favourite. If you should stumble across it in this (I can t direct you, sorry) go into Pogue Mahone s - A really lively pub with atmosphere steaming out of the windows. Another good one is The Old Fashioned Cafe, which is between Piazza Cadorna and Parc Sempione, hidden round the back of a building which looks very much like a theatre. They used to (and still might) do wicked international nightys of a Wednesday. Turn up early in order to get food and drink cheaper. Don t bother with beers, go for the killer cocktails.Parc Sempione is also attached to the lovely old Castello sforzesco - it s free to go in and look around, as is the museum, and it s a nice place to sit and eat lunch. Be prepared for the stray cats though. Finally, try to plan your visit to coincide with the festival of San Ambrogio. Every year, in November or December, a whole village of market stalls fills the streets around the private university (La Cattolica). It s nice to wander round the stalls with a cup of mulled wine picking out unusual Christmas presents.Oh, and if you are ever looking for rented accomodation in Milan, be very, VERY careful.     ']
filtered_hist_vote_written: ['    Milan undoubtedly has some of the finest designer boutiques in Europe, and the scope is incredible, with more or less entire streets filled with designer boutiques. Of course with the Italian Lire, the price tags run into the millions, and there is very little that anyone coming on holiday can really afford to substantially overhaul their wardrobe. Indeed becasue of Milan s status, there almost seems to be a slight premium on prices of clothes - a Milano tax  All the international names are present in Milan as well as a whole host of Italian designers, whose work is bubbling under the surface ready to make the big breakthrough. For an up and coming designer Milan is wonderful as you can see what is in and what to go for for next season, but for mere mortals, the prices are a bit out of the range of everyday shoppers.     ', '    I visited Milan in May of 1999. I m obsessed with fashion and I m ashamed to admit that it s my ambition to visit as many  fashion capitals  as I possibly can. Milan certainly didn t disappoint. It only cost us    40 return with  Buzz  Airlines and we managed to get cheap, but very nice as it turned out, accomodation over the internet. This gave us lots of spare spending money for shopping and to eat the gorgeous food that s on offer all over the city.Ok, there s no joking around about what you wear here. I dressed up to look around the centre, and still felt under-dressed  The trick is to wear as much high fashion as you can, whilst pretending that you re not at all uncomfortable. The Italians manage it perfectly. To ease any high-heel blisters, take the metro system around the town. Its cheap and easy to navigate. Only tip is, make sure you remember exactly which exit you came in from - there are so many different exits from each of the stations that you can easily get lost on your return. Buy a daily ticket, or better still a ticket for your entire stay, it works out a lot cheaper overall.Head for the Duomo - the centre of the action. Here you can shop in elegance and eat at some of the best (and not cheap) restaurants in the city. If you are doing some sight-seeing, venure up the Duomo. Hope that the lifts are working - the steps are a definite no go in your high heels - and wonder at the incredible (they really are) views at the top.      ', '    Hi all, first of all, forgive my mistakes but I am in italian girl and my Engish is not good ;)I would like to talk about Cagliari, the town where I live.Cagliari is situated on the south cost of Sardinia Island in the mediterranean sea. There are two parts of the town u have to visit: the old part called Castello, with old church and towers, with old streets, and the touristic part: the sea.near Cagliari, there are 7 km of white beach and clear sea where u can catch the sun and have a fun in the beach  This beach is called POETTO, but if u can move by car, u could should visit the several beaches in the south east part.In cagliari there are alot of hotel, cheap or expensive, there are discoes, cinemas...The Cagliari airport is 15minutes by bus far from the center, the port is in the main street of cagliari (Via Roma).Have a fun in CAgliari and if u need an help, pls contact me :)     ', '    Ravenna was, indeed, for a brief time the capital of Italy, but now it is most famous for the roman mosiacs which adorn here. She is a beautiful city, close to the coast, indeed, a good day trip from escapees from the Romagnola Riviera (Rimini being the most famous resort)A very compact city, it is easy to visit most of the more important attractions (these attractions being, primarily, the Roman mosiacs and the Cathedral and surrounding churches), in a day and still have time for a pleasant lunch, perhaps partaking of the speciality of Romagna, piadine. The mosaics remain what the city is most famous for, and they are housed a little way out of the city itself. There is a university in the city, which adds a bit of life to an otherwise pretty, but perhaps a little quiet, city. As the regional centre, as well as an important historical centre, Ravenna does her best to attract tourists, but has none of the rush evident in some of her more well known neighbours.  A town that grew from something of a historical curiousity and has retained a charm of a working city, make this a good place to stop for a while. There is enough to see to make it feel worthwhile without too much that you will feel you are missing out if you move on. There are a couple of churches of interest in the city, and one on the outskirts which takes a bit of finding, as well as the tomb of Dante, and lots of Roman excavations. It s an interesting detour, probably, rather than a place to visit in its own right.     ']

If you’re planning a trip to Milan, here’s a balanced insider’s view to help you navigate the city like a local. Public transport in Milan is generally excellent—trams run clean and on time, less hampered by traffic than buses, which, while modern and comfortable, can get delayed during rush hours. The integrated transport system offers great value for money, making it easy and affordable to explore the city and beyond, especially since Milan is well connected by train and airport links.

For cultural and historical highlights, don’t miss Parc Sempione and Castello Sforzesco—both beautiful, free to enter, and perfect for a leisurely stroll steeped in history. The Duomo, Milan’s iconic centerpiece, is a must-see not only for its stunning Gothic architecture but also for the spectacular views from its rooftop. Around the Duomo, you’ll find elegant shopping streets filled with high-end boutiques, showcasing Milan’s world-renowned fashion scene. While these designer stores are a feast for the eyes, be prepared for premium prices.

If you’re after authentic local experiences and better value, skip the pricey restaurants near the Duomo. Instead, explore the Monday morning market along the main canal for affordable clothes and goods, or visit the market near Piazzale Piemonte and Piazza Sicilia for excellent Italian meats and cheeses at market prices. Timing your visit during the San Ambrogio festival in late November or early December adds a charming cultural layer, with festive market stalls and a lively atmosphere.

product_reviews: ['    With Easyjet now offering budget flights to Budapest, wht better way of celebrating Hungary s accession to the European Union than a visit to one of Europe s most fascinating and exotic cities?Budapest is often described as one of the  great European capitals  and mentioned in the same breath as Vienna or Paris. However, mention the city to most people and they will associate it with the Communist era rather than the  belle epoque .In September 2003 I was lucky enough to travel round central and eastern Europe by train taking in 5 countries, all of which were formerly under the Soviet sphere of influence, behind the Iron Curtain. I have to say that of all the places I saw, Budapest was most like the cities of western Europe and seemed to have that cosmopolitan air that the grand European cities possess.This is for the most part due to it s history - it was the second city of the Habsburg empire and, up to the turn of the twentieth century, Budapest was close behind Paris with a reputation for hedonism and style. This is evident in the architecture of the Pest part of the city with wide, tree-lined boulevards, tenement blocks with those Art Deco wrought iron balconies and the covered arcades inside the tenements.It is also apparent from the number of cafes in the Parisienne/Viennese style. I would certainly recommend a visit to the  Gerbeaud Patisserie  at Vorosmarty ter - the largest and most famous of Budapest s confectioners.Budapest is, of course, made up of two quite distinct towns - Buda and Pest. Buda lies to the south of the Danube and is historically the town of royalty, whereas Pest is more closley associated with business and finance. Buda is quiet and tranquil, Pest is busy and lively and home to most of the sights that tourists make a beeline for.Buda---------The most popular sight in Buda is the Varhegy (Castle Hill). Standing atop a huge craggy hill is the Royal Palace which contains numerous visitor attractions. There are several ways to get to the top - walk (such hard work), take a bus (not very exciting) or take the funicular - by the far the best way and affords super views. It is an old restored 19th century funicular and comprises two tiny carriages, one behind the other.When you get to the top, you gat a tremendous view across to Pest and if you look down to your left you will see the impressive Gothic style  Parliament building with it s famous dome.There is a lot to see up on the hill and most of it is contained in the Royal Palace building - The Ludwig Collection (Museum Of Contemporary Art), the Hungarian National Gallery and the Budapest History Museum are just a couple. We only did the Ludwig Collection but I can thoroughly recommend it - there are some interesting Pop Art pieces including work by Warhol and Lichtenstein and a wonderful Picasso. There is a small entrance fee but admission is free with a Budapest Card (more on that later).There are usually loads of people milling around here and there are often musicians playing in the gardens of the palace. The flowers are beautiful and it is worth coming up here even if you do not visit any of the museums. Also up on the hill but in the old streets of the town, there are several pretty churches which are worth looking at and you should take a stroll through the scenic streets - there has been a fortress here since the 12th century and therefore settlements nearby so there is an enormous breadth of architectural history in these streets. Pest----------Pest, as I have said, is busier and more vital than Buda. If you are staying in a hotel it is more likely to be in Pest and it is probably where you will spend most of your time.Much of the architecture here dates from the late 19th century so it has more of a homogenous look to it than Buda. The Belvaros (inner city) is where it s all going on for visitors to Budapest and this is where you ll find mostof the bars and cafes. A good example is Vorosmarty ter  - an attractive square where you ll see buskers, portraitists, craft stalls and lovely fountains. If you go at Christmas, this is the place to sample some warming Hungarian street-fare.I love Lipotvaros (Leopold Town) which is the area around St. Stephens Basilica and leads down to the waterfront and the Chain Bridge where you can cross to Buda.  One of the most famous buildings here is the Gresahm Palace - a huge Art Nouveau building, originally built for an insurance company. It has beautiful wrought iron gates bearing a peacock design and stained-glass windows depicting Hungarian heroes.St. Stephens Basilica is one you HAVE to see but it s often only open at weekends, although they try to keep the giant door open so you can at least get a glimpse inside. The square in which it s situated is beautiful and is reminiscent of the great piazzas of Rome.One of the great attractions of Budapest are the baths - some are very old and ornate and they are popular with tourists and locals alike. The best known are probably the Gellert Baths close to the Danube in Buda. They are decorated with fantastic majolica tiles and the spa water gushes out of lion-headed spouts. These baths have a mixed sex thermal pool and there is an outdoor pool for use in summer too.There are baths all over the city but you should do your homework if you plan to visit any of them because some of them have separate bathing times for men and women. If you are hoping for relief from a particular medical complaint you should also read up on the subject because certain baths are recommended for particular conditions.My favourite place was about 10 kilometres southwest of the city, outside Buda and it is the Szorbopark - the Statue Park. After the fall of the Communists, the great iconic statues of Stalin and Lenin and those commemorating great achievements otr dedicated to the workers of Hungary were all removed from the streets and squares of Budapest. In the mid late 1990s some enterprising soul found them all in storage and thought that it would be interesting (and no doubt lucrative) to display them all in one place - so that Statue Park was born. As you walk round Communist marches are played over a loud-speaker and in the very centre of the park is a flower-bed with it s flowers trained to the shape of a red star - it s the most wonderful outdoor museum I have ever visited.Pick up a leaflet in a tourist information office or at a station for details on how to get there.That reminds me...public transport. I am glad to report that Budapest has an excellent public transport system. A combination of clean and frequent trams, undreground trains and buses makes Budapest an easy city to get round.  The metro covers most places tourists will want to get to and there are 3 lines, colour-coded which intersect at Deak ter in Pest. Between stations, the driver will announce the next stop and the direction of the train is indicated by the name of the station at the end of the line.Tickets are available for all transport from kiosks, tobacconists/newsagents and stations. Travel is cheap but you can make it even more so by buying a one day or three day card.The Budapest Card costs around 7.50 poundsfor 48 hours, but can be bought for 24 or 72 hours too. With it you get free entry into many museums and galleries, discounted entry into others and free travel on public transport. These are available from main stations and tourist information offices. When you buy it you are given a thick brochure with full details of where you can use it and it also includes a useful map.There is no shortage of places to eat in Budapest. There are plenty of restaurants serving local food which I always like to see because I think that these places are sometimes difficult to find in cosmopolitan cities. Therefore if you want to sample the goulash you have plenty of options. Vegetarians  - do not fear, you can order goulash in all kinds of ways including meat-free so you will not be left out. Freshwater fish is also common here - my partner sampled the carp and he reports that it was very good. For a special meal, I would recommend a great little restaurant at Hajos u. 43 (district VI) called  The Marquis de Salade  which served Azerbaijani, Hungarian and Russian cuisine. While it was fairly expensive by Hungarian standards, we had a good bottle of Hungarian wine and starters and mains for just over thirty pounds. I have to mention my starter in particular - it was a big domed mound of pickled herrings, covered with beetroot, then this was covered with an outer layer of chopped boiled eggs - scrumptious   Otherwise, as you would expect, there are the restaurants which you now find in every capital city - Mexican, sushi bars, pizza joints, etc.Pastry/bread type snacks are popular as street food and, especially in the stations, you will find stall selling vast arrays of these - the most popular ones in seem to be a sweet pastry swirl which is covered with a sticky looking glaze and sprinkled with cinnamon. Please beware if you buy a sandwich from one of these stalls - with only minutes to spare, I bought one to eat on a long train journey. It was a small baguette and seemed to have slices of salami and salad sticking out of it. When, on the train, I removed the three layers of clingfilm, the bread wasn t buttered and they were only half slices of tomato and salami, cleverly presented to make it look like the sandwich was crammed with filling We only really stuck to restaurants and bars for nightlife but there are some discos/nightclubs in the city and you can find details of what is on through listings magazines. Another useful point - most of the city has been fly-postered but it s always up to date so check them out if you fancy going to any gigs. Shopping in Budapest is not particularly exciting and souvenirs are pretty dull too - mass produced Russian dolls (you know, the kind that fit inside each other), fur hats with Communist insignia on the peak and dried chillis and paprika. Hotel accommodation in Budapest is not that cheap. Pensions are a bit cheaper but are starting to approach hotel prices. You will find most accommodation in Pest rather than Buda. If you are on a tight budget you should consider staying in private rooms. There are always loads of people offering private rooms when you arrive in any of the mainline train stations, or try at the tourist information offices. Always make sure you know how far out the place is before you agree.I  barely scratched the surface of Budapest when I visited but I can safely say that, at some point in the future, I will be back.  It is a city which hits you with new surprises each time you turn a corner. it is loud, it is grimy (grimy, not littered), and it can be very crowded but at the same time it is elegant, lively and exciting.However, do not go to Budapest expecting all of these things at knock-down prices. Budapest has been receiving visitors longer than Prague and it s prices are now edging up to those of other western European capitals. You can eat fairly cheaply and travel is reasonable but you will spend more than you expect.  It IS one of the great European capitals and I suggest you get yourself there as soon as possible but remember to take a bit of cash with you . Imagine having your first free elections in 1900? I found the history of Budapest very moving as it is related to the visitor in its proud displays of statues and monuments of war heroes, museums, palaces and art galleries.There are over sixty museums and art galleries in Budapest ranging from international collections (Why do I still get excited when I see an original Turner or a Van Gogh?) and others such as the Hungarian National Museum and more local interests. The city is a feast to wonder over and to be impressed by.Although we had booked for one week in the Gellert with its choice of several restaurants, on our first evening we were compelled to explore both Buda and Pest so we began our adventures by walking across the Elizabeth bridge, one of several,  to Pest. We found ourselves promenading  along the stylishly illuminated Vaci Street, the fashionable shopping area with spectacular statues, fountains, cafes and bars. Before long we were experiencing our first Hungarian meal of Goose Livers and Pancakes with Sheep  8217;s Cheese and Dill, washed down with local beer and wine in  a terrace restaurant on the Eastern Bank of the Danube with a spectacular view of the Royal Palace, and the funicular railway we planned for the next day, across the twinkling river. We also had our first taste of the Hungarian Gypsy violinist serenading me to Lara  8217;s Theme, the first of many         The  continental climate, with very hot summers and extreme winters, meant that September was an ideal time to visit as July and August are very hot indeed, and Budapest is a city meant to be explored on foot. Although there is an excellent public transport system of taxis, buses, trams and taxis, walking everywhere allowed us to soak up the atmosphere as well us giving us the excuse to take frequent breaks in the many pavement bars and cafes for excellent coffee and icy cold beers.There are a total of thirty one spa-water pools and thermal baths in Budapest fed by the mineral rich hot springs deep inside the earth. These are government subsidised  and regarded as a very important aspect of Budapest culture with health giving qualities. Several of the original Turkish built baths from the 16th Century  remains in operation. One of the most stunning examples of Ottoman architecture, the Rudas, is for men only with no need to wear a bathing suit as a small apron is provided So every morning, after a swim in the Gellert  8217;s marble columned indoor swimming pool and an excellent breakfast, we  8217;d plan our day. Just think architecture and history and culture. From Roman amphitheatres, medieval monuments, the Gothic period, the Turkish remains, the Baroque style of the Hapsburgs and the Neo-Classical structures all telling their own story of invasion, destroying and rebuilding as each new invader appeared to raze the existing city to the ground and set about rebuilding in their own style. We had expensive meals, thirty pounds for two with plenty of wine, and cheap ones, fifteen pounds for two and always with plenty of wine and beer. These are all things to do next time we visit Buda and Pest, the marriage of two halves forming Budapest, a magical and romantic city. There are details here:Hungarian National Tourist Office Embassy of the Republic of Hungary, 46 Eaton Place SW1X 8AL Tel: 020 782 1032     ', '    Budapest is one of the most beautiful and loveliest cities of planet earth. This city is the capital of Hungary - a country in central Europe. Budapest has two parts: Buda on hill and Pesti. Danube - the river, separates these two parts of the city from each other. Budapest has a very rich history, and it would take me years to mention it all. The city is known for its culture, for its bridges that were destroyed during the World War Two and  then rebuilt, for its Houses of Parliament (which to me are a smaller and simplier version of the British Houses of Parliament), for its castle on hill, for its wonderful thermal baths, for its delicious food and wine, and the list can go on and on and on ...  Since July 1998 I have visited the city several times, and frankly, I cannot get enough of it. It is a city that has everything. It is so beautiful and so romantic. The weather, food and wine are really divine. Budapest is one of the cheapest capital cities in Europe, and you can see a good three hours long jazz concert for as little as 50 pence.  How to get to Budapest? The easiest way is to fly. Most European airlines fly to Budapest at least once a day. Malev - the Hungarian airline does some cheap deals from time to time. Normally, I pay around    160 pounds for a return trip. If you pay more than that you know you are being ... . The following is a down to earth guide if you plan to visit Budapest. So, keep reading     Basic vocabulary:-  Ter  means  Square -  Utca  means  Street - Taxis and transport: Remember that you should always call City Taxi at 211-1111 when you need a taxi. Calling is always cheaper than picking up a taxi on the street. If you are not near a phone you may also take Fo, Buda, 6x6, or Radio taxis as well. ', '    Budapest is the capital of Hungary which was one of the first Eastern bloc countries to become more open in the late 1980s.    As the capital city it is home to many of Hungary s government buildings and historically important venues.  A city steeped in history it is a superb venue to visit for those with an interest in architecture - I found it one of the most fascinating cities I have visited.GETTING THEREBy air:Budapest is situated in central Hungary and is served by an international airport which is approximately 10miles from the city centre.  Flights from Britain to Hungary are by either Malev or British Airways.  The airport is quite small considering its international status and is easy to find your way around with a few small duty free shops.There are a number of choices to get from the airport to the city:Taxi - there are large numbers of taxis and private hire firms available but beware they can be very expensive.  If you chose to take a taxi negotiate a set fare for the journey beforehand.  The journey to the city centre takes around half an hour if the traffic is relatively busy.  Courtesy Buses - if you are staying at one of the higher star hotels these often lay on shuttle buses.  Check details beforehand, if booked with the hotel in question the bus is usually free but double check about any charges.Bus - there are frequent bus connections between the airport and city centre which is a lot cheaper than hiring a taxi.  This journey can take up to 40 minutes.  You can also take the bus to the nearest metro station and take the underground to the city centre for the remainder of the journey.  This is a good idea if you are staying outside of the city centre at an area nearer an underground station.  Good idea to get a metro map before arriving.By train:If interrailing etc there are a number of rail routes into Hungary mostly coming via Vienna.  There are three railway stations in Hungary - East, South and West so double check which station you are coming into. By road:As the capital Hungary is well served by a number of major motorways, once again the most popular route being up from Vienna, Austria.By boat:Another popular route to Budapest from Austria during the summer is by hydrofoil from Vienna. This journey can take up to five hours.THE CITYThe city is made of three towns but is mostly thought of as two halves - Buda and Pest.  Buda is on the right hand side of the Danube and has the more older, quaint feeling.  Pest is on the left hand side of the Danube and feels more built up with fine buildings thanks to its prosperous past and as the seat of many government buildings. The city is divided into 21 districts which are represented by Roman numerals.  The city is very large, approx  16 miles by 18 miles but there are many large parklands and green areas so it does not feel overly built up in areas.The area has very distinct seasons and I visited in summer which was typically very hot and very dry.  Whilst very hot during the day it became much cooler on an evening so I d suggest packing plenty of light layers.  GETTING AROUNDAs mentioned above there are numerous taxis but be aware they can sometimes be expensive and its wise to negotiate a price beforehand.  There is a good tram and bus network which is easy to figure out and relatively cheap all-day tickets etc make it a simple way to explore.  Being a large city it can be tough on the feet - take some comfortable shoes, it may sound like common sense but this is one city that really got to my feet There is also the metro system. Oh, this brings tears of laughter to the eyes.  With three lines it is hardly the London Underground and is very simple to use, with ticket machines in the stations and people were very helpful when I first tried to figure it out.  The first part of underground was opened in 1896, other lines opening in 1973 and 1979.  It is rather rickety and small but is worth the journey to see some wonderful tiling in the underground stations. HOTELSBudapest has a wide range of hotels from 5 to 1 star as well as guest houses and a youth hostel.  The price of the larger chain hotels is comparable with that in other capital cities.  The further from the city centre you stay the more reasonable the room rates become.  Unless adventurous I d ensure you have a room reserved beforehand as it is a very busy city especially as it holds many festivals, cultural and sporting events.  SHOPPPINGBefore going to Hungary I had read that it was both the centre of shopping for Eastern Europe and cheap.  In many respects I have to disagree with these two statements.  In Pest there were a number of larger, department style shops as you d expect in any large city.  However there were a number of shops and I was shocked to see the lack of stock they were carrying and the age behind it.  Many of the shops looked like British shops from 30 years ago.  In this area items were either old versions of those items that had lost there fashionable status in the west - especially electric carving knives   The department stores were very westernized as were many of their prices.  This was also noticeable in a number of the main chain hotels - the prices were comparable with other capital cities.  For more regional shopping I recommend you go into Buda were there are a number of smaller craft shops and stalls.  Particularly nice was the Hungarian lace and linen works, many highly embroided however, these still weren t cheap.. Leather goods were reasonable as were Hungarian woodwork and pottery. Overall I felt the shopping eluded me somewhat, I m sure it was hiding in a street I never found EATING OUT/FOOD   DRINKThere are a wide range of choices for eating out.  All the major hotels have open restaurants and there are a number of other restaurants lining the boulevards, many with outside eating areas.  The restaurants in the hotels serve an international menu on the whole but the overriding food choice at restaurants was very heavily red meat based.  If you are a red meat fan this is wonderful and I found the quality and value very good.  Possibly stodgy for some people the most popular meals were undoubtedly meat, potato and veg based, lots of stews..  As you d expect paprika is one of the major flavourings used. It is more difficult to find a wide selection for vegetarians and my veggie friend found her choice very limited, mainly to salad, cheese and potato dishes - however she made up for this on puddings.Hungary produces some superb puddings and cakes and I recommend you look out for the specialist cake and coffee rooms one of the most famous being Gerbeaud.  The range of coffees is vast and much of it I would use to tar roads but if that s your favourite taste you ll be in coffee heaven One area I cannot fault Hungary on - beer as well as their own makes beers from nearby Germany and Austria are very popular..  Proper big beer steins and glasses whilst sat out in the summer sun was the perfect break from sight seeing for me.Hungary is also famous for its own fruit brandies and some potent liquors which surely could double as rocket fuel.  One is a particularly powerful herbal liquor which has a distinctive taste you either love or hate   Oh and before you ask    yes there was a McDonalds - where isn t there one? NIGHTLIFEFor many people eating out is the nightlife and it can be made into a long evening especially when the weather allows for you to sit outside and watch the world go by.  The streets are very busy in the number of people but laid back on an evening, many people strolling along the Danube when night time markets are often held.  In the large city squares there is often street entertainment and other events often reflecting other events such as festivals in the city.  There are a number of nightclubs and discos catering for all tastes - check out the local English language newspaper (I think it was called the Budapest Sun) for more details.  There are often ballets and Operas at the State Opera House, even if you do not attend an event here be sure to visit to see the grand entrance and marble staircase.There are a number of popular casinos including a floating casino on the River Danube. SIGHTSEEINGThere is so much to see and do in Budapest I cannot begin to cover it all here so I will just give my edited highlights   Much of the sights can be seen on foot and via the tram/bus system.  My top tips:Simply walking around Buda is interesting and to get to Buda from Pest is the vernacular railway up Castle Hill which gives you a great view over Pest.TOP TIP - If you are a student make sure you have you International or National Student Union card with you - this will get you FREE into many museums and galleries and get you discounts on other tickets Castle Palace:Castle Palace is the impressive Palace on Buda which overlooks the Danube and Pest.  On an evening it is lit up and is a very beautiful sight.  The building is now home to the Hungarian National Gallery which  is on four floors and has art of both Hungarian and International importance.The exhibits were well laid out and the Palace has good natural light but many of the rooms felt sparse, cold and bear so it can become somewhat overbearing at times.  All the items were well labeled and a number of guide books were available.Chain Bridge:Chain Bridge adjoins Buda and Pest in front of the Castle Palace and is also lit on an evening making a striking display.  Fisherman s Bastion:This really is a strange and intriguing folly.  On Castle Hill, Buda the Fishermen of the Medieval times built this defence bastion in a neo-Romanesque side and it looks like a child s fairytale castle.  Off-white in colour it has fairytale like spires and towers and large sweeping staircases.  This makes any adult feel like a child again as it is large and imposing and cries for a game of hide and seek  It gives excellent, wide views of the city so is a must for the budding photographer.  In the courtyard is an impressive bronze statue of St Stephen sat upon a horse.  Matthias Church:Near the Fisherman s Bastion is Matthias Church.  This is a very grand and ornate church in a Gothic style.  It has a turbulent history having at one time being converted into a mosque when Hungary was invaded by the Turks in the 16th century and later it was taken over by the Jesuits and badly damaged in the Second World War.  The interior is stunning with many geometric designs and ornate stained glass windows.  Heroes Square (H   ns   k tere)Heroes Square is located slightly out of the city centre at H   ns   k tere which is easily accessible from the Metro (M1)Heroes Square  is an impressive square with a 118ft high column with a statue of the Angel Gabriel on top.  Around the bottom of the plinth are the sculptures of horsemen in bronze.  It is a very powerful area with the memorial to the Unknown Soldier incorporated. Museum of Fine Arts:The Museum of Fine Arts is located to the side of Heroes Square. This museum has 23 rooms though not all are always open to the public.  Unlike the National Museum this museum is more conventionally laid out with more intricate use of specialist lighting and better laid out overall.  Works include items of both Hungarian and International importance with special items on a visiting basis.  There s a nice caf    downstairs.  Parliament Building:I believe this building was partly designed on our own Palaces of Westminster and the resemblance is striking as it also has a waterfront fa   ade which is intricately carved with  88 figures of famous Hungarians including kings and military leaders.  The Parliament Building is topped by a large dome. There are a number of guided tours but the best view of the buildings fa   ade is from the other side of the river in Buda, from the Fisherman s Bastion.  SPASBudapest is famous for its spas as there are many mineral spas throughout the city which are believed to have many healing and relaxing qualities.  One of the most famous Spas is at G   llert which has various mud baths, steam rooms, sauna, brine, carbonic and wave baths.  The prices vary from spa to spa so check out the price list beforehand.  ATMOSPHEREBudapest is a large city yet even though I was there at a very busy time it never felt as crowded as most Western cities.  Admittedly I found it a rather dour city in places and noted many of the hotel workers were particularly gruff.  However, it was at a time when the Grand Prix was in so it was undoubtedly a stressful time for the tourist services.  I d also stay I felt this more in Pest than Buda.  Buda was a far more relaxed atmosphere and more traditional.  Pest felt very much as if it were being carried along on the commercialisation wave and I believe the city is in a great state of flux.  No doubt as the city finds its feet it will evolve.The grand buildings give the city a very serious feeling and a very historical sense with few large new buildings and those that have been built blend in well.  GENERALThe currency of Hungary is the forint.  I d strongly recommend you only cash in your traveler s cheques at your hotel or a bank.  Take care, I found a number of the banknotes looked very similar. I found a week in Budapest was sufficient to see al the sights within the city and if I visited for this length of time again I would divide my time between the city and a few days exploring outside the city where there are a number of Roman ruins and agricultural centres.  For a city break I believe a long weekend would give you plenty of time to see the major points of Budapest.  It is certainly an interesting city which I think will be of particular interest to people with an interest in architecture, art and Eastern European history and cultural.  For all there are a number of spas I didn t find it a particularly relaxing holiday though I would never go to a city for relaxation anyhow   It is a city that grabs you by the arm and drags you out to go sight-seeing and exploring.  I was disappointed with the shopping but have no doubt this is an area that will develop rapidly.       ', '    Though I knew very well that it had been years since the collapse of the Iron Curtain, nothing prepared me for how westernized Budapest actually is in the present day.  The only remnant of Communism I could immediately distinguish was the rather large proportion of shabby Lada cars on the streets of the Hungarian capital, probably dating back to pre-1990 days (for I doubt Hungarian Lada sales are all that significant now).Tourism has, of course, expanded rapidly since the Soviet Union  8217;s decline, and we were given ample indication of this over an hour before actually arriving in Budapest, when, on the train, we were given free maps of the city by young representatives of the Budapest Tourist Board (or something of the sort).  Another representative of the same organization, after finding out that we had already reserved a quad room at the Hostel Landler, directed us to their free minibus service outside the train station.  This entailed a journey across Budapest in a rundown 9-seater van, with an unresponsive driver; but we could not complain, since the trip was free, and saved us a great deal of hassle with public transportation and orientation.The Hostel Landler itself was a much less impressive proposition, though fittingly inexpensive at 3000 forints (   6.98) per person per night.  One of the so-called   8220;summer hostels  8221;, in practice this meant that Landler was nothing more than lived-in university dorms that had become temporarily free over the holidays.  Adorned with worn students  8217; posters on the wall, the room itself was of adequate size - as it should have been, since it was the abode of no less than four university students during term time.  The bathrooms and showers were, however, seemingly reminiscent of an army barracks.  The showers were vaguely divided into cubicles, with no shower curtains, and emitted a single, solid (and thus uncomfortable) stream of water when used.  The toilets had a fearful tendency to either fail to flush, or to run out of toilet paper, thus making the utilization of altogether more acceptable bathroom services in restaurants crucially important.Budapest is actually an amalgamation of two separate   8220;cities  8221;, Buda and Pest, which are divided by the renowned Danube River.  The Hostel Landler was located in Buda, so we decided to explore this side of the river first.  Here, in heavy rain, we walked to the Castle District, on a hill near the river.  The Matthias Church proved suitably impressive, and made quite a change from other European cathedrals, with its elegant patchwork of aquamarine, yellow, green, white, and maroon roof tiles.  The Fisherman  8217;s Bastion, a stone  8217;s throw from the church, offered a great view of the city, spoiled only by the adverse weather conditions.  Eventually, we found ourselves in the Castle grounds.  The rain had not abated, and an abortive attempt to exit the castle and descend towards our hostel was thwarted by an iron gate.  Dejected, we were nearly tempted to take a taxi back, but decided otherwise when a surprisingly honest taxi driver (there are, unfortunately, not a great deal of these to be found in Europe) informed us that our proposed journey would take at least half an hour, on account of traffic.A few hours  8217; rest after a tiring return journey meant that we only left the hostel, in search of dinner, after 2100.  We soon gathered that it was too late ( ) to find any open restaurants in this part of Buda   8211; in the end, we had no choice but to dine at Pizza Hut.The next day, after once again braving the necessary discomfort of the showers, we walked into Pest.  The first brief stop was the Hungarian National museum, with an entry fee of only 300 forints (   0.70).  This contained one principal exhibit on Hungarian history from before the 9th century AD to the present day.  This was just passable, as far as museums go, with significant emphasis on the wars with the Turks.  Most of the labels were in English as well as Hungarian, though there were a surprising number that the museum staff seemingly could not be bothered with, as far as translations were concerned.The next sight we encountered was St. Stephen  8217;s Basilica, one of Budapest  8217;s main attractions.  A marvelous white dome, and an awe-inspiring interior, was feast enough for the eyes.  Unfortunately, I could not help but be disappointed at my failure to see Saint Stephen  8217;s mummified right hand, a religious relic reportedly held on public display somewhere within the basilica.  I now know that the relic is to be found only after paying to go up the Panorama tower, which at the time I had dismissed as one of the least logical places for it to be held.After an amusing incident in which one of my friends was fined 1500 forints (   3.49) for showing up on the subway platform without a ticket (the regrettable thing being that he had never intended to take the Metro in the first place), we proceeded along the Andr   ssy    t to Heroes  8217; Square, this time in the baking heat of a sunny day.  We took a few pictures in the big square (about which we knew next to nothing, having failed to bring   8220;Let  8217;s Go Europe  8221; with us), and then proceeded to the outside of Vajdahunyad Castle in the nearby park.  This was supposedly built in a combination of Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque styles, though the time period of its construction, and the precise purpose for which it was built, are unclear to me even now.Budapest was the cheapest place we had visited, especially as far as eating out goes.  Massive three-course meals could be had for less than 1700 forints (   3.95), complete with the Hungarian specialty, Goulash soup.  Public transportation was also cheap, the few times we actually used it.  The tram system was exceedingly useful (especially for people who wish to take a ride without paying), and the subway was passable (forgetting, for a moment, the somewhat over-zealous platform inspectors).Just as suspicions of lingering Communism were doomed to be discarded, so too was this the case with reports of the post-Soviet mafia (according to   8220;Let  8217;s Go Europe  8221; especially active around Vaci    t) and gangs of roaming skinheads.  Budapest proved a cosmopolitan city, with a goodly number of tourists, though not nearly as many as in yet more westernized Prague.  I actually preferred Budapest to Prague, since a smaller number of tourists can mean a more authentic feel and, in this case, lower prices   8211; two things that should be prized by any average backpacker.
