Four pounds each  Your choice but those metro police don t half get stroppy.My advice on Budapest? Go before too many more MacDonalds appear. Beautiful, fun city.     ', '    I went to Budapest in 1996 as part of a college field trip. The city itself is stunning with beautiful Art Nouveau architecture and, if you re interested in art and design, a visit to the Museum of Decorative Arts in unmissable.For a cheap holiday, stay in Pest rather than Buda - the same for eating out. Local food is cheap and filling and evn the best restaurants are inexpensive. At that time we were able to get an excellent three course meal for under    10 in fantastic surroundings. Elsewhere was even cheaper.The nightlife is great - somewhere in Pest there is a bar with a swing in it, but unfortunately, as the nightlife is so great, I couldn t tell you where...Racism, however, is rife in Hungary, so if you are black or Asian, be aware that you may find yourself forced into uncomfortable situations, equally the case for white people travelling with black or Asian friends. We were spat on by both white and black people who felt that we shouldn t be mixing and some stores made black customers extremely unwelcome.Also, be wary of the public baths in the city - while it is an exoerience not to be missed, be careful which baths you attend. Tourist guides usually give good information about which are best for men and which for women.     ', '    1. Go the Gellert Bath House. The building itself resembles the interior of Buckingham Palace, rather than a swimming pool complex. Relax in the hot mineral pools, boil in the steam rooms, freeze in the plunge pools and above all, be sure and have a 30 minute massage for just 2 pounds  You ll feel at least 20 years younger 2. Walk across as many of the Danube bridges as possible, and marvel at the sheer length of the river. If going between October and April, wrap extra warm. I was there in February and it was -6 degrees Celsius, and the bitter wind made it feel even colder.3. Have a half-litre of Dreher lager for about 60 pence in any of the traditional pubs scattered around the city - it s very tasty indeed 4. Visit the magnificent Parliament buildings, and go early (before 11am) to get a tour inside.5. Have some of the delicious Goulash soup on offer in all restaurants and pubs. It s meaty, with loads of vegetables, tarragon and cream. Mmmm 6. Be sure and visit one of the many casinos. I recommend the Las Vegas Casino on the riverside. Minimum bet is only  2 on the Blackjack tables and you ll feel like James Bond or a high-class moll 7. Visit the Grand Palace - this beautiful and historic compound which overlooks the Danube contains the National Museum, Art Gallery as well as the Palace itself.8. Ride the metro - it s unbelievably punctual as well as frequent. If you feel the need to pay (no-one else seems to ), it s only 2 pounds for 4 days unlimited travel. Try and make someone smile whilst on the train - you ll find it impossible, as the Hungarians are a depressing (if stunningly attractive) lot.9. Boogie the night away in Bahnhof, an excellent nightclub for 20 somethings in Pest 6. A quid to get in and the drinks are cheap and cheerful.10. Ask your concierge to give you details of classical concerts that are taking place. they are really poorly advertised, but are superb and tickets cost about 2 pounds for a full opera      ', '    Ever fancied playing chess in the great outdoors almost entirely immersed in 37 degrees of thermal water? In March? In Eastern Europe? Hmmm, probably not, but I can assure you that it  8217;s a simple case of once bitten, forever smitten. My venture into the welcoming arms of the Magyar capital began when I was bargain city-break hunting on the web and found myself staring at 4 nights in a 4* hotel for    266. Not the best deal in the world, but the fact that I simply had to phone a free number and hand over my credit card details and Fred Olsen would do the rest was infinitely appealing at the time. Arriving at the airport after a couple of hours in the air, we retrieved our bags in record time and having waltzed through passport control (ok, so it was a cinch   8211; the guy had his head buried in the local rag) instantly saw the infamous   8216;Airport Minibus  8217; desk. This nifty facility means that you get transported to any address in the city for a happy    7.80 return, taking the hassle out of foreign-country, strange-language, dark-night accommodation location. Based in the Castle District in Buda on the western side of the Danube, we soon found our way across the river (a bit like the Thames, only less grotty) in search of the shops, restaurants and general social life of the plainer, flatter Pest. As warned by roons_y, the main drag, Vaci Utca, whilst unquestionably the centre of Budapest  8217;s shops and restaurants, features prices not disimilar to the UK   8211; which, in a city famed for being bargaintastic for us Brits, is not a welcome sight. Still, if you can side-step the pushy Hungarians ready to pounce on lost-looking tourists and lure them into their establishments, choose carefully and you can get some good grub   8211; we tried   8216;La Biere  8217;, an underground cavern of a restaurant which had delicious goulash, a welcoming English-speaking host and didn  8217;t put too great a strain on our pockets.Pest  8217;s District VII proved to be the most successful for us for eating and going out. Lizst Ferenc Ter (located by the Oktogon metro station), a square flanked by various haunts proclaimed to be   8216;trendy  8217; and   8216;in  8217; by the guide books, didn  8217;t particularly wet our whistle.  After a coke in the acclaimed   8216;Incognito  8217; (make that gloomy and uninspiring, during the day at least), we journeyed south-west and found the restaurant   8216;Kek Rasa  8217; (The Blue Rose), behind the synagogue on Wesseleny Utca. This was a tasty and cheap meal for us with beer for 50p, goulash soup for    1, and mains for    1.50. We then went onto the Old Man  8217;s Music Pub (Akacfa Utca) and saw quite possibly the greatest swing band in the world, for free, in a beer-coloured den of smoke and atmosphere.  So   8211; if you  8217;re in town on a Sunday   8211; don  8217;t miss   8216;em: The Cotton Club Singers (and if they don  8217;t play Sesame Street, you  8217;re being robbed ) Another area worth a look is the southern section of District V, also in Pest.  This area provided us with a great Greek place to eat (with   8216;Dolphin  8217; in the title) that did all manner of chicken-dishes and fantastic pizzas and then we went onto the Jazz Garden for cocktails, ice-cream and some authentic Hungarian jazz in intimate and slightly more upmarket surroundings.Obviously with the picturesque and hilly town of Buda, some serious sight-seeing has to happen. You can  8217;t possibly ignore the lure of the magnificent Royal Palace towering ominously over you from the hillside, or the intriguingly ornate churches. Get yourself up the hill via the many stairs or head towards the cable car and get wandering. The Royal Palace is also home to both the National Gallery and the Museum of Modern Art. If you  8217;re not much of a culture-vulture, the modern art is more accessible as there are a lot of human-interest photographs, which don  8217;t require a BA in art history to derive easy pleasure from. If it  8217;s something more traditional you fancy, the National  8217;s the one for you, but with it  8217;s many floors it can be a little dull unless you  8217;re a real art-lover.There are many more sites of interest, most of which can be enjoyed from afar as you walk across the river, which is just as well as quite frankly they are all too far apart and the underground doesn  8217;t go everywhere. One local phenomenon definitely worth visiting though, is a thermal bath. Although there are many harvesting the gurgling thermal waters which fester under the city  8217;s surface, if your party is made up of both sexes, you can  8217;t go far wrong hitting the Szechenyi baths in the City Park near Hero  8217;s Square. You literally get off the metro in the middle of the park and the big yellow building is it   8211; and it  8217;s beautiful.  As this is one of the largest baths in Europe, I advise that you and your party opt for cabins (rather than lockers) and stick together when you get changed.  I spent an awkward quarter of an hour shivering round the perimeter of the several out-door baths, squinting at all and sundry in attempt to spot my other half amidst the masses.  Once you  8217;ve been in the Jacuzzi and whirlpool sections of the 37 degree pools and done some lengths in the main pool (if you brought a swimming cap that is, although you can hire one), don  8217;t forget to go inside and visit one of the dozens of smaller pools, varying in temperature from seriously lobster to icy plunge.  Then to finish, sauna or steam any remaining toxins away or get a little more intellectual with a game of chess.  The choice, as they say, is yours.If a day of sight-seeing has put you in the mood for somewhere to take the weight off your feet and indulge in coffee and cakes, don  8217;t bother searching for the New York Caf   . The renowned neo-classical haven for the rich and famous of Hungary since 1854, is no more - it  8217;s currently boarded up and shut down (much to our disappointment). Instead, satisfy your sweet tooth at Caf    Gerbaud on Vorosmarty Ter   8211; ours weren  8217;t as nice as they looked, and you can  8217;t possibly have a cup of tea as it didn  8217;t seem to be on the menu (I think Hungarian tea is usually iced), but the interior is grand and if you can get a table by the window, people watching may prove an inexpensive way to pass the time.So, my concluding points (aka All The Little Things You Need To Know About Budapest But The Guidebooks Didn  8217;t Tell You) are as follows.  Bear in mind that the shops in Budapest shut down on Saturday afternoon and Sunday.  This is a good time to sight-see, visit the baths or if you  8217;re thinking of venturing to the Ecseri flea-market, go when the Hungarian  8217;s go   8211; on Saturday.  Don  8217;t forget to stamp your underground ticket to validate it   8211; being fined brings bad karma.  Understand that toilet-paper everywhere is like Tesco  8217;s value with a texture to it more reminiscent of the citrus section of a cheese grater than velvet.  Drink lots of beer   8211; it  8217;s so much cheaper than UK.  Understand that in this part of Europe it is proper to have a huge head on your pint - resist the temptation to show them how it  8217;s done   If anyone figures out how to pay for a bus, let me know.  Get your money out of the cash machines as and when you need it   8211; the rates of exchange are far better than you can get anywhere else.  The best guide-book you can buy is   8216;Budapest in your pocket  8217; which at 70p, is probably the most convenient and thoroughly useful guide we had.Budapest is a friendly and relatively good-value place to visit, with a lot of beautiful places to see and some good food and drink to be consumed.  Go in spring before it gets too hot as there  8217;s a lot of walking to be done      ', '    The capital city of Hungary was famously once two cities-Buda and Pest, divided by the River Danube. Indeed it still retains a feeling of being 2 separate places. Buda on the one hand has a very historical feel, with the presence of the Royal Palace on Castle Hill and the Freedom Monument adding to this impression. Pest, on the other hand, despite comprising mostly old buildings, feels much more the heart of modern day Budapest. This side of the Danube holds the business district, main train station, and the majority of the budget accommodation.On arrival in Budapest and checking into one of the hostels immediately surrounding the station, our first instinct was to get down to the river to get our bearings. The city is beautiful at night-the castle, freedom monument and parliament being among the illuminated highlights to be seen from the banks of the river. Arriving on a Sunday evening, it proved difficult to find an open restaurant with any tables available, but we eventually stumbled across a traditional Hungarian restaurant in the back streets of Pest where we enjoyed a typically paprika-dominated meal. The next day we headed to Buda, trekking up Gell   rt Hill to the Freedom monument commemorating the freeing of the city from Nazi rule in 1945. The views over Budapest are excellent; indeed the summit of this hill was used to site a fortress after the 1848 revolution to control the population. Soviet cannons remain trained on the city from this point, a reminder of the troubled times the capital had under communist rule. Walking parallel to the River, V   rhegy (Castle Hill) can be reached, with the impressive Royal Palace dominating this entire area. On the way back to Pest we crossed Margaret Bridge, which links both sides of the city to Margaret Island in the middle of the River. This is the place to go for any vaguely sporty local, with an athletics track, swimming pool, cycle hire and large open spaces. There is also an open air theatre and a casino hidden away at the far end of the Island. This is definitely a place to go to relax, away from the city streets. Another popular way to relax in Budapest is at one of the many thermal baths, one of which we went to the next day. You pay for a full day on entrance-2600 forints, but if you spend less than 3 hours you get 300ft back, and if you spend less than 2 hours you are refunded 600ft on your exit. However, there is so much to do any less than 2 hours seemed impossible. There were several pools, indoors and out, of varying temperatures, as well as saunas which start at 50  730;C, and rise up to 100, yes 100 degrees centigrade  All this proved a very relaxing way to pass an afternoon.There is an underground system in Budapest, which links the city very well, I didn t use this myself, prefering to soak up the whole experience on foot, but it would be very convenient for moving about the city.Budapest has a very rich cultural heritage, and yet it seems to embrace the 21st century more than the capital cities of other nearby countries, one gets the rare sense that this city would be just as vibrant and busy even without the hordes of tourists it attracts, as such you can gain a real insight on the workings of this wonderful city.     ']

If you’re considering Budapest for your next adventure, especially beyond the usual beach getaway, you’re in for a treat. This city truly shines during St Stephen’s Day festival, where the atmosphere buzzes with friendly crowds and spectacular fireworks lighting up the Danube—imagine standing by the river, soaking in history and celebration all at once. Budapest’s impressive architecture is a feast for the eyes: from the grand Parliament buildings (tip: go early for tours) to the stunning bridges connecting Buda and Pest, every corner tells a story.

Food lovers, rejoice! Budapest offers superb cuisine at very reasonable prices. Don’t miss trying the iconic goulash soup, which is delicious and widely available, and you’ll be pleasantly surprised by the quality of vegetarian options too. Dining out is a pleasure here, with excellent service—especially from younger staff who add a warm, welcoming touch.

Getting around is both easy and budget-friendly. The metro runs like clockwork, with cheap unlimited travel passes, but a heads-up: ticket inspectors are strict, so don’t risk fines by skipping your fare. Driving isn’t recommended, as many areas are under renovation; instead, embrace walking. Strolling across the Danube bridges, especially in crisp weather, is a memorable experience that captures Budapest’s romantic charm.

For a cultural fix, classical concerts and opera performances are superb and surprisingly affordable. And if relaxation is on your agenda, the Gellert Bath House is a must-visit—its stunning architecture and mineral pools offer a perfect blend of history and leisure.

Night owls will find nightlife options like Bahnhof nightclub with cheap entry and drinks, adding to the city’s vibrant vibe. Overall, Budapest balances rich history, cultural delights, and great value, making it a fantastic destination for curious travelers who appreciate detail, good food, and authentic experiences. Just pack comfy shoes and an open mind!
